Tassa mayhaṃ brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā aparisuddhakāyakammantā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, aparisuddhakāyakammantasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ aparisuddhakāyakammanto araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; parisuddhakāyakammantohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyakammantā [M 1.0021] araññavanapatthāni [V 1.0023] pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, parisuddhakāyakammataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

35. For me also, brahmin, before my full enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred: 'Forest and wilderness dwellings, which are remote resting places, are hard to endure. Seclusion is difficult, and it is hard to delight in being alone. The forests, it seems, carry away the mind of a monk who has not attained concentration.' To me, brahmin, this thought occurred: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to forest and wilderness dwellings, which are remote resting places, with impure bodily action, it is surely because of this cause, their fault of impure bodily action, that those venerable ascetics and brahmins summon unwholesome fear and terror. But I do not resort to forest and wilderness dwellings, which are remote resting places, with impure bodily action; I am of pure bodily action. I am one of those noble ones who, being of pure bodily action, resort to forest and wilderness dwellings, which are remote resting places.' Seeing in myself this purity of bodily action, brahmin, I attained even greater assurance for dwelling in the forest.

36. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā aparisuddhavacīkammantā…pe… aparisuddhamanokammantā [T 1.0030] …pe… aparisuddhājīvā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, aparisuddhājīvasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ aparisuddhājīvo araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; parisuddhājīvohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhājīvā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, parisuddhājīvataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

36. To me, brahmin, this thought occurred: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to forest and wilderness dwellings, which are remote resting places, with impure verbal action… with impure mental action… with impure livelihood, it is surely because of this cause, their fault of impure livelihood, that those venerable ascetics and brahmins summon unwholesome fear and terror. But I do not resort to forest and wilderness dwellings, which are remote resting places, with an impure livelihood; I am of pure livelihood. I am one of those noble ones who, being of pure livelihood, resort to forest and wilderness dwellings, which are remote resting places.' Seeing in myself this purity of livelihood, brahmin, I attained even greater assurance for dwelling in the forest.

37. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā abhijjhālū kāmesu tibbasārāgā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, abhijjhālukāmesutibbasārāgasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ abhijjhālu kāmesu tibbasārāgo araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; anabhijjhālūhamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā anabhijjhālū araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti[P 1.0018], tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, anabhijjhālutaṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

37. Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins who are covetous and have intense lust for sensual pleasures resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, it is because of the fault of their covetousness and intense lust for sensual pleasures that those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not covetous and do not have intense lust for sensual pleasures when I resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings; I am free from covetousness. Of those noble ones who, being free from covetousness, resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, I am one.’ Seeing this freedom from covetousness in myself, brahmin, I gained even greater confidence for dwelling in the forest.

38. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā byāpannacittā paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappā araññavanapatthāni [T 1.0031] pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, byāpannacittapaduṭṭhamanasaṅkappasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ byāpannacitto paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; mettacittohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā mettacittā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, mettacittataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

38. Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins with malevolent minds and corrupt intentions resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, it is because of the fault of their malevolent minds and corrupt intentions that those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings with a malevolent mind and corrupt intentions; I have a mind of loving-kindness. Of those noble ones who, having a mind of loving-kindness, resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, I am one.’ Seeing this mind of loving-kindness in myself, brahmin, I gained even greater confidence for dwelling in the forest.

39. “Tassa [M 1.0022][V 1.0024] mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā thīnamiddhapariyuṭṭhitā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, thīnamiddhapariyuṭṭhānasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ thīnamiddhapariyuṭṭhito araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; vigatathīnamiddhohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā vigatathīnamiddhā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, vigatathīnamiddhataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

39. Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins, being overcome by sloth and torpor, resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, it is because of the fault of being overcome by sloth and torpor that those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not overcome by sloth and torpor when I resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings; I am rid of sloth and torpor. Of those noble ones who, being rid of sloth and torpor, resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, I am one.’ Seeing this freedom from sloth and torpor in myself, brahmin, I gained even greater confidence for dwelling in the forest.

40. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā uddhatā avūpasantacittā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, uddhataavūpasantacittasandosahetu [T 1.0032] have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ uddhato avūpasantacitto araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; vūpasantacittohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā vūpasantacittā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, vūpasantacittataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

40. Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins who are restless and have unpacified minds resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, it is because of the fault of their restlessness and unpacified minds that those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not restless and do not have an unpacified mind when I resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings; I have a pacified mind. Of those noble ones who, having pacified minds, resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, I am one.’ Seeing this state of having a pacified mind in myself, brahmin, I gained even greater confidence for dwelling in the forest.

41. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kaṅkhī vicikicchī araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, kaṅkhivicikicchisandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ kaṅkhī vicikicchī araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; tiṇṇavicikicchohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā tiṇṇavicikicchā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, tiṇṇavicikicchataṃ attani sampassamāno [P 1.0019] bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

41. Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins who are doubtful and perplexed resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, it is because of the fault of their doubt and perplexity that those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not doubtful and perplexed when I resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings; I have overcome perplexity. Of those noble ones who, having overcome perplexity, resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, I am one.’ Seeing this state of having overcome perplexity in myself, brahmin, I gained even greater confidence for dwelling in the forest.

42. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā attukkaṃsakā paravambhī araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, attukkaṃsanaparavambhanasandosahetu have te bhonto [M 1.0023] samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti[T 1.0033]. Na kho panāhaṃ attukkaṃsako paravambhī araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi[V 1.0025]; anattukkaṃsako aparavambhīhamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā anattukkaṃsakā aparavambhī araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, anattukkaṃsakataṃ aparavambhitaṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

42. Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins who are self-praising and disparage others resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, it is because of the fault of self-praise and disparaging others that those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not self-praising and do not disparage others when I resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings; I am not self-praising and do not disparage others. Of those noble ones who are not self-praising and do not disparage others, who resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, I am one.’ Seeing this quality of not being self-praising and not disparaging others in myself, brahmin, I gained even greater confidence for dwelling in the forest.

43. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā chambhī bhīrukajātikā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, chambhibhīrukajātikasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ chambhī bhīrukajātiko araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; vigatalomahaṃsohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā vigatalomahaṃsā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, vigatalomahaṃsataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

43. Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins who are terrified and of a timid nature resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, it is because of the fault of being terrified and of a timid nature that those venerable ascetics and brahmins surely invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not terrified and not of a timid nature when I resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings; I am free from terror. Of those noble ones who are free from terror, who resort to remote forest and woodland lodgings, I am one.’ Seeing this freedom from terror in myself, brahmin, I gained even greater confidence for dwelling in the forest.

44. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nikāmayamānā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, lābhasakkārasilokanikāmana nikāmayamāna (sī. syā.) sandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nikāmayamāno [T 1.0034] araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; appicchohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā appicchā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, appicchataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

44. Brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while desiring gain, honor, and praise, it is surely because of this fault of desiring gain, honor, and praise that those venerable ascetics and brahmins invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while desiring gain, honor, and praise. I am of few desires. Indeed, I am one of those noble ones who, being of few desires, resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings.’ Brahmin, seeing in myself this quality of having few desires, I gained an even greater comfort for dwelling in the forest.

45. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kusītā hīnavīriyā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti[M 1.0024], kusītahīnavīriyasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ kusīto hīnavīriyo araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; āraddhavīriyohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā āraddhavīriyā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, āraddhavīriyataṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

45. Brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being lazy and of deficient energy, it is surely because of this fault of being lazy and of deficient energy that those venerable ascetics and brahmins invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being lazy and of deficient energy. My energy is aroused. Indeed, I am one of those noble ones who, with aroused energy, resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings.’ Brahmin, seeing in myself this quality of aroused energy, I gained an even greater comfort for dwelling in the forest.

46. “Tassa [V 1.0026] mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye [P 1.0020] kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā muṭṭhassatī asampajānā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, muṭṭhassatiasampajānasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ muṭṭhassati asampajāno araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; upaṭṭhitassatihamasmi. Ye [T 1.0035] hi vo ariyā upaṭṭhitassatī araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, upaṭṭhitassatitaṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

46. Brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being of lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension, it is surely because of this fault of lapsed mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension that those venerable ascetics and brahmins invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being of lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension. My mindfulness is established. Indeed, I am one of those noble ones who, with established mindfulness, resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings.’ Brahmin, seeing in myself this quality of established mindfulness, I gained an even greater comfort for dwelling in the forest.

47. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā asamāhitā vibbhantacittā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, asamāhitavibbhantacittasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ asamāhito vibbhantacitto araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; samādhisampannohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā samādhisampannā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, samādhisampadaṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

47. Brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being unconcentrated and of wandering mind, it is surely because of this fault of being unconcentrated and of wandering mind that those venerable ascetics and brahmins invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being unconcentrated and of wandering mind. I am accomplished in concentration. Indeed, I am one of those noble ones who, being accomplished in concentration, resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings.’ Brahmin, seeing in myself this accomplishment in concentration, I gained an even greater comfort for dwelling in the forest.

48. “Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā duppaññā eḷamūgā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti, duppaññaeḷamūgasandosahetu have te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā akusalaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti. Na kho panāhaṃ duppañño eḷamūgo [M 1.0025] araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi; paññāsampannohamasmi. Ye hi vo ariyā paññāsampannā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti tesamahaṃ [T 1.0036] aññataro’ti. Etamahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, paññāsampadaṃ attani sampassamāno bhiyyo pallomamāpādiṃ araññe vihārāya.

48. Brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being unwise and driveling, it is surely because of this fault of being unwise and driveling that those venerable ascetics and brahmins invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings while being unwise and driveling. I am accomplished in wisdom. Indeed, I am one of those noble ones who, being accomplished in wisdom, resort to remote jungle and forest lodgings.’ Brahmin, seeing in myself this accomplishment in wisdom, I gained an even greater comfort for dwelling in the forest.

Soḷasapariyāyaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The sixteenfold discourse is concluded.

49. “Tassa [V 1.0027] mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ yā tā rattiyo abhiññātā abhilakkhitā – cātuddasī pañcadasī aṭṭhamī ca pakkhassa – tathārūpāsu rattīsu yāni tāni ārāmacetiyāni vanacetiyāni rukkhacetiyāni bhiṃsanakāni salomahaṃsāni tathārūpesu senāsanesu vihareyyaṃ appeva nāmāhaṃ bhayabheravaṃ passeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, aparena samayena yā tā rattiyo abhiññātā abhilakkhitā – cātuddasī pañcadasī aṭṭhamī ca pakkhassa – tathārūpāsu rattīsu yāni tāni ārāmacetiyāni vanacetiyāni rukkhacetiyāni bhiṃsanakāni salomahaṃsāni tathārūpesu senāsanesu viharāmi. Tattha ca me, brāhmaṇa, viharato mago vā āgacchati, moro vā kaṭṭhaṃ [P 1.0021] pāteti, vāto vā paṇṇakasaṭaṃ paṇṇasaṭaṃ (sī. pī.) ereti; tassa mayhaṃ brāhmaṇa etadahosi tassa mayhaṃ evaṃ hoti (sī. syā.) – ‘etaṃ nūna taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchatī’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, etadahosi – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ aññadatthu bhayapaṭikaṅkhī bhayapāṭikaṅkhī (sī.) viharāmi? Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yathābhūtaṃ yathābhūtassa yathābhūtassa yathābhūtassa (sī. syā.) me taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchati, tathābhūtaṃ tathābhūtova yathābhūto yathābhūtova (sī. syā.) taṃ bhayabheravaṃ paṭivineyya’nti. Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, caṅkamantassa taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchati. So kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, neva tāva tiṭṭhāmi [T 1.0037] na nisīdāmi na nipajjāmi, yāva caṅkamantova taṃ bhayabheravaṃ paṭivinemi. Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, ṭhitassa taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchati. So kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, neva tāva caṅkamāmi na nisīdāmi na nipajjāmi. Yāva ṭhitova taṃ bhayabheravaṃ paṭivinemi. Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, nisinnassa taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchati. So kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, neva tāva nipajjāmi na tiṭṭhāmi [M 1.0026] na caṅkamāmi, yāva nisinnova taṃ bhayabheravaṃ paṭivinemi. Tassa mayhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, nipannassa taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchati. So kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, neva tāva nisīdāmi na tiṭṭhāmi na caṅkamāmi, yāva nipannova taṃ bhayabheravaṃ paṭivinemi.

49. “Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘Suppose I were to dwell in those fearful and hair-raising places—such as park shrines, forest shrines, and tree shrines—on those nights known and marked, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the lunar fortnight. Perhaps I might encounter that fear and terror.’ So, brahmin, at a later time I dwelled in those fearful and hair-raising places—park shrines, forest shrines, and tree shrines—on those nights known and marked, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the lunar fortnight. While I was dwelling there, brahmin, a beast would come, or a peacock would knock down a twig, or the wind would rustle a heap of leaves. Then it occurred to me: ‘Surely, this is that fear and terror coming!’ Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘Why do I dwell just expecting fear? Suppose that as that fear and terror comes to me, in whatever posture I am in, I were to dispel that fear and terror in that very posture.’ While I was walking, brahmin, that fear and terror came. So, brahmin, I did not stand still, nor sit down, nor lie down until I had dispelled that fear and terror while walking. While I was standing still, brahmin, that fear and terror came. So, brahmin, I neither walked, nor sat down, nor lay down until I had dispelled that fear and terror while standing still. While I was sitting, brahmin, that fear and terror came. So, brahmin, I neither lay down, nor stood up, nor walked until I had dispelled that fear and terror while sitting. While I was lying down, brahmin, that fear and terror came. So, brahmin, I neither sat down, nor stood up, nor walked until I had dispelled that fear and terror while lying down.”

50. “Santi kho pana, brāhmaṇa, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā rattiṃyeva samānaṃ divāti sañjānanti, divāyeva samānaṃ rattīti sañjānanti. Idamahaṃ tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sammohavihārasmiṃ vadāmi. Ahaṃ kho pana, brāhmaṇa, rattiṃyeva samānaṃ rattīti sañjānāmi, divāyeva samānaṃ divāti sañjānāmi. Yaṃ kho taṃ, brāhmaṇa, sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘asammohadhammo satto loke uppanno bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna’nti, mameva taṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘asammohadhammo satto loke uppanno bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna’nti.

50. “There are, brahmin, some ascetics and brahmins who perceive what is night as day, and what is day as night. This I declare to be their dwelling in delusion. But I, brahmin, perceive what is night as night, and what is day as day. If anyone, speaking rightly, were to say, ‘A being of undeluded nature has arisen in the world for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans,’ it is of me alone that one, speaking rightly, could say this: ‘A being of undeluded nature has arisen in the world for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.’”

51. “Āraddhaṃ [T 1.0038][V 1.0028] kho pana me, brāhmaṇa, vīriyaṃ ahosi asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā appammuṭṭhā (syā.), passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ. So kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ [P 1.0022] avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca vihāsiṃ, sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesiṃ; yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

51. “Brahmin, my energy was roused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unclouded, my body was tranquil and unperturbed, my mind was concentrated and one-pointed. Then, brahmin, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of initial and sustained thought, I entered and dwelled in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, I dwelled equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and I experienced happiness with the body. I entered and dwelled in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells happily.’ With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelled in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.”

52. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ [M 1.0027] anussarāmi, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe [T 1.0039] anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe – ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, brāhmaṇa, rattiyā paṭhame yāme paṭhamā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā, tamo vihato āloko uppanno, yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

52. “With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of corruptions, pliant, workable, steady, and unshakable, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives. I recollected my many kinds of past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, and many eons of cosmic contraction and expansion. ‘There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a life-span. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There, too, I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a life-span. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.’ Thus, with their aspects and details, I recollected my many kinds of past lives. This, Brahmin, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligently, ardently, and resolutely.”

53. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ [V 1.0029] upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā [P 1.0023] vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā [T 1.0040] sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā; te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti. Iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, brāhmaṇa, rattiyā majjhime yāme dutiyā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā, tamo vihato āloko uppanno, yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

53. “With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of corruptions, pliant, workable, steady, and unshakable, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I understood how beings fare in accordance with their kamma: ‘Indeed, these venerable beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong view. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower worlds, in hell. But these venerable beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right view. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a good destination, in the heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I understood how beings fare in accordance with their kamma. This, Brahmin, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligently, ardently, and resolutely.”

54. “So [M 1.0028] evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. ‘Ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ ahosi. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsiṃ. Ayaṃ [T 1.0041] kho me, brāhmaṇa, rattiyā pacchime yāme tatiyā vijjā adhigatā, avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā, tamo vihato āloko uppanno, yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

54. “With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of corruptions, pliant, workable, steady, and unshakable, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘This is suffering.’ I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘These are the taints.’ I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’ I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints.’ I directly knew, as it truly is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ For me, knowing thus and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, the knowledge arose: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ This, Brahmin, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligently, ardently, and resolutely.”

55. “Siyā kho pana te, brāhmaṇa, evamassa – ‘ajjāpi nūna samaṇo gotamo avītarāgo avītadoso avītamoho, tasmā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevatī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, brāhmaṇa, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dve kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, atthavase sampassamāno araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevāmi – attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ sampassamāno, pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamāno”ti.

55. “Brahmin, it might occur to you: ‘Surely, even now the ascetic Gotama is not free from lust, not free from hatred, not free from delusion; that is why he frequents remote forest and wilderness resting places.’ But it should not be seen like that, Brahmin. Seeing two benefits, Brahmin, I frequent remote forest and wilderness resting places: seeing a pleasant abiding for myself in this very life, and being compassionate towards the future generation.”

56. “Anukampitarūpā [V 1.0030] vatāyaṃ bhotā gotamena pacchimā janatā[P 1.0024], yathā taṃ arahatā sammāsambuddhena. Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama! Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya – ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti; evamevaṃ bhotā gotamena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

56. “The Venerable Gotama has indeed shown compassion to the future generation, just as an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, would show compassion. Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Just as, Venerable Gotama, one might set upright what has been overturned, or reveal what has been hidden, or show the way to one who is lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that ‘those with eyes may see forms’; even so, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Venerable Gotama in many ways. I go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth, for as long as life lasts.”

Bhayabheravasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The fourth, the Discourse on Fear and Terror, is concluded.

5. Anaṅgaṇasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Blemishes

57. Evaṃ [M 1.0029][V 1.0031][T 1.0042] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso, bhikkhave”ti. “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca –

57. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus!” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

“Cattārome, āvuso, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Idha panāvuso, ekacco puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Idha panāvuso, ekacco puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ sāṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ hīnapuriso akkhāyati. Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ sāṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyati[T 1.0043]. Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova [P 1.0025] samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ anaṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ hīnapuriso akkhāyati. Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ anaṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyatī”ti.

“Friends, there are these four individuals found existing in the world. What four? Here, friends, a certain individual, being with a blemish, does not know as it really is: ‘There is a blemish within me.’ Then again, friends, a certain individual, being with a blemish, knows as it really is: ‘There is a blemish within me.’ Here, friends, a certain individual, being without a blemish, does not know as it really is: ‘There is no blemish within me.’ Then again, friends, a certain individual, being without a blemish, knows as it really is: ‘There is no blemish within me.’ Among them, friends, that individual who, being with a blemish, does not know as it really is, ‘There is a blemish within me’—this one, of these two individuals who are with a blemish, is said to be the inferior person. Among them, friends, that individual who, being with a blemish, knows as it really is, ‘There is a blemish within me’—this one, of these two individuals who are with a blemish, is said to be the superior person. Among them, friends, that individual who, being without a blemish, does not know as it really is, ‘There is no blemish within me’—this one, of these two individuals who are without a blemish, is said to be the inferior person. Among them, friends, that individual who, being without a blemish, knows as it really is, ‘There is no blemish within me’—this one, of these two individuals who are without a blemish, is said to be the superior person.”

58. Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā mahāmoggallāno āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca –

58. When this was said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“Ko nu kho, āvuso sāriputta, hetu ko paccayo yenimesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ sāṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ eko hīnapuriso akkhāyati, eko seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyati? Ko panāvuso [V 1.0032] sāriputta, hetu ko [M 1.0030] paccayo yenimesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ anaṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ eko hīnapuriso akkhāyati, eko seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyatī”ti?

“Friend Sāriputta, what is the cause, what is the condition, whereby of these two individuals who are with a blemish, one is said to be the inferior person and one is said to be the superior person? And what, friend Sāriputta, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby of these two individuals who are without a blemish, one is said to be the inferior person and one is said to be the superior person?”

59. “Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – na chandaṃ janessati na vāyamissati na vīriyaṃ ārabhissati tassaṅgaṇassa pahānāya; so sarāgo sadoso samoho sāṅgaṇo saṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā rajena ca malena ca pariyonaddhā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā na ceva paribhuñjeyyuṃ na ca pariyodapeyyuṃ pariyodāpeyyuṃ (?), rajāpathe ca naṃ nikkhipeyyuṃ. Evañhi sā, āvuso, kaṃsapāti aparena samayena saṃkiliṭṭhatarā [T 1.0044] assa malaggahitā”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Evameva kho, āvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – na chandaṃ janessati na vāyamissati na vīriyaṃ ārabhissati tassaṅgaṇassa pahānāya; so sarāgo sadoso samoho sāṅgaṇo saṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati.

59. “Among them, friend, as to that individual who, being with a blemish, does not know as it really is, ‘There is a blemish within me,’ it is to be expected of him that he will not generate desire, will not make an effort, and will not arouse energy for the abandoning of that blemish. He will die with lust, with aversion, with delusion, with a blemish, and with a defiled mind. Just as, friend, a bronze bowl brought from a shop or a smith’s family might be covered with dust and dirt. Its owners would neither use it nor clean it, but would place it on a dusty road. In this way, friend, would not that bronze bowl in time become even more defiled and caked with grime?” “So it is, friend.” “Even so, friend, as to that individual who, being with a blemish, does not know as it really is, ‘There is a blemish within me,’ it is to be expected of him that he will not generate desire, will not make an effort, and will not arouse energy for the abandoning of that blemish. He will die with lust, with aversion, with delusion, with a blemish, and with a defiled mind.

“Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – chandaṃ janessati vāyamissati vīriyaṃ ārabhissati tassaṅgaṇassa pahānāya; so arāgo adoso amoho anaṅgaṇo asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā rajena ca malena ca pariyonaddhā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā paribhuñjeyyuñceva pariyodapeyyuñca, na ca naṃ rajāpathe nikkhipeyyuṃ. Evañhi [P 1.0026] sā, āvuso, kaṃsapāti aparena samayena parisuddhatarā assa pariyodātā”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Evameva kho, āvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo sāṅgaṇova samāno ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – chandaṃ janessati vāyamissati vīriyaṃ ārabhissati tassaṅgaṇassa pahānāya; so arāgo adoso amoho anaṅgaṇo asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati.

“Friend Moggallāna, among these, a person who, while being with defilement, knows in accordance with reality, ‘There is defilement within me,’—it is to be expected of them that they will generate desire, strive, and exert effort for the abandoning of that defilement. They will pass away without lust, without hatred, without delusion, without defilement, and with an undefiled mind. Suppose, friend, a bronze bowl is brought from a shop or a smith's family, covered with dust and dirt. Its owners would both use it and clean it, and would not place it on a dusty path. Thus, friend, that bronze bowl would at a later time become purer and brighter.” “So it is, friend.” “In the same way, friend, a person who, while being with defilement, knows in accordance with reality, ‘There is defilement within me,’—it is to be expected of them that they will generate desire, strive, and exert effort for the abandoning of that defilement. They will pass away without lust, without hatred, without delusion, without defilement, and with an undefiled mind.

“Tatrāvuso[M 1.0031], yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ [T 1.0045] – subhanimittaṃ manasi karissati, tassa subhanimittassa manasikārā rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃsessati; so sarāgo sadoso samoho sāṅgaṇo saṃkiliṭṭhacitto [V 1.0033] kālaṃ karissati. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā parisuddhā pariyodātā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā na ceva paribhuñjeyyuṃ na ca pariyodapeyyuṃ, rajāpathe ca naṃ nikkhipeyyuṃ. Evañhi sā, āvuso, kaṃsapāti aparena samayena saṃkiliṭṭhatarā assa malaggahitā”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Evameva kho, āvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – subhanimittaṃ manasi karissati, tassa subhanimittassa manasikārā rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃsessati;so sarāgo sadoso samoho sāṅgaṇo saṃkiliṭṭhacittokālaṃkarissati.

“Friend Moggallāna, among these, a person who, while being without defilement, does not know in accordance with reality, ‘There is no defilement within me,’—it is to be expected of them that they will attend to a sign of beauty. Because of attending to that sign of beauty, lust will assail their mind. That person will pass away with lust, with hatred, with delusion, with defilement, and with a defiled mind. Suppose, friend, a bronze bowl is brought from a shop or a smith's family, pure and bright. Its owners would neither use it nor clean it, and would place it on a dusty path. Thus, friend, that bronze bowl would at a later time become more defiled and stained with dirt.” “So it is, friend.” “In the same way, friend, a person who, while being without defilement, does not know in accordance with reality, ‘There is no defilement within me,’—it is to be expected of them that they will attend to a sign of beauty. Because of attending to that sign of beauty, lust will assail their mind. That person will pass away with lust, with hatred, with delusion, with defilement, and with a defiled mind.

“Tatrāvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – subhanimittaṃ na manasi karissati, tassa subhanimittassa amanasikārā rāgo cittaṃ nānuddhaṃsessati; so arāgo adoso amoho anaṅgaṇo asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā parisuddhā pariyodātā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā paribhuñjeyyuñceva pariyodapeyyuñca, na ca naṃ rajāpathe nikkhipeyyuṃ. Evañhi sā, āvuso, kaṃsapāti aparena samayena parisuddhatarā assa pariyodātā”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Evameva [T 1.0046] kho, āvuso, yvāyaṃ puggalo anaṅgaṇova samāno ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇa’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – subhanimittaṃ na manasi karissati, tassa subhanimittassa amanasikārā rāgo cittaṃ nānuddhaṃsessati; so arāgo adoso amoho anaṅgaṇo asaṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati.

“Friend Moggallāna, among these, a person who, while being without defilement, knows in accordance with reality, ‘There is no defilement within me,’—it is to be expected of them that they will not attend to a sign of beauty. Because of not attending to that sign of beauty, lust will not assail their mind. That person will pass away without lust, without hatred, without delusion, without defilement, and with an undefiled mind. Suppose, friend, a bronze bowl is brought from a shop or a smith's family, pure and bright. Its owners would both use it and clean it, and would not place it on a dusty path. Thus, friend, that bronze bowl would at a later time become purer and brighter.” “So it is, friend.” “In the same way, friend, a person who, while being without defilement, knows in accordance with reality, ‘There is no defilement within me,’—it is to be expected of them that they will not attend to a sign of beauty. Because of not attending to that sign of beauty, lust will not assail their mind. That person will pass away without lust, without hatred, without delusion, without defilement, and with an undefiled mind.

“Ayaṃ kho, āvuso moggallāna[P 1.0027], hetu ayaṃ paccayo yenimesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ sāṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ eko hīnapuriso akkhāyati, eko seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyati. Ayaṃ panāvuso moggallāna, hetu ayaṃ [M 1.0032] paccayo yenimesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ anaṅgaṇānaṃyeva sataṃ eko hīnapuriso akkhāyati, eko seṭṭhapuriso akkhāyatī”ti.

“This, friend Moggallāna, is the cause, this is the condition, why of these two persons who are both with defilement, one is called an inferior person and one is called a superior person. And this, friend Moggallāna, is the cause, this is the condition, why of these two persons who are both without defilement, one is called an inferior person and one is called a superior person.”

60. “Aṅgaṇaṃ aṅgaṇanti, āvuso, vuccati. Kissa nu kho etaṃ, āvuso, adhivacanaṃ yadidaṃ aṅgaṇa”nti? “Pāpakānaṃ kho etaṃ, āvuso, akusalānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ aṅgaṇa”nti.

60. “‘Defilement, defilement,’ it is said, friend Sāriputta. Of what, friend, is this a designation, this word ‘defilement’?” “Friend Moggallāna, ‘defilement’ is a designation for evil, unwholesome states that are the resort of desire.”

“Ṭhānaṃ [V 1.0034] kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘āpattiñca vata āpanno assaṃ, na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ āpattiṃ āpanno’ti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ – ‘āpattiṃ āpanno’ti. ‘Jānanti maṃ bhikkhū āpattiṃ āpanno’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

“Friend Moggallāna, this possibility exists: that for a certain bhikkhu here this desire might arise: ‘Suppose I have committed an offense; may the bhikkhus not know that I have committed an offense!’ And this possibility exists, friend: that the bhikkhus might know of that bhikkhu, ‘He has committed an offense.’ Thinking, ‘The bhikkhus know that I have committed an offense,’ he becomes angry and displeased. Whatever anger there is, friend, and whatever displeasure—both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ [T 1.0047] kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘āpattiñca vata āpanno assaṃ, anuraho maṃ bhikkhū codeyyuṃ, no saṅghamajjhe’ti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū saṅghamajjhe codeyyuṃ, no anuraho. ‘Saṅghamajjhe maṃ bhikkhū codenti, no anuraho’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

“Friend Moggallāna, this possibility exists: that for a certain bhikkhu here this desire might arise: ‘Suppose I have committed an offense; may the bhikkhus admonish me in private, not in the midst of the Saṅgha!’ And this possibility exists, friend: that the bhikkhus might admonish that bhikkhu in the midst of the Saṅgha, not in private. Thinking, ‘The bhikkhus admonish me in the midst of the Saṅgha, not in private,’ he becomes angry and displeased. Whatever anger there is, friend, and whatever displeasure—both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘āpattiñca vata āpanno assaṃ, sappaṭipuggalo maṃ codeyya, no appaṭipuggalo’ti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ appaṭipuggalo codeyya, no sappaṭipuggalo. ‘Appaṭipuggalo maṃ codeti, no sappaṭipuggalo’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, this is a possible case, wherein a certain monk in this Dispensation such a wish might arise: 'Oh, that I might have committed an offense, and that a person of equal standing would admonish me, not a person of unequal standing.' Friend, this is a possible case, wherein a person of unequal standing would admonish that monk, not a person of equal standing. Thinking, 'A person of unequal standing admonishes me, not a person of equal standing,' that monk becomes angry and displeased. Friend, whatever anger and whatever displeasure there is, both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata mameva satthā paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya, na aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ satthā paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyā’ti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ satthā paṭipucchitvā [M 1.0033] paṭipucchitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya, na taṃ bhikkhuṃ [P 1.0028] satthā [T 1.0048] paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya. ‘Aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ satthā paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, na maṃ satthā paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desetī’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, this is a possible case, wherein a certain monk in this Dispensation such a wish might arise: 'Oh, that the Teacher, having questioned only me repeatedly, would teach the Dhamma to the monks, and not, having questioned another monk repeatedly, teach the Dhamma to the monks.' Friend, this is a possible case, wherein the Teacher, having questioned another monk repeatedly, would teach the Dhamma to the monks, and not, having questioned that monk repeatedly, teach the Dhamma to the monks. Thinking, 'The Teacher, having questioned another monk repeatedly, teaches the Dhamma to the monks, and does not, having questioned me repeatedly, teach the Dhamma to the monks,' that monk becomes angry and displeased. Friend, whatever anger and whatever displeasure there is, both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ [V 1.0035] kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata mameva bhikkhū purakkhatvā purakkhatvā gāmaṃ bhattāya paviseyyuṃ, na aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū purakkhatvā purakkhatvā gāmaṃ bhattāya paviseyyu’nti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū purakkhatvā purakkhatvā gāmaṃ bhattāya paviseyyuṃ, na taṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū purakkhatvā purakkhatvā gāmaṃ bhattāya paviseyyuṃ. ‘Aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū purakkhatvā purakkhatvā gāmaṃ bhattāya pavisanti, na maṃ bhikkhū purakkhatvā purakkhatvā gāmaṃ bhattāya pavisantī’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, this is a possible case, wherein a certain monk in this Dispensation such a wish might arise: 'Oh, that the monks, placing only me at the forefront, would enter the village for alms-food, and not, placing another monk at the forefront, enter the village for alms-food.' Friend, this is a possible case, wherein the monks, placing another monk at the forefront, would enter the village for alms-food, and not, placing that monk at the forefront, enter the village for alms-food. Thinking, 'The monks, placing another monk at the forefront, enter the village for alms-food, and do not, placing me at the forefront, enter the village for alms-food,' that monk becomes angry and displeased. Friend, whatever anger and whatever displeasure there is, both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata ahameva labheyyaṃ bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ, na añño bhikkhu labheyya bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍa’nti. Ṭhānaṃ kho [T 1.0049] panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ añño bhikkhu labheyya bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ, na so bhikkhu labheyya bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ. ‘Añño bhikkhu labhati bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ, nāhaṃ labhāmi bhattagge aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍa’nti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, this is a possible case, wherein a certain monk in this Dispensation such a wish might arise: 'Oh, that only I might receive the first seat, the first water, and the first alms-food in the refectory, and not another monk receive the first seat, the first water, and the first alms-food in the refectory.' Friend, this is a possible case, wherein another monk might receive the first seat, the first water, and the first alms-food in the refectory, and that monk might not receive them. Thinking, 'Another monk receives the first seat, the first water, and the first alms-food in the refectory, and I do not receive them,' that monk becomes angry and displeased. Friend, whatever anger and whatever displeasure there is, both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata ahameva bhattagge bhuttāvī anumodeyyaṃ, na añño bhikkhu bhattagge bhuttāvī anumodeyyā’ti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ añño bhikkhu bhattagge bhuttāvī anumodeyya, na so bhikkhu bhattagge bhuttāvī anumodeyya. ‘Añño bhikkhu bhattagge bhuttāvī [M 1.0034] anumodati, nāhaṃ bhattagge bhuttāvī anumodāmī’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, this is a possible case, wherein a certain monk in this Dispensation such a wish might arise: 'Oh, that only I, having eaten, might give the blessing of appreciation in the refectory, and not another monk, having eaten, give the blessing of appreciation.' Friend, this is a possible case, wherein another monk, having eaten, might give the blessing of appreciation in the refectory, and that monk, having eaten, might not give the blessing of appreciation. Thinking, 'Another monk, having eaten, gives the blessing of appreciation in the refectory, and I, having eaten, do not give the blessing of appreciation,' that monk becomes angry and displeased. Friend, whatever anger and whatever displeasure there is, both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata ahameva ārāmagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, na añño bhikkhu ārāmagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyā’ti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ añño bhikkhu [V 1.0036] ārāmagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya, na so bhikkhu ārāmagatānaṃ [P 1.0029] bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya. ‘Añño bhikkhu ārāmagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ [T 1.0050] deseti, nāhaṃ ārāmagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desemī’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, this is a possible case, wherein a certain monk in this Dispensation such a wish might arise: 'Oh, that only I might teach the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery, and not another monk teach the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery.' Friend, this is a possible case, wherein another monk might teach the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery, and that monk might not teach the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery. Thinking, 'Another monk teaches the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery, and I do not teach the Dhamma to the monks who have come to the monastery,' that monk becomes angry and displeased. Friend, whatever anger and whatever displeasure there is, both of these are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata ahameva ārāmagatānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ…pe… upāsakānaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ…pe… upāsikānaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, na añño bhikkhu ārāmagatānaṃ upāsikānaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyā’ti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ añño bhikkhu ārāmagatānaṃ upāsikānaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya, na so bhikkhu ārāmagatānaṃ upāsikānaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya. ‘Añño bhikkhu ārāmagatānaṃ upāsikānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, nāhaṃ ārāmagatānaṃ upāsikānaṃ dhammaṃ desemī’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, it is possible that in this Dispensation a certain monk might have an evil wish arise thus: ‘Oh, that I alone might teach the Dhamma to the nuns who have come to the monastery... to the male lay disciples... to the female lay disciples who have come to the monastery, and that no other monk might teach the Dhamma to the female lay disciples who have come to the monastery!’ And it is possible, friend, that another monk teaches the Dhamma to the female lay disciples who have come to the monastery, while that first monk does not. Then, thinking, ‘Another monk teaches the Dhamma to the female lay disciples who have come to the monastery, not I,’ he becomes angry and displeased. Friend, both this anger and this displeasure are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata mameva bhikkhū sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ garukareyyuṃ (sī. syā. pī.) māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, na aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyu’nti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, na taṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ. ‘Aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū sakkaronti garuṃ [M 1.0035] karonti mānenti pūjenti[T 1.0051], na maṃ bhikkhū sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjentī’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, it is possible that in this Dispensation a certain monk might have an evil wish arise thus: ‘Oh, that the monks might respect, revere, esteem, and honor only me, and that they might not respect, revere, esteem, and honor any other monk!’ And it is possible, friend, that the monks respect, revere, esteem, and honor another monk, while they do not respect, revere, esteem, and honor that first monk. Then, thinking, ‘The monks respect, revere, esteem, and honor another monk, but they do not respect, revere, esteem, and honor me,’ he becomes angry and displeased. Friend, both this anger and this displeasure are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata mameva bhikkhuniyo…pe… upāsakā…pe… upāsikā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, na aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ upāsikā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyu’nti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ upāsikā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ, na taṃ bhikkhuṃ upāsikā sakkareyyuṃ garuṃ [V 1.0037] kareyyuṃ māneyyuṃ pūjeyyuṃ. ‘Aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ upāsikā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti, na maṃ upāsikā sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjentī’ti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, it is possible that in this Dispensation a certain monk might have an evil wish arise thus: ‘Oh, that the nuns... the male lay disciples... the female lay disciples might respect, revere, esteem, and honor only me, and that the female lay disciples might not respect, revere, esteem, and honor any other monk!’ And it is possible, friend, that the female lay disciples respect, revere, esteem, and honor another monk, while they do not respect, revere, esteem, and honor that first monk. Then, thinking, ‘The female lay disciples respect, revere, esteem, and honor another monk, but they do not respect, revere, esteem, and honor me,’ he becomes angry and displeased. Friend, both this anger and this displeasure are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata ahameva lābhī assaṃ paṇītānaṃ cīvarānaṃ, na añño bhikkhu lābhī assa paṇītānaṃ cīvarāna’nti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ añño [P 1.0030] bhikkhu lābhī assa paṇītānaṃ cīvarānaṃ, na so bhikkhu lābhī assa paṇītānaṃ cīvarānaṃ. ‘Añño bhikkhu lābhī lābhī assa (ka.) paṇītānaṃ cīvarānaṃ, nāhaṃ lābhī [T 1.0052] lābhī assaṃ (ka.) paṇītānaṃ cīvarāna’nti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, it is possible that in this Dispensation a certain monk might have an evil wish arise thus: ‘Oh, that I alone might be a recipient of excellent robes, and that no other monk might be a recipient of excellent robes!’ And it is possible, friend, that another monk is a recipient of excellent robes, while that first monk is not. Then, thinking, ‘Another monk is a recipient of excellent robes, but I am not,’ he becomes angry and displeased. Friend, both this anger and this displeasure are a defilement.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ idhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya – ‘aho vata ahameva lābhī assaṃ paṇītānaṃ piṇḍapātānaṃ…pe… paṇītānaṃ senāsanānaṃ…pe… paṇītānaṃ gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ, na añño bhikkhu lābhī assa paṇītānaṃ gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna’nti. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, āvuso, vijjati yaṃ añño bhikkhu lābhī assa paṇītānaṃ gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ, na so bhikkhu lābhī assa paṇītānaṃ gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ. ‘Añño bhikkhu [M 1.0036] lābhī lābhī assa (ka.) paṇītānaṃ gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ, nāhaṃ lābhī lābhī assaṃ (ka.) paṇītānaṃ gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna’nti – iti so kupito hoti appatīto. Yo ceva kho, āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo – ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ.

Friend, it is possible that in this Dispensation a certain monk might have an evil wish arise thus: ‘Oh, that I alone might be a recipient of excellent almsfood... of excellent lodgings... of excellent medicines and requisites for the sick, and that no other monk might be a recipient of excellent medicines and requisites for the sick!’ And it is possible, friend, that another monk is a recipient of excellent medicines and requisites for the sick, while that first monk is not. Then, thinking, ‘Another monk is a recipient of excellent medicines and requisites for the sick, but I am not,’ he becomes angry and displeased. Friend, both this anger and this displeasure are a defilement.

“Imesaṃ kho etaṃ, āvuso, pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ aṅgaṇa”nti.

Friend, this term ‘defilement’ is indeed a designation for these evil, unwholesome states that move in the sphere of evil wishes.

61. “Yassa kassaci, āvuso, bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti āraññiko pantasenāsano piṇḍapātiko [V 1.0038] sapadānacārī paṃsukūliko lūkhacīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī na ceva sakkaronti na garuṃ karonti na mānenti na pūjenti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Te hi tassa [T 1.0053] āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā parisuddhā pariyodātā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā ahikuṇapaṃ vā kukkurakuṇapaṃ vā manussakuṇapaṃ vā racayitvā aññissā kaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjitvā antarāpaṇaṃ paṭipajjeyyuṃ. Tamenaṃ jano disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ambho, kimevidaṃ harīyati jaññajaññaṃ viyā’ti? Tamenaṃ uṭṭhahitvā apāpuritvā avāpuritvā (sī.) olokeyya. Tassa sahadassanena amanāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyya, pāṭikulyatā paṭikūlatā (ka.), pāṭikūlyatā (syā.) ca saṇṭhaheyya, jegucchatā ca jegucchitā ca (pī. ka.) saṇṭhaheyya; jighacchitānampi na bhottukamyatā assa, pageva suhitānaṃ. Evameva kho, āvuso, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti āraññiko pantasenāsano piṇḍapātiko sapadānacārī paṃsukūliko lūkhacīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī na ceva sakkaronti na garuṃ karonti [P 1.0031] na mānenti na pūjenti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Te hi tassa āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca.

61. Friend, if any monk is seen and heard to have these evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire still unabandoned, even if he is a forest-dweller, one who resorts to remote lodgings, an alms-food eater, one who goes on alms-round from house to house without omission, a wearer of rag-robes, and a wearer of coarse robes, still his companions in the holy life do not respect, revere, esteem, or venerate him. For what reason? Because in that venerable one, those evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire are seen and heard to be still unabandoned. Suppose, friend, a bronze bowl brought from a shop or a smith's forge is clean and bright. Its owners might fill it with the carcass of a snake, a dog, or a human, cover it with another bronze bowl, and proceed into the marketplace. Seeing it, a person might say: ‘Sir, what is this being carried as if it were something precious?’ Then, having lifted it and uncovered it, they would look inside. At the mere sight of it, displeasure would arise, revulsion would arise, and disgust would arise; even for the hungry there would be no desire to eat, how much more so for the well-fed. In the same way, friend, if any monk is seen and heard to have these evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire still unabandoned, even if he is a forest-dweller, one who resorts to remote lodgings, an alms-food eater, one who goes on alms-round from house to house without omission, a wearer of rag-robes, and a wearer of coarse robes, still his companions in the holy life do not respect, revere, esteem, or venerate him. For what reason? Because in that venerable one, those evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire are seen and heard to be still unabandoned.

62. “Yassa kassaci, āvuso, bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti gāmantavihārī [M 1.0037] nemantaniko gahapaticīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti. Taṃ kissa hetu[T 1.0054]? Te hi tassa āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṃsapāti ābhatā āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā parisuddhā pariyodātā. Tamenaṃ sāmikā sālīnaṃ odanaṃ vicitakāḷakaṃ vicinitakāḷakaṃ (ka.) anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjanaṃ racayitvā aññissā kaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjitvā antarāpaṇaṃ paṭipajjeyyuṃ. Tamenaṃ jano disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ambho, kimevidaṃ harīyati jaññajaññaṃ viyā’ti? Tamenaṃ uṭṭhahitvā apāpuritvā olokeyya. Tassa saha dassanena manāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyya, appāṭikulyatā ca saṇṭhaheyya, ajegucchatā ca saṇṭhaheyya; suhitānampi bhottukamyatā assa, pageva jighacchitānaṃ. Evameva kho, āvuso, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno ime pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, kiñcāpi so hoti gāmantavihārī nemantaniko gahapaticīvaradharo, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti[V 1.0039]. Taṃ kissa hetu? Te hi tassa āyasmato pāpakā akusalā icchāvacarā pahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti cā”ti.

62. Friend, if any monk is seen and heard to have these evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire abandoned, even if he is one who dwells near a village, an acceptor of invitations, and a wearer of robes given by householders, his companions in the holy life respect, revere, esteem, and venerate him. For what reason? Because in that venerable one, those evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire are seen and heard to be abandoned. Suppose, friend, a bronze bowl brought from a shop or a smith's forge is clean and bright. Its owners might fill it with rice from fine grain, with dark grains picked out, with many kinds of curry and condiments, cover it with another bronze bowl, and proceed into the marketplace. Seeing it, a person might say: ‘Sir, what is this being carried as if it were something precious?’ Then, having lifted it and uncovered it, they would look inside. At the mere sight of it, delight would arise, non-revulsion would arise, and non-disgust would arise; even for the well-fed there would be a desire to eat, how much more so for the hungry. In the same way, friend, if any monk is seen and heard to have these evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire abandoned, even if he is one who dwells near a village, an acceptor of invitations, and a wearer of robes given by householders, his companions in the holy life respect, revere, esteem, and venerate him. For what reason? Because in that venerable one, those evil, unwholesome volitions prompted by desire are seen and heard to be abandoned.

63. Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā mahāmoggallāno āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca – “upamā maṃ, āvuso sāriputta, paṭibhātī”ti. “Paṭibhātu taṃ, āvuso moggallānā”ti. “Ekamidāhaṃ, āvuso, samayaṃ rājagahe viharāmi giribbaje. Atha khvāhaṃ, āvuso, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā [T 1.0055] pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ. Tena kho pana samayena samīti yānakāraputto rathassa nemiṃ tacchati. Tamenaṃ paṇḍuputto ājīvako purāṇayānakāraputto paccupaṭṭhito hoti. Atha kho, āvuso, paṇḍuputtassa ājīvakassa purāṇayānakāraputtassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘aho vatāyaṃ samīti yānakāraputto imissā nemiyā imañca vaṅkaṃ imañca jimhaṃ imañca dosaṃ taccheyya, evāyaṃ nemi apagatavaṅkā apagatajimhā apagatadosā suddhā assa suddhāssa (sī. pī.), suddhā (ka.) sāre patiṭṭhitā’ti[P 1.0032]. Yathā yathā kho, āvuso, paṇḍuputtassa ājīvakassa purāṇayānakāraputtassa cetaso parivitakko hoti, tathā tathā [M 1.0038] samīti yānakāraputto tassā nemiyā tañca vaṅkaṃ tañca jimhaṃ tañca dosaṃ tacchati. Atha kho, āvuso, paṇḍuputto ājīvako purāṇayānakāraputto attamano attamanavācaṃ nicchāresi – ‘hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchatī’ti.

63. When this was said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to the Venerable Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, a simile occurs to me.' 'Let it occur to you, friend Moggallāna.' 'Once, friend, I was dwelling at Rājagaha in the mountain-girt city. Then, friend, in the morning, having dressed, I took my bowl and robe and entered Rājagaha for alms. Now at that time, Samīti, a chariot-maker’s son, was trimming the felly of a chariot wheel. And Paṇḍuputta, an Ājīvaka, the son of a former chariot-maker, was standing by. Then, friend, this thought arose in the mind of Paṇḍuputta, the Ājīvaka, son of a former chariot-maker: ‘Oh, if only this Samīti, the chariot-maker’s son, would trim away this bend, this crookedness, and this flaw from this felly! Then this felly would be without bend, without crookedness, and without flaw; it would be pure, established in the heartwood.’ And just as that thought occurred to Paṇḍuputta, the Ājīvaka, son of a former chariot-maker, so did Samīti, the chariot-maker’s son, trim away that bend, that crookedness, and that flaw from that felly. Then, friend, Paṇḍuputta, the Ājīvaka, son of a former chariot-maker, being pleased, uttered a joyous utterance: ‘It is as though he trims knowing my heart with his own heart!’

“Evameva kho, āvuso, ye te puggalā assaddhā, jīvikatthā na saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, saṭhā māyāvino ketabino keṭubhino (bahūsu) uddhatā unnaḷā capalā mukharā vikiṇṇavācā, indriyesu aguttadvārā, bhojane amattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttā, sāmaññe anapekkhavanto, sikkhāya na tibbagāravā, bāhulikā sāthalikā, okkamane pubbaṅgamā, paviveke nikkhittadhurā, kusītā hīnavīriyā muṭṭhassatī asampajānā asamāhitā [T 1.0056] vibbhantacittā duppaññā eḷamūgā, tesaṃ āyasmā sāriputto iminā dhammapariyāyena hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya tacchati.

In the same way, friend, there are those individuals who, being faithless, have gone forth from the household life into homelessness not out of faith but for the sake of a livelihood; they are deceitful, fraudulent, treacherous, restless, haughty, fickle, harsh-spoken, of scattered speech, with sense-faculties unguarded, immoderate in eating, not devoted to wakefulness, without regard for the ascetic life, not having keen respect for the training, given to abundance, lax, foremost in backsliding, having thrown off the yoke in seclusion, lazy, of deficient energy, of lapsed mindfulness, not clearly comprehending, unconcentrated, of bewildered mind, of little wisdom, dull and stupid. It is as though the Venerable Sāriputta, by means of this Dhamma discourse, trims them, knowing their hearts with his own heart.

“Ye pana te kulaputtā saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, asaṭhā amāyāvino aketabino anuddhatā anunnaḷā acapalā amukharā avikiṇṇavācā, indriyesu guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā, sāmaññe apekkhavanto, sikkhāya tibbagāravā, na bāhulikā [V 1.0040] na sāthalikā, okkamane nikkhittadhurā, paviveke pubbaṅgamā, āraddhavīriyā pahitattā upaṭṭhitassatī sampajānā samāhitā ekaggacittā paññavanto aneḷamūgā, te āyasmato sāriputtassa imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā pivanti maññe, ghasanti maññe vacasā ceva manasā ca – ‘sādhu vata, bho, sabrahmacārī akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpetī’ti. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, itthī vā puriso vā daharo yuvā maṇḍanakajātiko sīsaṃnhāto uppalamālaṃ vā vassikamālaṃ vā atimuttakamālaṃ adhimuttakamālaṃ (syā.) vā labhitvā ubhohi hatthehi paṭiggahetvā uttamaṅge sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhapeyya, evameva kho, āvuso, ye te kulaputtā saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā, asaṭhā amāyāvino aketabino anuddhatā anunnaḷā acapalā amukharā avikiṇṇavācā, indriyesu guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā, sāmaññe apekkhavanto, sikkhāya tibbagāravā, na [T 1.0057] bāhulikā na sāthalikā, okkamane nikkhittadhurā, paviveke pubbaṅgamā, āraddhavīriyā pahitattā upaṭṭhitassatī [M 1.0039] sampajānā samāhitā ekaggacittā paññavanto aneḷamūgā, te āyasmato sāriputtassa imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā pivanti maññe, ghasanti maññe vacasā ceva manasā ca – ‘sādhu vata, bho, sabrahmacārī akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā kusale patiṭṭhāpetī’ti. Itiha te ubho mahānāgā aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ samanumodiṃsū”ti.

“But those sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, who are not deceitful, not fraudulent, not hypocritical, not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not garrulous, and of restrained speech; who have guarded the doors of their sense faculties, are moderate in eating, are devoted to wakefulness, have regard for the state of a recluse, have strong respect for the training, are not given to abundance and are not lax, have laid down the burden in what leads downwards, are foremost in seclusion, have aroused their energy, have directed their minds, have established mindfulness, are clearly comprehending, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, possess wisdom, and are not dull-witted—when they hear this exposition of the Dhamma from the Venerable Sāriputta, it is as if they drink it, as if they savor it with both speech and mind, thinking: ‘It is excellent, friends, that a fellow practitioner, having raised us from unwholesome states, establishes us in wholesome states!’ Just as a young woman or man, fond of adornments, having bathed their head, might receive a garland of blue lotuses, jasmine, or Arabian jasmine with both hands and place it on their head, the most excellent limb, so too, friends, do those sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, who are not deceitful, not fraudulent, not hypocritical, not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not garrulous, and of restrained speech; who have guarded the doors of their sense faculties, are moderate in eating, are devoted to wakefulness, have regard for the state of a recluse, have strong respect for the training, are not given to abundance and are not lax, have laid down the burden in what leads downwards, are foremost in seclusion, have aroused their energy, have directed their minds, have established mindfulness, are clearly comprehending, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, possess wisdom, and are not dull-witted—when they hear this exposition of the Dhamma from the Venerable Sāriputta, it is as if they drink it, as if they savor it with both speech and mind, thinking: ‘It is excellent, friends, that a fellow practitioner, having raised us from unwholesome states, establishes us in wholesome states!’ Thus, these two great beings mutually rejoiced in each other’s well-spoken words.”

Anaṅgaṇasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, the fifth, is concluded.

6. Ākaṅkheyyasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Aspirations

64. Evaṃ [T 1.0058][V 1.0041][P 1.0033] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

64. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharatha sampannapātimokkhā; pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā viharatha ācāragocarasampannā aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvino; samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesu.

“Monks, dwell accomplished in virtue, accomplished in the Pātimokkha. Dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, accomplished in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults. Having undertaken them, train in the training rules.”

65. “Ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu – ‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā’ti manāpo garubhāvaniyo cāti (sī.), sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno vipassanāya samannāgato brūhetā suññāgārānaṃ.

65. “If, monks, a monk should wish, ‘May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow practitioners, respected and esteemed by them,’ he should be one who fulfills the virtues, is devoted to internal serenity of mind, does not neglect jhāna, is endowed with insight, and is a developer of empty abodes.”
