He is making this statement in the assembly at Vesālī: ‘The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry, based on his own intuition. And the Dhamma taught by him for a specific goal leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.’”

147. “Kodhano heso, sāriputta, sunakkhatto moghapuriso. Kodhā ca panassa esā vācā bhāsitā. ‘Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsissāmī’ti kho, sāriputta, sunakkhatto moghapuriso vaṇṇaṃyeva tathāgatassa [V 1.0100] bhāsati[P 1.0069]. Vaṇṇo heso, sāriputta, tathāgatassa yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yassa ca khvāssa atthāya dhammo desito so niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā’ti.

147. “Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta is given to anger. And this statement of his is spoken out of anger. Sāriputta, thinking, ‘I will speak dispraise,’ the foolish man Sunakkhatta actually speaks the praise of the Tathāgata. For this, Sāriputta, is a praise of the Tathāgata, that one should say: ‘The Dhamma he has taught for a purpose is such that it leads one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.’”

“Ayampi hi nāma, sāriputta, sunakkhattassa moghapurisassa mayi dhammanvayo na bhavissati – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi, satthā devamanussānaṃ, buddho bhagavā’ti.

“Sāriputta, for the foolish man Sunakkhatta, this inferential knowledge of the Dhamma regarding me will surely not arise: ‘For this reason, the Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sublime One, the Knower of worlds, the unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’”

“Ayampi hi nāma, sāriputta, sunakkhattassa moghapurisassa mayi [T 1.0139] dhammanvayo na bhavissati – ‘itipi so bhagavā anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti – ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti; āvibhāvaṃ, tirobhāvaṃ; tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati, seyyathāpi ākāse; pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti, seyyathāpi udake; udakepi abhijjamāno gacchati, seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ; ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamati, seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇo; imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parimasati parimajjati; yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattetī’ti.

“Sāriputta, for the foolish man Sunakkhatta, this inferential knowledge of the Dhamma regarding me will surely not arise: ‘For this reason, the Blessed One wields the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without sinking as if it were earth; seated cross-legged, he travels through the sky like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand this sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahmā world.’”

“Ayampi [M 1.0099] hi nāma, sāriputta, sunakkhattassa moghapurisassa mayi dhammanvayo na bhavissati – ‘itipi so bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇāti – dibbe ca mānuse ca, ye dūre santike cā’ti.

“Sāriputta, for the foolish man Sunakkhatta, this inferential knowledge of the Dhamma regarding me will surely not arise: ‘For this reason, the Blessed One, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far and near.’”

“Ayampi hi nāma, sāriputta, sunakkhattassa moghapurisassa mayi dhammanvayo na bhavissati – ‘itipi so bhagavā parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāti – sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti pajānāti, vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ vītarāgaṃ cittanti pajānāti; sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ sadosaṃ cittanti pajānāti, vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ vītadosaṃ cittanti pajānāti; samohaṃ vā cittaṃ samohaṃ cittanti pajānāti, vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ vītamohaṃ cittanti pajānāti; saṃkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ saṃkhittaṃ cittanti pajānāti[T 1.0140], vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ vikkhittaṃ cittanti pajānāti; mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ mahaggataṃ cittanti pajānāti, amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ amahaggataṃ cittanti pajānāti; sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ sauttaraṃ cittanti pajānāti, anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ anuttaraṃ cittanti pajānāti; samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ samāhitaṃ cittanti [V 1.0101] pajānāti, asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ asamāhitaṃ cittanti pajānāti; vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ cittanti pajānāti, avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ avimuttaṃ cittanti pajānātī’ti.

“Sāriputta, for the foolish man Sunakkhatta, this inferential knowledge of the Dhamma regarding me will surely not arise: ‘For this reason, the Blessed One, having encompassed with his own mind the minds of other beings, of other persons, knows them. He knows a mind with lust as a mind with lust, and a mind without lust as a mind without lust; he knows a mind with hate as a mind with hate, and a mind without hate as a mind without hate; he knows a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; he knows a constricted mind as a constricted mind, and a scattered mind as a scattered mind; he knows a lofty mind as a lofty mind, and a mind that is not lofty as a mind that is not lofty; he knows a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, and an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind; he knows a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; he knows a liberated mind as a liberated mind, and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.’”

148. “Dasa kho panimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalāni yehi balehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti. Katamāni dasa?

148. “Sāriputta, there are these ten powers of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel. What are the ten?”

“Idha, sāriputta, tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa [P 1.0070] tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

“Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, cause as cause and non-cause as non-cause. And that the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, cause as cause and non-cause as non-cause—this, Sāriputta, is a power that belongs to the Tathāgata, relying on which the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.”

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ kammasamādānānaṃ ṭhānaso hetuso vipākaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ kammasamādānānaṃ ṭhānaso hetuso vipākaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ [M 1.0100] ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the result of actions undertaken in the past, future, and present, by way of condition and by way of root-cause. And that the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the result of actions undertaken in the past, future, and present, by way of condition and by way of root-cause—this, Sāriputta, is a power that belongs to the Tathāgata, relying on which the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.”

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato sabbatthagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi[T 1.0141], sāriputta, tathāgato sabbatthagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the path that leads to all destinations. And that the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the path that leads to all destinations—this, Sāriputta, is a power that belongs to the Tathāgata, relying on which the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.”

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato anekadhātunānādhātulokaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato anekadhātunānādhātulokaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

“Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the world with its many and various elements. And that the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the world with its many and various elements—this, Sāriputta, is a power that belongs to the Tathāgata, relying on which the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.”

“Puna [V 1.0102] caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikataṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikataṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the various dispositions of beings. And, Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the various dispositions of beings—this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata-power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the state of maturity and immaturity of the faculties of superior and inferior beings and individuals. And, Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the state of maturity and immaturity of the faculties of superior and inferior beings and individuals—this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata-power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ [T 1.0142] saṃkilesaṃ vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence concerning the absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. And, Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata knows distinctly, as it really is, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence concerning the absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments—this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata-power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.

“Puna [M 1.0101] caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe – ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion. ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, had such food, experienced such pleasure and pain, and had such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; there too, I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, had such food, experienced such pleasure and pain, and had such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I have been reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. And, Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives—that is, one birth, two births… and so on… thus with their aspects and details he recollects his manifold past lives—this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata-power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena [T 1.0143] satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage [V 1.0103] satte pajānāti – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā [P 1.0071] paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti. Iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne [M 1.0102] paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti. Iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti. Idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, of good complexion and bad complexion, in good destinations and in bad destinations; he understands beings who fare according to their kamma: ‘Indeed, these venerable beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, in hell. Or indeed, these venerable beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, were not revilers of the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, of good complexion and bad complexion, in good destinations and in bad destinations, and understands beings who fare according to their kamma. And, Sāriputta, that the Tathāgata, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, of good complexion and bad complexion, in good destinations and in bad destinations, and understands beings who fare according to their kamma: ‘Indeed, these venerable beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, in hell. Or indeed, these venerable beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, were not revilers of the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, of good complexion and bad complexion, in good destinations and in bad destinations, and understands beings who fare according to their kamma—this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata-power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the foremost position, roars the lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel.

“Puna caparaṃ, sāriputta, tathāgato āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Yampi, sāriputta, tathāgato āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati, idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ hoti yaṃ balaṃ āgamma tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge, enters and abides in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life. That the Tathāgata, Sāriputta, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge, enters and abides in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life—this too, Sāriputta, is a power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahma.

“Imāni kho, sāriputta, dasa tathāgatassa tathāgatabalāni yehi balehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahma.

149. “Yo [V 1.0104] kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso; takkapariyāhataṃ [T 1.0144] samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme [M 1.0103] aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya, taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.

149. Sāriputta, should anyone, knowing me thus and seeing me thus, say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, followed by investigation, and of his own devising’—without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if brought there. Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, do I declare this to be the outcome. Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if brought there.

150. “Cattārimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa vesārajjāni yehi vesārajjehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti. Katamāni cattāri?

150. Sāriputta, there are these four grounds of self-confidence of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahma. What are the four?

“‘Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā’ti. Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena [P 1.0072] paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ etampahaṃ (sī. pī.), sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘While you claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, these dhammas have not been fully awakened to by you’—that an ascetic or a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this, in accordance with the Dhamma: this ground, Sāriputta, I do not see. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I abide secure, fearless, and self-confident.

“‘Khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato ime āsavā aparikkhīṇā’ti. Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto [T 1.0145] vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints have not been completely destroyed by you’—that an ascetic or a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this, in accordance with the Dhamma: this ground, Sāriputta, I do not see. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I abide secure, fearless, and self-confident.

“‘Ye kho pana te antarāyikā dhammā vuttā, te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti. Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘Those things declared by you to be obstructive are not capable of obstructing one who engages in them’—that an ascetic or a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this, in accordance with the Dhamma: this ground, Sāriputta, I do not see. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I abide secure, fearless, and self-confident.

“‘Yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito, so na niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā’ti[V 1.0105]. Tatra vata maṃ samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci vā lokasmiṃ sahadhammena paṭicodessatī’ti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

‘The Dhamma taught by you for a certain purpose does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering’—that an ascetic or a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me on this, in accordance with the Dhamma: this ground, Sāriputta, I do not see. Not seeing this ground, Sāriputta, I abide secure, fearless, and self-confident.

“Imāni [M 1.0104] kho, sāriputta, cattāri tathāgatassa vesārajjāni yehi vesārajjehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti.

These, Sāriputta, are the four grounds of self-confidence of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahma.

“Yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme [T 1.0146] aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.

Sāriputta, should anyone, knowing me thus and seeing me thus, say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, followed by investigation, and of his own devising’—without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if brought there. Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, do I declare this to be the outcome. Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if brought there.

151. “Aṭṭha kho imā, sāriputta, parisā. Katamā aṭṭha? Khattiyaparisā, brāhmaṇaparisā, gahapatiparisā, samaṇaparisā, cātumahārājikaparisā cātummahārājikā (sī. syā. pī.), tāvatiṃsaparisā, māraparisā, brahmaparisā – imā kho, sāriputta, aṭṭha parisā. Imehi kho, sāriputta, catūhi vesārajjehi samannāgato tathāgato imā aṭṭha parisā upasaṅkamati ajjhogāhati. Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, anekasataṃ khattiyaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā. Tatrapi mayā sannisinnapubbañceva, sallapitapubbañca, sākacchā ca samāpajjitapubbā. Tatra vata maṃ bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā okkamissatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto viharāmi.

151. Sāriputta, there are these eight assemblies. Which eight? The assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā—these, Sāriputta, are the eight assemblies. Endowed with these four kinds of intrepidity, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata approaches and enters these eight assemblies. I recall, Sāriputta, having approached many hundreds of assemblies of nobles. There I have sat with them before, conversed with them before, engaged in discussion, and entered into attainment. That any fear or timidity should overcome me there—such a possibility, Sāriputta, I do not perceive. Not perceiving such a possibility, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, attained fearlessness, and attained intrepidity.

“Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisaṃ…pe… gahapatiparisaṃ… samaṇaparisaṃ… cātumahārājikaparisaṃ… tāvatiṃsaparisaṃ… māraparisaṃ… brahmaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā. Tatrapi mayā sannisinnapubbañceva, sallapitapubbañca, sākacchā ca samāpajjitapubbā. Tatra vata maṃ bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā okkamissatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta[V 1.0106], na samanupassāmi. Etamahaṃ, sāriputta, nimittaṃ asamanupassanto khemappatto abhayappatto vesārajjappatto [P 1.0073] viharāmi.

I recall, Sāriputta, having approached many hundreds of assemblies of brahmins... assemblies of householders... assemblies of ascetics... assemblies of the Four Great Kings... assemblies of the Thirty-three... assemblies of Māra... and assemblies of Brahmā. There too I have sat with them before, conversed with them before, engaged in discussion, and entered into attainment. That any fear or timidity should overcome me there—such a possibility, Sāriputta, I do not perceive. Not perceiving such a possibility, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, attained fearlessness, and attained intrepidity.

“Yo [M 1.0105] kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā [T 1.0147] alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.

Indeed, Sāriputta, whoever, knowing me thus and seeing me thus, should say: 'The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, pursued by investigation, and self-devised'—Sāriputta, without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if carried and placed there. Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom might attain Arahantship in this very life, so certain is this consequence, I declare. Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if carried and placed there.

152. “Catasso kho imā, sāriputta, yoniyo. Katamā catasso? Aṇḍajā yoni, jalābujā yoni, saṃsedajā yoni, opapātikā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, aṇḍajā yoni? Ye kho te, sāriputta, sattā aṇḍakosaṃ abhinibbhijja jāyanti – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, aṇḍajā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, jalābujā yoni? Ye kho te, sāriputta, sattā vatthikosaṃ abhinibbhijja jāyanti – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, jalābujā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, saṃsedajā yoni? Ye kho te, sāriputta, sattā pūtimacche vā jāyanti pūtikuṇape vā pūtikummāse vā candanikāye vā oḷigalle vā jāyanti – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, saṃsedajā yoni. Katamā ca, sāriputta, opapātikā yoni? Devā, nerayikā, ekacce ca manussā, ekacce ca vinipātikā – ayaṃ vuccati, sāriputta, opapātikā yoni. Imā kho, sāriputta, catasso yoniyo.

152. Sāriputta, there are these four modes of generation. What are the four? Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, and spontaneous generation. And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born generation? Those beings who are born by breaking through an eggshell—this is called egg-born generation, Sāriputta. And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born generation? Those beings who are born by breaking through the womb—this is called womb-born generation, Sāriputta. And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born generation? Those beings who are born in rotten fish, or in a rotten corpse, or in rotten dough, or in a cesspool, or in a drain—this is called moisture-born generation, Sāriputta. And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous generation? Gods, beings in hell, certain human beings, and certain beings in the states of deprivation—this is called spontaneous generation, Sāriputta. These, Sāriputta, are the four modes of generation.

“Yo [T 1.0148] kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti, taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ [V 1.0107] sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi. Taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye.

Indeed, Sāriputta, whoever, knowing me thus and seeing me thus, should say: 'The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, pursued by investigation, and self-devised'—Sāriputta, without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if carried and placed there. Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom might attain Arahantship in this very life, so certain is this consequence, I declare. Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if carried and placed there.

153. “Pañca [M 1.0106] kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo. Katamā pañca? Nirayo, tiracchānayoni, pettivisayo, manussā, devā. Nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, nirayagāmiñca maggaṃ, nirayagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Tiracchānayoniñcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, tiracchānayonigāmiñca maggaṃ, tiracchānayonigāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Pettivisayaṃ cāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, pettivisayagāmiñca maggaṃ, pettivisayagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Manusse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, manussalokagāmiñca maggaṃ[T 1.0149], manussalokagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Deve cāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, devalokagāmiñca maggaṃ, devalokagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Nibbānañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi, nibbānagāmiñca maggaṃ, nibbānagāminiñca [P 1.0074] paṭipadaṃ; yathā paṭipanno ca āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati tañca pajānāmi.

153. Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of petas, human beings, and devas. Sāriputta, I know hell, the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell; and I know how one who has so practiced, on the dissolution of the body, after death, is reborn in the plane of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. Sāriputta, I know the animal realm, the path leading to the animal realm, and the practice leading to the animal realm; and I know how one who has so practiced, on the dissolution of the body, after death, is reborn in the animal realm. Sāriputta, I know the realm of petas, the path leading to the realm of petas, and the practice leading to the realm of petas; and I know how one who has so practiced, on the dissolution of the body, after death, is reborn in the realm of petas. Sāriputta, I know human beings, the path leading to the human world, and the practice leading to the human world; and I know how one who has so practiced, on the dissolution of the body, after death, is reborn among human beings. Sāriputta, I know the devas, the path leading to the world of devas, and the practice leading to the world of devas; and I know how one who has so practiced, on the dissolution of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Sāriputta, I know Nibbāna, the path leading to Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna; and I know how one who has so practiced, through the destruction of the taints, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, enters upon and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom.

154. “Idhāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantadukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, aṅgārakāsu sādhikaporisā pūrā aṅgārānaṃ vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva aṅgārakāsuṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca [T 1.0150] iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva aṅgārakāsuṃ āgamissatī’ti[V 1.0108]. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tassā aṅgārakāsuyā [M 1.0107] patitaṃ, ekantadukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantadukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

154. Here, Sāriputta, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know them thus: ‘This person is practicing in such a way, is striving in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the plane of misery, a bad destination, a state of perdition, in hell.’ Then at a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has been reborn in the plane of misery, a bad destination, a state of perdition, in hell, experiencing exclusively painful, severe, and sharp feelings. Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals, flameless and smokeless. Then a man would come along—scorched and overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched—traveling by the one-way path heading right for that same charcoal pit. A man with good sight, seeing him, would say: ‘This gentleman is practicing in such a way, is striving in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that he will come to this very charcoal pit.’ Then at a later time, he would see him fallen into that charcoal pit, experiencing exclusively painful, severe, and sharp feelings. In the same way, Sāriputta, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know them thus: ‘This person is practicing in such a way, is striving in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the plane of misery, a bad destination, a state of perdition, in hell.’ Then at a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see that on the dissolution of the body, after death, he has been reborn in the plane of misery, a bad destination, a state of perdition, in hell, experiencing exclusively painful, severe, and sharp feelings.

“Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapannaṃ, dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, gūthakūpo sādhikaporiso, pūro gūthassa. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto [P 1.0075] kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva gūthakūpaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā [T 1.0151] ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā imaṃyeva gūthakūpaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tasmiṃ gūthakūpe patitaṃ, dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tiracchānayoniṃ upapannaṃ, dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is striving in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the animal realm.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in the animal realm, experiencing painful, severe, and harsh feelings. Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a cesspit deeper than a man's height, full of filth. Then a man would come along—afflicted by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched—traveling by a direct path, heading straight for that very cesspit. A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘This good man has practiced in such a way, is striving in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that he will come to this very cesspit.’ At a later time, he would see that man fallen into that cesspit, experiencing painful, severe, and harsh feelings. Even so, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is striving in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the animal realm.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in the animal realm, experiencing painful, severe, and harsh feelings.

“Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ [M 1.0108] passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapannaṃ, dukkhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, rukkho visame bhūmibhāge jāto tanupattapalāso kabaracchāyo[V 1.0109]. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva rukkhaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva rukkhaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya[T 1.0152], aparena samayena tassa rukkhassa chāyāya nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā dukkhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā pettivisayaṃ upapannaṃ, dukkhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the realm of petas.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in the realm of petas, experiencing feelings of abundant suffering. Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a tree growing on an uneven patch of ground, with sparse leaves and foliage, and patchy shade. Then a man would come along—afflicted by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched—traveling by a single path, heading straight for that very tree. A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘This good man has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that he will come to this very tree.’ At a later time, he would see that man sitting or lying down in the shade of that tree, experiencing feelings of abundant suffering. Even so, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the realm of petas.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in the realm of petas, experiencing feelings of abundant suffering.

“Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapannaṃ, sukhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, rukkho same bhūmibhāge jāto bahalapattapalāso sandacchāyo saṇḍacchāyo (syā.), santacchāyo (ka.). Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva rukkhaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imameva rukkhaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tassa rukkhassa chāyāya nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā sukhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ [T 1.0153] puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā [M 1.0109] manussesu upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā manussesu upapannaṃ, sukhabahulā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn among humans.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn among humans, experiencing feelings of abundant pleasure. Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a tree growing on a level patch of ground, with dense leaves and foliage, and deep shade. Then a man would come along—afflicted by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched—traveling by a single path, heading straight for that very tree. A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘This good man has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that he will come to this very tree.’ At a later time, he would see that man sitting or lying down in the shade of that tree, experiencing feelings of abundant pleasure. Even so, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn among humans.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn among humans, experiencing feelings of abundant pleasure.

“Idha [P 1.0076] panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā [V 1.0110] visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, pāsādo, tatrāssa kūṭāgāraṃ ullittāvalittaṃ nivātaṃ phusitaggaḷaṃ pihitavātapānaṃ. Tatrāssa pallaṅko gonakatthato paṭikatthato paṭalikatthato kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇo sauttaracchado ubhatolohitakūpadhāno. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva pāsādaṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva pāsādaṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena tasmiṃ pāsāde tasmiṃ kūṭāgāre tasmiṃ pallaṅke nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ [T 1.0154] puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho yathā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant. Suppose, Sāriputta, there were a palace, and in it an upper chamber, plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with bolts fastened and windows closed. In it there would be a couch spread with a long-fleeced woolen rug, a white woolen rug, a woolen rug with floral designs, and a spread of the finest antelope hide, with a canopy above, and with red cushions at both ends. Then a man would come along—afflicted by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched—traveling by a single path, heading straight for that very palace. A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘This good man has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that he will arrive at this very palace.’ At a later time, he would see him seated or lying down in that palace, in that upper chamber, on that couch, experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant. Even so, Sāriputta, in this world, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I know him thus: ‘This person has practiced in such a way, is conducting himself in such a way, and has embarked on such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ At a later time, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I see him, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant.

“Idha panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaccaṃ puggalaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissatīti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, pokkharaṇī acchodakā [M 1.0110] sātodakā sītodakā setakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā. Avidūre cassā tibbo vanasaṇḍo. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito ekāyanena maggena tameva pokkharaṇiṃ paṇidhāya. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘tathā bhavaṃ puriso paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā imaṃyeva pokkharaṇiṃ āgamissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passeyya aparena samayena taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā nhāyitvā ca pivitvā ca sabbadarathakilamathapariḷāhaṃ paṭippassambhetvā [T 1.0155] paccuttaritvā tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ [P 1.0077] vā, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, idhekaccaṃ puggalaṃ evaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāmi – tathāyaṃ puggalo paṭipanno tathā ca iriyati tañca maggaṃ samārūḷho, yathā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ [V 1.0111] abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissatī’ti. Tamenaṃ passāmi aparena samayena āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantaṃ, ekantasukhā vedanā vedayamānaṃ. Imā kho, sāriputta, pañca gatiyo.

Here, Sāriputta, I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my mind thus: 'This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a manner, and has embarked on such a path, that through the destruction of the taints, he will in this very life realize for himself the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having directly known and attained it, and will dwell therein.' Then, at a later time, I see that person, through the destruction of the taints, realizing for himself the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom in this very life, and dwelling therein, experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant. Just as, Sāriputta, there might be a lotus pond with clear, pleasant, cool, and pure water, with good fords, delightful. Not far from it there might be a dense forest grove. Then a man might come along, scorched and overcome by the heat, weary, thirsty, and parched, traveling along a single path, heading straight for that very lotus pond. A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say: 'This worthy man is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a manner, and has embarked on such a path that he will come to this very lotus pond.' Then, at a later time, he would see that man having plunged into the pond, bathed, drunk, and with all his torment, weariness, and feverishness subsided, come out and sit or lie down in that forest grove, experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant. In the same way, Sāriputta, I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my mind thus: 'This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a manner, and has embarked on such a path that, through the destruction of the taints, he will in this very life realize for himself the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having directly known and attained it, and will dwell therein.' Then, at a later time, I see that person, through the destruction of the taints, realizing for himself the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom in this very life, and dwelling therein, experiencing feelings that are exclusively pleasant. These, Sāriputta, are the five destinations.

“Yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jānantaṃ evaṃ passantaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso; takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhāna’nti taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi ‘taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye’.

Sāriputta, whoever, knowing me thus and seeing me thus, should say: 'The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction of noble knowledge and vision; the ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, followed up by investigation, self-devised'—Sāriputta, without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if he had been carried there. Just as, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, might attain final knowledge in this very life, so, Sāriputta, do I declare this to be the case: 'Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, without relinquishing that view, he is deposited in hell just as if he had been carried there.'

155. “Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ [T 1.0156] caritā caritvā (ka.) – tapassī sudaṃ homi paramatapassī, lūkho sudaṃ lūkhassudaṃ (sī. pī.) homi paramalūkho, jegucchī sudaṃ homi paramajegucchī, pavivitto sudaṃ pavivittassudaṃ (sī. pī.) homi paramapavivitto[M 1.0111]. Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, tapassitāya hoti – acelako homi muttācāro hatthāpalekhano hatthāvalekhano (syā.), na ehibhaddantiko na tiṭṭhabhaddantiko; nābhihaṭaṃ na uddissakataṃ na nimantanaṃ sādiyāmi. So na kumbhimukhā paṭiggaṇhāmi, na kaḷopimukhā paṭiggaṇhāmi, na eḷakamantaraṃ, na daṇḍamantaraṃ, na musalamantaraṃ, na dvinnaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ, na gabbhiniyā, na pāyamānāya pāyantiyā (ka.), na purisantaragatāya, na saṅkittīsu, na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti, na yattha makkhikā saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī; na macchaṃ na maṃsaṃ na suraṃ na merayaṃ na thusodakaṃ pivāmi; so ekāgāriko vā homi ekālopiko, dvāgāriko [P 1.0078] vā homi dvālopiko…pe… sattāgāriko vā homi sattālopiko; ekissāpi dattiyā yāpemi, dvīhipi dattīhi yāpemi…pe… sattahipi dattīhi yāpemi; ekāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāremi, dvīhikampi āhāraṃ āhāremi…pe… sattāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāremi; iti evarūpaṃ addhamāsikampi pariyāyabhattabhojanānuyogamanuyutto viharāmi.

155. Sāriputta, I recall having practiced the holy life endowed with four aspects: I was an ascetic, a foremost ascetic; I was austere, foremost in austerity; I was scrupulous, foremost in scrupulousness; I was secluded, foremost in seclusion. And this, Sāriputta, was my asceticism: I went without clothes, was of unrestrained conduct, and licked my hands clean. I would not come when invited with ‘Venerable sir, please come,’ nor would I stop when requested with ‘Venerable sir, please stay.’ I did not accept food brought to me, food prepared specially for me, or an invitation. I did not accept food from the mouth of a pot or a pan. I did not accept it across a threshold, across a stick, or across a pestle; nor from two people eating together when one of them would give; nor from a pregnant woman, a nursing woman, or a woman who had been with a man; nor from food collected at a public distribution; nor where a dog was waiting; nor where flies were swarming. I did not accept fish or meat; I did not drink liquor, spirits, or fermented gruel. I was one who took alms from only one house, taking only one mouthful; or from two houses, taking two mouthfuls… or from seven houses, taking seven mouthfuls. I subsisted on one small bowl, on two small bowls… or on seven small bowls. I took food once every other day, once every third day… or once every eighth day. Thus I lived devoted to the practice of eating at fixed intervals, even up to once a fortnight.

“So sākabhakkho vā homi, sāmākabhakkho vā homi, nīvārabhakkho vā homi, daddulabhakkho vā homi, haṭabhakkho vā homi, kaṇabhakkho vā [T 1.0157] homi, ācāmabhakkho vā homi[V 1.0112], piññākabhakkho vā homi, tiṇabhakkho vā homi, gomayabhakkho vā homi, vanamūlaphalāhāro yāpemi pavattaphalabhojī.

I was one who ate leafy greens, or millet, or wild rice, or leather scraps, or moss, or rice bran, or rice scum, or oil-seed refuse, or grass, or cow dung. I subsisted on forest roots and fruits, feeding on fruits that had fallen on their own.

“So sāṇānipi dhāremi, masāṇānipi dhāremi, chavadussānipi dhāremi, paṃsukūlānipi dhāremi, tirīṭānipi dhāremi, ajinampi dhāremi, ajinakkhipampi dhāremi, kusacīrampi dhāremi, vākacīrampi dhāremi, phalakacīrampi dhāremi, kesakambalampi dhāremi, vāḷakambalampi dhāremi, ulūkapakkhampi dhāremi; kesamassulocakopi homi kesamassulocanānuyogamanuyutto; ubbhaṭṭhakopi homi āsanapaṭikkhitto; ukkuṭikopi homi ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutto; kaṇṭakāpassayikopi homi kaṇṭakāpassaye seyyaṃ kappemi imassānantare aññopi koci pāṭhapadeso aññesu ājīvakavatadīpakasuttesu dissati; sāyatatiyakampi udakorohanānuyogamanuyutto viharāmi – iti evarūpaṃ anekavihitaṃ kāyassa [M 1.0112] ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto viharāmi. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, tapassitāya hoti.

I wore garments of hemp, of mixed hemp, of shroud-cloth, of rags from a dust heap, of tree bark, of antelope hide, and a strip of antelope hide. I wore a garment of kusa grass, a garment of bark fibers, a garment of wooden splints, a blanket of human hair, a blanket of horsehair, and a garment of owl's wings. I was one who plucked out my hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out hair and beard. I was one who stood upright, rejecting seats. I was one who squatted, devoted to the exertion of squatting. I was one who lay on a bed of thorns; I made my bed on a plank of thorns. I lived devoted to the practice of immersing myself in water three times a day, including in the evening. Thus, in these various ways, I lived devoted to the practice of tormenting and torturing the body. This, Sāriputta, was my asceticism.

156. “Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, lūkhasmiṃ hoti – nekavassagaṇikaṃ rajojallaṃ kāye sannicitaṃ hoti papaṭikajātaṃ. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, tindukakhāṇu nekavassagaṇiko sannicito hoti papaṭikajāto, evamevāssu me, sāriputta, nekavassagaṇikaṃ rajojallaṃ kāye sannicitaṃ hoti papaṭikajātaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, na evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vatāhaṃ imaṃ rajojallaṃ pāṇinā parimajjeyyaṃ, aññe vā pana me imaṃ rajojallaṃ pāṇinā parimajjeyyu’nti. Evampi me, sāriputta[T 1.0158], na hoti. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, lūkhasmiṃ hoti.

156. Herein, Sāriputta, this was my austerity: the dust and dirt of many years accumulated on my body, forming a crust. Just as a tinduka tree stump over many years accumulates a crust, so too the dust and dirt of many years accumulated on my body, forming a crust. It never occurred to me, Sāriputta, ‘Oh, if only I could wipe this dust and dirt off with my hand, or if only others would wipe this dust and dirt off me with their hands!’ It never occurred to me thus. This, Sāriputta, was my austerity.

“Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, jegucchismiṃ hoti – so kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, satova abhikkamāmi, satova paṭikkamāmi, yāva udakabindumhipi me dayā paccupaṭṭhitā hoti – ‘māhaṃ khuddake pāṇe visamagate saṅghātaṃ āpādesi’nti. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, jegucchismiṃ hoti.

Herein, Sāriputta, this was my scrupulousness: I walked forward mindfully, I walked back mindfully. Even for a drop of water, compassion was established in me, thinking, ‘May I not bring to destruction the tiny creatures in uneven places.’ This, Sāriputta, was my scrupulousness.

“Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputta, pavivittasmiṃ hoti – so kho [P 1.0079] ahaṃ, sāriputta, aññataraṃ araññāyatanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā viharāmi. Yadā passāmi gopālakaṃ vā pasupālakaṃ vā tiṇahārakaṃ vā kaṭṭhahārakaṃ vā vanakammikaṃ vā, vanena vanaṃ gahanena gahanaṃ ninnena ninnaṃ thalena thalaṃ saṃpatāmi papatāmi (sī. syā. pī.). Taṃ kissa hetu? Mā maṃ te addasaṃsu ahañca mā te addasanti. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, āraññako mago manusse disvā vanena vanaṃ gahanena gahanaṃ ninnena ninnaṃ [V 1.0113] thalena thalaṃ saṃpatati, evameva kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, yadā passāmi gopālakaṃ vā pasupālakaṃ vā tiṇahārakaṃ vā kaṭṭhahārakaṃ vā vanakammikaṃ vā vanena vanaṃ gahanena gahanaṃ ninnena ninnaṃ thalena thalaṃ saṃpatāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Mā maṃ te addasaṃsu ahañca mā te addasanti. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, pavivittasmiṃ hoti.

Herein, Sāriputta, this was my seclusion: I would enter some forest haunt and dwell there. When I saw a cowherd, a shepherd, a grass-cutter, a wood-gatherer, or a forest-worker, I would flee from forest to forest, from thicket to thicket, from low ground to low ground, from high ground to high ground. For what reason? ‘May they not see me, and may I not see them.’ Just as a wild deer, upon seeing humans, flees from forest to forest, from thicket to thicket, from low ground to low ground, from high ground to high ground, so too, Sāriputta, when I saw a cowherd, a shepherd, a grass-cutter, a wood-gatherer, or a forest-worker, I would flee from forest to forest, from thicket to thicket, from low ground to low ground, from high ground to high ground. For what reason? ‘May they not see me, and may I not see them.’ This, Sāriputta, was my seclusion.

“So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ye te goṭṭhā paṭṭhitagāvo apagatagopālakā, tattha catukkuṇḍiko upasaṅkamitvā yāni tāni vacchakānaṃ [T 1.0159] taruṇakānaṃ dhenupakānaṃ gomayāni tāni sudaṃ āhāremi. Yāvakīvañca me[M 1.0113], sāriputta, sakaṃ muttakarīsaṃ apariyādinnaṃ hoti, sakaṃyeva sudaṃ muttakarīsaṃ āhāremi. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, mahāvikaṭabhojanasmiṃ hoti.

Sāriputta, I would go on all fours to the cattle pens after the cows had left and the cowherds were gone, and I would eat the dung of the young, suckling calves. And as long as my own urine and feces were not exhausted, I would eat my own urine and feces. This, Sāriputta, was my partaking of grossly foul food.

157. “So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, aññataraṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ ajjhogāhetvā viharāmi. Tatrāssudaṃ, sāriputta, bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hoti – yo koci avītarāgo taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati, yebhuyyena lomāni haṃsanti. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, yā tā rattiyo sītā hemantikā antaraṭṭhakā himapātasamayā antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye (sī. pī.) tathārūpāsu rattīsu rattiṃ abbhokāse viharāmi, divā vanasaṇḍe; gimhānaṃ pacchime māse divā abbhokāse viharāmi, rattiṃ vanasaṇḍe. Apissu maṃ, sāriputta, ayaṃ anacchariyagāthā paṭibhāsi pubbe assutapubbā –

157. Sāriputta, I would dwell, having entered a certain terrifying forest grove. And in that terrifying forest grove, Sāriputta, such was its terrifying nature that any person not free from passion who entered it would, for the most part, have their hair stand on end. Sāriputta, during those nights that were cold and wintry, during the eight-day winter intervals, a time of snowfall, on such nights I would dwell at night in the open and during the day in the forest grove; and in the last month of summer, I would dwell during the day in the open and at night in the forest grove. And then, Sāriputta, this amazing verse, never heard before, occurred to me:

“Sotatto sosinno sosīno (sī. pī. ka.), sosino (syā.), sosindo (saddanīti) ceva, eko bhiṃsanake vane;

Naggo na caggimāsīno, esanāpasuto munī”ti.

‘Scorched and drenched, alone in a terrifying forest, naked, not sitting by a fire, the sage devoted to the quest.’

“So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, susāne seyyaṃ kappemi chavaṭṭhikāni upadhāya. Apissu maṃ, sāriputta, gāmaṇḍalā gomaṇḍalā (bahūsu) cariyāpiṭakaaṭṭhakathā oloketabbā upasaṅkamitvā oṭṭhubhantipi, omuttentipi, paṃsukenapi okiranti, kaṇṇasotesupi salākaṃ pavesenti. Na kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, abhijānāmi tesu pāpakaṃ cittaṃ uppādetā. Idaṃsu me, sāriputta, upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hoti.

Sāriputta, I would make my bed in a charnel ground, using the bones of the dead as a pillow. And, Sāriputta, village youths would come up to me and spit on me, urinate on me, sprinkle dust on me, and insert sticks into my ear-holes. But, Sāriputta, I do not recall having generated an evil thought towards them. This, Sāriputta, was my abiding in equanimity.

158. “Santi [T 1.0160][P 1.0080] kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘āhārena [V 1.0114] suddhī’ti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kolehi yāpemā’ti. Te kolampi khādanti, kolacuṇṇampi khādanti, kolodakampi pivanti – anekavihitampi kolavikatiṃ paribhuñjanti. Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva kolaṃ āhāraṃ āhāritā. Siyā kho pana te, sāriputta, evamassa – ‘mahā nūna tena samayena kolo ahosī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tadāpi etaparamoyeva kolo ahosi seyyathāpi etarahi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva [M 1.0114] kolaṃ āhāraṃ āhārayato adhimattakasimānaṃ patto kāyo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā, evamevassu me aṅgapaccaṅgāni bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma oṭṭhapadaṃ, evamevassu me ānisadaṃ hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma vaṭṭanāvaḷī, evamevassu me piṭṭhikaṇṭako unnatāvanato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma jarasālāya gopānasiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti, evamevassu me phāsuḷiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti, evamevassu me akkhikūpesu akkhitārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma tittakālābuāmakacchinno vātātapena saṃphuṭito samphusito (syā.), saṃpuṭito (pī. ka.) ettha saṃphuṭitoti saṅkucitoti attho hoti sammilāto, evamevassu [T 1.0161] me sīsacchavi saṃphuṭitā hoti sammilātā tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘udaracchaviṃ parimasissāmī’ti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, ‘piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ parimasissāmī’ti udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, yāvassu me, sāriputta, udaracchavi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karissāmī’ti tattheva avakujjo papatāmi tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, tameva kāyaṃ assāsento pāṇinā gattāni anomajjāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, pāṇinā gattāni anomajjato pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā patanti tāyevappāhāratāya.

158. There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view: ‘Purity comes through food.’ They say: ‘Let us subsist on jujubes.’ They eat jujubes, jujube powder, and drink jujube water—they consume various kinds of jujube preparations. But, Sāriputta, I recall having eaten just a single jujube as my food. It might occur to you, Sāriputta: ‘Surely the jujube must have been large at that time.’ But it should not be seen that way, Sāriputta. At that time the jujube was the very same size as it is now. From eating just that one jujube, Sāriputta, my body became extremely emaciated. My limbs became like the joints of an āsītika creeper or a kāḷa creeper, on account of that little food. My buttocks became like a camel’s hoof, on account of that little food. My spine, with its vertebrae protruding and receding, became like a string of beads, on account of that little food. My ribs jutted out like the rafters of a dilapidated shed, on account of that little food. The pupils of my eyes, sunk deep in their sockets, appeared like the reflection of stars in the water of a deep well, on account of that little food. The skin of my head became shriveled and withered like a bitter gourd cut while raw and withered by wind and sun, on account of that little food. When, Sāriputta, I thought to touch the skin of my belly, I would grasp my spine; when I thought to touch my spine, I would grasp the skin of my belly—so close was the skin of my belly stuck to my spine, on account of that little food. When, Sāriputta, I thought to defecate or urinate, I would fall down right there on my face, on account of that little food. When, Sāriputta, comforting this very body, I would rub my limbs with my hand, the hairs, their roots rotted, would fall out from my body, on account of that little food.

159. “Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘āhārena suddhī’ti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘muggehi yāpema…pe… tilehi yāpema…pe… taṇḍulehi yāpemā’ti. Te taṇḍulampi khādanti, taṇḍulacuṇṇampi khādanti, taṇḍulodakampi [P 1.0081] pivanti – anekavihitampi taṇḍulavikatiṃ paribhuñjanti. Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva taṇḍulaṃ āhāraṃ āhāritā. Siyā kho pana te, sāriputta, evamassa – ‘mahā nūna tena samayena taṇḍulo ahosī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tadāpi etaparamoyeva taṇḍulo ahosi[V 1.0115], seyyathāpi [M 1.0115] etarahi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, ekaṃyeva taṇḍulaṃ āhāraṃ āhārayato adhimattakasimānaṃ [T 1.0162] patto kāyo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā, evamevassu me aṅgapaccaṅgāni bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma oṭṭhapadaṃ, evamevassu me ānisadaṃ hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma vaṭṭanāvaḷī, evamevassu me piṭṭhikaṇṭako unnatāvanato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma jarasālāya gopānasiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti, evamevassu me phāsuḷiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti, evamevassu me akkhikūpesu akkhitārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma tittakālābu āmakacchinno vātātapena saṃphuṭito hoti sammilāto, evamevassu me sīsacchavi saṃphuṭitā hoti sammilātā tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘udaracchaviṃ parimasissāmī’ti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, ‘piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ parimasissāmī’ti udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi. Yāvassu me, sāriputta, udaracchavi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, ‘vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karissāmī’ti tattheva avakujjo papatāmi tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, tameva kāyaṃ assāsento pāṇinā gattāni anomajjāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, sāriputta, pāṇinā gattāni anomajjato pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā patanti tāyevappāhāratāya.

159. There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view: ‘Purity comes through food.’ They say: ‘Let us subsist on mung beans… let us subsist on sesame… let us subsist on rice.’ They eat rice, rice powder, and drink rice-water—they consume various kinds of rice preparations. But, Sāriputta, I recall having eaten just a single grain of rice as my food. It might occur to you, Sāriputta: ‘Surely the grain of rice must have been large at that time.’ But it should not be seen that way, Sāriputta. At that time the grain of rice was the very same size as it is now. From eating just that one grain of rice, Sāriputta, my body became extremely emaciated. My limbs became like the joints of an āsītika creeper or a kāḷa creeper, on account of that little food. My buttocks became like a camel’s hoof, on account of that little food. My spine, with its vertebrae protruding and receding, became like a string of beads, on account of that little food. My ribs jutted out like the rafters of a dilapidated shed, on account of that little food. The pupils of my eyes, sunk deep in their sockets, appeared like the reflection of stars in the water of a deep well, on account of that little food. The skin of my head became shriveled and withered like a bitter gourd cut while raw and withered by wind and sun, on account of that little food. When, Sāriputta, I thought to touch the skin of my belly, I would grasp my spine; when I thought to touch my spine, I would grasp the skin of my belly—so close was the skin of my belly stuck to my spine, on account of that little food. When, Sāriputta, I thought to defecate or urinate, I would fall down right there on my face, on account of that little food. When, Sāriputta, comforting this very body, I would rub my limbs with my hand, the hairs, their roots rotted, would fall out from my body, on account of that little food.

“Tāyapi kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, iriyāya tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamaṃ uttariṃ manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Imissāyeva ariyāya paññāya anadhigamā, yāyaṃ ariyā paññā adhigatā ariyā niyyānikā, niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

Yet, Sāriputta, by that exertion, by that practice, by that difficult austerity, I did not attain any state beyond human states, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. For what reason? Because of not attaining this noble wisdom, which, when attained, is noble, liberating, and leads one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.

160. “Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘saṃsārena suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so na kho paneso (sī. syā.), sāriputta, saṃsāro sulabharūpo [M 1.0116] yo mayā asaṃsaritapubbo [P 1.0082] iminā dīghena addhunā, aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehi. Suddhāvāse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, deve saṃsareyyaṃ, nayimaṃ lokaṃ punarāgaccheyyaṃ.

160. Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and have this doctrine: ‘Purification is through wandering in saṃsāra.’ But, Sāriputta, it is not easy to find a round of rebirth that I have not already wandered through in this long journey, except for the devas of the Pure Abodes. And if I were to wander among the devas of the Pure Abodes, Sāriputta, I would not return to this world again.

“Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘upapattiyā [V 1.0116] suddhī’ti. Na kho pana sā, sāriputta[T 1.0163], upapatti sulabharūpā yā mayā anupapannapubbā iminā dīghena addhunā, aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehi. Suddhāvāse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, deve upapajjeyyaṃ, nayimaṃ lokaṃ punarāgaccheyyaṃ.

Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and declare: ‘Purification is through rebirth.’ But, Sāriputta, a rebirth in which I have not previously been reborn in this long journey is not easy to find, except among the devas of the Pure Abodes. And if I were to be reborn among the devas of the Pure Abodes, Sāriputta, I would not return to this world again.

“Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘āvāsena suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so, sāriputta, āvāso sulabharūpo yo mayā anāvuṭṭhapubbo anāvutthapubbo (sī. pī.) iminā dīghena addhunā, aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehi. Suddhāvāse cāhaṃ, sāriputta, deve āvaseyyaṃ, nayimaṃ lokaṃ punarāgaccheyyaṃ.

Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and declare: ‘Purification is through dwelling.’ But, Sāriputta, a dwelling in which I have not previously dwelt in this long journey is not easy to find, except among the devas of the Pure Abodes. And if I were to dwell among the devas of the Pure Abodes, Sāriputta, I would not return to this world again.

“Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yaññena suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so, sāriputta, yañño sulabharūpo yo mayā ayiṭṭhapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā, tañca kho raññā vā satā khattiyena muddhāvasittena brāhmaṇena vā mahāsālena.

Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and declare: ‘Purification is through sacrifice.’ But, Sāriputta, a sacrifice that I have not previously performed in this long journey is not easy to find, and I have performed it as a king, an anointed khattiya, or as a wealthy brahmin.

“Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘aggiparicariyāya suddhī’ti. Na kho pana so, sāriputta, aggi sulabharūpo yo mayā apariciṇṇapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā, tañca kho raññā vā satā khattiyena muddhāvasittena brāhmaṇena vā mahāsālena.
