Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view and declare: ‘Purification is through tending the fire.’ But, Sāriputta, a fire that I have not previously tended in this long journey is not easy to find, and I have tended it as a king, an anointed khattiya, or as a wealthy brahmin.

161. “Santi kho pana, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yāvadevāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso daharo hoti yuvā [T 1.0164] susukāḷakeso bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato paṭhamena vayasā tāvadeva paramena paññāveyyattiyena samannāgato hoti. Yato ca kho ayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso jiṇṇo hoti vuddho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto, āsītiko vā nāvutiko vā vassasatiko vā jātiyā, atha tamhā paññāveyyattiyā, parihāyatī’ti. Na kho panetaṃ, sāriputta[M 1.0117], evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ahaṃ kho pana, sāriputta, etarahi jiṇṇo vuddho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto, āsītiko me vayo vattati. Idha me assu, sāriputta, cattāro sāvakā vassasatāyukā vassasatajīvino, paramāya satiyā ca gatiyā ca dhitiyā ca samannāgatā paramena ca paññāveyyattiyena. Seyyathāpi, sāriputta, daḷhadhammā daḷhadhammo (bahūsu) ṭīkā ca moggallānabyākaraṇaṃ ca oloketabbaṃ dhanuggaho sikkhito katahattho katūpāsano lahukena asanena appakasireneva tiriyaṃ tālacchāyaṃ atipāteyya, evaṃ adhimattasatimanto [V 1.0117] evaṃ adhimattagatimanto evaṃ [P 1.0083] adhimattadhitimanto evaṃ paramena paññāveyyattiyena samannāgatā. Te maṃ catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ upādāyupādāya pañhaṃ puccheyyuṃ, puṭṭho puṭṭho cāhaṃ tesaṃ byākareyyaṃ, byākatañca me byākatato dhāreyyuṃ, na ca maṃ dutiyakaṃ uttari paṭipuccheyyuṃ. Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitā aññatra uccārapassāvakammā, aññatra niddākilamathapaṭivinodanā apariyādinnāyevassa, sāriputta, tathāgatassa dhammadesanā, apariyādinnaṃyevassa tathāgatassa dhammapadabyañjanaṃ, apariyādinnaṃyevassa tathāgatassa pañhapaṭibhānaṃ[T 1.0165]. Atha me te cattāro sāvakā vassasatāyukā vassasatajīvino vassasatassa accayena kālaṃ kareyyuṃ. Mañcakena cepi maṃ, sāriputta, pariharissatha, nevatthi tathāgatassa paññāveyyattiyassa aññathattaṃ. Yaṃ kho taṃ yaṃ kho panetaṃ (sī.), sāriputta, sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘asammohadhammo satto loke uppanno bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna’nti, mameva taṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyya ‘asammohadhammo satto loke uppanno bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna’”nti.

161. Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this view, who have this doctrine: ‘For as long as this good man is young, a youth with fine black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, for that long is he endowed with supreme, manifest wisdom. But when this good man is old, aged, venerable, has passed a long time, and has reached the final stage of life—being eighty, ninety, or a hundred years of age by birth—then he declines from that manifest wisdom.’ But, Sāriputta, it should not be regarded so. I, Sāriputta, am now old, aged, venerable, have passed a long time, and have reached the final stage of life; my age is eighty years. Suppose, Sāriputta, I had four disciples in this Dispensation, each with a hundred-year lifespan, living for a hundred years, endowed with supreme mindfulness, quickness, and steadfastness, and with supreme wisdom capable of explaining cause and effect. Just as, Sāriputta, a renowned archer with a powerful bow, skilled, practiced, and having demonstrated his art, could with a light arrow and with little effort shoot across the shadow of a palm tree, so too would they be endowed with exceedingly great mindfulness, exceedingly great quickness, exceedingly great steadfastness, and with supreme wisdom capable of explaining cause and effect. They would question me again and again on the four foundations of mindfulness, and as I was questioned each time, I would be able to answer them. And they would be able to retain what I had explained just as I had explained it, and they would not question me further a second time, apart from when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; apart from the act of passing excrement and urine; apart from dispelling sleep and fatigue. Sāriputta, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma would be inexhaustible, the Tathāgata’s words and phrases of the Dhamma would be inexhaustible, and the Tathāgata’s ability to answer questions would be inexhaustible. Then those four disciples of mine, with their hundred-year lifespans, living for a hundred years, would pass away at the end of a hundred years. Even if, Sāriputta, you were to carry me on a couch, there would be no alteration in the Tathāgata’s state of wisdom capable of explaining cause and effect. Sāriputta, if one were to speak rightly, one would say: ‘A being whose nature is without delusion has arisen in the world for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the good, for the benefit, and for the happiness of gods and humans.’ It is of me that one, speaking rightly, would say this.

162. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā nāgasamālo bhagavato piṭṭhito ṭhito hoti bhagavantaṃ bījayamāno. Atha kho āyasmā nāgasamālo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Api hi me, bhante, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā lomāni haṭṭhāni. Konāmo ayaṃ, bhante, dhammapariyāyo”ti? “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, nāgasamāla, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ lomahaṃsanapariyāyo tveva naṃ dhārehī”ti.

162. At that time, the Venerable Nāgasamāla was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him. Then the Venerable Nāgasamāla said this to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! Indeed, venerable sir, having heard this discourse on the Dhamma, my body-hairs have bristled. What, venerable sir, is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma?” “Therefore, Nāgasamāla, you should remember this discourse on the Dhamma as ‘The Hair-Raising Discourse.’”

Idamavoca [M 1.0118] bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā nāgasamālo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Nāgasamāla, his mind uplifted, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Mahāsīhanādasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Second Mahāsīhanāda Sutta is finished.

3. Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ

3. The Greater Discourse on the Mass of Suffering.

163. Evaṃ [T 1.0166][V 1.0118] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya [P 1.0084] sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃsu. Atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “atippago kho tāva sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya carituṃ, yaṃ nūna mayaṃ yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkameyyāmā”ti. Atha kho te bhikkhū yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu; sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho te bhikkhū te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā etadavocuṃ – “samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema; samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema; samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema; idha no, āvuso, ko viseso, ko adhippayāso, kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa amhākaṃ vā – yadidaṃ dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesanaṃ, anusāsaniyā vā anusāsani”nti? Atha kho te bhikkhū tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ bhāsitaṃ neva [T 1.0167] abhinandiṃsu, nappaṭikkosiṃsu; anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃsu – “bhagavato santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmā”ti.

163. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then, in the morning, a number of monks, having dressed and taken their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: 'It is still too early to walk for alms in Sāvatthī. Suppose we were to go to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects.' Then those monks went to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. When they had exchanged courteous and memorable talk, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to them: 'Friends, the ascetic Gotama makes known the full understanding of sensual pleasures; we too make known the full understanding of sensual pleasures. Friends, the ascetic Gotama makes known the full understanding of forms; we too make known the full understanding of forms. Friends, the ascetic Gotama makes known the full understanding of feelings; we too make known the full understanding of feelings. Here, friends, what is the distinction, what is the aim, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, between his teaching of the Dhamma and our teaching of the Dhamma, or between his instruction and our instruction?' Then those monks neither welcomed nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other sects. Without welcoming or rejecting it, they got up from their seats and left, thinking: 'We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'

164. Atha kho te bhikkhū sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “idha mayaṃ, bhante, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ [M 1.0119] piṇḍāya pāvisimha. Tesaṃ no, bhante, amhākaṃ etadahosi – ‘atippago kho tāva sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya carituṃ, yaṃ nūna mayaṃ yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkameyyāmā’ti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkamimha; upasaṅkamitvā tehi aññatitthiyehi [V 1.0119] paribbājakehi saddhiṃ sammodimha; sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdimha. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho amhe, bhante, te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā etadavocuṃ – ‘samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema[P 1.0085]. Samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema. Samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeti, mayampi vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapema. Idha no, āvuso, ko viseso, ko adhippayāso, kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ [T 1.0168] samaṇassa vā gotamassa amhākaṃ vā, yadidaṃ dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesanaṃ anusāsaniyā vā anusāsani’nti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ bhāsitaṃ neva abhinandimha, nappaṭikkosimha; anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamimha – ‘bhagavato santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmā’”ti.

164. Then those monks, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from their alms round after the meal, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: 'Here, venerable sir, in the morning, having dressed and taken our bowls and robes, we entered Sāvatthī for alms. It occurred to us, venerable sir: "It is still too early to walk for alms in Sāvatthī. Suppose we were to go to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects." Then, venerable sir, we went to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, we exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. When we had exchanged courteous and memorable talk, we sat down to one side. While we were sitting there, venerable sir, those wanderers of other sects said to us: "Friends, the ascetic Gotama makes known the full understanding of sensual pleasures; we too make known the full understanding of sensual pleasures. Friends, the ascetic Gotama makes known the full understanding of forms; we too make known the full understanding of forms. Friends, the ascetic Gotama makes known the full understanding of feelings; we too make known the full understanding of feelings. Here, friends, what is the distinction, what is the aim, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, between his teaching of the Dhamma and our teaching of the Dhamma, or between his instruction and our instruction?" Then, venerable sir, we neither welcomed nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other sects. Without welcoming or rejecting it, we rose from our seats and left, thinking: "We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One."

165. “Evaṃvādino, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘ko panāvuso, kāmānaṃ assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Ko rūpānaṃ assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Ko vedanānaṃ assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa’nti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā na ceva sampāyissanti, uttariñca vighātaṃ āpajjissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasmiṃ. Nāhaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, passāmi sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya yo imesaṃ pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyya, aññatra tathāgatena vā tathāgatasāvakena vā, ito vā pana sutvā.

165. “Monks, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows: ‘But friends, what is the gratification in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, and what is the escape? What is the gratification in forms, what is the danger, and what is the escape? What is the gratification in feelings, what is the danger, and what is the escape?’ Questioned thus, monks, those wanderers of other sects will be unable to answer, and moreover, will fall into vexation. For what reason? Because, monks, it is beyond their domain. Monks, I do not see in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind with an explanation of these questions, except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.”

166. “Ko ca, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ assādo? Pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā, sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā [M 1.0120]… jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā – ime [T 1.0169] kho, bhikkhave, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo.

166. “And what, monks, is the gratification in sensual pleasures? There are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear… odors cognizable by the nose… flavors cognizable by the tongue… tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing—these, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. Monks, whatever happiness and joy arise in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure—this is the gratification in sensual pleasures.”

167. “Ko ca, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo? Idha, bhikkhave, kulaputto yena sippaṭṭhānena [V 1.0120] jīvikaṃ kappeti – yadi muddāya yadi gaṇanāya yadi saṅkhānena saṅkhāya (ka.) yadi kasiyā yadi vaṇijjāya yadi gorakkhena yadi issatthena yadi rājaporisena yadi sippaññatarena – sītassa purakkhato uṇhassa purakkhato ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīṃsapasamphassehi rissamāno īrayamāno (ka.), samphassamāno (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasutta 136) khuppipāsāya mīyamāno; ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ [P 1.0086] kāmānameva hetu.

167. And what, bhikkhus, is the drawback of sensual pleasures? Here, bhikkhus, a clansman makes a living by some occupation—whether by finger-reckoning, by counting, by computation, by farming, by trade, by cattle-herding, by archery, by royal service, or by any other such craft. He is afflicted by cold, afflicted by heat, harassed by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and dying from hunger and thirst. This, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering that has sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures.

“Tassa ce, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā nābhinipphajjanti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati, sammohaṃ āpajjati – ‘moghaṃ vata me uṭṭhānaṃ, aphalo vata me vāyāmo’ti. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

If, bhikkhus, while that clansman is thus striving, making a sustained effort, and exerting himself, that wealth is not produced for him, he sorrows, becomes weary, and laments; beating his breast, he cries aloud and falls into confusion, thinking: ‘Alas, my striving is in vain! Alas, my exertion is fruitless!’ This, too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering that has sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures.

“Tassa ce, bhikkhave, kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā abhinipphajjanti. So tesaṃ bhogānaṃ ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti – ‘kinti me bhoge neva rājāno hareyyuṃ, na corā hareyyuṃ, na aggi daheyya, na udakaṃ vaheyya vāheyya (ka.), na appiyā dāyādā hareyyu’nti. Tassa [T 1.0170] evaṃ ārakkhato gopayato te bhoge rājāno vā haranti, corā vā haranti, aggi vā dahati, udakaṃ vā vahati, appiyā vā dāyādā haranti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati, sammohaṃ āpajjati – ‘yampi me ahosi tampi no natthī’ti. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

If, bhikkhus, while that clansman is thus striving, making a sustained effort, and exerting himself, that wealth is produced for him, then on account of protecting that wealth he experiences pain and distress, thinking: ‘Lest kings take my wealth, or thieves take it, or fire burn it, or water carry it away, or unloved heirs take it!’ And while he is thus guarding and protecting it, kings do take his wealth, or thieves take it, or fire burns it, or water carries it away, or unloved heirs take it. He sorrows, becomes weary, and laments; beating his breast, he cries aloud and falls into confusion, thinking: ‘That which I once had, is no more!’ This, too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering that has sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures.

168. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu rājānopi rājūhi vivadanti, khattiyāpi khattiyehi vivadanti[M 1.0121], brāhmaṇāpi brāhmaṇehi vivadanti, gahapatīpi gahapatīhi vivadanti, mātāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi mātarā vivadati, pitāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi pitarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhātarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhaginiyā vivadati, bhaginīpi bhātarā vivadati, sahāyopi sahāyena vivadati. Te tattha kalahaviggahavivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ pāṇīhipi upakkamanti, leḍḍūhipi upakkamanti, daṇḍehipi upakkamanti, satthehipi upakkamanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ[V 1.0121]. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

168. Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasures as the cause, sensual pleasures as the source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders; a mother quarrels with her son, a son with his mother; a father quarrels with his son, a son with his father; a brother quarrels with a brother, a brother with a sister, a sister with a brother; a friend quarrels with a friend. Having fallen into quarrels, conflicts, and disputes, they attack one another with their hands, with clods of earth, with staves, and with swords. There they meet with death or with suffering equivalent to death. This, too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering that has sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, ubhatobyūḷhaṃ saṅgāmaṃ pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu[T 1.0171], sattīsupi khippamānāsu, asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasures as the cause, sensual pleasures as the source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures, taking up sword and shield, buckling on bow and quiver, they plunge into a battle arrayed on both sides, while arrows are being shot, spears are being hurled, and swords are flashing. There they pierce with arrows and spears, and cut off heads with swords. There they meet with death or with suffering equivalent to death. This, too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering that has sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, addāvalepanā aṭṭāvalepanā (syā. ka.) upakāriyo pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu, sattīsupi khippamānāsu[P 1.0087], asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, chakaṇakāyapi pakaṭṭhiyāpi (sī.) osiñcanti, abhivaggenapi omaddanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasures as the cause, sensual pleasures as the source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures, taking up sword and shield, buckling on bow and quiver, they charge the fortifications plastered with wet cow-dung, while arrows are being shot, spears are being hurled, and swords are flashing. There they pierce with arrows and spears, douse with boiling liquid cow-dung, crush with a pile of logs, and cut off heads with swords. There they meet with death or with suffering equivalent to death. This, too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering that has sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, arising simply on account of sensual pleasures.

169. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu sandhimpi chindanti, nillopampi haranti, ekāgārikampi karonti, paripanthepi tiṭṭhanti, paradārampi gacchanti. Tamenaṃ rājāno gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārenti – kasāhipi tāḷenti, vettehipi tāḷenti, aḍḍhadaṇḍakehipi tāḷenti; hatthampi chindanti, pādampi chindanti, hatthapādampi [T 1.0172] chindanti, kaṇṇampi chindanti, nāsampi chindanti, kaṇṇanāsampi chindanti; bilaṅgathālikampi karonti[M 1.0122], saṅkhamuṇḍikampi karonti, rāhumukhampi karonti, jotimālikampi karonti, hatthapajjotikampi karonti, erakavattikampi karonti, cīrakavāsikampi karonti, eṇeyyakampi karonti, baḷisamaṃsikampi karonti, kahāpaṇikampi karonti, khārāpatacchikampi karonti, palighaparivattikampi karonti, palālapīṭhakampi karonti, tattenapi telena osiñcanti, sunakhehipi khādāpenti, jīvantampi sūle uttāsenti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti[V 1.0122]. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

169. Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as the cause, with sensual pleasures as the origin, with sensual pleasures as the basis, for the very reason of sensual pleasures, people break into houses, carry out violent plunder, commit single-house robbery, practice highway robbery, and commit adultery. Then kings, having seized them, inflict various tortures—they have them flogged with whips, beaten with canes, struck with half-split batons; they cut off their hands, cut off their feet, cut off both hands and feet; they cut off their ears, cut off their noses, cut off both ears and noses; they perform the 'gruel pot' torture, the 'conch-shell head' torture, the 'Rāhu's mouth' torture, the 'garland of flames' torture, the 'hand-lamp' torture, the 'grass-strip' torture, the 'bark-garment' torture, the 'antelope' torture, the 'flesh-hook' torture, the 'coin-piece' torture, the 'lye-pickling' torture, the 'turning-bar' torture, the 'straw-mattress' torture; they pour boiling oil over them, have them devoured by dogs, impale them alive on a stake, and cut off their heads with a sword. There they meet death or suffering equivalent to death. This, monks, is a visible drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as the cause, with sensual pleasures as the origin, with sensual pleasures as the basis, for the very reason of sensual pleasures.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu kāyena duccaritaṃ caranti, vācāya duccaritaṃ caranti, manasā duccaritaṃ caranti. Te kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṃ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Ayampi, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo samparāyiko, dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as the cause, with sensual pleasures as the origin, with sensual pleasures as the basis, for the very reason of sensual pleasures, people engage in misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, on the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, a place of downfall, in hell. This, monks, is a future drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering with sensual pleasures as the cause, with sensual pleasures as the origin, with sensual pleasures as the basis, for the very reason of sensual pleasures.

170. “Kiñca, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo kho, bhikkhave, kāmesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

170. And what, monks, is the escape from sensual pleasures? It is the removal of desire and lust for sensual pleasures, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.

“Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ [T 1.0173] kāmānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā kāme parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno kāme parijānissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā [P 1.0088] evaṃ kāmānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, te vata sāmaṃ vā kāme parijānissanti paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno kāme parijānissatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.

Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape, that they themselves will fully comprehend sensual pleasures, or that they will establish another in that state whereby one who has practiced accordingly will fully comprehend sensual pleasures—this is not possible. But, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do understand as it really is the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape, that they themselves will fully comprehend sensual pleasures, or that they will establish another in that state whereby one who has practiced accordingly will fully comprehend sensual pleasures—this is possible.

171. “Ko ca, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ assādo? Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, khattiyakaññā vā brāhmaṇakaññā vā gahapatikaññā vā pannarasavassuddesikā vā soḷasavassuddesikā vā, nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷī nāccodātā paramā sā, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ samaye subhā [M 1.0123] vaṇṇanibhāti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, subhaṃ vaṇṇanibhaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ rūpānaṃ assādo.

171. And what, monks, is the gratification of forms? Suppose, monks, there is a maiden of the warrior caste, or the brahmin caste, or the householder caste, fifteen or sixteen years of age, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair—at that time, monks, is her beautiful appearance not supreme? 'Just so, venerable sir.' The pleasure and mental joy that arise in dependence on that beautiful appearance—this is the gratification of forms.

“Ko ca, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo? Idha, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya aparena samayena āsītikaṃ vā nāvutikaṃ vā vassasatikaṃ vā jātiyā, jiṇṇaṃ gopānasivaṅkaṃ [V 1.0123] bhoggaṃ daṇḍaparāyanaṃ pavedhamānaṃ gacchantiṃ āturaṃ gatayobbanaṃ khaṇḍadantaṃ khaṇḍadantiṃ (sī. pī.) palitakesaṃ palitakesiṃ, vilūnaṃ khalitasiraṃ valinaṃ tilakāhatagattaṃ tilakāhatagattiṃ (bahūsu) aṭṭhakathā ṭīkā oloketabbā. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā [T 1.0174] sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

And what, monks, is the drawback of forms? Here, monks, one might see that same sister at a later time, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, bent like a roof-rafter, stooped, relying on a staff, going along trembling, ailing, her youth gone, broken-toothed, with white hair, with sparse hair, bald-headed, wrinkled, her body spotted with moles. What do you think, monks? That former beautiful appearance that was, has it vanished, and has the drawback become manifest? ‘Just so, venerable sir.’ This, too, monks, is a drawback of forms.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya ābādhikaṃ dukkhitaṃ bāḷhagilānaṃ, sake muttakarīse palipannaṃ semānaṃ seyyamānaṃ (ka.), aññehi vuṭṭhāpiyamānaṃ, aññehi saṃvesiyamānaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister sick, suffering, gravely ill, lying fallen in her own urine and feces, being lifted up by others, being put to bed by others. What do you think, monks? That former beautiful appearance that was, has it vanished, and has the drawback become manifest? ‘Just so, venerable sir.’ This, too, monks, is a drawback of forms.

172. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – ekāhamataṃ vā dvīhamataṃ vā tīhamataṃ vā, uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakajātaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

172. Furthermore, monks, one might see the body of that same sister discarded in a charnel ground—dead for one day, two days, or three days, bloated, discolored, and festering. What do you think, monks? That former beautiful appearance that was, has it vanished, and has the drawback become manifest? ‘Just so, venerable sir.’ This, too, monks, is a drawback of forms.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – kākehi vā khajjamānaṃ, kulalehi vā khajjamānaṃ, gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, kaṅkehi vā khajjamānaṃ, sunakhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, byagghehi vā khajjamānaṃ, dīpīhi vā khajjamānaṃ, siṅgālehi vā khajjamānaṃ, vividhehi vā pāṇakajātehi khajjamānaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave[P 1.0089], yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister’s body discarded in a charnel ground—being devoured by crows, or being devoured by hawks, or being devoured by vultures, or being devoured by herons, or being devoured by dogs, or being devoured by tigers, or being devoured by leopards, or being devoured by jackals, or being devoured by various kinds of creatures. What do you think, monks? Has that former beautiful complexion vanished, and has the drawback become manifest? ‘Even so, venerable sir.’ This, too, monks, is the drawback of forms.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ, aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ [T 1.0175] nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ [M 1.0124] nhārusambandhaṃ, aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ, aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhāni disāvidisāvikkhittāni – aññena hatthaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena pādaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena gopphakaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena jaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena ūruṭṭhikaṃ, aññena kaṭiṭṭhikaṃ, aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena piṭṭhiṭṭhikaṃ, aññena khandhaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena gīvaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena hanukaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena dantaṭṭhikaṃ, aññena [V 1.0124] sīsakaṭāhaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister’s body discarded in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood, bound by sinews; a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, bound by sinews; a skeleton without flesh and blood, bound by sinews; bones with their connections gone, scattered in all directions—in one direction a hand bone, in another a foot bone, in another an ankle bone, in another a shin bone, in another a thigh bone, in another a hip bone, in another a rib bone, in another a backbone, in another a shoulder bone, in another a neck bone, in another a jawbone, in another a tooth bone, in another the skull. What do you think, monks? Has that former beautiful complexion vanished, and has the drawback become manifest? ‘Even so, venerable sir.’ This, too, monks, is the drawback of forms.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, tameva bhaginiṃ passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ – aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgāni, aṭṭhikāni puñjakitāni terovassikāni, aṭṭhikāni pūtīni cuṇṇakajātāni. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yā purimā subhā vaṇṇanibhā sā antarahitā, ādīnavo pātubhūtoti? ‘Evaṃ, bhante’. Ayampi, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ ādīnavo.

Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister’s body discarded in a charnel ground—bones, white, like the color of a conch shell; bones heaped up, more than a year old; bones, rotten and crumbled to dust. What do you think, monks? Has that former beautiful complexion vanished, and has the drawback become manifest? ‘Even so, venerable sir.’ This, too, monks, is the drawback of forms.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, rūpesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

And what, monks, is the escape from forms? It is, monks, the subduing of desire and lust for forms, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from forms.

“Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ rūpānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā rūpe parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno rūpe parijānissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ rūpānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā rūpe parijānissanti paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno rūpe parijānissatīti [T 1.0176] – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.

Monks, whatever recluses or brahmins do not understand as it actually is the gratification in forms as gratification, the drawback in forms as drawback, and the escape from forms as escape, it is not possible that they themselves will fully comprehend forms, or that they will establish another to that end, such that one who practices accordingly will fully comprehend forms. But, monks, whatever recluses or brahmins understand as it actually is the gratification in forms as gratification, the drawback in forms as drawback, and the escape from forms as escape, it is possible that they themselves will fully comprehend forms, or that they will establish another to that end, such that one who practices accordingly will fully comprehend forms.

173. “Ko ca, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ assādo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, neva tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na parabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na ubhayabyābādhāyapi [P 1.0090] ceteti[M 1.0125]; abyābajjhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Abyābajjhaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ assādaṃ vadāmi.

173. And what, monks, is the gratification in feelings? Here, monks, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. At the time, monks, when a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both. At that time, he experiences a feeling that is unafflicted. I say, monks, that unafflictedness is the highest gratification in feelings.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ [V 1.0125] avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati…pe… yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā, upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti yaṃ taṃ ariyā [T 1.0177] ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati…pe… yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, neva tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na parabyābādhāyapi ceteti, na ubhayabyābādhāyapi ceteti; abyābajjhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Abyābajjhaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ assādaṃ vadāmi.

Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is filled with the rapture and happiness born of concentration… Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells happily.’… Furthermore, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. At that time, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both; at that time, he experiences a feeling that is unafflicted. I say, monks, that unafflictedness is the highest gratification in feelings.

174. “Ko ca, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ ādīnavo? Yaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā – ayaṃ vedanānaṃ ādīnavo.

174. And what, monks, is the drawback of feelings? That feelings, monks, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the drawback of feelings.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, vedanānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, vedanāsu chandarāgavinayo, chandarāgappahānaṃ – idaṃ vedanānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

And what, monks, is the escape from feelings? It is, monks, the subduing of desire and lust for feelings, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from feelings.

“Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ vedanānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti, te vata sāmaṃ vā vedanaṃ parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno vedanaṃ parijānissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ye ca kho [T 1.0178] keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā evaṃ vedanānaṃ assādañca assādato ādīnavañca ādīnavato nissaraṇañca nissaraṇato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti te vata sāmaṃ vā vedanaṃ parijānissanti, paraṃ vā tathattāya samādapessanti yathā paṭipanno vedanaṃ parijānissatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī”ti.

Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as they really are the gratification of feelings as gratification, the danger in feelings as danger, and the escape from feelings as escape—that they themselves will fully comprehend feelings, or will establish another for that purpose so that one who practices accordingly will fully comprehend feelings—this possibility does not exist. And, bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do understand as they really are the gratification of feelings as gratification, the danger in feelings as danger, and the escape from feelings as escape—that they themselves will fully comprehend feelings, or will establish another for that purpose so that one who practices accordingly will fully comprehend feelings—this possibility exists.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The third, the Greater Discourse on the Mass of Suffering, is concluded.

4. Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ

4. The Lesser Discourse on the Mass of Suffering

175. Evaṃ [M 1.0126][P 1.0091][V 1.0126][T 1.0179] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ nigrodhārāme. Atha kho mahānāmo sakko yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho mahānāmo sakko bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “dīgharattāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā evaṃ dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi – ‘lobho cittassa upakkileso, doso cittassa upakkileso, moho cittassa upakkileso’ti. Evañcāhaṃ evaṃpāhaṃ (ka.), bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi – ‘lobho cittassa upakkileso, doso cittassa upakkileso, moho cittassa upakkileso’ti. Atha ca pana me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, evaṃ hoti – ‘kosu nāma me dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī’”ti.

175. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in Kapilavatthu at the Banyan Tree Monastery. Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, for a long time I have known the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: "Greed is a corruption of the mind; hatred is a corruption of the mind; delusion is a corruption of the mind." And although I know the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way, venerable sir, yet at times states of greed overcome my mind and remain; states of hatred overcome my mind and remain; and states of delusion overcome my mind and remain. To me, venerable sir, this thought occurs: "What quality, indeed, has not been abandoned within me, by which at times states of greed overcome my mind and remain, states of hatred overcome my mind and remain, and states of delusion overcome my mind and remain?"'

176. “So eva kho te, mahānāma, dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno yena te ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, dosadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, mohadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. So ca hi te, mahānāma, dhammo ajjhattaṃ pahīno abhavissa, na tvaṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvaseyyāsi, na kāme paribhuñjeyyāsi. Yasmā ca kho te, mahānāma, so eva dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno tasmā tvaṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasasi, kāme paribhuñjasi.

176. Mahānāma, it is that very quality that has not been abandoned within you, by which at times states of greed overcome your mind and remain, states of hatred overcome your mind and remain, and states of delusion overcome your mind and remain. For if, Mahānāma, that quality had been abandoned within you, you would not dwell in a household, you would not indulge in sensual pleasures. But because, Mahānāma, that very quality has not been abandoned within you, you dwell in a household and indulge in sensual pleasures.

177. “‘Appassādā [T 1.0180] kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo bahūpāyāsā (sī. syā. pī.) ettha bhiyyo’ti – iti cepi, mahānāma, ariyasāvakassa yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti, so ca sova (ka.) aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ nādhigacchati, aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; atha kho so neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hoti. Yato ca kho, mahānāma, ariyasāvakassa ‘appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo [M 1.0127] ettha bhiyyo’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya [V 1.0127] sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti, so ca aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ adhigacchati aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; atha kho so anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hoti.

177. Mahānāma, even if a noble disciple has clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is that 'sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, and much tribulation; the danger in them is far greater,' if he does not attain a joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or another state more peaceful than that, then he is not yet one who is non-returning to sensual pleasures. But when, Mahānāma, a noble disciple has clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is that 'sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, and much tribulation; the danger in them is far greater,' and he does attain a joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or another state more peaceful than that, then he is one who is non-returning to sensual pleasures.

“Mayhampi kho, mahānāma[P 1.0092], pubbeva sambodhā, anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato, ‘appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti, so ca aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ nājjhagamaṃ, aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; atha khvāhaṃ neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu paccaññāsiṃ. Yato ca kho me, mahānāma, ‘appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ ahosi, so ca sova (ka.) aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ ajjhagamaṃ, aññaṃ vā tato santataraṃ; athāhaṃ anāvaṭṭī kāmesu paccaññāsiṃ.

For me also, Mahānāma, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, I had clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is that 'sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, and much tribulation; the danger in them is far greater.' Yet, as long as I had not attained a joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or another state more peaceful than that, I did not claim to be non-returning to sensual pleasures. But when, Mahānāma, I had clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is that 'sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, and much tribulation; the danger in them is far greater,' and I had attained a joy and pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, or another state more peaceful than that, then I claimed to be non-returning to sensual pleasures.

178. “Ko ca, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ assādo? Pañcime, mahānāma, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā; sotaviññeyyā saddā…pe… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā… jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā – ime kho, mahānāma, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yaṃ kho, mahānāma, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo.

178. And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification of sensual pleasures? There are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear... smells cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. These, Mahānāma, are the five cords of sensual pleasure. Whatever happiness and joy arises in dependence on these five cords of sensual pleasure—this is the gratification of sensual pleasures.

“Ko ca, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo? Idha, mahānāma, kulaputto yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvikaṃ kappeti – yadi muddāya yadi gaṇanāya yadi saṅkhānena yadi kasiyā yadi vaṇijjāya yadi gorakkhena yadi issatthena yadi rājaporisena yadi sippaññatarena, sītassa purakkhato uṇhassa purakkhato ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīṃsapasamphassehi rissamāno khuppipāsāya mīyamāno; ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ [T 1.0182] kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

And what, Mahānāma, is the drawback of sensual pleasures? Here, Mahānāma, a son of a good family earns a living by some skill—whether by counting on the fingers, by calculation, by computation, by farming, by trade, by cattle-herding, by archery, by royal service, or by any other such skill. He is oppressed by cold and oppressed by heat, tormented by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and dying from hunger and thirst. This, Mahānāma, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible in the present life, which has sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and arises for the sake of sensual pleasure alone.

“Tassa [M 1.0128] ce mahānāma kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā nābhinipphajjanti, so socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati ‘moghaṃ [V 1.0128] vata me uṭṭhānaṃ, aphalo vata me vāyāmo’ti. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

If, Mahānāma, for that son of a good family who is thus striving, making effort, and exerting himself, those possessions are not produced, he sorrows, becomes weary, and laments; beating his breast, he wails and falls into bewilderment, thinking: 'Alas, my striving is in vain! Alas, my exertion is fruitless!' This too, Mahānāma, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible in the present life, which has sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and arises for the sake of sensual pleasure alone.

“Tassa ce, mahānāma, kulaputtassa evaṃ uṭṭhahato ghaṭato vāyamato te bhogā abhinipphajjanti. So tesaṃ bhogānaṃ ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti – ‘kinti me bhoge neva rājāno hareyyuṃ, na corā hareyyuṃ, na aggi daheyya, na udakaṃ vaheyya, na appiyā vā dāyādā hareyyu’nti. Tassa evaṃ ārakkhato gopayato te bhoge rājāno vā haranti, corā vā haranti, aggi vā dahati, udakaṃ vā vahati, appiyā vā dāyādā haranti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati – ‘yampi me ahosi tampi no natthī’ti. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

If, Mahānāma, for that son of a good family who is thus striving, making effort, and exerting himself, those possessions are produced, he, on account of protecting those possessions, experiences bodily suffering and mental distress: 'How might neither kings take away my possessions, nor thieves take them away, nor fire burn them, nor water carry them away, nor unloved heirs take them away?' While he is thus guarding and protecting them, either kings take away those possessions, or thieves take them away, or fire burns them, or water carries them away, or unloved heirs take them away. He sorrows, becomes weary, and laments; beating his breast, he wails and falls into bewilderment, thinking: 'That which I had, that too is no more!' This too, Mahānāma, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible in the present life, which has sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and arises for the sake of sensual pleasure alone.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu rājānopi rājūhi vivadanti, khattiyāpi khattiyehi vivadanti, brāhmaṇāpi brāhmaṇehi vivadanti, gahapatīpi gahapatīhi vivadanti, mātāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi mātarā vivadati, pitāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi pitarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhātarā vivadati, bhātāpi bhaginiyā vivadati, bhaginīpi bhātarā vivadati, sahāyopi sahāyena vivadati. Te tattha kalahaviggahavivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ pāṇīhipi upakkamanti, leḍḍūhipi upakkamanti, daṇḍehipi upakkamanti, satthehipi upakkamanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ[T 1.0183]. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, due to sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, based on sensual pleasures, and for the sake of sensual pleasure alone, kings dispute with kings, nobles with nobles, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders; a mother disputes with her son, a son with his mother; a father disputes with his son, a son with his father; a brother disputes with a brother, a brother with a sister, a sister with a brother; a friend disputes with a friend. Having fallen into quarrels, conflicts, and disputes, they attack one another with their hands, with clods of earth, with staves, and with weapons. There they meet death, or suffering comparable to death. This too, Mahānāma, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible in the present life, due to sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, based on sensual pleasures, and for the sake of sensual pleasure alone.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, ubhatobyūḷhaṃ saṅgāmaṃ pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu, sattīsupi khippamānāsu, asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, asināpi sīsaṃ [M 1.0129] chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, due to sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, based on sensual pleasures, and for the sake of sensual pleasure alone, taking up sword and shield, having fastened on bow and quiver, they rush into a battle arrayed on both sides, while arrows are being shot, spears are being hurled, and swords are flashing. There they are pierced by arrows and by spears, and their heads are cut off by swords. There they meet death, or suffering comparable to death. This too, Mahānāma, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible in the present life, due to sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, based on sensual pleasures, and for the sake of sensual pleasure alone.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṃ [V 1.0129] gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā, addāvalepanā upakāriyo pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu, sattīsupi khippamānāsu, asīsupi vijjotalantesu. Te tattha usūhipi vijjhanti, sattiyāpi vijjhanti, chakaṇakāyapi osiñcanti, abhivaggenapi omaddanti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, due to sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, based on sensual pleasures, and for the sake of sensual pleasure alone, taking up sword and shield, having fastened on bow and quiver, they rush into fortifications smeared with hot mire, while arrows are being shot, spears are being hurled, and swords are flashing. There they are pierced by arrows and by spears, drenched with boiling cow-dung, crushed by logs, and their heads are cut off by swords. There they meet death, or suffering comparable to death. This too, Mahānāma, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible in the present life, due to sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, based on sensual pleasures, and for the sake of sensual pleasure alone.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu sandhimpi chindanti, nillopampi haranti, ekāgārikampi [T 1.0184] karonti, paripanthepi tiṭṭhanti, paradārampi gacchanti. Tamenaṃ rājāno gahetvā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārenti – kasāhipi tāḷenti, vettehipi tāḷenti, aḍḍhadaṇḍakehipi tāḷenti; hatthampi chindanti, pādampi chindanti, hatthapādampi chindanti, kaṇṇampi chindanti, nāsampi chindanti, kaṇṇanāsampi chindanti; bilaṅgathālikampi karonti, saṅkhamuṇḍikampi karonti, rāhumukhampi karonti, jotimālikampi karonti, hatthapajjotikampi karonti, erakavattikampi karonti, cīrakavāsikampi karonti, eṇeyyakampi karonti, baḷisamaṃsikampi karonti, kahāpaṇikampi karonti, khārāpatacchikampi karonti, palighaparivattikampi karonti, palālapīṭhakampi karonti, tattenapi telena osiñcanti, sunakhehipi khādāpenti, jīvantampi sūle uttāsenti, asināpi sīsaṃ chindanti. Te tattha maraṇampi nigacchanti, maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo sandiṭṭhiko dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, on account of sensual pleasures, because of sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures, for the very reason of sensual pleasures, people break into houses, plunder, commit burglary, lie in wait on highways, and go to others’ wives. Then, kings have them arrested and inflict various kinds of punishments on them. They flog them with whips, strike them with canes, and strike them with split batons; they cut off their hands, cut off their feet, cut off both hands and feet, cut off their ears, cut off their noses, cut off both ears and noses. They inflict the ‘gruel-pot torture,’ the ‘conch-shell tonsure,’ the ‘Rāhu’s mouth,’ the ‘flaming garland,’ the ‘hand-torch,’ the ‘reed-strip torture,’ the ‘bark-dress torture,’ the ‘antelope torture,’ the ‘flesh-hooking,’ the ‘coin-cutting,’ the ‘caustic-rubbing,’ the ‘pivot-pin torture,’ and the ‘straw-mattress torture.’ They pour boiling oil over them, have them fed to dogs, impale them alive, and cut off their heads with swords. There they meet death or suffering like death. This, Mahānāma, is a visible drawback of sensual pleasures—a visible mass of suffering, on account of sensual pleasures, because of sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures, for the very reason of sensual pleasures.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahānāma, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu kāyena duccaritaṃ caranti, vācāya duccaritaṃ caranti, manasā duccaritaṃ caranti. Te kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṃ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā, apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Ayampi, mahānāma, kāmānaṃ ādīnavo samparāyiko[M 1.0130], dukkhakkhandho kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, on account of sensual pleasures, because of sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures, for the very reason of sensual pleasures, they misconduct themselves by body, speech, and mind. Having misconducted themselves by body, speech, and mind, on the dissolution of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. This too, Mahānāma, is a drawback of sensual pleasures in the future life, a mass of suffering on account of sensual pleasures, because of sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures, for the very reason of sensual pleasures.

179. “Ekamidāhaṃ, mahānāma, samayaṃ rājagahe viharāmi gijjhakūṭe pabbate. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā nigaṇṭhā niganthā (syā. ka.) isigilipasse kāḷasilāyaṃ [T 1.0185] ubbhaṭṭhakā honti āsanapaṭikkhittā, opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti. Atha khvāhaṃ, mahānāma, sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena isigilipasse kāḷasilā yena te nigaṇṭhā [V 1.0130] tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā te nigaṇṭhe etadavocaṃ – ‘kinnu tumhe, āvuso, nigaṇṭhā ubbhaṭṭhakā āsanapaṭikkhittā, opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayathā’ti? Evaṃ vutte, mahānāma, te nigaṇṭhā maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘nigaṇṭho, āvuso, nāṭaputto nāthaputto (sī. pī.) sabbaññū sabbadassāvī aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti – “carato ca me tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa [P 1.0093] ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhita”nti. So evamāha – “atthi kho vo atthi kho bho (syā. ka.), nigaṇṭhā, pubbe pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, taṃ imāya kaṭukāya dukkarakārikāya nijjīretha nijjaretha (sī. syā. pī.); yaṃ panettha mayaṃ panettha (ka.) etarahi kāyena saṃvutā vācāya saṃvutā manasā saṃvutā taṃ āyatiṃ pāpassa kammassa akaraṇaṃ; iti purāṇānaṃ kammānaṃ tapasā byantibhāvā, navānaṃ kammānaṃ akaraṇā, āyatiṃ anavassavo; āyatiṃ anavassavā kammakkhayo, kammakkhayā dukkhakkhayo, dukkhakkhayā vedanākkhayo, vedanākkhayā sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Tañca panamhākaṃ ruccati ceva khamati ca, tena camha attamanā’ti.

179. On one occasion, Mahānāma, I was dwelling at Rājagaha, on Vulture Peak Mountain. At that time, a number of Nigaṇṭhas were standing upright on the Black Rock on the side of Isigili, rejecting seats, experiencing painful, intense, harsh, and bitter feelings born of their own exertion. Then, Mahānāma, in the evening, having risen from seclusion, I approached the Black Rock on the side of Isigili, where those Nigaṇṭhas were. Having approached, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas: ‘Why, friends Nigaṇṭhas, are you standing upright, rejecting seats, experiencing painful, intense, harsh, and bitter feelings born of your own exertion?’ When this was said, Mahānāma, those Nigaṇṭhas said to me: ‘Friend, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, asserting complete knowledge and vision thus: “Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and constantly present in me.” He says: “Nigaṇṭhas, you have done evil deeds in the past. Exhaust them by this harsh, difficult practice. And as for what is restrained here and now by body, speech, and mind, that is the non-doing of evil deeds for the future. Thus, by austerity, old deeds are exhausted; by not doing new deeds, there is no influx for the future. With no influx for the future, there is the exhaustion of deeds; with the exhaustion of deeds, there is the exhaustion of suffering; with the exhaustion of suffering, there is the exhaustion of feeling; with the exhaustion of feeling, all suffering will be completely exhausted.” And this pleases and satisfies us, and so we are content.’

180. “Evaṃ [T 1.0186] vutte, ahaṃ, mahānāma, te nigaṇṭhe etadavocaṃ – ‘kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – ahuvamheva mayaṃ pubbe na nāhuvamhā’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – akaramheva mayaṃ pubbe pāpakammaṃ na nākaramhā’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā pāpakammaṃ akaramhā’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ, ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjīretabbaṃ[M 1.0131], ettakamhi vā dukkhe nijjiṇṇe sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissatī’ti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’. ‘Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, jānātha – diṭṭheva dhamme akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampada’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’.

180. When this was said, Mahānāma, I said to those Nigaṇṭhas: ‘But do you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, know: “We certainly existed in the past; it is not that we did not exist”?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘But do you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, know: “We certainly did evil deeds in the past; it is not that we did not do them”?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘But do you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, know: “We did evil deeds of such and such a kind”?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘But do you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, know: “So much suffering has been exhausted, so much suffering is to be exhausted, or when so much suffering has been exhausted, all suffering will be exhausted”?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘But do you, friends Nigaṇṭhas, know of the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states in this very life?’ ‘No, friend.’

“‘Iti kira tumhe, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, na jānātha – ahuvamheva mayaṃ pubbe na nāhuvamhāti, na jānātha – akaramheva mayaṃ pubbe pāpakammaṃ na nākaramhāti, na jānātha – evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā pāpakammaṃ akaramhāti, na jānātha – ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ, ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjīretabbaṃ, ettakamhi vā dukkhe nijjiṇṇe sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ bhavissatīti. Na jānātha – diṭṭheva dhamme akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadaṃ. Evaṃ sante, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, ye loke luddā lohitapāṇino kurūrakammantā manussesu [V 1.0131] paccājātā te nigaṇṭhesu pabbajantī’ti? ‘Na [T 1.0187] kho, āvuso gotama, sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ; sukhena cāvuso [P 1.0094] gotama, sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ abhavissa, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhaṃ adhigaccheyya, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhavihāritaro āyasmatā gotamenā’ti.

‘So it seems, friends Nigaṇṭhas, you do not know: “We existed in the past; it is not that we did not exist.” You do not know: “We did evil kamma in the past; it is not that we did not do it.” You do not know: “We did such and such evil kamma.” You do not know: “This much suffering has been exhausted,” or “This much suffering is to be exhausted,” or “When this much suffering is exhausted, all suffering will have been exhausted.” You do not know the abandoning of unwholesome states and the undertaking of wholesome states in this very life. This being so, friends Nigaṇṭhas, is it that those in the world who are cruel, bloody-handed, and engaged in brutal actions are reborn among humans and go forth among the Nigaṇṭhas?’ ‘Indeed, friend Gotama, happiness is not to be attained by happiness; happiness is to be attained by suffering. If, friend Gotama, happiness were to be attained by happiness, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would attain happiness, for King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha lives more happily than the venerable Gotama.’

“‘Addhāyasmantehi nigaṇṭhehi sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā vācā bhāsitā – na kho, āvuso gotama, sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ; sukhena cāvuso gotama, sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ abhavissa, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhaṃ adhigaccheyya, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhavihāritaro āyasmatā gotamenā”ti. Api ca ahameva tattha paṭipucchitabbo – ko nu kho āyasmantānaṃ sukhavihāritaro rājā vā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro āyasmā vā gotamo’ti? Addhāvuso gotama, amhehi sahasā appaṭisaṅkhā vācā bhāsitā, na kho, āvuso gotama, sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, dukkhena kho sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ; sukhena cāvuso gotama, sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ abhavissa, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhaṃ adhigaccheyya, rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro sukhavihāritaro āyasmatā gotamenāti. Api ca tiṭṭhatetaṃ, idānipi mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ gotamaṃ pucchāma – ko nu kho āyasmantānaṃ sukhavihāritaro rājā vā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro āyasmā vā gotamo’ti?

‘Certainly, venerable Nigaṇṭhas, you have spoken rashly and without reflection, saying: “Indeed, friend Gotama, happiness is not to be attained by happiness; happiness is to be attained by suffering. If, friend Gotama, happiness were to be attained by happiness, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would attain happiness, for King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha lives more happily than the venerable Gotama.” But in this matter, I myself should have been questioned: “Who indeed lives more happily: King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, or the venerable Gotama?”’ ‘Certainly, friend Gotama, we spoke rashly and without reflection, saying: “Indeed, friend Gotama, happiness is not to be attained by happiness; happiness is to be attained by suffering. If, friend Gotama, happiness were to be attained by happiness, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha would attain happiness, for King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha lives more happily than the venerable Gotama.” But let that be. Even now we ask the venerable Gotama: “Who indeed lives more happily: King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, or the venerable Gotama?”’

“‘Tena [M 1.0132] hāvuso nigaṇṭhā, tumheva tattha paṭipucchissāmi, yathā vo khameyya tathā naṃ byākareyyātha. Taṃ kiṃ maññathāvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahoti rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro, aniñjamāno [T 1.0188] kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, satta rattindivāni ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharitu’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’.

‘In that case, friends Nigaṇṭhas, I will question you in return on this matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas, is King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha able to dwell for seven days and nights experiencing exclusively happiness, without moving his body or speaking a word?’ ‘No, friend, this is not possible.’

“‘Taṃ kiṃ maññathāvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahoti rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro, aniñjamāno kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, cha rattindivāni…pe… pañca rattindivāni… cattāri rattindivāni… tīṇi rattindivāni… dve rattindivāni… ekaṃ rattindivaṃ ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharitu’nti? ‘No hidaṃ, āvuso’.

‘What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas, is King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha able to dwell for six days and nights… five days and nights… four days and nights… three days and nights… two days and nights… one day and night experiencing exclusively happiness, without moving his body or speaking a word?’ ‘No, friend, this is not possible.’

“‘Ahaṃ [V 1.0132] kho, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahomi aniñjamāno kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, ekaṃ rattindivaṃ ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharituṃ. Ahaṃ kho, āvuso nigaṇṭhā, pahomi aniñjamāno kāyena, abhāsamāno vācaṃ, dve rattindivāni… tīṇi rattindivāni… cattāri rattindivāni… pañca rattindivāni… cha rattindivāni… satta rattindivāni ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī viharituṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññathāvuso nigaṇṭhā, evaṃ sante ko sukhavihāritaro rājā vā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro ahaṃ vā’ti? ‘Evaṃ sante āyasmāva gotamo [P 1.0095] sukhavihāritaro raññā māgadhena seniyena bimbisārenā’”ti.

‘Friends Nigaṇṭhas, I am able to dwell for one day and one night experiencing exclusively happiness, without moving my body or speaking a word. I am able, friends Nigaṇṭhas, to dwell for two days and nights… three days and nights… four days and nights… five days and nights… six days and nights… seven days and nights experiencing exclusively happiness, without moving my body or speaking a word. What do you think, friends Nigaṇṭhas, this being so, who dwells more happily—King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, or I?’ ‘This being so, Venerable Gotama dwells more happily than King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.’

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano mahānāmo sakko bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. Elated, Mahānāma the Sakyan rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Shorter Discourse on the Mass of Suffering, the fourth, is finished.

5. Anumānasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Inference

181. Evaṃ [T 1.0189][V 1.0133] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhaggesu viharati susumāragire suṃsumāragire (sī. syā. pī.) bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Tatra kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso, bhikkhavo”ti. “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca –

181. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. There, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:

“Pavāreti [M 1.0133] cepi, āvuso, bhikkhu – ‘vadantu maṃ āyasmanto, vacanīyomhi āyasmantehī’ti, so ca hoti dubbaco, dovacassakaraṇehi dhammehi samannāgato, akkhamo appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ, atha kho naṃ sabrahmacārī na ceva vattabbaṃ maññanti, na ca anusāsitabbaṃ maññanti, na ca tasmiṃ puggale vissāsaṃ āpajjitabbaṃ maññanti.

“Friends, even if a bhikkhu invites correction, saying, ‘May the venerable ones correct me; I am to be corrected by the venerable ones,’ yet he is difficult to correct, possesses qualities that make him difficult to correct, is intolerant, and does not accept instruction respectfully, then his companions in the holy life do not consider him fit to be spoken to, nor fit to be instructed, nor do they think it fit to place trust in that person.

“Katame cāvuso, dovacassakaraṇā dhammā? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu pāpiccho hoti, pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ vasaṃ gato. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu pāpiccho hoti, pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ vasaṃ gato – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

“And what, friends, are the qualities that make one difficult to correct? Here, friends, a bhikkhu has evil desires; he has fallen under the sway of evil desires. Friends, that a bhikkhu has evil desires and has fallen under the sway of evil desires—this is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu attukkaṃsako hoti paravambhī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu attukkaṃsako hoti paravambhī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu exalts himself and disparages others. Friends, that a bhikkhu exalts himself and disparages others—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhābhibhūto. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhābhibhūto – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is given to anger and is overcome by anger. Friends, that a bhikkhu is given to anger and is overcome by anger—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso[T 1.0190], bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu upanāhī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu upanāhī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is given to anger and, on account of anger, bears a grudge. Friends, that a bhikkhu is given to anger and, on account of anger, bears a grudge—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu abhisaṅgī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhahetu abhisaṅgī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is given to anger and, on account of anger, clings to it. Friends, that a bhikkhu is given to anger and, on account of anger, clings to it—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna [V 1.0134] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhasāmantā kodhasāmantaṃ (syā. pī. ka.) vācaṃ nicchāretā. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti kodhasāmantā vācaṃ nicchāretā – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is given to anger and utters speech connected with anger. Friends, that a bhikkhu is given to anger and utters speech connected with anger—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito cudito (sī. syā. pī.) codakena codakaṃ paṭippharati. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakaṃ paṭippharati – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, when admonished by an admonisher, a bhikkhu opposes the admonisher. Friends, that a bhikkhu, when admonished by an admonisher, opposes the admonisher—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna [M 1.0134] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakaṃ apasādeti. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakaṃ apasādeti – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, when admonished by an admonisher, a bhikkhu disparages the admonisher. Friends, that a bhikkhu, when admonished by an admonisher, disparages the admonisher—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ[P 1.0096], āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakassa paccāropeti. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena codakassa paccāropeti – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, when admonished by an admonisher, a bhikkhu accuses the admonisher in return. Friends, that a bhikkhu, when admonished by an admonisher, accuses the admonisher in return—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmeti, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, when admonished by an admonisher, a bhikkhu evades the issue, leads the discussion astray, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment. Friends, that a bhikkhu, when admonished by an admonisher, evades the issue, leads the discussion astray, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena apadāne [T 1.0191] na sampāyati. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu codito codakena apadāne na sampāyati – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, when admonished by an admonisher, a bhikkhu is unable to account for his conduct. Friends, that a bhikkhu, when admonished by an admonisher, is unable to account for his conduct—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu makkhī hoti paḷāsī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu makkhī hoti paḷāsī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is contemptuous and contentious. Friends, that a bhikkhu is contemptuous and contentious—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu issukī hoti maccharī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu issukī hoti maccharī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is envious and miserly. Friends, that a bhikkhu is envious and miserly—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu saṭho hoti māyāvī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu saṭho hoti māyāvī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is fraudulent and crafty. Friends, that a bhikkhu is fraudulent and crafty—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna [V 1.0135] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu thaddho hoti atimānī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu thaddho hoti atimānī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is obstinate and conceited. Friends, that a bhikkhu is obstinate and conceited—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī. Yampāvuso, bhikkhu sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī – ayampi dhammo dovacassakaraṇo. Ime vuccantāvuso, dovacassakaraṇā dhammā.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu clings to his own views, holding to them firmly and relinquishing them with difficulty. Friends, that a bhikkhu clings to his own views, holding to them firmly and relinquishing them with difficulty—this, too, is a quality that makes one difficult to correct. These, friends, are called the qualities that make one difficult to correct.
