Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Satisfied, those monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

Vanapatthasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Vanapattha Sutta, the seventh, is concluded.

8. Madhupiṇḍikasuttaṃ

8. The Honey-ball Sutta

199. Evaṃ [T 1.0220][V 1.0155] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ nigrodhārāme. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kapilavatthuṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Kapilavatthusmiṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena mahāvanaṃ tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya. Mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā beluvalaṭṭhikāya mūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Daṇḍapāṇipi kho sakko jaṅghāvihāraṃ jaṅghavihāraṃ (ka.) anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno yena mahāvanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā yena beluvalaṭṭhikā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā daṇḍamolubbha ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho daṇḍapāṇi sakko bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kiṃvādī samaṇo kimakkhāyī”ti? “Yathāvādī kho, āvuso, sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya [M 1.0155] sadevamanussāya na kenaci loke viggayha tiṭṭhati, yathā ca pana kāmehi visaṃyuttaṃ viharantaṃ taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ akathaṃkathiṃ chinnakukkuccaṃ bhavābhave vītataṇhaṃ saññā nānusenti – evaṃvādī kho ahaṃ, āvuso, evamakkhāyī”ti.

199. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu, after the meal, on returning from his alms round, he went to the Great Wood for the day’s abiding. Having entered the Great Wood, he sat down at the foot of a beluva sapling for the day’s abiding. Now, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the Great Wood. Having entered the Great Wood, he went to the beluva sapling where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When this courteous and memorable talk was concluded, leaning on his staff, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: “What is the ascetic’s doctrine? What does he proclaim?” “Friend, I profess a doctrine whereby one does not stand in conflict with anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, with its population of ascetics and brahmins, devas and humans. And perceptions do not obsess that brahmin who dwells disjoined from sensual pleasures, who is free from doubt, whose perplexity is cut off, and who is without craving for any state of existence. This, friend, is my doctrine; this is what I proclaim.”

“Evaṃ vutte daṇḍapāṇi sakko sīsaṃ okampetvā[P 1.0109], jivhaṃ nillāḷetvā, tivisākhaṃ nalāṭikaṃ [T 1.0221] nalāṭe vuṭṭhāpetvā daṇḍamolubbha pakkāmi.

When this was said, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan shook his head, stuck out his tongue, and drew up three wrinkles upon his forehead. Then, leaning on his staff, he departed.

200. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena nigrodhārāmo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kapilavatthuṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ. Kapilavatthusmiṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena mahāvanaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃ divāvihārāya. Mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā beluvalaṭṭhikāya mūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdiṃ. Daṇḍapāṇipi kho, bhikkhave, sakko jaṅghāvihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno yena mahāvanaṃ tenupasaṅkami. Mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā yena beluvalaṭṭhikā yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā mayā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā daṇḍamolubbha ekamantaṃ [V 1.0156] aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho, bhikkhave, daṇḍapāṇi sakko maṃ etadavoca – ‘kiṃvādī samaṇo kimakkhāyī’ti?

200. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and went to Nigrodha’s Park. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Here, bhikkhus, in the morning, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu, after the meal, on returning from my alms round, I went to the Great Wood for the day’s abiding. Having entered the Great Wood, I sat down at the foot of a beluva sapling for the day’s abiding. Now, bhikkhus, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the Great Wood. Having entered the Great Wood, he came to the beluva sapling where I was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with me. When this courteous and memorable talk was concluded, leaning on his staff, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, bhikkhus, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan said to me: ‘What is the ascetic’s doctrine? What does he proclaim?’”

“Evaṃ vutte ahaṃ, bhikkhave, daṇḍapāṇiṃ sakkaṃ etadavocaṃ – yathāvādī kho, āvuso, sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya na kenaci loke viggayha tiṭṭhati, yathā ca pana kāmehi visaṃyuttaṃ viharantaṃ taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ akathaṃkathiṃ chinnakukkuccaṃ bhavābhave vītataṇhaṃ saññā nānusenti – evaṃvādī kho ahaṃ, āvuso, evamakkhāyī”ti. “Evaṃ vutte bhikkhave, daṇḍapāṇi sakko sīsaṃ [T 1.0222] okampetvā, jivhaṃ nillāḷetvā, tivisākhaṃ nalāṭikaṃ nalāṭe vuṭṭhāpetvā daṇḍamolubbha pakkāmī”ti.

“When this was said, bhikkhus, I said to Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan: ‘Friend, I profess a doctrine whereby one does not stand in conflict with anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, with its population of ascetics and brahmins, devas and humans. And perceptions do not obsess that brahmin who dwells disjoined from sensual pleasures, who is free from doubt, whose perplexity is cut off, and who is without craving for any state of existence. This, friend, is my doctrine; this is what I proclaim.’ When this was said, bhikkhus, Daṇḍapāṇi the Sakyan shook his head, stuck out his tongue, and drew up three wrinkles upon his forehead. Then, leaning on his staff, he departed.”

201. Evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kiṃvādī pana, bhante, bhagavā sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya na kenaci loke viggayha tiṭṭhati? Kathañca pana, bhante, bhagavantaṃ kāmehi visaṃyuttaṃ viharantaṃ taṃ [M 1.0156] brāhmaṇaṃ akathaṃkathiṃ chinnakukkuccaṃ bhavābhave vītataṇhaṃ saññā nānusentī”ti? “Yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ, esevanto paṭighānusayānaṃ, esevanto diṭṭhānusayānaṃ[P 1.0110], esevanto vicikicchānusayānaṃ, esevanto mānānusayānaṃ, esevanto bhavarāgānusayānaṃ, esevanto avijjānusayānaṃ, esevanto daṇḍādāna-satthādāna-kalaha-viggaha-vivāda-tuvaṃtuvaṃ-pesuñña-musāvādānaṃ. Etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’ti. Idamavoca bhagavā. Idaṃ vatvāna sugato uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi.

201. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, holding what doctrine does the Blessed One not stand in conflict with anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, with its population of ascetics and brahmins, devas and humans? And for what reason do perceptions not obsess the Blessed One, that brahmin who dwells disjoined from sensual pleasures, who is free from doubt, whose perplexity is cut off, and who is without craving for any state of existence?” “Bhikkhu, the source from which the host of perceptions and concepts born of proliferation assails a person—if, regarding this, there is nothing to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to, this itself is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust, the end of the underlying tendencies to aversion, the end of the underlying tendencies to views, the end of the underlying tendencies to doubt, the end of the underlying tendencies to conceit, the end of the underlying tendencies to craving for existence, and the end of the underlying tendencies to ignorance. This is the end of taking up rods and weapons, of quarrels, conflicts, disputes, recrimination, slander, and false speech. It is here that these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.” This the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

202. Atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ acirapakkantassa bhagavato etadahosi – “idaṃ kho no, āvuso, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā, vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā, uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – ‘yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ [T 1.0223] abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ…pe… etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’ti[V 1.0157]. Ko nu kho imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajeyyā”ti? Atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “ayaṃ kho āyasmā mahākaccāno satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ. Pahoti cāyasmā mahākaccāno imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajituṃ. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkameyyāma; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyāmā”ti.

202. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, this thought occurred to those bhikkhus: 'Friends, the Blessed One, having pointed out this summary in brief without analyzing the meaning in detail, has risen from his seat and entered the monastery, saying: “Bhikkhu, from whatever source collections of perceptions born of proliferation assail a person, if, in this, there is nothing to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to, this itself is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust... Herein, these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.” Now, who indeed could analyze in detail the meaning of this summary pointed out in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been analyzed in detail?' Then this thought occurred to those bhikkhus: 'This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise spiritual companions. Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this summary pointed out in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been analyzed in detail. Let us then approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and ask him about this matter.'

Atha kho te bhikkhū yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā mahākaccānena saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavocuṃ – “idaṃ kho no, āvuso kaccāna, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – ‘yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto [M 1.0157] rāgānusayānaṃ…pe… etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’ti. Tesaṃ no, āvuso kaccāna, amhākaṃ acirapakkantassa bhagavato etadahosi – ‘idaṃ kho no, āvuso, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – “yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha [T 1.0224] ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ…pe… etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī”ti. Ko nu kho imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajeyyāti? Tesaṃ no, āvuso kaccāna, amhākaṃ etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā mahākaccāno satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ, pahoti [P 1.0111] cāyasmā mahākaccāno imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena [V 1.0158] uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajituṃ. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkameyyāma; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyāmā’ti. Vibhajatāyasmā mahākaccāno”ti.

Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna. Having approached, they exchanged joyful greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna. When this courteous and memorable talk was concluded, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: 'Friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One, having pointed out this summary in brief without analyzing the meaning in detail, has risen from his seat and entered the monastery, saying: “Bhikkhu, from whatever source collections of perceptions born of proliferation assail a person, if, in this, there is nothing to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to, this itself is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust... Herein, these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.” To us, friend Kaccāna, soon after the Blessed One had departed, this thought occurred: “Friends, the Blessed One, having pointed out this summary in brief without analyzing the meaning in detail, has risen from his seat and entered the monastery, saying: ‘Bhikkhu, from whatever source collections of perceptions born of proliferation assail a person, if, in this, there is nothing to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to, this itself is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust... Herein, these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.’ Now, who indeed could analyze in detail the meaning of this summary pointed out in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been analyzed in detail?” Then, friend Kaccāna, this thought occurred to us: “This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise spiritual companions. Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this summary pointed out in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been analyzed in detail. Let us then approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and ask him about this matter.” May the Venerable Mahākaccāna analyze it.'

203. “Seyyathāpi, āvuso, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva mūlaṃ, atikkamma khandhaṃ, sākhāpalāse sāraṃ pariyesitabbaṃ maññeyya; evaṃsampadamidaṃ āyasmantānaṃ satthari sammukhībhūte, taṃ bhagavantaṃ atisitvā[T 1.0225], amhe etamatthaṃ paṭipucchitabbaṃ maññatha. So hāvuso, bhagavā jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passati, cakkhubhūto ñāṇabhūto dhammabhūto brahmabhūto, vattā pavattā, atthassa ninnetā, amatassa dātā, dhammassāmī tathāgato. So ceva panetassa kālo ahosi, yaṃ bhagavantaṃyeva etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha. Yathā vo bhagavā byākareyya tathā naṃ dhāreyyāthā”ti. “Addhāvuso kaccāna, bhagavā jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passati, cakkhubhūto ñāṇabhūto dhammabhūto brahmabhūto, vattā pavattā, atthassa ninnetā, amatassa dātā, dhammassāmī tathāgato. So ceva panetassa kālo ahosi, yaṃ bhagavantaṃyeva etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyāma. Yathā no bhagavā byākareyya tathā naṃ dhāreyyāma. Api cāyasmā mahākaccāno satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ, pahoti [M 1.0158] cāyasmā mahākaccāno imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajituṃ. Vibhajatāyasmā mahākaccāno agaruṃ katvā”ti agarukatvā (sī.), agarukaritvā (syā. pī.). “Tena hāvuso, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasikarotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahākaccānassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā mahākaccāno etadavoca –

203. “Friends, it is as if a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would pass over the root and the trunk of a great, standing tree possessing heartwood, thinking that heartwood should be sought among the branches and leaves. Such is this case with you venerable ones, who, when the Teacher was present before you, passed over that Blessed One and think that we should be asked about this matter. For, friends, that Blessed One, knowing, knows; seeing, sees. He has become the eye, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become sublime. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the expounder of the meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. That was the very time when you should have asked the Blessed One himself about this matter. As the Blessed One would have explained to you, so you should have remembered it.”

“Surely, friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One, knowing, knows; seeing, sees. He has become the eye, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become sublime. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the expounder of the meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. That was the very time when we should have asked the Blessed One himself about this matter. As the Blessed One would have explained to us, so we would have remembered it. And yet, the Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise spiritual companions. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this summary pointed out in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been analyzed in detail. May the Venerable Mahākaccāna analyze it, not taking it as a burden.”

“In that case, friends, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.”

“Very well, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāna. The Venerable Mahākaccāna said this:

204. “Yaṃ kho no, āvuso, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – ‘yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti[T 1.0226]. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ, esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ…pe… etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’ti, imassa kho ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmi –

204. Venerable sirs, the Blessed One, having stated an exposition in brief without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling: 'Monk, from what source do perceptions of conceptual proliferation assail a person? If, in this regard, there is nothing to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust... Herein, these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.' Venerable sirs, of this exposition stated in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which was not analyzed in detail, I understand the meaning in detail in this way:

“Cakkhuñcāvuso, paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā [V 1.0159] vedanā, yaṃ vedeti taṃ sañjānāti[P 1.0112], yaṃ sañjānāti taṃ vitakketi, yaṃ vitakketi taṃ papañceti, yaṃ papañceti tatonidānaṃ purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti atītānāgatapaccuppannesu cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu. Sotañcāvuso, paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ…pe… ghānañcāvuso, paṭicca gandhe ca uppajjati ghānaviññāṇaṃ…pe… jivhañcāvuso, paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ…pe… kāyañcāvuso, paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca uppajjati kāyaviññāṇaṃ…pe… manañcāvuso, paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, yaṃ vedeti taṃ sañjānāti, yaṃ sañjānāti taṃ vitakketi, yaṃ vitakketi taṃ papañceti, yaṃ papañceti tatonidānaṃ purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti atītānāgatapaccuppannesu manoviññeyyesu dhammesu.

Venerable sirs, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. What one feels, that one perceives. What one perceives, that one thinks about. What one thinks about, that one conceptually proliferates. Conditioned by that which one conceptually proliferates, perceptions of conceptual proliferation assail a person with respect to forms cognizable by the eye in the past, future, and present. Venerable sirs, dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises... and so on... Venerable sirs, dependent on the nose and smells, nose-consciousness arises... and so on... Venerable sirs, dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises... and so on... Venerable sirs, dependent on the body and tangible objects, body-consciousness arises... and so on... Venerable sirs, dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. What one feels, that one perceives. What one perceives, that one thinks about. What one thinks about, that one conceptually proliferates. Conditioned by that which one conceptually proliferates, perceptions of conceptual proliferation assail a person with respect to mental objects cognizable by the mind in the past, future, and present.

“So vatāvuso, cakkhusmiṃ sati rūpe sati cakkhuviññāṇe sati phassapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Phassapaññattiyā sati vedanāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Vedanāpaññattiyā sati saññāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Saññāpaññattiyā sati [M 1.0159] vitakkapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Vitakkapaññattiyā sati papañcasaññāsaṅkhāsamudācaraṇapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. So vatāvuso, sotasmiṃ sati sadde sati…pe… [V 1.0160][T 1.0227] ghānasmiṃ sati gandhe sati…pe… jivhāya sati rase sati…pe… kāyasmiṃ sati phoṭṭhabbe sati…pe… manasmiṃ sati dhamme sati manoviññāṇe sati phassapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Phassapaññattiyā sati vedanāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Vedanāpaññattiyā sati saññāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Saññāpaññattiyā sati vitakkapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Vitakkapaññattiyā sati papañcasaññāsaṅkhāsamudācaraṇapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – ṭhānametaṃ vijjati.

Indeed, venerable sirs, when the eye exists, when forms exist, and when eye-consciousness exists, it is possible that one will designate contact. When the designation of contact exists, it is possible that one will designate feeling. When the designation of feeling exists, it is possible that one will designate perception. When the designation of perception exists, it is possible that one will designate thought. When the designation of thought exists, it is possible that one will designate the assailing by perceptions of conceptual proliferation. Indeed, venerable sirs, when the ear exists, when sounds exist... and so on... when the nose exists, when smells exist... and so on... when the tongue exists, when tastes exist... and so on... when the body exists, when tangible objects exist... and so on... when the mind exists, when mental objects exist, and when mind-consciousness exists, it is possible that one will designate contact. When the designation of contact exists, it is possible that one will designate feeling. When the designation of feeling exists, it is possible that one will designate perception. When the designation of perception exists, it is possible that one will designate thought. When the designation of thought exists, it is possible that one will designate the assailing by perceptions of conceptual proliferation.

“So vatāvuso, cakkhusmiṃ asati rūpe asati cakkhuviññāṇe asati phassapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Phassapaññattiyā asati vedanāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Vedanāpaññattiyā asati saññāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Saññāpaññattiyā asati vitakkapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Vitakkapaññattiyā asati papañcasaññāsaṅkhāsamudācaraṇapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. So vatāvuso, sotasmiṃ [T 1.0229] asati sadde asati…pe… ghānasmiṃ asati gandhe asati…pe… jivhāya asati rase asati…pe… kāyasmiṃ asati phoṭṭhabbe asati…pe… manasmiṃ asati dhamme asati manoviññāṇe [V 1.0161] asati phassapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Phassapaññattiyā asati vedanāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Vedanāpaññattiyā asati saññāpaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Saññāpaññattiyā asati vitakkapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Vitakkapaññattiyā asati papañcasaññāsaṅkhāsamudācaraṇapaññattiṃ paññāpessatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

Indeed, venerable sirs, when the eye does not exist, when forms do not exist, and when eye-consciousness does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate contact. When the designation of contact does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate feeling. When the designation of feeling does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate perception. When the designation of perception does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate thought. When the designation of thought does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate the assailing by perceptions of conceptual proliferation. Indeed, venerable sirs, when the ear does not exist, when sounds do not exist... and so on... when the nose does not exist, when smells do not exist... and so on... when the tongue does not exist, when tastes do not exist... and so on... when the body does not exist, when tangible objects do not exist... and so on... when the mind does not exist, when mental objects do not exist, and when mind-consciousness does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate contact. When the designation of contact does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate feeling. When the designation of feeling does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate perception. When the designation of perception does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate thought. When the designation of thought does not exist, it is not possible that one will designate the assailing by perceptions of conceptual proliferation.

“Yaṃ kho no, āvuso, bhagavā saṃkhittena [P 1.0113] uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – ‘yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ…pe… etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’ti, imassa kho ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā [M 1.0160] saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmi. Ākaṅkhamānā ca pana tumhe āyasmanto bhagavantaṃyeva upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha. Yathā no bhagavā byākaroti tathā naṃ dhāreyyāthā”ti.

Venerable sirs, the Blessed One, having stated an exposition in brief without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling: 'Monk, from what source do perceptions of conceptual proliferation assail a person? If, in this regard, there is nothing to be delighted in, welcomed, or clung to, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust... Herein, these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.' Venerable sirs, of this exposition stated in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which was not analyzed in detail, I understand the meaning in detail in this way. But if you, venerable sirs, so desire, you may approach the Blessed One himself and question him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you bear it in mind.

205. Atha kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahākaccānassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “yaṃ kho no, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – ‘yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ…pe… etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī’ti. Tesaṃ no, bhante, amhākaṃ acirapakkantassa bhagavato etadahosi – ‘idaṃ kho no, āvuso, bhagavā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvā vitthārena atthaṃ avibhajitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ paviṭṭho – “yatonidānaṃ, bhikkhu, purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ. Esevanto rāgānusayānaṃ, esevanto paṭighānusayānaṃ, esevanto diṭṭhānusayānaṃ, esevanto vicikicchānusayānaṃ, esevanto mānānusayānaṃ, esevanto bhavarāgānusayānaṃ[V 1.0162], esevanto avijjānusayānaṃ, esevanto daṇḍādāna-satthādāna-kalaha-viggaha-vivādatuvaṃtuvaṃ-pesuñña-musāvādānaṃ. Etthete pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantī”ti. Ko nu kho imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajeyyā’ti? Tesaṃ no, bhante, amhākaṃ etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā mahākaccāno satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ, pahoti cāyasmā mahākaccāno [T 1.0230] imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena uddesassa uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajituṃ, yaṃnūna mayaṃ yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkameyyāma; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyāmā’ti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkamimha; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ [M 1.0161] mahākaccānaṃ [P 1.0114] etamatthaṃ paṭipucchimha. Tesaṃ no, bhante, āyasmatā mahākaccānena imehi ākārehi imehi padehi imehi byañjanehi attho vibhatto”ti. “Paṇḍito, bhikkhave, mahākaccāno; mahāpañño, bhikkhave, mahākaccāno. Maṃ cepi tumhe, bhikkhave, etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyaṃ yathā taṃ mahākaccānena byākataṃ. Eso cevetassa attho. Evañca evemeva ca (ka.) naṃ dhārethā”ti.

205. Then those monks, having greatly delighted in and rejoiced at the words of the Venerable Mahākaccāna, rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One, having set forth a summary in brief for us without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: “O monk, owing to what source do the multitudes of perceptions of proliferation assail a person? If, in this regard, there is nothing to be delighted in, spoken of with attachment, or clung to, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust… and so on… Herein, these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.” Venerable sir, to us, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this thought occurred: “Friends, the Blessed One, having set forth this summary in brief for us without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying: ‘O monk, owing to what source do the multitudes of perceptions of proliferation assail a person? If, in this regard, there is nothing to be delighted in, spoken of with attachment, or clung to, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to lust, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to aversion, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to views, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to doubt, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to conceit, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to craving for existence, this is the end of the underlying tendencies to ignorance, this is the end of taking up rods and weapons, of quarrels, disputes, arguments, strife, contentiousness, slander, and false speech. Herein, these evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.’ Who, now, could analyze in detail the meaning of this summary set forth in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which was not analyzed?” Then, venerable sir, it occurred to us: “This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise companions in the holy life. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this summary set forth in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which was not analyzed. What if we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and ask him about this matter?” So, venerable sir, we approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna and asked him about this matter. Venerable sir, the meaning was analyzed for us by the Venerable Mahākaccāna with these aspects, with these words, with these phrases.' 'Mahākaccāna is a scholar, O monks; Mahākaccāna is of great wisdom, O monks. If you were to ask me about this matter, O monks, I too would explain it in the very same way as it was explained by Mahākaccāna. This indeed is its meaning, and so should you bear it in mind.'

Evaṃ vutte āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “seyyathāpi, bhante, puriso jighacchādubbalyapareto madhupiṇḍikaṃ adhigaccheyya, so yato yato sāyeyya, labhetheva sādurasaṃ asecanakaṃ. Evameva kho, bhante, cetaso bhikkhu dabbajātiko, yato yato imassa dhammapariyāyassa paññāya atthaṃ upaparikkheyya, labhetheva attamanataṃ, labhetheva cetaso pasādaṃ. Ko nāmo ayaṃ ko nāmāyaṃ (syā.), bhante, dhammapariyāyo”ti? “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, ānanda, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ madhupiṇḍikapariyāyo tveva naṃ dhārehī”ti.

When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: 'Just as, venerable sir, a person afflicted by hunger and weakness might come upon a honey-ball, and from whatever part he might taste it, he would find a sweet, delectable flavor; in the very same way, venerable sir, a monk of wise nature, from whatever part he might investigate the meaning of this Dhamma exposition with wisdom, would surely find gladness, would surely find mental clarity. What, venerable sir, is the name of this Dhamma exposition?' 'Therefore, Ānanda, you should bear this Dhamma exposition in mind as “The Discourse on the Honey-ball”.'

Idamavoca [T 1.0231] bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā ānando bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. Gladdened, the Venerable Ānanda greatly delighted in the Blessed One's words.

Madhupiṇḍikasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The eighth, the Discourse on the Honey-ball, is concluded.

9. Dvedhāvitakkasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on the Two Kinds of Thought

206. Evaṃ [V 1.0163][T 1.0232] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

206. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this:

“Pubbeva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvā vitakke vihareyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yo cāyaṃ kāmavitakko yo ca byāpādavitakko yo ca vihiṃsāvitakko – imaṃ ekaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ[M 1.0162]; yo cāyaṃ nekkhammavitakko yo ca abyāpādavitakko yo ca avihiṃsāvitakko – imaṃ dutiyaṃ bhāgamakāsiṃ.

“Monks, before my supreme awakening, when I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta, it occurred to me: ‘Suppose I were to dwell having divided my thoughts into two parts.’ So, monks, I set on one side thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of violence; and I set on the other side thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-violence.

207. “Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati [P 1.0115] kāmavitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ kāmavitakko. So ca kho attabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, parabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, ubhayabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’ anibbānasaṃvattaniko”ti (?). ‘Attabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘parabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; [T 1.0233] ‘paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, uppannuppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ pajahameva atītakālikakiriyāpadāniyeva vinodameva atītakālikakiriyāpadāniyeva byantameva byanteva (sī. syā. pī.) naṃ akāsiṃ.

207. “Monks, as I was dwelling thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—a thought of sensual desire arose in me. I understood it thus: ‘This thought of sensual desire has arisen in me. It leads to my own affliction, to the affliction of others, and to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna.’ As I reflected, ‘It leads to my own affliction,’ it subsided in me. As I reflected, ‘It leads to the affliction of others,’ it subsided in me. As I reflected, ‘It leads to the affliction of both,’ it subsided in me. As I reflected, ‘It obstructs wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna,’ it subsided in me. Monks, I would abandon, dispel, and make an end of each thought of sensual desire as it arose.

208. “Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati byāpādavitakko…pe… uppajjati vihiṃsāvitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ vihiṃsāvitakko. So ca kho attabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, parabyābādhāyapi [V 1.0164] saṃvattati, ubhayabyābādhāyapi saṃvattati, paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’. ‘Attabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘parabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattatī’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati; ‘paññānirodhiko vighātapakkhiko anibbānasaṃvattaniko’tipi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, uppannuppannaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ pajahameva vinodameva byantameva naṃ akāsiṃ.

208. “Monks, as I was dwelling thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—a thought of ill will arose in me… a thought of violence arose in me. I understood it thus: ‘This thought of violence has arisen in me. It leads to my own affliction, to the affliction of others, and to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna.’ As I reflected, ‘It leads to my own affliction,’ it subsided in me. As I reflected, ‘It leads to the affliction of others,’ it subsided in me. As I reflected, ‘It leads to the affliction of both,’ it subsided in me. As I reflected, ‘It obstructs wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna,’ it subsided in me. Monks, I would abandon, dispel, and make an end of each thought of violence as it arose.

“Yaññadeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, tathā tathā nati hoti cetaso. Kāmavitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi [M 1.0163] anuvicāreti, pahāsi nekkhammavitakkaṃ, kāmavitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassa taṃ [T 1.0234] kāmavitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Byāpādavitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave…pe… vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi avihiṃsāvitakkaṃ, vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassa taṃ vihiṃsāvitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye kiṭṭhasambādhe gopālako gāvo rakkheyya. So tā gāvo tato tato daṇḍena ākoṭeyya paṭikoṭeyya sannirundheyya sannivāreyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Passati hi so, bhikkhave, gopālako tatonidānaṃ vadhaṃ vā bandhanaṃ vā jāniṃ vā garahaṃ vā. Evameva kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, addasaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ vodānapakkhaṃ.

“Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that will be the inclination of his mind. If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of sensual desire, he has abandoned the thought of renunciation to cultivate the thought of sensual desire, and his mind inclines to thoughts of sensual desire. If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of ill will… If a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of violence, he has abandoned the thought of non-violence to cultivate the thought of violence, and his mind inclines to thoughts of violence. It is like a cowherd in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, who would guard his cows in a field dense with crops. He would strike and prod them from here and there with his stick, restraining and checking them. For what reason is this? Because the cowherd sees that from that cause there could be death, bondage, loss, or blame. In the same way, monks, I saw the danger, degradation, and defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit and purifying aspect of renunciation in wholesome states.

209. “Tassa [P 1.0116] mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati nekkhammavitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ nekkhammavitakko. So ca kho nevattabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na parabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattati, paññāvuddhiko avighātapakkhiko nibbānasaṃvattaniko’. Rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Divasaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Rattindivaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Api ca kho me aticiraṃ anuvitakkayato anuvicārayato kāyo kilameyya[V 1.0165]. Kāye kilante kilamante (ka.) cittaṃ [T 1.0235] ūhaññeyya. Ūhate citte ārā cittaṃ samādhimhāti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi ekodi karomi (pī.) samādahāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Mā me cittaṃ ūhaññī’ti ugghāṭīti (syā. ka.), ūhanīti (pī.).

209. “Monks, as I was dwelling thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—a thought of renunciation arose in me. I understood it thus: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It does not lead to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it enhances wisdom, is not on the side of distress, and leads to Nibbāna.’ If I were to think and ponder on it for a night, I would see no danger from that cause. If I were to think and ponder on it for a day, I would see no danger from that cause. If I were to think and ponder on it for a day and a night, I would see no danger from that cause. However, by thinking and pondering on it for too long, my body would become weary. When the body is weary, the mind becomes agitated. When the mind is agitated, it is far from concentration. So, monks, I established my mind internally, settled it, made it one-pointed, and concentrated it. For what reason? ‘Lest my mind be agitated.’

210. “Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati abyāpādavitakko…pe… uppajjati avihiṃsāvitakko. So evaṃ pajānāmi – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ avihiṃsāvitakko. So ca kho nevattabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na parabyābādhāya saṃvattati, na ubhayabyābādhāya [M 1.0164] saṃvattati, paññāvuddhiko avighātapakkhiko nibbānasaṃvattaniko’. Rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Divasaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Rattindivaṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyaṃ anuvicāreyyaṃ, neva tatonidānaṃ bhayaṃ samanupassāmi. Api ca kho me aticiraṃ anuvitakkayato anuvicārayato kāyo kilameyya. Kāye kilante cittaṃ ūhaññeyya. Ūhate citte ārā cittaṃ samādhimhāti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi, sannisādemi, ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? ‘Mā me cittaṃ ūhaññī’ti.

210. “While I was dwelling thus, monks, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a thought of non-ill will arose in me… a thought of non-cruelty arose in me. I understood thus: ‘This thought of non-cruelty has arisen in me. And it does not lead to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both. It is conducive to the growth of wisdom, is not on the side of distress, and leads to Nibbāna.’ Even if, monks, I were to think and ponder on it continually at night, I would see no danger arising from that source. Even if, monks, I were to think and ponder on it continually during the day, I would see no danger arising from that source. Even if, monks, I were to think and ponder on it continually night and day, I would see no danger arising from that source. However, if I were to think and ponder on it for too long, my body would become weary. When the body is weary, the mind would be disturbed. When the mind is disturbed, it is far from concentration. Therefore, monks, I establish my mind right within, cause it to settle down, make it one-pointed, and concentrate it. For what reason? ‘May my mind not be disturbed.’”

“Yaññadeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, tathā tathā nati hoti cetaso. Nekkhammavitakkañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi [T 1.0236] kāmavitakkaṃ, nekkhammavitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassaṃ taṃ nekkhammavitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Abyāpādavitakkañce, bhikkhave…pe… avihiṃsāvitakkañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulamanuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ, avihiṃsāvitakkaṃ bahulamakāsi, tassa taṃ avihiṃsāvitakkāya cittaṃ namati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse sabbasassesu gāmantasambhatesu gopālako gāvo rakkheyya[P 1.0117], tassa rukkhamūlagatassa vā abbhokāsagatassa vā satikaraṇīyameva hoti – ‘etā ete (ka.) gāvo’ti. Evamevaṃ kho, bhikkhave, satikaraṇīyameva ahosi – ‘ete dhammā’ti.

“Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and considers, the inclination of his mind is in that direction. If, monks, a monk frequently thinks and considers thoughts of renunciation, he abandons the thought of sensual pleasure and frequently cultivates the thought of renunciation; his mind inclines towards the thought of renunciation. If, monks, he considers thoughts of non-ill will… If, monks, a monk frequently thinks and considers thoughts of non-cruelty, he abandons the thought of cruelty and frequently cultivates the thought of non-cruelty; his mind inclines towards the thought of non-cruelty. Just as, monks, in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been brought near the village, a cowherd would guard the cows; whether he is at the foot of a tree or in the open, it is only a matter of maintaining mindfulness thus: ‘These are the cows.’ In the very same way, monks, for me it was only a matter of maintaining mindfulness thus: ‘These are the dharmas.’”

211. “Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, bhikkhave, vīriyaṃ ahosi asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā[V 1.0166], passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca vihāsiṃ sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesiṃ, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti ‘upekkhako satimā [M 1.0165] sukhavihārī’ti, tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

211. “But, monks, my energy was roused and not sluggish, my mindfulness was established and not confused, my body was tranquil and not agitated, my mind was concentrated and one-pointed. Secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelled in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, I entered and dwelled in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, I dwelled in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experienced happiness with the body; I entered and dwelled in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘One who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily.’ With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelled in the fourth jhāna, which is without suffering and without happiness, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

212. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi jātiṃ…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Ayaṃ kho [T 1.0237] me, bhikkhave, rattiyā paṭhame yāme paṭhamā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

212. “When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, without blemish, free from corruptions, become malleable, workable, steady, and attained to the imperturbable, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of recollecting past abodes. I recollected my manifold past abodes. That is: one birth… thus, with their aspects and details, I recollected my manifold past abodes. This, monks, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as it does for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.”

213. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne…pe… ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā…pe… iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate, yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, bhikkhave, rattiyā majjhime yāme dutiyā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

213. “When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, without blemish, free from corruptions, become malleable, workable, steady, and attained to the imperturbable, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing… ‘Indeed, these honorable beings were endowed with bad conduct of body…’ Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, of good appearance and bad appearance, in good destinations and bad destinations; I understood beings faring on according to their kamma. This, monks, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as it does for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.”

214. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ[M 1.0166]. ‘Ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ [V 1.0167] āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ [T 1.0238] āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ ahosi – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsiṃ. Ayaṃ kho me, bhikkhave, rattiyā pacchime yāme tatiyā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato.

214. “With my mind thus concentrated, purified, and cleansed, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliable, workable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I knew as it really is: ‘This is suffering.’ I knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ I knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ I knew as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I knew as it really is: ‘These are the taints.’ I knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’ I knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints.’ I knew as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ For me, thus knowing and thus seeing, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual pleasure, my mind was liberated from the taint of being, and my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there arose the knowledge: ‘I am liberated.’ I knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ This, bhikkhus, was the third knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as it does for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.”

215. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, araññe pavane mahantaṃ ninnaṃ pallalaṃ. Tamenaṃ mahāmigasaṅgho upanissāya vihareyya. Tassa kocideva puriso uppajjeyya anatthakāmo ahitakāmo ayogakkhemakāmo. So yvāssa maggo khemo sovatthiko pītigamanīyo taṃ maggaṃ pidaheyya, vivareyya kummaggaṃ, odaheyya okacaraṃ, ṭhapeyya okacārikaṃ. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāmigasaṅgho aparena samayena [T 1.0239] anayabyasanaṃ anayabyasanaṃ tanuttaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) āpajjeyya. Tasseva kho pana, bhikkhave, mahato migasaṅghassa kocideva puriso uppajjeyya atthakāmo hitakāmo yogakkhemakāmo. So yvāssa maggo khemo sovatthiko pītigamanīyo taṃ maggaṃ vivareyya, pidaheyya kummaggaṃ, ūhaneyya okacaraṃ, nāseyya okacārikaṃ. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāmigasaṅgho aparena samayena vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjeyya.

215. “Suppose, bhikkhus, in a forest, in a grove, there were a great, low-lying marsh, and a great herd of deer lived depending on it. Then a certain man would appear, wishing for their disadvantage, harm, and lack of security from the yokes. He would block off the safe path, which is conducive to well-being and leads to delight, open up a wrong path, set up a decoy, and place a decoy doe. Thus, bhikkhus, in time that great herd of deer would meet with ruin and disaster. But then, bhikkhus, for that same great herd of deer, a certain man would appear, wishing for their welfare, benefit, and security from the yokes. He would open up the safe path, which is conducive to well-being and leads to delight, block off the wrong path, remove the decoy, and destroy the decoy doe. Thus, bhikkhus, in time that great herd of deer would attain growth, increase, and expansion.”

“Upamā kho me ayaṃ, bhikkhave, katā atthassa viññāpanāya[P 1.0118]. Ayaṃ cevettha attho – mahantaṃ ninnaṃ pallalanti kho, bhikkhave, kāmānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Mahāmigasaṅghoti kho, bhikkhave, sattānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Puriso anatthakāmo ahitakāmo ayogakkhemakāmoti kho, bhikkhave, mārassetaṃ pāpimato adhivacanaṃ. Kummaggoti kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhaṅgikassetaṃ micchāmaggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – micchādiṭṭhiyā micchāsaṅkappassa micchāvācāya micchākammantassa micchāājīvassa micchāvāyāmassa micchāsatiyā micchāsamādhissa. Okacaroti kho, bhikkhave, nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Okacārikāti [M 1.0167] kho, bhikkhave, avijjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Puriso atthakāmo hitakāmo yogakkhemakāmoti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Khemo maggo sovatthiko pītigamanīyoti kho[V 1.0168], bhikkhave, ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhiyā sammāsaṅkappassa sammāvācāya sammākammantassa sammāājīvassa sammāvāyāmassa sammāsatiyā sammāsamādhissa.

“Bhikkhus, this simile has been made by me to make the meaning known. And this is the meaning here: ‘A great, low-lying marsh’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. ‘A great herd of deer’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for beings. ‘A man wishing for their disadvantage, harm, and lack of security from the yokes’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for Māra, the Evil One. ‘The wrong path’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, namely: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. ‘The decoy’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for delight and lust. ‘The decoy doe’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for ignorance. ‘A man wishing for their welfare, benefit, and security from the yokes’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. ‘The safe path, conducive to well-being, and leading to delight’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”

“Iti kho, bhikkhave, vivaṭo mayā khemo maggo sovatthiko pītigamanīyo, pihito kummaggo, ūhato okacaro, nāsitā okacārikā. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā. Etāni, bhikkhave[T 1.0240], rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni; jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti.

“Thus, bhikkhus, the safe path, conducive to well-being, and leading to delight has been opened by me; the wrong path has been blocked; the decoy has been uprooted; the decoy doe has been destroyed. Whatever, bhikkhus, should be done by a teacher for his disciples, seeking their welfare, being compassionate, out of compassion, that has been done for you by me. These, bhikkhus, are the roots of trees, these are empty dwellings. Meditate, bhikkhus, do not be heedless; do not be remorseful later. This is our instruction to you.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Dvedhāvitakkasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The Discourse on the Two Kinds of Thought, the ninth, is concluded.

10. Vitakkasaṇṭhānasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Stilling of Thoughts

216. Evaṃ [T 1.0241][V 1.0169] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti [P 1.0119] te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

216. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” they replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Adhicittamanuyuttena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā pañca nimittāni kālena kālaṃ manasi kātabbāni. Katamāni pañca? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno yaṃ nimittaṃ āgamma yaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tamhā nimittā aññaṃ nimittaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ. Tassa tamhā nimittā aññaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ ye pāpakā akusalā [M 1.0168] vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti ekodibhoti (syā. ka.) samādhiyati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho palagaṇḍo vā palagaṇḍantevāsī vā sukhumāya āṇiyā oḷārikaṃ āṇiṃ abhinihaneyya abhinīhareyya abhinivatteyya abhinivajjeyya (sī. pī.); evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno yaṃ nimittaṃ āgamma yaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi [T 1.0242] mohūpasaṃhitāpi, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tamhā nimittā aññaṃ nimittaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ. Tassa tamhā nimittā aññaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to five themes. What are the five? Here, bhikkhus, if, when a bhikkhu attends to a certain theme, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in him, then that bhikkhu should attend to another theme connected with what is wholesome. When he attends to another theme connected with what is wholesome, those evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated. Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled carpenter or his apprentice would use a fine peg to strike, remove, and extract a coarse one; so too, bhikkhus, if, when a bhikkhu attends to a certain theme, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in him, then that bhikkhu should attend to another theme connected with what is wholesome. When he attends to another theme connected with what is wholesome, those evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated.

217. “Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno tamhā nimittā aññaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ ādīnavo upaparikkhitabbo – ‘itipime vitakkā akusalā, itipime vitakkā sāvajjā, itipime vitakkā [V 1.0170] dukkhavipākā’ti. Tassa tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ ādīnavaṃ upaparikkhato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, itthī vā puriso vā daharo yuvā maṇḍanakajātiko ahikuṇapena vā kukkurakuṇapena vā manussakuṇapena [P 1.0120] vā kaṇṭhe āsattena aṭṭiyeyya harāyeyya jiguccheyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, tassa ce bhikkhuno tamhāpi nimittā aññaṃ nimittaṃ [T 1.0243] manasikaroto kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ ādīnavo upaparikkhitabbo – ‘itipime vitakkā akusalā, itipime [M 1.0169] vitakkā sāvajjā, itipime vitakkā dukkhavipākā’ti. Tassa tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ ādīnavaṃ upaparikkhato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati.

217. “Bhikkhus, if, when that bhikkhu is attending to another theme connected with what is wholesome, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, then that bhikkhu should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts: ‘Thus these thoughts are unwholesome, thus these thoughts are blameworthy, thus these thoughts result in suffering.’ As he examines the drawbacks of those thoughts, the evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated. Just as, bhikkhus, a young woman or man fond of adornment would be horrified, humiliated, and disgusted if the carcass of a snake, a dog, or a human were hung around their neck; so too, bhikkhus, if, when that bhikkhu is attending to another theme connected with what is wholesome, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, then that bhikkhu should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts: ‘Thus these thoughts are unwholesome, thus these thoughts are blameworthy, thus these thoughts result in suffering.’ As he examines the drawbacks of those thoughts, the evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated.

218. “Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno tesampi vitakkānaṃ ādīnavaṃ upaparikkhato uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ asatiamanasikāro āpajjitabbo. Tassa tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ asatiamanasikāraṃ āpajjato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, cakkhumā puriso āpāthagatānaṃ rūpānaṃ adassanakāmo assa; so nimīleyya vā aññena vā apalokeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tassa ce bhikkhuno tesampi vitakkānaṃ ādīnavaṃ upaparikkhato uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi, te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati.

218. “Bhikkhus, if, when that bhikkhu is examining the drawbacks of even those thoughts, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, then that bhikkhu should resort to non-recollection and non-attention towards those thoughts. When he resorts to non-recollection and non-attention towards those thoughts, the evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated. Just as, bhikkhus, a man with eyes, if he did not wish to see forms that had come into range, would close his eyes or look away; so too, bhikkhus, if, when that bhikkhu is examining the drawbacks of even those thoughts, evil unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, they are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated.

219. “Tassa [T 1.0244] ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno tesampi vitakkānaṃ asatiamanasikāraṃ āpajjato [V 1.0171] uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhānaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Tassa tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhānaṃ manasikaroto ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sīghaṃ gaccheyya. Tassa evamassa – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ sīghaṃ gacchāmi? Yaṃnūnāhaṃ saṇikaṃ gaccheyya’nti. So saṇikaṃ gaccheyya. Tassa evamassa – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ saṇikaṃ gacchāmi? Yaṃnūnāhaṃ tiṭṭheyya’nti. So tiṭṭheyya[M 1.0170]. Tassa evamassa – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ ṭhito? Yaṃnūnāhaṃ nisīdeyya’nti. So nisīdeyya. Tassa evamassa – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ nisinno? Yaṃnūnāhaṃ nipajjeyya’nti. So nipajjeyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, puriso oḷārikaṃ oḷārikaṃ iriyāpathaṃ abhinivajjetvā abhinissajjetvā (syā.) sukhumaṃ sukhumaṃ iriyāpathaṃ kappeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tassa ce bhikkhuno tesampi vitakkānaṃ asatiamanasikāraṃ āpajjato uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati.

219. Bhikkhus, if, when that bhikkhu is not attending to even those thoughts, evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, then that bhikkhu should attend to the causal source of those thoughts. As he attends to the causal source of those thoughts, the evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and go to cessation. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated. Just as, bhikkhus, if a man were walking quickly, he might think: ‘Why am I walking quickly? What if I were to walk slowly?’ So he would walk slowly. He might think: ‘Why am I walking slowly? What if I were to stand?’ So he would stand. He might think: ‘Why am I standing? What if I were to sit down?’ So he would sit down. He might think: ‘Why am I sitting? What if I were to lie down?’ So he would lie down. In this way, bhikkhus, that man, giving up the coarser postures, would adopt the more refined postures. So too, bhikkhus, if, when that bhikkhu is not attending to even those thoughts, evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, they are abandoned and go to cessation. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated.

220. “Tassa [T 1.0245] ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno tesampi vitakkānaṃ vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhānaṃ manasikaroto uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi. Tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā dantebhidantamādhāya dante + abhidantaṃ + ādhāyāti ṭīkāyaṃ padacchedo, dantebhīti panettha karaṇattho yutto viya dissati jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhitabbaṃ abhinippīḷetabbaṃ abhisantāpetabbaṃ[P 1.0121]. Tassa dantebhidantamādhāya jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, balavā puriso dubbalataraṃ purisaṃ sīse vā gale vā khandhe vā gahetvā abhiniggaṇheyya abhinippīḷeyya abhisantāpeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, tassa ce bhikkhuno tesampi vitakkānaṃ vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhānaṃ manasikaroto uppajjanteva pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi. Tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā dantebhidantamādhāya [V 1.0172] jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhitabbaṃ abhinippīḷetabbaṃ abhisantāpetabbaṃ. Tassa dantebhidantamādhāya jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi [T 1.0246] mohūpasaṃhitāpi [M 1.0171] te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati.

220. Bhikkhus, if, while a bhikkhu is attending to the causal source of those thoughts, evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should clench his teeth, press his tongue against the palate, and restrain, suppress, and afflict his mind with his mind. As he clenches his teeth, presses his tongue against the palate, and restrains, suppresses, and afflicts his mind with his mind, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and go to cessation. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated. Just as a strong man might seize a weaker man by the head, the throat, or the shoulder, and restrain, suppress, and afflict him; so too, bhikkhus, if, while a bhikkhu is attending to the causal source of those thoughts, evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion still arise in him, then that bhikkhu should clench his teeth, press his tongue against the palate, and restrain, suppress, and afflict his mind with his mind. As he clenches his teeth, presses his tongue against the palate, and restrains, suppresses, and afflicts his mind with his mind, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned and go to cessation. With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, composed, unified, and concentrated.

221. “Yato kho yato ca kho (syā. ka.), bhikkhave, bhikkhuno yaṃ nimittaṃ āgamma yaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi, tassa tamhā nimittā aññaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Tesampi vitakkānaṃ ādīnavaṃ upaparikkhato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Tesampi vitakkānaṃ asatiamanasikāraṃ āpajjato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Tesampi vitakkānaṃ vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhānaṃ manasikaroto ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi [T 1.0247] te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti samādhiyati. Dantebhidantamādhāya jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato ye pāpakā akusalā vitakkā chandūpasaṃhitāpi dosūpasaṃhitāpi mohūpasaṃhitāpi te pahīyanti te abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Tesaṃ pahānā ajjhattameva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati sannisīdati ekodi hoti [P 1.0122] samādhiyati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vasī vitakkapariyāyapathesu. Yaṃ vitakkaṃ ākaṅkhissati taṃ vitakkaṃ vitakkessati, yaṃ vitakkaṃ nākaṅkhissati na taṃ vitakkaṃ vitakkessati. Acchecchi taṇhaṃ, vivattayi vāvattayi (sī. pī.) saṃyojanaṃ, sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”ti.

221. O monks, when evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in a monk attending to a certain sign, then for that monk, by attending to another sign connected with the wholesome, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned; they go to cessation. Due to their abandonment, the mind becomes steady internally, settles down, becomes unified, and is concentrated. For him who investigates the danger of those very thoughts, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned; they go to cessation. Due to their abandonment, the mind becomes steady internally, settles down, becomes unified, and is concentrated. For him who attains non-recollection and non-attention towards those very thoughts, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned; they go to cessation. Due to their abandonment, the mind becomes steady internally, settles down, becomes unified, and is concentrated. For him who attends to the causal basis of the formation of those very thoughts, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned; they go to cessation. Due to their abandonment, the mind becomes steady internally, settles down, becomes unified, and is concentrated. For that monk who, placing tooth upon tooth, pressing his tongue against the palate, restrains, crushes, and afflicts the mind with the mind, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion are abandoned; they go to cessation. Due to their abandonment, the mind becomes steady internally, settles down, becomes unified, and is concentrated. This, O monks, is called a monk who is a master in the paths of the courses of thought. Whatever thought he wishes to think, that thought he will think; whatever thought he does not wish to think, that thought he will not think. He has cut off craving, turned away the fetter, and by the right full understanding of conceit, has made an end of suffering.

Idamavoca [M 1.0172][V 1.0173] bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Those monks, being delighted, greatly rejoiced in the Blessed One's speech.

Vitakkasaṇṭhānasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta, the tenth, is concluded.

Sīhanādavaggo niṭṭhito dutiyo.

The Sīhanāda Vagga, the second, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that chapter:

Cūḷasīhanādalomahaṃsavaro, mahācūḷadukkhakkhandhaanumānikasuttaṃ;

Khilapatthamadhupiṇḍikadvidhāvitakka, pañcanimittakathā puna vaggo.

The Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta and the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta; the Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta, the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta, and the Anumāna Sutta; the Cetokhila Sutta and the Vanapattha Sutta; the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta; the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta; and again, the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta, which is the discourse on the five signs. This is the chapter that was taught.

3. Opammavaggo

3. The Chapter on Similes

1. Kakacūpamasuttaṃ

1. The Simile of the Saw

222. Evaṃ [T 1.0248][M 1.0173][V 1.0174] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā moḷiyaphagguno bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ ativelaṃ saṃsaṭṭho viharati. Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho āyasmā moḷiyaphagguno bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ viharati – sace koci bhikkhu āyasmato moḷiyaphaggunassa sammukhā tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, tenāyasmā moḷiyaphagguno kupito anattamano adhikaraṇampi karoti. Sace pana koci bhikkhu tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ sammukhā āyasmato moḷiyaphaggunassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, tena tā bhikkhuniyo kupitā anattamanā adhikaraṇampi karonti. Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho āyasmā moḷiyaphagguno bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ viharati. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “āyasmā, bhante, moḷiyaphagguno bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ ativelaṃ saṃsaṭṭho viharati. Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho, bhante, āyasmā moḷiyaphagguno bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ viharati – sace koci bhikkhu āyasmato moḷiyaphaggunassa sammukhā tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, tenāyasmā moḷiyaphagguno kupito anattamano [T 1.0249] adhikaraṇampi karoti. Sace pana koci bhikkhu tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ sammukhā āyasmato moḷiyaphaggunassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, tena tā bhikkhuniyo kupitā anattamanā adhikaraṇampi karonti. Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho, bhante, āyasmā moḷiyaphagguno bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ viharatī”ti.

222. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna was living in overly close association with the nuns. The Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna was living in such close association with the nuns that if any monk spoke disparagingly of those nuns in the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna’s presence, then the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna would become angry and displeased and would even create a dispute. But if any monk spoke disparagingly of the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna in the presence of those nuns, then those nuns would become angry and displeased and would even create a dispute. Thus the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna was living in overly close association with the nuns. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna is living in overly close association with the nuns. He is living in such close association with the nuns that if any monk speaks disparagingly of those nuns in the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna’s presence, then the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna becomes angry and displeased and even creates a dispute. But if any monk speaks disparagingly of the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna in the presence of those nuns, then those nuns become angry and displeased and even create a dispute. Venerable sir, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna is living in overly close association with the nuns in this way.”

223. Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ[P 1.0123], bhikkhu, mama vacanena moḷiyaphaggunaṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantehi – ‘satthā taṃ, āvuso phagguna, āmantetī’”ti. “Evaṃ[V 1.0175], bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā moḷiyaphagguno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ moḷiyaphaggunaṃ etadavoca – “satthā taṃ, āvuso phagguna, āmantetī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā moḷiyaphagguno tassa [M 1.0174] bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ moḷiyaphaggunaṃ bhagavā etadavoca –

223.
