Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk: “Come, monk, in my name summon the monk Moḷiyaphagguna, saying, ‘The Teacher calls you, friend Phagguna.’” “Yes, venerable sir,” that monk replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna and said to him, “The Teacher calls you, friend Phagguna.” “Very well, friend,” the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna replied to that monk. He then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna as he was sitting to one side:

“Saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, phagguna, bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ ativelaṃ saṃsaṭṭho viharasi? Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho kira tvaṃ, phagguna, bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ viharasi – sace koci bhikkhu tuyhaṃ sammukhā tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, tena tvaṃ kupito anattamano adhikaraṇampi karosi. Sace pana koci bhikkhu tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ sammukhā tuyhaṃ avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, tena tā bhikkhuniyo kupitā anattamanā adhikaraṇampi karonti. Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho kira tvaṃ, phagguna, bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ viharasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Nanu tvaṃ, phagguna, kulaputto saddhā [T 1.0250] agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”ti.

“Is it true, Phagguna, that you live in excessive association with the nuns? Is it true that you live in such association with the nuns that if any monk speaks dispraise of those nuns in your presence, you become angry and displeased and even create a dispute? And if any monk speaks dispraise of you in the presence of those nuns, those nuns become angry and displeased and even create a dispute? Is it true that you live in such association with the nuns?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Phagguna, are you not a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

224. “Na kho te etaṃ, phagguna, patirūpaṃ kulaputtassa saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitassa, yaṃ tvaṃ bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ ativelaṃ saṃsaṭṭho vihareyyāsi. Tasmātiha, phagguna, tava cepi koci sammukhā tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyya, tatrāpi tvaṃ, phagguna, ye gehasitā gehassitā (?) chandā ye gehasitā vitakkā te pajaheyyāsi. Tatrāpi te, phagguna, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘na ceva me cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāmi, hitānukampī ca viharissāmi mettacitto, na dosantaro’ti. Evañhi te, phagguna, sikkhitabbaṃ.

224. “Phagguna, it is not suitable for you, a clansman who has gone forth in faith from the household life into homelessness, to live in overly close association with the nuns. Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone should speak disparagingly of those nuns in your presence, you should abandon any desires and thoughts connected with the household life. In that case, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will not be altered, nor will I utter evil speech; I will dwell compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, and without inner hatred.’ Thus, Phagguna, you should train yourself.

“Tasmātiha, phagguna, tava cepi koci sammukhā tāsaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ pāṇinā pahāraṃ dadeyya, leḍḍunā pahāraṃ dadeyya, daṇḍena pahāraṃ dadeyya, satthena pahāraṃ dadeyya. Tatrāpi tvaṃ, phagguna, ye gehasitā chandā ye gehasitā vitakkā te pajaheyyāsi. Tatrāpi te, phagguna, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘na ceva me cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāmi, hitānukampī ca viharissāmi mettacitto, na dosantaro’ti. Evañhi te, phagguna, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone in your presence should strike those nuns with a hand, a clod, a stick, or a knife, you should abandon any desires and thoughts connected with the household life. In that case, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will not be altered, nor will I utter evil speech; I will dwell compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, and without inner hatred.’ Thus, Phagguna, you should train yourself.

“Tasmātiha, phagguna, tava cepi koci sammukhā avaṇṇaṃ bhāseyya, tatrāpi tvaṃ, phagguna[V 1.0176], ye gehasitā chandā ye gehasitā vitakkā te [M 1.0175] pajaheyyāsi. Tatrāpi te, phagguna, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘na ceva me cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāmi, hitānukampī ca viharissāmi mettacitto, na dosantaro’ti. Evañhi [T 1.0251] te, phagguna, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone should speak disparagingly of you in your presence, you should abandon any desires and thoughts connected with the household life. In that case, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will not be altered, nor will I utter evil speech; I will dwell compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, and without inner hatred.’ Thus, Phagguna, you should train yourself.

“Tasmātiha, phagguna, tava cepi koci pāṇinā pahāraṃ dadeyya, leḍḍunā pahāraṃ dadeyya, daṇḍena pahāraṃ dadeyya, satthena pahāraṃ [P 1.0124] dadeyya, tatrāpi tvaṃ, phagguna, ye gehasitā chandā ye gehasitā vitakkā te pajaheyyāsi. Tatrāpi te, phagguna, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘na ceva me cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāmi, hitānukampī ca viharissāmi mettacitto, na dosantaro’ti. Evañhi te, phagguna, sikkhitabba”nti.

“Therefore, Phagguna, even if someone should strike you with a hand, a clod, a stick, or a knife, you should abandon any desires and thoughts connected with the household life. In that case, Phagguna, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will not be altered, nor will I utter evil speech; I will dwell compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, and without inner hatred.’ Thus, Phagguna, you should train yourself.”

225. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “ārādhayiṃsu vata me, bhikkhave, bhikkhū ekaṃ samayaṃ cittaṃ. Idhāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhū āmantesiṃ – ahaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ekāsanabhojanaṃ bhuñjāmi. Ekāsanabhojanaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, bhuñjamāno appābādhatañca sañjānāmi appātaṅkatañca lahuṭṭhānañca balañca phāsuvihārañca. Etha tumhepi, bhikkhave, ekāsanabhojanaṃ bhuñjatha. Ekāsanabhojanaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tumhepi bhuñjamānā appābādhatañca sañjānissatha appātaṅkatañca lahuṭṭhānañca balañca phāsuvihārañcāti. Na me, bhikkhave, tesu bhikkhūsu anusāsanī karaṇīyā ahosi; satuppādakaraṇīyameva me, bhikkhave, tesu bhikkhūsu ahosi.

225. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Indeed, monks, the monks once pleased my mind. Here, monks, I addressed the monks: ‘I, monks, eat a single meal. Eating a single meal, monks, I am aware of having little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, monks, you too eat a single meal. Eating a single meal, monks, you too will be aware of having little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding.’ There was no need for me to give instructions to those monks, monks; there was only a need for me to arouse mindfulness in them.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, subhūmiyaṃ catumahāpathe ājaññaratho yutto assa ṭhito odhastapatodo. Tamenaṃ dakkho yoggācariyo assadammasārathi abhiruhitvā, vāmena hatthena rasmiyo gahetvā, dakkhiṇena hatthena patodaṃ gahetvā, yenicchakaṃ yadicchakaṃ [T 1.0252] sāreyyapi paccāsāreyyapi. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, na me tesu bhikkhūsu anusāsanī karaṇīyā ahosi, satuppādakaraṇīyameva me, bhikkhave, tesu bhikkhūsu ahosi. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, tumhepi akusalaṃ pajahatha, kusalesu dhammesu āyogaṃ karotha. Evañhi tumhepi imasmiṃ dhammavinaye vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissatha.

“Just as, monks, on level ground at a four-way intersection, a thoroughbred chariot stands harnessed, with the goad laid down. Then a skilled trainer, a charioteer of tamed horses, mounts it, takes the reins in his left hand, takes the goad in his right hand, and drives it forward and back as he wishes. In the same way, monks, there was no need for me to give those monks instructions; there was only a need for me to arouse mindfulness in them. Therefore, monks, you too should abandon the unwholesome and apply yourselves to wholesome qualities. For thus, you too will attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Discipline.”

“Seyyathāpi[M 1.0176][V 1.0177], bhikkhave, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre mahantaṃ sālavanaṃ. Tañcassa eḷaṇḍehi sañchannaṃ. Tassa kocideva puriso uppajjeyya atthakāmo hitakāmo yogakkhemakāmo. So yā tā sālalaṭṭhiyo kuṭilā ojāpaharaṇiyo ojaharaṇiyo (ka.) tā chetvā tacchetvā (sī. syā. pī.) bahiddhā nīhareyya, antovanaṃ suvisodhitaṃ visodheyya. Yā pana tā sālalaṭṭhiyo ujukā sujātā tā sammā parihareyya. Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, sālavanaṃ aparena samayena vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tumhepi akusalaṃ pajahatha, kusalesu dhammesu āyogaṃ karotha. Evañhi [P 1.0125] tumhepi imasmiṃ dhammavinaye vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissatha.

“Just as, monks, near a village or town, there might be a large sal grove overgrown with castor-oil plants. A person might arise who desires its welfare, benefit, and security from bondage. He would cut down and remove the crooked sal saplings that are detrimental to its vigor, and he would thoroughly clear the inner grove. He would properly tend the straight and well-grown sal saplings. Thus, monks, that sal grove would in time attain growth, increase, and abundance. In the same way, monks, you too should abandon the unwholesome and apply yourselves to wholesome qualities. For thus, you too will attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Discipline.”

226. “Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, imissāyeva sāvatthiyā vedehikā nāma gahapatānī ahosi. Vedehikāya, bhikkhave, gahapatāniyā evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘soratā vedehikā gahapatānī, nivātā vedehikā gahapatānī, upasantā vedehikā gahapatānī’ti. Vedehikāya kho pana, bhikkhave, gahapatāniyā kāḷī nāma dāsī ahosi dakkhā analasā [T 1.0253] susaṃvihitakammantā.

226. “Once, monks, right here in Sāvatthī, there was a householder’s wife named Vedehikā. A good reputation had gone out about Vedehikā the householder’s wife: ‘Vedehikā the householder’s wife is amiable, Vedehikā the householder’s wife is humble, Vedehikā the householder’s wife is tranquil.’ Now, monks, Vedehikā the householder’s wife had a slave woman named Kāḷī, who was skilled, tireless, and well-organized in her work.”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, kāḷiyā dāsiyā etadahosi – ‘mayhaṃ kho ayyāya evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – “soratā vedehikā gahapatānī, nivātā vedehikā gahapatānī, upasantā vedehikā gahapatānī”ti. Kiṃ nu kho me ayyā santaṃyeva nu kho ajjhattaṃ kopaṃ na pātukaroti udāhu asantaṃ udāhu mayhamevete mayhevete (sī. pī.) kammantā susaṃvihitā yena me ayyā santaṃyeva ajjhattaṃ kopaṃ na pātukaroti, no asantaṃ? Yaṃnūnāhaṃ ayyaṃ vīmaṃseyya’nti. Atha kho, bhikkhave, kāḷī dāsī divā uṭṭhāsi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, vedehikā gahapatānī kāḷiṃ dāsiṃ etadavoca – ‘he je kāḷī’ti. ‘Kiṃ, ayye’ti? ‘Kiṃ, je, divā uṭṭhāsī’ti? ‘Na khvayye na kho ayye (sī. pī.), kiñcī’ti. ‘No vata re kiñci, pāpi dāsi pāpadāsi (syā. ka.), divā uṭṭhāsī’ti kupitā anattamanā bhākuṭiṃ bhūkuṭiṃ (sī. pī.), bhakuṭīṃ (syā.) akāsi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, kāḷiyā dāsiyā [M 1.0177] etadahosi – ‘santaṃyeva kho me ayyā ajjhattaṃ kopaṃ na pātukaroti, no asantaṃ; mayhamevete kammantā susaṃvihitā, yena me ayyā santaṃyeva ajjhattaṃ kopaṃ na pātukaroti, no asantaṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhiyyosomattāya ayyaṃ vīmaṃseyya’”nti.

“Then, monks, the slave girl Kāḷī thought: ‘My lady has such a fine reputation: “The householder’s wife Vedehikā is amiable, the householder’s wife Vedehikā is humble, the householder’s wife Vedehikā is peaceful.” Does my lady truly not reveal inner anger when it is present, or is it absent? Or is it because my tasks are so well-arranged that my lady does not reveal inner anger even when it is present, and not because it is absent? What if I were to test my lady?’ Then, monks, the slave girl Kāḷī got up late in the day. Then, monks, the householder’s wife Vedehikā said to the slave girl Kāḷī: ‘Hey, Kāḷī!’ ‘What is it, madam?’ ‘Why, girl, did you get up late in the day?’ ‘It is nothing, madam.’ ‘It’s not nothing, you wicked slave, that you got up late in the day!’ Angry and displeased, she frowned. Then, monks, the slave girl Kāḷī thought: ‘My lady does indeed have inner anger that she does not reveal; it is not that it is absent. It is because my tasks are so well-arranged that my lady does not reveal her inner anger even when it is present, not because it is absent. What if I were to test her even further?’”

“Atha [V 1.0178] kho, bhikkhave, kāḷī dāsī divātaraṃyeva uṭṭhāsi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, vedehikā gahapatānī kāḷiṃ dāsiṃ etadavoca – ‘he je, kāḷī’ti. ‘Kiṃ, ayye’ti? ‘Kiṃ, je, divātaraṃ uṭṭhāsī’ti? ‘Na khvayye, kiñcī’ti. ‘No vata re kiñci, pāpi dāsi, divātaraṃ [T 1.0254] uṭṭhāsī’ti kupitā anattamanā anattamanavācaṃ nicchāresi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, kāḷiyā dāsiyā etadahosi – ‘santaṃyeva kho me ayyā ajjhattaṃ kopaṃ na pātukaroti, no asantaṃ. Mayhamevete kammantā susaṃvihitā, yena me ayyā santaṃyeva ajjhattaṃ kopaṃ na pātukaroti, no asantaṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhiyyosomattāya ayyaṃ vīmaṃseyya’nti.

“Then, monks, the slave girl Kāḷī got up even later in the day. Then, monks, the householder’s wife Vedehikā said to the slave girl Kāḷī: ‘Hey, Kāḷī!’ ‘What is it, madam?’ ‘Why, slave girl, did you get up even later in the day?’ ‘It is nothing, madam.’ ‘It’s not nothing, you wicked slave, that you get up even later in the day!’ Angry and displeased, she uttered words of displeasure. Then, monks, the slave girl Kāḷī thought: ‘My lady does indeed have inner anger that she does not reveal; it is not that it is absent. It is because my tasks are so well-arranged that my lady does not reveal her inner anger even when it is present, not because it is absent. What if I were to test her even further?’”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, kāḷī dāsī divātaraṃyeva uṭṭhāsi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, vedehikā gahapatānī kāḷiṃ dāsiṃ etadavoca [P 1.0126] – ‘he je, kāḷī’ti. ‘Kiṃ, ayye’ti? ‘Kiṃ, je, divā uṭṭhāsī’ti? ‘Na khvayye, kiñcī’ti. ‘No vata re kiñci, pāpi dāsi, divā uṭṭhāsī’ti kupitā anattamanā aggaḷasūciṃ gahetvā sīse pahāraṃ adāsi, sīsaṃ vobhindi vi + ava + bhindi = vobhindi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, kāḷī dāsī bhinnena sīsena lohitena galantena paṭivissakānaṃ ujjhāpesi – ‘passathayye, soratāya kammaṃ; passathayye, nivātāya kammaṃ, passathayye, upasantāya kammaṃ! Kathañhi nāma ekadāsikāya divā uṭṭhāsīti kupitā anattamanā aggaḷasūciṃ gahetvā sīse pahāraṃ dassati, sīsaṃ vobhindissatī’ti.

“Then, monks, the slave girl Kāḷī got up even later in the day. Then, monks, the householder’s wife Vedehikā said to the slave girl Kāḷī: ‘Hey, Kāḷī!’ ‘What is it, madam?’ ‘Why, slave girl, did you get up late in the day?’ ‘It is nothing, madam.’ ‘It’s not nothing, you wicked slave, that you get up late in the day!’ Angry and displeased, she took a latch-pin and struck her on the head, splitting it open. Then, monks, the slave girl Kāḷī, with her head split open and blood streaming down, complained to the neighbors: ‘See, madams, the deed of the amiable one! See, madams, the deed of the humble one! See, madams, the deed of the peaceful one! How could she, angry and displeased at a single slave girl for getting up late in the day, take a latch-pin and strike her on the head, splitting it open!’”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, vedehikāya gahapatāniyā aparena samayena evaṃ pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchi – ‘caṇḍī vedehikā gahapatānī, anivātā vedehikā gahapatānī, anupasantā vedehikā gahapatānī’ti.

“Then, monks, after some time, this bad report about the householder’s wife Vedehikā arose: ‘The householder’s wife Vedehikā is fierce, the householder’s wife Vedehikā is not humble, the householder’s wife Vedehikā is not peaceful.’”

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu tāvadeva soratasorato hoti nivātanivāto [T 1.0255] hoti upasantūpasanto hoti yāva na amanāpā vacanapathā phusanti. Yato ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṃ [M 1.0178] amanāpā vacanapathā phusanti, atha bhikkhu ‘sorato’ti veditabbo, ‘nivāto’ti veditabbo, ‘upasanto’ti veditabbo. Nāhaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṃ ‘suvaco’ti vadāmi yo cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārahetu suvaco hoti, sovacassataṃ āpajjati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tañhi so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ [V 1.0179] alabhamāno na suvaco hoti, na sovacassataṃ āpajjati. Yo ca kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammaṃyeva sakkaronto, dhammaṃ garuṃ karonto, dhammaṃ mānento, dhammaṃ pūjento, dhammaṃ apacāyamāno dhammaṃ yeva sakkaronto dhammaṃ garukaronto dhammaṃ apacāyamāno (sī. syā. pī.) suvaco hoti, sovacassataṃ āpajjati, tamahaṃ ‘suvaco’ti vadāmi. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘dhammaṃyeva sakkarontā, dhammaṃ garuṃ karontā, dhammaṃ mānentā, dhammaṃ pūjentā, dhammaṃ apacāyamānā suvacā bhavissāma, sovacassataṃ āpajjissāmā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“Just so, monks, a certain monk is very agreeable, very humble, and very peaceful only as long as unpleasant courses of speech do not touch him. But when, monks, unpleasant courses of speech touch a monk, only then is he to be known as ‘agreeable,’ to be known as ‘humble,’ and to be known as ‘peaceful.’ I do not call a monk ‘easy to admonish’ who is easy to admonish and becomes compliant for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. Why is that? Because if that monk does not get robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites, he is not easy to admonish and does not become compliant. But a monk who, honoring only the Dhamma, respecting the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, venerating the Dhamma, and esteeming the Dhamma, is easy to admonish and becomes compliant, him I call ‘easy to admonish.’ Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Honoring only the Dhamma, respecting the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, venerating the Dhamma, and esteeming the Dhamma, we will be easy to admonish and will become compliant.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”

227. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, vacanapathā yehi vo pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ – kālena vā akālena vā; bhūtena vā abhūtena vā; saṇhena vā pharusena vā; atthasaṃhitena vā anatthasaṃhitena vā; mettacittā vā dosantarā vā. Kālena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ akālena vā; bhūtena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ abhūtena vā; saṇhena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ pharusena vā; atthasaṃhitena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ anatthasaṃhitena [P 1.0127] vā[T 1.0256]; mettacittā vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ dosantarā vā. Tatrāpi vo, bhikkhave, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘na ceva no cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāma, hitānukampī ca viharissāma mettacittā, na dosantarā. Tañca puggalaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā pharitvā viharissāma, tadārammaṇañca sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cittena vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena abyāpajjhena (sī. syā. pī.), abyāpajjena (ka.) aṅguttaratikanipātaṭīkā oloketabbā pharitvā viharissāmā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

227. “Monks, there are these five courses of speech by which others may address you: timely or untimely; factually or unfactually; gently or harshly; beneficially or unbeneficially; with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hate. Monks, others may address you in a timely or untimely way; factually or unfactually; gently or harshly; beneficially or unbeneficially; with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hate. In such cases, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our minds will remain unaltered, and we will utter no evil words. We will abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate. We will dwell pervading that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and with that as our object, we will dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without affliction.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”

228. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso āgaccheyya kudālapiṭakaṃ kuddālapiṭakaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) ādāya. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ imaṃ mahāpathaviṃ apathaviṃ karissāmī’ti[M 1.0179]. So tatra tatra vikhaṇeyya khaṇeyya (sī. syā. pī.), tatra tatra vikireyya, tatra tatra oṭṭhubheyya, tatra tatra omutteyya – ‘apathavī bhavasi, apathavī bhavasī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu so puriso imaṃ mahāpathaviṃ apathaviṃ kareyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Ayañhi, bhante, mahāpathavī gambhīrā appameyyā. Sā na sukarā apathavī kātuṃ; yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, pañcime vacanapathā yehi vo pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ – kālena vā akālena vā; bhūtena vā abhūtena vā; saṇhena vā pharusena vā; atthasaṃhitena vā anatthasaṃhitena vā; mettacittā vā dosantarā vā. Kālena vā[V 1.0180], bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ akālena [T 1.0257] vā; bhūtena vā bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ abhūtena vā; saṇhena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ pharusena vā; atthasaṃhitena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ anatthasaṃhitena vā; mettacittā vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ dosantarā vā. Tatrāpi vo, bhikkhave, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘na ceva no cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāma, hitānukampī ca viharissāma mettacittā na dosantarā. Tañca puggalaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā pharitvā viharissāma, tadārammaṇañca sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ pathavisamena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharissāmā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

228. “Suppose, monks, a man were to come along carrying a hoe and a basket. He would say, ‘I will make this great earth be without earth!’ He would dig here and there, scatter soil here and there, spit here and there, and urinate here and there, saying, ‘Be without earth! Be without earth!’ What do you think, monks, could that man make this great earth be without earth?” “No, venerable sir.” “Why is that?” “Because, venerable sir, this great earth is deep and immeasurable. It is not easy to make it be without earth. That man would only partake of weariness and frustration.” “Just so, monks, there are these five courses of speech by which others may address you—timely or untimely; factually or unfactually; gently or harshly; beneficially or unbeneficially; with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hate. Others may address you, monks, in a timely or untimely way; factually or unfactually; gently or harshly; beneficially or unbeneficially; with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hate. In such cases, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our minds will remain unaltered, and we will utter no evil words. We will abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate. We will dwell pervading that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and with that as our object, we will dwell pervading the entire world with a mind like the earth—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without affliction.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”

229. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso āgaccheyya lākhaṃ vā haliddiṃ vā nīlaṃ vā mañjiṭṭhaṃ vā ādāya. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ imasmiṃ ākāse rūpaṃ likhissāmi, rūpapātubhāvaṃ karissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu so puriso imasmiṃ ākāse rūpaṃ likheyya, rūpapātubhāvaṃ kareyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Ayañhi, bhante, ākāso arūpī anidassano. Tattha na sukaraṃ rūpaṃ likhituṃ, rūpapātubhāvaṃ kātuṃ; yāvadeva ca pana [P 1.0128] so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, pañcime vacanapathā yehi vo pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ kālena vā akālena vā [T 1.0258] …pe… ‘na ceva… tadārammaṇañca [M 1.0180] sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ ākāsasamena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharissāmā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

229. “Suppose, monks, a man were to come carrying lac, turmeric, blue dye, or madder. He would say, ‘I will draw a form in the sky and make it appear.’ What do you think, monks? Could that man draw a form in the sky and make it appear?” “No, venerable sir.” “Why is that?” “Because, venerable sir, the sky is formless and invisible. It is not easy to draw a form there or make it appear; that man would only partake of weariness and frustration.” “Just so, monks, there are these five ways of speech by which others might address you. In such cases, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our minds will remain unaffected, and we will utter no evil words. We will abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate. We will dwell pervading that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and making that the object, we will dwell pervading the entire world with a mind like space, abundant, exalted, measureless, without hostility and without ill will.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.

230. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso āgaccheyya ādittaṃ tiṇukkaṃ ādāya. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ imāya ādittāya tiṇukkāya gaṅgaṃ nadiṃ santāpessāmi saṃparitāpessāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu so puriso ādittāya tiṇukkāya gaṅgaṃ nadiṃ santāpeyya saṃparitāpeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Gaṅgā hi, bhante, nadī gambhīrā appameyyā. Sā na sukarā ādittāya tiṇukkāya santāpetuṃ saṃparitāpetuṃ; yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, pañcime vacanapathā yehi vo pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ kālena vā akālena [V 1.0181] vā…pe… ‘na ceva… tadārammaṇañca sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ gaṅgāsamena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharissāmā”ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

230. “Suppose, monks, a man were to come carrying a blazing torch of grass. He would say: ‘With this blazing torch of grass, I will heat up and scorch the river Ganges.’ What do you think, monks? Would that man be able to heat up and scorch the river Ganges with that blazing torch of grass?” “No, venerable sir.” “Why is that?” “Because, venerable sir, the river Ganges is deep and immeasurable. It is not easy to heat and scorch it with a blazing torch of grass. That man would only partake of weariness and frustration.” “Just so, monks, there are these five ways of speech by which others might address you. In such cases, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our minds will remain unaffected, and we will utter no evil words. We will abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate. We will dwell pervading that person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and making that the object, we will dwell pervading the entire world with a mind like the river Ganges, abundant, exalted, measureless, without hostility and without ill will.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”

231. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, biḷārabhastā madditā sumadditā suparimadditā, mudukā tūlinī chinnasassarā chinnabhabbharā. Atha puriso āgaccheyya kaṭṭhaṃ vā kathalaṃ kaṭhalaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) vā ādāya. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahaṃ imaṃ biḷārabhastaṃ madditaṃ sumadditaṃ suparimadditaṃ, mudukaṃ tūliniṃ, chinnasassaraṃ chinnabhabbharaṃ kaṭṭhena vā kathalena vā sarasaraṃ karissāmi bharabharaṃ karissāmī’ti[T 1.0259]. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu so puriso amuṃ biḷārabhastaṃ madditaṃ sumadditaṃ suparimadditaṃ, mudukaṃ tūliniṃ, chinnasassaraṃ chinnabhabbharaṃ kaṭṭhena vā kathalena vā sarasaraṃ kareyya, bharabharaṃ kareyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Amu hi, bhante, biḷārabhastā madditā sumadditā suparimadditā, mudukā tūlinī, chinnasassarā chinnabhabbharā. Sā na sukarā kaṭṭhena vā kathalena vā sarasaraṃ kātuṃ bharabharaṃ kātuṃ; yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, pañcime vacanapathā yehi vo pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ kālena vā [P 1.0129] akālena vā; bhūtena vā abhūtena vā; saṇhena [M 1.0181] vā pharusena vā; atthasaṃhitena vā anatthasaṃhitena vā; mettacittā vā dosantarā vā. Kālena vā bhikkhave pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ akālena vā; bhūtena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ abhūtena vā; saṇhena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ pharusena vā; atthasaṃhitena vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ anatthasaṃhitena vā; mettacittā vā, bhikkhave, pare vadamānā vadeyyuṃ dosantarā vā. Tatrāpi vo, bhikkhave, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘na ceva no cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāma hitānukampī ca viharissāma mettacittā na dosantarā. Tañca puggalaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā pharitvā viharissāma, tadārammaṇañca sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ biḷārabhastāsamena cetasā [T 1.0260] vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharissāmā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

231. “Suppose, monks, there were a cat-skin bag that had been kneaded, thoroughly kneaded, and perfectly kneaded—soft, like cotton-wool, with its rustling and rattling sounds cut off. Then a man were to come carrying a stick or a potsherd. He might say: ‘With this stick or potsherd, I will make this cat-skin bag—kneaded, thoroughly kneaded, and perfectly kneaded, soft, like cotton-wool, with its rustling and rattling sounds cut off—rustle and rattle.’ What do you think, monks? Would that man be able to make that cat-skin bag—kneaded, thoroughly kneaded, and perfectly kneaded, soft, like cotton-wool, with its rustling and rattling sounds cut off—rustle and rattle with a stick or a potsherd?” “No, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable sir, that cat-skin bag has been kneaded, thoroughly kneaded, and perfectly kneaded—soft, like cotton-wool, with its rustling and rattling sounds cut off. It is not easy to make it rustle or rattle with a stick or a potsherd; that man would only reap weariness and vexation.” “Just so, monks, are these five ways of speaking by which others may address you—whether timely or untimely; with what is true or untrue; gently or harshly; connected with benefit or not connected with benefit; with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hatred. Whether timely or untimely, monks, others may address you; whether with what is true or untrue, others may address you; whether gently or harshly, others may address you; whether connected with benefit or not connected with benefit, others may address you; whether with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hatred, others may address you. In such a case, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our minds will remain unaffected; we will utter no evil words; we will abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hatred. We will dwell pervading that person with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, and making that the object, we will dwell pervading the entire world with a mind like a cat-skin bag—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will.’ Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.”

232. “Ubhatodaṇḍakena cepi, bhikkhave, kakacena corā ocarakā aṅgamaṅgāni okanteyyuṃ, tatrāpi yo mano padūseyya, na me so tena sāsanakaro. Tatrāpi vo, bhikkhave[V 1.0182], evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘na ceva no cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati, na ca pāpikaṃ vācaṃ nicchāressāma, hitānukampī ca viharissāma mettacittā na dosantarā. Tañca puggalaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā pharitvā viharissāma tadārammaṇañca sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharissāmā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

232. “Even if, monks, base thieves were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, one who corrupts their mind on that account would not be a follower of my teaching. In that situation, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our minds will remain unaffected; we will utter no evil words; we will abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hatred. We will dwell pervading that person with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, and making that the object, we will dwell pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will.’ Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.”

233. “Imañca imañce (?) tumhe, bhikkhave, kakacūpamaṃ ovādaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ manasi kareyyātha. Passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, taṃ vacanapathaṃ, aṇuṃ vā thūlaṃ vā, yaṃ tumhe nādhivāseyyāthā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, imaṃ kakacūpamaṃ ovādaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ manasikarotha. Taṃ vo bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.

233. “And, bhikkhus, you should frequently keep in mind this instruction on the simile of the saw. Do you see, bhikkhus, any way of speaking, subtle or gross, that you would not tolerate?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, bhikkhus, frequently keep in mind this instruction on the simile of the saw. That will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. The bhikkhus, gratified, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Kakacūpamasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The first Discourse on the Simile of the Saw is finished.

2. Alagaddūpamasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the Simile of the Water Snake

234. Evaṃ [T 1.0261][M 1.0182][V 1.0183][P 1.0130] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena ariṭṭhassa nāma bhikkhuno gaddhabādhipubbassa gandhabādhipubbassa (ka.) evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā”ti. Assosuṃ kho sambahulā bhikkhū – “ariṭṭhassa kira nāma bhikkhuno gaddhabādhipubbassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’”ti. Atha kho te bhikkhū yena ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ etadavocuṃ – “saccaṃ kira te, āvuso ariṭṭha, evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’”ti. “Evaṃbyākho evaṃ kho (?) bhagavato sammukhāyevassa “evaṃbyākho”ti ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā”ti.

234. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time a bhikkhu named Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, had conceived this evil wrong view: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them.” A number of bhikkhus heard: “It seems that the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, has conceived this evil wrong view: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them.’” Then those bhikkhus approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, and said to him: “Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that this evil wrong view has arisen in you: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them’?” “Exactly so, friends. As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them.”

Atha kho tepi bhikkhū ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ etasmā [T 1.0262] pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecetukāmā samanuyuñjanti samanugāhanti samanuggāhanti (syā.) samanubhāsanti – “mā hevaṃ, āvuso ariṭṭha, avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi; na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ abbhācikkhanaṃ (ka.), na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Anekapariyāyenāvuso ariṭṭha, antarāyikā dhammā antarāyikā vuttā bhagavatā, alañca pana te paṭisevato antarāyāya. Appassādā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā,ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā…pe… maṃsapesūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… tiṇukkūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… supinakūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… yācitakūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… asisūnūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… sattisūlūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā… sappasirūpamā kāmā vuttā [M 1.0183] bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”ti. Evampi kho ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo [V 1.0184] tehi bhikkhūhi samanuyuñjiyamāno samanugāhiyamāno samanuggāhiyamāno (syā. vinayepi) samanubhāsiyamāno tadeva tatheva taṃ (vinaye) pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa voharati – “evaṃbyākho ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā”ti.

Then those bhikkhus, wishing to make the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, abandon that evil wrong view, questioned him, examined him, and asked for his reasons: “Do not say so, friend Ariṭṭha! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One! It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus. In many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, obstructive things have been described as obstructive by the Blessed One, and they are indeed able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them. The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures have little delight, much suffering, and much tribulation, and that the danger in them is greater. The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton… like a piece of meat… like a grass torch… like a pit of glowing coals… like a dream… like borrowed goods… like the fruit of a tree… like a butcher’s knife… like a spear and stake… like a snake’s head—having much suffering and much tribulation, and that the danger in them is greater.” Yet, even when questioned, examined, and asked for his reasons by those bhikkhus, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, adhered to that same evil wrong view, holding to it forcefully and with wrong consideration, saying: “Exactly so, friends, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them.”

235. Yato kho te bhikkhū nāsakkhiṃsu ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ [T 1.0263][P 1.0131] etasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecetuṃ, atha kho te bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “ariṭṭhassa nāma, bhante, bhikkhuno gaddhabādhipubbassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti. Assumha kho mayaṃ, bhante – ‘ariṭṭhassa kira nāma bhikkhuno gaddhabādhipubbassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, yena ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo tenupasaṅkamimha; upasaṅkamitvā ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ etadavocumha – ‘saccaṃ kira te, āvuso ariṭṭha, evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti?

235. When those bhikkhus were unable to make the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, abandon that evil wrong view, they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Once seated, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, the bhikkhu named Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, has conceived this evil wrong view: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them.’ We heard, Venerable Sir, that ‘the bhikkhu named Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, has conceived this evil wrong view: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them.”’ Then, Venerable Sir, we approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers, and said to him: ‘Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, as is rumored, that this evil wrong view has arisen in you: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to be an obstruction for one who partakes of them”’?”

“Evaṃ vutte, bhante, ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo amhe etadavoca – ‘evaṃbyākho ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ etasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecetukāmā samanuyuñjimha samanugāhimha samanubhāsimha [T 1.0264] – ‘mā hevaṃ, āvuso ariṭṭha, avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi; na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ[M 1.0184], na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Anekapariyāyenāvuso ariṭṭha, antarāyikā dhammā antarāyikā vuttā bhagavatā, alañca pana te paṭisevato antarāyāya. Appassādā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā…pe… sappasirūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo’ti. Evampi kho, bhante, ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo amhehi samanuyuñjiyamāno samanugāhiyamāno [V 1.0185] samanubhāsiyamāno tadeva pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa voharati – ‘evaṃbyākho ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’ti. Yato kho mayaṃ, bhante, nāsakkhimha ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ etasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecetuṃ, atha mayaṃ etamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocemā”ti.

“Venerable Sir, when this was said, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, said to us: ‘Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to cause obstruction for one who partakes of them.’ Then, Venerable Sir, wishing to dissuade the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, from that evil view, we questioned him, pressed him, and cross-examined him: ‘Do not say so, friend Ariṭṭha! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One! It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus. In many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, the Blessed One has described obstructive things as obstructive, and they are indeed able to obstruct one who partakes of them. The Blessed One has described sensual pleasures as providing little gratification, much suffering, and much tribulation, and that the danger in them is greater. The Blessed One has described sensual pleasures as being like a skeleton… and so on… like a snake’s head—having much suffering and much tribulation, and that the danger in them is greater.’ Yet, Venerable Sir, even as we questioned, pressed, and cross-examined him in this way, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, obstinately clung to and insisted upon that same evil view, saying: ‘Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to cause obstruction for one who partakes of them.’ When, Venerable Sir, we were unable to dissuade the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, from that evil view, we reported this matter to the Blessed One.”

236. Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ āmantehi – ‘satthā taṃ, āvuso ariṭṭha, āmantetī’”ti. “Evaṃ[P 1.0132], bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā, yena ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ etadavoca – “satthā [T 1.0265] taṃ, āvuso ariṭṭha, āmantetī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “saccaṃ kira te, ariṭṭha, evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’”ti?

236. Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu: “Come, bhikkhu, go to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, and in my name say to him: ‘The Teacher calls you, friend Ariṭṭha.’” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. He went to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, and said: “The Teacher calls you, friend Ariṭṭha.” “Yes, friend,” replied the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer. He went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, as he was sitting to one side: “Is it true, Ariṭṭha, that such an evil view as this has arisen in you: ‘This is how I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to cause obstruction for one who partakes of them’?”

“Evaṃbyākho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi – ‘yathā yeme antarāyikā dhammā vuttā bhagavatā te paṭisevato nālaṃ antarāyāyā’”ti. “Kassa kho nāma tvaṃ, moghapurisa, mayā evaṃ dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāsi? Nanu mayā, moghapurisa, anekapariyāyena antarāyikā dhammā antarāyikā vuttā? Alañca pana te paṭisevato antarāyāya. Appassādā kāmā vuttā mayā, bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… maṃsapesūpamā [M 1.0185] kāmā vuttā mayā… tiṇukkūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… supinakūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… yācitakūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… asisūnūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… sattisūlūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā… sappasirūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā, bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Atha ca pana tvaṃ, moghapurisa, attanā duggahitena [T 1.0266] amhe ceva abbhācikkhasi, attānañca khanasi, bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavasi. Tañhi te, moghapurisa, bhavissati dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.

“It is indeed so, Venerable Sir, that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not able to cause obstruction for one who partakes of them.” “Worthless man, to whom do you understand me to have taught the Dhamma in such a way? Worthless man, have I not in many ways declared obstructive things to be obstructive? And they are indeed able to cause obstruction for one who partakes of them. I have declared sensual pleasures to be of little gratification, of much suffering, and of much tribulation; the danger in them is greater. I have declared sensual pleasures to be like a skeleton, like a piece of meat, like a grass torch, like a pit of hot coals, like a dream, like borrowed goods, like fruit on a tree, like a butcher’s block, like a spear and stake, and like the head of a snake—of much suffering and of much tribulation; the danger in them is greater. And yet you, worthless man, through your own wrong grasp, not only misrepresent me but you also destroy yourself and generate much demerit. That, worthless man, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.”

Atha [V 1.0186] kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nāyaṃ ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo usmīkatopi imasmiṃ dhammavinaye”ti? “Kiñhi kiṃti (ka.) siyā, bhante; no hetaṃ, bhante”ti. Evaṃ vutte, ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo tuṇhībhūto maṅkubhūto pattakkhandho adhomukho pajjhāyanto appaṭibhāno nisīdi. Atha kho bhagavā ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ maṅkubhūtaṃ pattakkhandhaṃ adhomukhaṃ pajjhāyantaṃ appaṭibhānaṃ viditvā ariṭṭhaṃ bhikkhuṃ gaddhabādhipubbaṃ etadavoca – “paññāyissasi kho tvaṃ, moghapurisa, etena sakena pāpakena diṭṭhigatena. Idhāhaṃ bhikkhū paṭipucchissāmī”ti.

Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus? Does this bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, have even a spark of warmth in this Dhamma and Vinaya?” “How could he, Venerable Sir? No, Venerable Sir.” When this was said, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, sat silent, dismayed, with drooping shoulders, his face downcast, brooding, and at a loss for a reply. Then the Blessed One, seeing that the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, was silent, dismayed, with drooping shoulders, his face downcast, brooding, and at a loss for a reply, said to him: “You will be known by this evil view of your own, worthless man. Now, I will question the bhikkhus.”

237. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “tumhepi me, bhikkhave[P 1.0133], evaṃ dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānātha yathāyaṃ ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo attanā duggahitena amhe ceva abbhācikkhati, attānañca khanati, bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavatī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante. Anekapariyāyena hi no, bhante, antarāyikā dhammā antarāyikā vuttā bhagavatā; alañca pana te paṭisevato antarāyāya. Appassādā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā…pe… sappasirūpamā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā[T 1.0267], ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”ti. “Sādhu sādhu, bhikkhave, sādhu, kho me tumhe, bhikkhave, evaṃ dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānātha. Anekapariyāyena hi kho, bhikkhave, antarāyikā dhammā vuttā mayā, alañca pana te paṭisevato antarāyāya. Appassādā kāmā vuttā mayā[M 1.0186], bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā…pe… sappasirūpamā kāmā vuttā mayā, bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo. Atha ca panāyaṃ ariṭṭho bhikkhu gaddhabādhipubbo attanā duggahitena amhe ceva abbhācikkhati, attānañca khanati, bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavati. Tañhi tassa moghapurisassa bhavissati dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya. So vata, bhikkhave, aññatreva kāmehi aññatra kāmasaññāya aññatra kāmavitakkehi kāme paṭisevissatīti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati”.

237. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, do you also understand the Dhamma taught by me in such a way as this monk Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers’ clan, who, through his own wrong grasp, both misrepresents us and undermines himself, and generates much demerit?” “No, venerable sir. For in many ways, venerable sir, obstructive things have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive; and they are indeed sufficient to cause an obstruction for one who indulges in them. Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be of little satisfaction, of much suffering, of much tribulation, and the danger in them is greater. Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a chain of bones… and so on… Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a snake’s head, of much suffering, of much tribulation, and the danger in them is greater.” “Good, good, monks. It is good that you, monks, understand the Dhamma taught by me in such a way. For in many ways, monks, obstructive things have been declared by me, and they are indeed sufficient to cause an obstruction for one who indulges in them. Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be of little satisfaction, of much suffering, of much tribulation, and the danger in them is greater. Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a chain of bones… and so on… Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a snake’s head, of much suffering, of much tribulation, and the danger in them is greater. And yet this monk Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture-killers’ clan, through his own wrong grasp, both misrepresents us and undermines himself, and generates much demerit. That will be for that foolish man’s long-lasting harm and suffering. For, monks, that one should indulge in sensual pleasures apart from sensual desires, apart from the perception of sensual pleasures, apart from thoughts of sensual pleasures—this is not possible.”

238. “Idha, bhikkhave, ekacce moghapurisā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti – suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthaṃ, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallaṃ. Te taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññāya atthaṃ na upaparikkhanti. Tesaṃ te dhammā paññāya atthaṃ anupaparikkhataṃ [V 1.0187] na nijjhānaṃ khamanti. Te upārambhānisaṃsā ceva dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā ca. Yassa catthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti tañcassa atthaṃ [T 1.0268] nānubhonti. Tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitā dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ.

238. “Here, monks, some foolish men learn the Dhamma—discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, ‘thus-said’ discourses, birth stories, amazing things, and analytical teachings. Having learned that Dhamma, they do not investigate the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. For them, as they do not investigate the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not become clear upon reflection. They learn the Dhamma for the sake of criticizing others and for the sake of release from refutation. And they do not experience the purpose for which they learn the Dhamma. For them, those teachings, being wrongly grasped, lead to their long-lasting harm and suffering. For what reason? Because of the wrong grasp of the teachings, monks.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko alagaddagavesī alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno. So passeyya mahantaṃ alagaddaṃ. Tamenaṃ bhoge vā naṅguṭṭhe vā gaṇheyya. Tassa so alagaddo paṭiparivattitvā paṭinivattitvā (syā. ka.) hatthe vā bāhāya vā aññatarasmiṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅge ḍaṃseyya ḍaseyya (sī. pī.). So tatonidānaṃ [P 1.0134] maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā, bhikkhave, alagaddassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacce moghapurisā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti – suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthaṃ, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallaṃ. Te taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññāya atthaṃ na upaparikkhanti. Tesaṃ te dhammā paññāya atthaṃ anupaparikkhataṃ na nijjhānaṃ khamanti. Te upārambhānisaṃsā ceva dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā ca. Yassa catthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhonti. Tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitā dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Duggahitattā bhikkhave dhammānaṃ.

“Suppose, monks, a man needing a venomous snake, seeking a venomous snake, would wander in search of a venomous snake. He might see a large venomous snake and grasp it by its coils or by its tail. That venomous snake, turning back, might bite him on the hand, the arm, or on some other major or minor limb. From that cause, he would meet with death or with suffering equal to death. For what reason? Because of the wrong grasp of the venomous snake, monks. In the same way, monks, some foolish men here learn the Dhamma—discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, ‘thus-said’ discourses, birth stories, amazing things, and analytical teachings. Having learned that Dhamma, they do not investigate the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. For them, as they do not investigate the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not become clear upon reflection. They learn the Dhamma for the sake of criticizing others and for the sake of release from refutation. And they do not experience the purpose for which they learn the Dhamma. For them, those teachings, being wrongly grasped, lead to their long-lasting harm and suffering. For what reason? Because of the wrong grasp of the teachings, monks.

239. “Idha [M 1.0187] pana, bhikkhave, ekacce kulaputtā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti – suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthaṃ, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallaṃ. Te taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññāya atthaṃ upaparikkhanti. Tesaṃ te dhammā paññāya atthaṃ upaparikkhataṃ nijjhānaṃ [T 1.0269] khamanti. Te na ceva upārambhānisaṃsā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti na itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā ca na ca itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā (?). Yassa catthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti tañcassa atthaṃ anubhonti. Tesaṃ te dhammā suggahitā dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Suggahitattā bhikkhave dhammānaṃ.

239. “But here, monks, some clansmen learn the Dhamma—discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, ‘thus-said’ discourses, birth stories, amazing things, and analytical teachings. Having learned that Dhamma, they investigate the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. For them, as they investigate the meaning with wisdom, those teachings become clear upon reflection. They do not learn the Dhamma for the sake of criticizing others, nor for the sake of release from refutation. And they experience the purpose for which they learn the Dhamma. For them, those teachings, being well-grasped, lead to their long-lasting welfare and happiness. For what reason? Because of the well-grasping of the teachings, monks.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko alagaddagavesī alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno. So passeyya mahantaṃ alagaddaṃ. Tamenaṃ ajapadena daṇḍena suniggahitaṃ niggaṇheyya. Ajapadena daṇḍena suniggahitaṃ niggahitvā, gīvāya suggahitaṃ gaṇheyya. Kiñcāpi so, bhikkhave[V 1.0188], alagaddo tassa purisassa hatthaṃ vā bāhaṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ bhogehi paliveṭheyya, atha kho so neva tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Suggahitattā, bhikkhave, alagaddassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacce kulaputtā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti – suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthaṃ, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallaṃ. Te taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paññāya atthaṃ upaparikkhanti. Tesaṃ te dhammā paññāya atthaṃ upaparikkhataṃ nijjhānaṃ khamanti. Te na ceva upārambhānisaṃsā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, na itivādappamokkhānisaṃsā ca. Yassa catthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, tañcassa atthaṃ anubhonti. Tesaṃ te dhammā suggahitā dīgharattaṃ atthāya hitāya sukhāya saṃvattanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Suggahitattā, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, yassa [T 1.0270] me bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājāneyyātha, tathā naṃ dhāreyyātha. Yassa ca pana me bhāsitassa atthaṃ na ājāneyyātha, ahaṃ vo tattha paṭipucchitabbo, ye vā panāssu viyattā bhikkhū.

Just as, monks, a man wanting a venomous snake, seeking a venomous snake, wanders in search of a venomous snake. He might see a large venomous snake. He would press it down firmly with a forked stick. Having pressed it down firmly with a forked stick, he would seize it securely by the neck. Even though, monks, that venomous snake might coil around his hand or arm or any other limb with its body, still he would not thereby meet death or deadly suffering. Why is that? Because of the secure grasp of the venomous snake, monks. In the same way, monks, here some clansmen learn the Dhamma—discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, thus-saids, birth stories, amazing things, and analytical teachings. Having learned that Dhamma, they examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. As they examine the meaning with wisdom, those teachings become clear to them. They learn the Dhamma neither for the sake of criticizing others nor for the sake of escaping refutation. And they experience the purpose for which they learned the Dhamma. For them, those teachings, being well-grasped, lead to their long-lasting benefit, welfare, and happiness. Why is that? Because of the well-grasping of the teachings, monks. Therefore, monks, when you understand the meaning of what I have said, you should bear it in mind accordingly. But if you do not understand the meaning of what I have said, you should question me about it, or you should question those monks who are expert.

240. “Kullūpamaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi nittharaṇatthāya, no gahaṇatthāya. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasikarotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “seyyathāpi[M 1.0188], bhikkhave, puriso addhānamaggappaṭipanno. So passeyya mahantaṃ udakaṇṇavaṃ, orimaṃ tīraṃ sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, pārimaṃ tīraṃ khemaṃ appaṭibhayaṃ; na cassa nāvā santāraṇī uttarasetu vā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya. Tassa evamassa [P 1.0135] – ‘ayaṃ kho mahāudakaṇṇavo, orimaṃ tīraṃ sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, pārimaṃ tīraṃ khemaṃ appaṭibhayaṃ; natthi ca nāvā santāraṇī uttarasetu vā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā, kullaṃ bandhitvā, taṃ kullaṃ nissāya hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṃ uttareyya’nti. Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā, kullaṃ bandhitvā taṃ kullaṃ nissāya hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṃ uttareyya. Tassa purisassa uttiṇṇassa tiṇṇassa (pī. ka.) pāraṅgatassa evamassa – ‘bahukāro kho me ayaṃ kullo; imāhaṃ kullaṃ nissāya hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṃ uttiṇṇo. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ kullaṃ sīse vā āropetvā khandhe [T 1.0271] vā uccāretvā uccopetvā (ka.) yena kāmaṃ pakkameyya’nti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu so puriso evaṃkārī tasmiṃ kulle kiccakārī assā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Kathaṃkārī ca so, bhikkhave, puriso tasmiṃ kulle kiccakārī assa? Idha, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa uttiṇṇassa pāraṅgatassa evamassa – ‘bahukāro kho me ayaṃ kullo; imāhaṃ kullaṃ nissāya [V 1.0189] hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṃ uttiṇṇo. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ kullaṃ thale vā ussādetvā ussāretvā (ka.) udake vā opilāpetvā yena kāmaṃ pakkameyya’nti. Evaṃkārī kho so, bhikkhave, puriso tasmiṃ kulle kiccakārī assa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, kullūpamo mayā dhammo desito nittharaṇatthāya, no gahaṇatthāya. Kullūpamaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desitaṃ, ājānantehi dhammāpi vo pahātabbā pageva adhammā.

240. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma with the simile of the raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping. Listen to it and attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, Bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a person on a long journey were to see a great expanse of water, with the near shore perilous and fearful, and the far shore safe and free from fear; but there is no ferryboat or bridge for going from the near to the far shore. It would occur to him: ‘This is a great expanse of water, with the near shore perilous and fearful, and the far shore safe and free from fear; but there is no ferryboat or bridge for going from the near to the far shore. What if I were to gather grass, wood, branches, and leaves, and having tied them into a raft, and relying on that raft, striving with my hands and feet, I could cross over safely to the far shore?’ Then, bhikkhus, that person would gather grass, wood, branches, and leaves, bind them together into a raft, and relying on that raft, striving with his hands and feet, would cross over safely to the far shore. Having crossed over and reached the far shore, it would occur to that person: ‘This raft has been very helpful to me; relying on this raft, striving with my hands and feet, I have crossed over safely to the far shore. What if I were to lift this raft onto my head or carry it on my shoulder and go wherever I wish?’ What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that person, by doing so, be doing what should be done with that raft?” “No, Bhante.” “And how, bhikkhus, would that person be doing what should be done with that raft? Here, bhikkhus, having crossed over and reached the far shore, it would occur to that person: ‘This raft has been very helpful to me; relying on this raft, striving with my hands and feet, I have crossed over safely to the far shore. What if I were to haul this raft onto dry land or set it adrift in the water and go wherever I wish?’ By doing so, bhikkhus, that person would be doing what should be done with that raft. In the same way, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been taught by me with the simile of the raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping. Bhikkhus, for you who understand the Dhamma taught with the simile of the raft, even righteous things are to be abandoned, how much more so unrighteous things.”

241. “Chayimāni, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni. Katamāni cha? Idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto, rūpaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti [M 1.0189] samanupassati; vedanaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati; saññaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati; saṅkhāre ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso [T 1.0272] me attā’ti samanupassati; yampi taṃ diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ, anuvicaritaṃ manasā tampi ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati; yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ – so loko so attā, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo[P 1.0136], sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmīti – tampi ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati. Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto, rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati; vedanaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati; saññaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati; saṅkhāre ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati; yampi taṃ diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ, anuvicaritaṃ manasā, tampi ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati; yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ – so loko so attā, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmīti – tampi ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassati. So evaṃ samanupassanto asati na paritassatī”ti.

241. “Bhikkhus, there are these six grounds for views. What six? Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person, who does not see the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who does not see superior persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of superior persons, and is untrained in the Dhamma of superior persons, regards form thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ He regards feeling thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ He regards perception thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ He regards volitional formations thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ And whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and explored by the mind—that too he regards thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ And that which is a ground for views—‘That which is the world, that is the self. After death I shall be that—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I shall remain the same for all eternity’—that too he regards thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ But a learned noble disciple, bhikkhus, who sees the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who sees superior persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of superior persons, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of superior persons, regards form thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ He regards feeling thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ He regards perception thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ He regards volitional formations thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ And whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and explored by the mind—that too he regards thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ And that which is a ground for views—‘That which is the world, that is the self. After death I shall be that—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I shall remain the same for all eternity’—that too he regards thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Regarding thus, he is not agitated about what is non-existent.”

242. Evaṃ vutte, aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “siyā nu kho, bhante, bahiddhā asati paritassanā”ti? “Siyā, bhikkhū”ti – bhagavā [T 1.0273] avoca. “Idha bhikkhu ekaccassa [V 1.0190] evaṃ hoti – ‘ahu vata me, taṃ vata me natthi; siyā vata me, taṃ vatāhaṃ na labhāmī’ti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, bahiddhā asati paritassanā hotī”ti.

242. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, could there be agitation about what is external when it is non-existent?” “There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, it occurs to someone: ‘Alas, it was mine, but now it is not! Alas, may it be mine, but I do not obtain it!’ He sorrows, becomes weary, laments, beats his breast, and falls into bewilderment. Thus, bhikkhu, there is agitation about what is external when it is non-existent.”

“Siyā pana, bhante, bahiddhā asati aparitassanā”ti? “Siyā, bhikkhū”ti – bhagavā avoca. “Idha bhikkhu ekaccassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘ahu vata me, taṃ vata me natthi; siyā vata me, taṃ vatāhaṃ na labhāmī’ti. So na socati [M 1.0190] na kilamati na paridevati na urattāḷiṃ kandati na sammohaṃ āpajjati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, bahiddhā asati aparitassanā hotī”ti.

“But, venerable sir, could there be non-agitation about what is external when it is non-existent?” “There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, it does not occur to someone: ‘Alas, it was mine, but now it is not! Alas, may it be mine, but I do not obtain it!’ He does not sorrow, does not become weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into bewilderment. Thus, bhikkhu, there is non-agitation about what is external when it is non-existent.”

“Siyā nu kho, bhante, ajjhattaṃ asati paritassanā”ti? “Siyā, bhikkhū”ti – bhagavā avoca. “Idha, bhikkhu, ekaccassa evaṃ diṭṭhi hoti – ‘so loko so attā, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmī’ti. So suṇāti tathāgatassa vā tathāgatasāvakassa vā sabbesaṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānapariyuṭṭhānābhinivesānusayānaṃ samugghātāya sabbasaṅkhārasamathāya sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggāya taṇhākkhayāya virāgāya nirodhāya nibbānāya dhammaṃ desentassa. Tassa evaṃ hoti [P 1.0137] – ‘ucchijjissāmi nāmassu, vinassissāmi nāmassu, nassu nāma bhavissāmī’ti. So socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, ajjhattaṃ asati paritassanā hotī”ti.

“Venerable sir, could there be agitation about what is internal when it is non-existent?” “There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, someone holds this view: ‘That which is the world, that is the self. After death I shall be that—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I shall remain the same for all eternity.’ He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all grounds for views, determinations, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies; for the stilling of all formations; for the relinquishing of all acquisitions; for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, for Nibbāna. It occurs to him: ‘Indeed, I shall be annihilated! Indeed, I shall be destroyed! Indeed, I shall no longer exist!’ He sorrows, becomes weary, laments, beats his breast, and falls into bewilderment. Thus, bhikkhu, there is agitation about what is internal when it is non-existent.”

“Siyā pana, bhante, ajjhattaṃ asati aparitassanā”ti? “Siyā, bhikkhū”ti [T 1.0274] bhagavā avoca. “Idha, bhikkhu, ekaccassa na evaṃ diṭṭhi hoti – ‘so loko so attā, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmī’ti. So suṇāti tathāgatassa vā tathāgatasāvakassa vā sabbesaṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānapariyuṭṭhānābhinivesānusayānaṃ samugghātāya sabbasaṅkhārasamathāya sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggāya taṇhākkhayāya virāgāya nirodhāya nibbānāya dhammaṃ desentassa. Tassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘ucchijjissāmi nāmassu, vinassissāmi nāmassu, nassu nāma bhavissāmī’ti. So na socati [V 1.0191] na kilamati na paridevati na urattāḷiṃ kandati na sammohaṃ āpajjati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, ajjhattaṃ asati aparitassanā hoti”.

“But, venerable sir, could there be non-agitation about what is internal when it is non-existent?” “There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, someone does not hold this view: ‘That which is the world, that is the self. After death I shall be that—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I shall remain the same for all eternity.’ He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all grounds for views, determinations, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies; for the stilling of all formations; for the relinquishing of all acquisitions; for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, for Nibbāna. It does not occur to him: ‘Indeed, I shall be annihilated! Indeed, I shall be destroyed! Indeed, I shall no longer exist!’ He does not sorrow, does not become weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into bewilderment. Thus, bhikkhu, there is non-agitation about what is internal when it is non-existent.”

243. “Taṃ tañca (ka.), bhikkhave, pariggahaṃ pariggaṇheyyātha, yvāssa yvāssu (ka.) pariggaho nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, sassatisamaṃ tatheva tiṭṭheyya. Passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, taṃ pariggahaṃ yvāssa pariggaho nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, sassatisamaṃ tatheva tiṭṭheyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sādhu, bhikkhave. Ahampi kho taṃ, bhikkhave, pariggahaṃ na samanupassāmi [M 1.0191] yvāssa pariggaho nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṃ tatheva tiṭṭheyya.

243. “Bhikkhus, you should take up that possession, a possession that would be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and would remain just so forever. Do you, bhikkhus, see any such possession, a possession that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and would remain just so forever?” “No, venerable sir.” “Good, bhikkhus. I too do not perceive any such possession, a possession that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and would remain just so forever.”

“Taṃ, bhikkhave, attavādupādānaṃ upādiyetha, yaṃsa yassa (syā. ka.) attavādupādānaṃ upādiyato na uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, taṃ attavādupādānaṃ [T 1.0275] yaṃsa attavādupādānaṃ upādiyato na uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sādhu, bhikkhave. Ahampi kho taṃ, bhikkhave, attavādupādānaṃ na samanupassāmi yaṃsa attavādupādānaṃ upādiyato na uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā.

“Bhikkhus, you should take up that clinging to a doctrine of self, by taking up which sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise. Do you, bhikkhus, see any such clinging to a doctrine of self, by taking up which sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?” “No, venerable sir.” “Good, bhikkhus. I too do not perceive any such clinging to a doctrine of self, by taking up which sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise.”

“Taṃ, bhikkhave, diṭṭhinissayaṃ nissayetha yaṃsa diṭṭhinissayaṃ nissayato na uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā. Passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, taṃ diṭṭhinissayaṃ yaṃsa diṭṭhinissayaṃ nissayato na uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sādhu, bhikkhave. Ahampi kho taṃ, bhikkhave, diṭṭhinissayaṃ na samanupassāmi yaṃsa diṭṭhinissayaṃ nissayato [P 1.0138] na uppajjeyyuṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”.

“Bhikkhus, you should rely on that basis for views, by relying on which sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise. Do you, bhikkhus, see any such basis for views, by relying on which sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?” “No, venerable sir.” “Good, bhikkhus. I too do not perceive any such basis for views, by relying on which sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise.”

244. “Attani vā, bhikkhave, sati attaniyaṃ me ti assā”ti?

244. “Bhikkhus, if there were a self, would there be what belongs to my self?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“So it is, venerable sir.”

“Attaniye vā, bhikkhave, sati attā me ti assā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Bhikkhus, if there were what belongs to self, would there be ‘my self’?” “So it is, venerable sir.”

“Attani [V 1.0192] ca, bhikkhave, attaniye ca saccato thetato anupalabbhamāne, yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ – ‘so loko so attā, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmī’ti – nanāyaṃ na ca khoyaṃ (ka.), bhikkhave, kevalo paripūro bāladhammo’”ti?

“Bhikkhus, when a self and what belongs to a self are not found in truth and reality, then as to that standpoint for views—‘That is the world, that is the self; after death I will be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I will remain just so forever’—is this not, bhikkhus, an entirely and completely foolish doctrine?”

“Kiñhi no siyā, bhante, kevalo hi, bhante, paripūro kevalo paripūro (sī. pī.) bāladhammo”ti.

“How could it not be, venerable sir? It is, venerable sir, an entirely and completely foolish doctrine.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”[T 1.0276].

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“And what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti?

“And what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“No, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“What do you think, bhikkhus, is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ [M 1.0192] vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“And what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ [V 1.0193] panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti?

“And what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“No, venerable sir.”

“Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ, ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā[P 1.0139], oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā, hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ, ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā, hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti – evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ”.

“Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever formations… whatever consciousness—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”

245. “Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmiṃ nibbindati, vedanāya nibbindati, saññāya nibbindati, saṅkhāresu nibbindati, viññāṇasmiṃ nibbindati, nibbidā virajjati nibbindaṃ virajjati (sī. syā. pī.), virāgā vimuccati[T 1.0277], vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.
