Te tattha anupakhajja mucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā madaṃ āpajjiṃsu, mattā samānā pamādaṃ āpajjiṃsu, pamattā samānā yathākāmakaraṇīyā ahesuṃ mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmise. Evañhi te, bhikkhave, dutiyāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa [P 1.0157] iddhānubhāvā. Seyyathāpi te, bhikkhave, dutiyā migajātā tathūpame ahaṃ ime dutiye samaṇabrāhmaṇe vadāmi.

In the last month of the hot season, when grass and water were exhausted, their bodies became exceedingly emaciated. Their bodies having become exceedingly emaciated, their strength and energy diminished. With their strength and energy diminished, their freedom of mind diminished. With their freedom of mind diminished, they returned to that very sown pasture of Māra and to those worldly allurements. There, having approached them, they became infatuated and consumed those nutriments. Consuming those nutriments there with infatuation, they fell into intoxication. Being intoxicated, they fell into heedlessness. Being heedless, they became subject to Māra's will with regard to that pasture and those worldly allurements. Thus, Bhikkhus, even those second ascetics and brahmins were not freed from Māra's domain. Just as that second group of deer, Bhikkhus, so do I declare these second ascetics and brahmins to be comparable.

269. “Tatra, bhikkhave, tatiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃ samacintesuṃ – ‘ye kho te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni…pe…. Evañhi te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yepi te dutiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃ samacintesuṃ – ‘ye kho te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni…pe…. Evañhi te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ sabbaso nivāpabhojanā lokāmisā paṭivirameyyāma, bhayabhogā paṭiviratā araññāyatanāni ajjhogāhetvā vihareyyāmā’ti. Te sabbaso nivāpabhojanā lokāmisā [M 1.0212] paṭiviramiṃsu. Bhayabhogā paṭiviratā araññāyatanāni ajjhogāhetvā vihariṃsu. Te tattha sākabhakkhāpi ahesuṃ…pe… pavattaphalabhojī. Tesaṃ gimhānaṃ [V 1.0215] pacchime māse tiṇodakasaṅkhaye adhimattakasimānaṃ [T 1.0307] patto kāyo hoti. Tesaṃ adhimattakasimānaṃ pattakāyānaṃ balavīriyaṃ parihāyi, balavīriye parihīne cetovimutti parihāyi, cetovimuttiyā parihīnāya tameva nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa paccāgamiṃsu tāni ca lokāmisāni. Te tattha anupakhajja mucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjiṃsu. Te tattha anupakhajja mucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā madaṃ āpajjiṃsu, mattā samānā pamādaṃ āpajjiṃsu, pamattā samānā yathākāmakaraṇīyā ahesuṃ mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmise. Evañhi te dutiyāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni upanissāya āsayaṃ kappeyyāma, tatrāsayaṃ kappetvā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjissāma, ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā na madaṃ āpajjissāma, amattā samānā na pamādaṃ āpajjissāma, appamattā samānā na yathākāmakaraṇīyā bhavissāma mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmise”ti.

269. “Therein, monks, the third group of ascetics and brahmins reflected thus: ‘Indeed, those first ascetics and brahmins who partook of that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly enticements… thus indeed, those first ascetics and brahmins were not freed from Māra’s domain. And those second ascetics and brahmins reflected thus: “Indeed, those first ascetics and brahmins… thus indeed, those first ascetics and brahmins were not freed from Māra’s domain. What if we were to abstain completely from consuming the bait and worldly enticements? Having abstained from consuming out of fear, we should enter the wilderness areas and dwell there.” They completely abstained from consuming the bait and worldly enticements. Having abstained from consuming out of fear, they entered the wilderness areas and dwelt there. There, they were eaters of greens… they subsisted on fallen fruit. In the last month of the hot season, when grass and water were exhausted, their bodies became exceedingly emaciated. With their bodies exceedingly emaciated, their strength and energy declined. With their strength and energy declined, their mental resolve declined. With their mental resolve declined, they returned to that very bait laid out by Māra and to those worldly enticements. There, having plunged in and being infatuated, they partook of the food. While partaking of the food there, having plunged in and being infatuated, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they fell into negligence; being negligent, they became subject to Māra’s will with regard to that bait and those worldly enticements. Thus indeed, those second ascetics and brahmins also were not freed from Māra’s domain. What if we were to establish a dwelling place relying on that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly enticements? Having established a dwelling place there, we will partake of that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly enticements without plunging in and without being infatuated. While partaking of the food without plunging in and without being infatuated, we will not fall into intoxication; being unintoxicated, we will not fall into negligence; being heedful, we will not become subject to Māra’s will with regard to that bait and those worldly enticements.’”

“Te amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni upanissāya āsayaṃ kappayiṃsu. Tatrāsayaṃ kappetvā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjiṃsu. Te tattha ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā na madaṃ āpajjiṃsu, amattā samānā na pamādaṃ āpajjiṃsu, appamattā samānā na yathākāmakaraṇīyā ahesuṃ mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmise[T 1.0308]. Api ca kho evaṃdiṭṭhikā ahesuṃ – sassato loko itipi, asassato loko itipi; antavā loko itipi, anantavā loko itipi; taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīraṃ itipi, aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīraṃ itipi; hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itipi, na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itipi, hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itipi, neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itipi[P 1.0158]. Evañhi te, bhikkhave, tatiyāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā [M 1.0213] na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Seyyathāpi te, bhikkhave, tatiyā migajātā tathūpame ahaṃ ime tatiye samaṇabrāhmaṇe vadāmi.

“They established their dwelling relying on that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly enticements. Having established their dwelling there, they partook of that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly enticements without plunging in and without being infatuated. While partaking of the food there without plunging in and without being infatuated, they did not fall into intoxication; being unintoxicated, they did not fall into negligence; being heedful, they did not become subject to Māra’s will with regard to that bait and those worldly enticements. However, they became holders of such views as: ‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘The world is not eternal’; ‘The world is finite,’ or ‘The world is infinite’; ‘The soul is the same as the body,’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body another’; ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’ Thus indeed, monks, those third ascetics and brahmins also were not freed from Māra’s domain. Just as that third herd of deer, monks, so do I declare these third ascetics and brahmins to be comparable.”

270. “Tatra, bhikkhave, catutthā samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃ samacintesuṃ – ‘ye kho te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa…pe…. Evañhi te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu [V 1.0216] mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yepi te dutiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃ samacintesuṃ – ‘ye kho te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā…pe…. Evañhi te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ sabbaso nivāpabhojanā lokāmisā paṭivirameyyāma bhayabhogā paṭiviratā araññāyatanāni ajjhogāhetvā vihareyyāmā’ti. Te sabbaso nivāpabhojanā lokāmisā paṭiviramiṃsu…pe…. Evañhi te dutiyāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yepi te tatiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃ samacintesuṃ ye kho te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā [T 1.0309] …pe…. Evañhi te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yepi te dutiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃ samacintesuṃ ye kho te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā…pe…. Evañhi te paṭhamā samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ sabbaso nivāpabhojanā lokāmisā paṭivirameyyāma, bhayabhogā paṭiviratā araññāyatanāni ajjhogāhetvā vihareyyāmā’ti. Te sabbaso nivāpabhojanā lokāmisā paṭiviramiṃsu…pe…. Evañhi te dutiyāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni upanissāya āsayaṃ kappeyyāma. Tatrāsayaṃ kappetvā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjissāma, ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā na madaṃ āpajjissāma, amattā samānā na pamādaṃ āpajjissāma, appamattā samānā na yathākāmakaraṇīyā bhavissāma mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmiseti.

270. “Then, Bhikkhus, the fourth group of ascetics and brahmins considered thus: ‘Indeed, those first ascetics and brahmins… they were not freed from Māra’s power and domain. And indeed, those second ascetics and brahmins… they too were not freed from Māra’s power and domain. And indeed, those third ascetics and brahmins… they too were not freed from Māra’s power and domain. What if we were to establish our dwelling relying on that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly allurements? Having established our dwelling there, we would partake of the foods without approaching them greedily and without infatuation. Partaking of the foods without approaching them greedily and without infatuation, we would not become intoxicated. Being unintoxicated, we would not become negligent. Being heedful, we would not become beings who could be dealt with as Māra wished in regard to that bait and those worldly allurements.’”

“Te amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni upanissāya āsayaṃ kappayiṃsu. Tatrāsayaṃ kappetvā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjiṃsu. Te tattha ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā na madaṃ āpajjiṃsu. Amattā samānā [M 1.0214] na pamādaṃ āpajjiṃsu. Appamattā samānā na yathākāmakaraṇīyā ahesuṃ mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmise. Api ca kho evaṃdiṭṭhikā ahesuṃ sassato loko itipi…pe… neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itipi. Evañhi te tatiyāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā na parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ yattha agati mārassa ca māraparisāya ca tatrāsayaṃ kappeyāma. Tatrāsayaṃ kappetvā amuṃ nivāpaṃ nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni [T 1.0310] ca lokāmisāni ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjissāma, ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā na madaṃ āpajjissāma, amattā samānā na pamādaṃ āpajjissāma, appamattā samānā na yathākāmakaraṇīyā bhavissāma mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmiseti.

“They established their dwelling relying on that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly allurements. Having established their dwelling there, they partook of the foods without approaching them greedily and without infatuation. Partaking of the foods there without approaching them greedily and without infatuation, they did not fall into intoxication. Being unintoxicated, they did not fall into negligence. Being heedful, they did not become beings who could be dealt with as Māra wished in regard to that bait and those worldly allurements. Moreover, they came to hold such views as: ‘The world is eternal,’… ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’ Thus, indeed, those third ascetics and brahmins also were not freed from Māra’s power and domain. Then the thought arose: ‘What if we were to establish our dwelling in a place that is inaccessible to Māra and Māra’s retinue? Having established our dwelling there, we would partake of the foods without approaching them greedily and without infatuation. Partaking of the foods without approaching them greedily and without infatuation, we would not become intoxicated. Being unintoxicated, we would not become negligent. Being heedful, we would not become beings who could be dealt with as Māra wished in regard to that bait and those worldly allurements.’”

“Te [V 1.0217] yattha agati mārassa ca māraparisāya ca tatrāsayaṃ kappayiṃsu. Tatrāsayaṃ kappetvā amuṃ nivāpaṃ [P 1.0159] nivuttaṃ mārassa amūni ca lokāmisāni ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjiṃsu, te tattha ananupakhajja amucchitā bhojanāni bhuñjamānā na madaṃ āpajjiṃsu, amattā samānā na pamādaṃ āpajjiṃsu, appamattā samānā na yathākāmakaraṇīyā ahesuṃ mārassa amusmiṃ nivāpe amusmiñca lokāmise. Evañhi te, bhikkhave, catutthā samaṇabrāhmaṇā parimucciṃsu mārassa iddhānubhāvā. Seyyathāpi te, bhikkhave, catutthā migajātā tathūpame ahaṃ ime catutthe samaṇabrāhmaṇe vadāmi.

“There, in a place inaccessible to Māra and Māra’s retinue, they established their dwelling. Having established their dwelling there, they partook of the foods without approaching them greedily or infatuation. Partaking of the foods there without approaching them greedily or infatuation, they did not fall into intoxication. Being unintoxicated, they did not fall into negligence. Being heedful, they did not become beings who could be dealt with as Māra wished regarding that bait and those worldly allurements. Thus, Bhikkhus, these fourth ascetics and brahmins were freed from Māra’s power and domain. Just as with that fourth group of deer, Bhikkhus, so I declare these fourth ascetics and brahmins to be comparable to them.”

271. “Kathañca, bhikkhave, agati mārassa ca māraparisāya ca? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu andhamakāsi māraṃ, apadaṃ vadhitvā māracakkhuṃ adassanaṃ gato pāpimato.

271. “And how, Bhikkhus, is there a place inaccessible to Māra and Māra’s retinue? Here, Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This, Bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra, has destroyed Māra's eye leaving no trace, and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.”

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave…pe… pāpimato.

“Furthermore, Bhikkhus, with the stilling of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and is filled with rapture and happiness born of concentration. This, Bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra, has destroyed Māra's eye leaving no trace, and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.”

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti [M 1.0215] ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave…pe… pāpimato.

“Furthermore, Bhikkhus, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body—that of which the Noble Ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells happily’—he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This, Bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra, has destroyed Māra's eye leaving no trace, and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.”

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ [T 1.0311] upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave…pe… pāpimato.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and features the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra; having destroyed Māra's eye, he has become untraceable and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā [V 1.0218] nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave…pe… pāpimato.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, [thinking,] ‘Space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra; having destroyed Māra's eye, he has become untraceable and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave…pe… pāpimato.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of the sphere of infinite space, [thinking,] ‘Consciousness is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra; having destroyed Māra's eye, he has become untraceable and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma [P 1.0160] ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave…pe… pāpimato.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of the sphere of infinite consciousness, [thinking,] ‘There is nothing,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra; having destroyed Māra's eye, he has become untraceable and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave…pe… pāpimato.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of the sphere of nothingness, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra; having destroyed Māra's eye, he has become untraceable and has gone out of sight of the Evil One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati. Paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu andhamakāsi māraṃ, apadaṃ vadhitvā māracakkhuṃ adassanaṃ gato pāpimato tiṇṇo loke visattika”nti.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. And, having seen with wisdom, his taints are completely destroyed. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra; having destroyed Māra's eye, he has become untraceable and has gone out of sight of the Evil One, having crossed over the entanglement in the world.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Pleased, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Nivāpasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Nivāpa Sutta, the fifth, is concluded.

6. Pāsarāsisuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on the Mass of Snares

272. Evaṃ [M 1.0216][V 1.0219][T 1.0312] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavocuṃ – “cirassutā no, āvuso ānanda, bhagavato sammukhā dhammī kathā. Sādhu mayaṃ, āvuso ānanda, labheyyāma bhagavato sammukhā dhammiṃ kathaṃ savanāyā”ti. “Tena hāyasmanto yena rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assamo tenupasaṅkamatha; appeva nāma labheyyātha bhagavato sammukhā dhammiṃ kathaṃ savanāyā”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato ānandassa paccassosuṃ.

272. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then many bhikkhus approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they said to the Venerable Ānanda: “It has been long, friend Ānanda, since we heard a Dhamma talk in the Blessed One's presence. It would be good, friend Ānanda, if we might get to hear a Dhamma talk in the Blessed One's presence.” “In that case, venerable sirs, approach the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka; it is possible you might get to hear a Dhamma talk in the Blessed One's presence.” “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda.

Atha kho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “āyāmānanda, yena pubbārāmo migāramātupāsādo tenupasaṅkamissāma divāvihārāyā”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paccassosi. Atha [P 1.0161] kho bhagavā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ yena pubbārāmo migāramātupāsādo tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “āyāmānanda, yena [T 1.0313] pubbakoṭṭhako tenupasaṅkamissāma gattāni parisiñcitu”nti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paccassosi.

Then the Blessed One, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern Park, to Migāra's Mother's Mansion, for the day's sojourn.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the Eastern Park, Migāra's Mother's Mansion, for the day's sojourn. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from seclusion and addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Come, Ānanda, let us go to the eastern bathing place to bathe our limbs.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

273. Atha kho bhagavā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ yena pubbakoṭṭhako tenupasaṅkami gattāni parisiñcituṃ. Pubbakoṭṭhake gattāni parisiñcitvā paccuttaritvā ekacīvaro aṭṭhāsi gattāni pubbāpayamāno. Atha kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ, bhante, rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assamo avidūre. Ramaṇīyo, bhante, rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assamo; pāsādiko, bhante, rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assamo. Sādhu, bhante, bhagavā yena rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assamo tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

273. Then the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the eastern bathing place to bathe his limbs. Having bathed his limbs at the eastern bathing place and come out, he stood in one robe, drying his limbs. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, this hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka is not far. The hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka is delightful, venerable sir; the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka is lovely. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka out of compassion.” The Blessed One consented in silence.

Atha [M 1.0217][V 1.0220] kho bhagavā yena rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assamo tenupasaṅkami. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assame dhammiyā kathāya sannisinnā honti. Atha kho bhagavā bahidvārakoṭṭhake aṭṭhāsi kathāpariyosānaṃ āgamayamāno. Atha kho bhagavā kathāpariyosānaṃ viditvā ukkāsitvā aggaḷaṃ ākoṭesi. Vivariṃsu kho te bhikkhū bhagavato dvāraṃ. Atha kho bhagavā rammakassa brāhmaṇassa assamaṃ pavisitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kāyanuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā? Kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti[T 1.0314]? “Bhagavantameva kho no, bhante, ārabbha dhammī kathā vippakatā, atha bhagavā anuppatto”ti. “Sādhu, bhikkhave! Etaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ patirūpaṃ kulaputtānaṃ saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitānaṃ yaṃ tumhe dhammiyā kathāya sannisīdeyyātha. Sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ – dhammī vā kathā, ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”.

Then the Blessed One approached the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. At that time, many bhikkhus were seated together in the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka for a Dhamma discussion. Then the Blessed One stood outside the door-frame, waiting for the discussion to end. Then, when the Blessed One knew that the discussion had ended, he cleared his throat and knocked on the door-bar. Those bhikkhus opened the door for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka and sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “For what discussion were you seated together just now, bhikkhus? And what was your interrupted conversation?” “Venerable sir, our Dhamma discussion that was interrupted was about the Blessed One himself, and then the Blessed One arrived.” “Good, bhikkhus! It is fitting for you, sons of good families who have gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, that you be seated together for a Dhamma discussion. When you have gathered together, bhikkhus, there are two things to be done: either Dhamma discussion or noble silence.”

274. “Dvemā, bhikkhave, pariyesanā – ariyā ca pariyesanā, anariyā ca pariyesanā.

274. Monks, there are these two searches: the noble search and the ignoble search.

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, anariyā pariyesanā? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhammaṃyeva pariyesati, attanā jarādhammo samāno jarādhammaṃyeva [P 1.0162] pariyesati, attanā byādhidhammo samāno byādhidhammaṃyeva pariyesati, attanā maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇadhammaṃyeva pariyesati, attanā sokadhammo samāno sokadhammaṃyeva pariyesati, attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, someone who is himself subject to birth, seeks only what is subject to birth. Being himself subject to aging, he seeks only what is subject to aging. Being himself subject to illness, he seeks only what is subject to illness. Being himself subject to death, he seeks only what is subject to death. Being himself subject to sorrow, he seeks only what is subject to sorrow. Being himself subject to defilement, he seeks only what is subject to defilement.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, jātidhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, jātidhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ jātidhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ jātidhammaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ jātidhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ jātidhammaṃ, jātarūparajataṃ jātidhammaṃ. Jātidhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo. Etthāyaṃ gathito gadhīto (syā. ka.) mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to birth? Children and a wife, monks, are subject to birth; female and male slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; fowl and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. These, monks, are attachments that are subject to birth. Being greedy for, infatuated with, and overcome by these, one who is himself subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, jarādhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, jarādhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ jarādhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ jarādhammaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ [T 1.0315] jarādhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ jarādhammaṃ[M 1.0218], jātarūparajataṃ [V 1.0221] jarādhammaṃ. Jarādhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo. Etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā jarādhammo samāno jarādhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to aging? Children and a wife, monks, are subject to aging; female and male slaves are subject to aging; goats and sheep are subject to aging; fowl and pigs are subject to aging; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to aging; gold and silver are subject to aging. These, monks, are attachments that are subject to aging. Being greedy for, infatuated with, and overcome by these, one who is himself subject to aging seeks only what is subject to aging.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, byādhidhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, byādhidhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ byādhidhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ byādhidhammaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ byādhidhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ byādhidhammaṃ. Byādhidhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo. Etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā byādhidhammo samāno byādhidhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to illness? Children and a wife, monks, are subject to illness; female and male slaves are subject to illness; goats and sheep are subject to illness; fowl and pigs are subject to illness; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to illness. These, monks, are attachments that are subject to illness. Being greedy for, infatuated with, and overcome by these, one who is himself subject to illness seeks only what is subject to illness.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, maraṇadhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, maraṇadhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ maraṇadhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ maraṇadhammaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ maraṇadhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ maraṇadhammaṃ. Maraṇadhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo. Etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇadhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to death? Children and a wife, monks, are subject to death; female and male slaves are subject to death; goats and sheep are subject to death; fowl and pigs are subject to death; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to death. These, monks, are attachments that are subject to death. Being greedy for, infatuated with, and overcome by these, one who is himself subject to death seeks only what is subject to death.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, sokadhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, sokadhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ sokadhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ sokadhammaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ sokadhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ sokadhammaṃ. Sokadhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo. Etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā sokadhammo samāno sokadhammaṃyeva pariyesati.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to sorrow? Children and a wife, monks, are subject to sorrow; female and male slaves are subject to sorrow; goats and sheep are subject to sorrow; fowl and pigs are subject to sorrow; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sorrow. These, monks, are attachments that are subject to sorrow. Being greedy for, infatuated with, and overcome by these, one who is himself subject to sorrow seeks only what is subject to sorrow.

“Kiñca, bhikkhave, saṃkilesadhammaṃ vadetha? Puttabhariyaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃkilesadhammaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃ[T 1.0316], kukkuṭasūkaraṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃ, jātarūparajataṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃ. Saṃkilesadhammā hete, bhikkhave, upadhayo. Etthāyaṃ gathito mucchito ajjhāpanno attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva pariyesati. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, anariyā pariyesanā.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to defilement? Children and a wife, monks, are subject to defilement; female and male slaves are subject to defilement; goats and sheep are subject to defilement; fowl and pigs are subject to defilement; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to defilement; gold and silver are subject to defilement. These, monks, are attachments that are subject to defilement. Being greedy for, infatuated with, and overcome by these, one who is himself subject to defilement seeks only what is subject to defilement. This, monks, is the ignoble search.

275. “Katamā ca, bhikkhave, ariyā pariyesanā? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā [P 1.0163] ajātaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati, attanā jarādhammo samāno jarādhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajaraṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati, attanā byādhidhammo samāno byādhidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā abyādhiṃ anuttaraṃ [V 1.0222] yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati, attanā maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇadhamme [M 1.0219] ādīnavaṃ viditvā amataṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati, attanā sokadhammo samāno sokadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asokaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati, attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesati. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyā pariyesanā.

275. And what, monks, is the noble search? Here, monks, someone, being himself subject to birth, having known the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being himself subject to aging, having known the danger in what is subject to aging, he seeks the unaging, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being himself subject to illness, having known the danger in what is subject to illness, he seeks the illness-free, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being himself subject to death, having known the danger in what is subject to death, he seeks the deathless, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being himself subject to sorrow, having known the danger in what is subject to sorrow, he seeks the sorrowless, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being himself subject to defilement, having known the danger in what is subject to defilement, he seeks the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. This, monks, is the noble search.

276. “Ahampi sudaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddho bodhisattova samāno attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi, attanā jarādhammo samāno jarādhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi, attanā [T 1.0317] byādhidhammo samāno byādhidhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi, attanā maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇadhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi, attanā sokadhammo samāno sokadhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi, attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi, attanā jarādhammo samāno…pe… byādhidhammo samāno… maraṇadhammo samāno… sokadhammo samāno… attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva pariyesāmi? Yaṃnūnāhaṃ attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajātaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyeseyyaṃ, attanā jarādhammo samāno jarādhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajaraṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyeseyyaṃ, attanā byādhidhammo samāno byādhidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā abyādhiṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyeseyyaṃ, attanā maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā amataṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyeseyyaṃ, attanā sokadhammo samāno sokadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asokaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyeseyyaṃ, attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyeseyya’nti.

276. “Monks, before my awakening, when I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta, I too, being myself subject to birth, sought only what was subject to birth. Being myself subject to aging, I sought only what was subject to aging. Being myself subject to illness, I sought only what was subject to illness. Being myself subject to death, I sought only what was subject to death. Being myself subject to sorrow, I sought only what was subject to sorrow. Being myself subject to defilement, I sought only what was subject to defilement. Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘Why, being myself subject to birth, do I seek only what is subject to birth? Being myself subject to aging… illness… death… sorrow… defilement, do I seek only what is subject to defilement? What if I, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, were to seek the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna? Being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, were to seek the unaging, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna? Being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in what is subject to illness, were to seek the illness-free, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna? Being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, were to seek the deathless, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna? Being myself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in what is subject to sorrow, were to seek the sorrowless, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna? Being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, were to seek the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna?’”

277. “So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, aparena samayena daharova samāno susukāḷakeso[T 1.0318], bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato paṭhamena vayasā akāmakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ assumukhānaṃ rudantānaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni [M 1.0220] vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajiṃ. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno kiṃ kusalagavesī kiṃkusalaṃgavesī (ka.) anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ. Upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso kālāma, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye [V 1.0223] brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, bhikkhave, āḷāro kālāmo maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā; tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso [P 1.0164] nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca vadāmi theravādañca, ‘jānāmi passāmī’ti ca paṭijānāmi ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti; addhā āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ viharatī’ti.

277. “Then, monks, at a later time—while still young, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth in the first stage of life—I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, though my parents wished otherwise and were weeping with tearful faces. Having gone forth thus, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unexcelled, supreme state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him: ‘Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.’ When this was said, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma replied: ‘The venerable one may stay. This Dhamma is such that an intelligent person can soon realize for themselves their own teacher’s doctrine, and having attained it with direct knowledge, abide therein.’ Before long, monks, I quickly mastered that Dhamma. Monks, just to that extent, with the mere striking of the lips, with the mere act of recitation, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders. I would claim, ‘I know, I see,’ and others would claim this as well. Then this thought occurred to me: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma does not declare this Dhamma merely out of faith, saying, “I abide having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and entered upon it.” Surely, Āḷāra Kālāma abides knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’”

“Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti upasampajja pavedesīti (sī. syā. pī.)? Evaṃ vutte, bhikkhave, āḷāro kālāmo ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ [T 1.0319] pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi vīriyaṃ, mayhaṃpatthi vīriyaṃ; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi sati, mayhaṃpatthi sati; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi samādhi, mayhaṃpatthi samādhi; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ āḷāro kālāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti, tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

“Then, monks, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him: ‘Friend Kālāma, to what extent do you declare this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge and entered upon it?’ When this was said, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the sphere of nothingness. Then this thought occurred to me, monks: ‘It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith; I too have faith. It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has energy; I too have energy. It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has mindfulness; I too have mindfulness. It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has concentration; I too have concentration. It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has wisdom; I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declares he abides in, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge and entered upon it?’ Then, monks, in no long time, I quickly realized that Dhamma for myself with direct knowledge, and having entered upon it, I abode.”

“Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ –

“Then, monks, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and, having approached, said this to him:”

‘Ettāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti?

“‘Friend Kālāma, is it to this extent that you declare this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge and entered upon it?’”

‘Ettāvatā [M 1.0221] kho ahaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemī’ti.

“‘Friend, it is to this extent that I declare this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and entered upon it.’”

‘Ahampi [V 1.0224] kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti.

“‘Friend, I too, to this extent, abide, having realized this Dhamma for myself with direct knowledge and entered upon it.’”

‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi. Yaṃ tvaṃ [P 1.0165] dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā [T 1.0320] sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi, yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi. Iti yādiso ahaṃ tādiso tuvaṃ, yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso ahaṃ. Ehi dāni, āvuso, ubhova santā imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharāmā’ti. Iti kho, bhikkhave, āḷāro kālāmo ācariyo me samāno (attano) ( ) natthi (sī. syā. pī.) antevāsiṃ maṃ samānaṃ attanā attano (sī. pī.) samasamaṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva ākiñcaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

‘Friend, it is a gain for us, friend, it is a great good fortune for us, that we see such a venerable companion in the holy life. The Dhamma that I make known, having realized it for myself through direct knowledge and attained it, is the very Dhamma that you dwell in, having realized it for yourself through direct knowledge and attained it. The Dhamma that you dwell in, having realized it for yourself through direct knowledge and attained it, is the very Dhamma that I make known, having realized it for myself through direct knowledge and attained it. Thus, the Dhamma I know, you know; the Dhamma you know, I know. Thus, as I am, so are you; as you are, so am I. Come now, friend, let us both lead this group.’ Thus, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma, being my teacher, placed me, his student, on an equal footing with himself and honored me with high honor. To me, monks, this thought occurred: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna; it leads only to rebirth in the sphere of nothingness.’ So, monks, not finding that Dhamma satisfactory, I became disenchanted with it and departed.

278. “So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, kiṃ kusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena udako uddako (sī. syā. pī.) rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso āvuso rāma (sī. syā. ka.) mahāsatto rāmaputtameva avoca, na rāmaṃ, rāmo hi tattha gaṇācariyo bhaveyya, tadā ca kālaṅkato asanto. tenevettha rāmāyattāni kriyapadāni atītakālavasena āgatāni, udako ca rāmaputto mahāsattassa sabrahmacārītveva vutto, na ācariyoti. ṭīkāyaṃ ca “pāḷiyaṃ rāmasseva samāpattilābhitā āgatā na udakassā”ti ādi pacchābhāge pakāsitā, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, bhikkhave, udako rāmaputto maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā; tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho [M 1.0222] ahaṃ, bhikkhave, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca vadāmi [T 1.0321] theravādañca, ‘jānāmi passāmī’ti ca paṭijānāmi ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesi; addhā rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ vihāsī’ti.

278. “So I, monks, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, sublime state of peace, went to where Udaka Rāmaputta was. Having approached, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.’ When this was said, monks, Udaka Rāmaputta said to me: ‘The venerable one may stay. This Dhamma is such that a wise person could, in no long time, realize his own teacher's doctrine for himself through direct knowledge, and having attained it, dwell therein.’ So I, monks, in no long time, very quickly, mastered that Dhamma. So I, monks, by so much as lip-recital and repetition of what was said, spoke the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders, and I claimed, ‘I know, I see’—I myself professed this, and so did others. To me, monks, this thought occurred: ‘Rāma did not make known this Dhamma from mere faith alone, declaring, “I dwell having realized it for myself through direct knowledge and attained it.” Surely Rāma dwelt knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’”

“Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja [V 1.0225] viharāmīti pavedesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, bhikkhave, udako rāmaputto nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmasseva ahosi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho rāmasseva ahosi vīriyaṃ[P 1.0166], mayhaṃpatthi vīriyaṃ; na kho rāmasseva ahosi sati, mayhaṃpatthi sati; na kho rāmasseva ahosi samādhi, mayhaṃpatthi samādhi, na kho rāmasseva ahosi paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesi, tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

“Then, monks, I went to where Udaka Rāmaputta was. Having approached, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, to what extent did Rāma make known this Dhamma, declaring that he himself, having realized it through direct knowledge and attained it, dwelled therein?’ When this was said, monks, Udaka Rāmaputta made known the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. To me, monks, this thought occurred: ‘It was not to Rāma alone that there was faith; I too have faith. It was not to Rāma alone that there was energy; I too have energy. It was not to Rāma alone that there was mindfulness; I too have mindfulness. It was not to Rāma alone that there was concentration; I too have concentration. It was not to Rāma alone that there was wisdom; I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma made known, declaring that he himself, having realized it through direct knowledge and attained it, dwelled therein?’ So, monks, in no long time, very quickly, having realized that Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge and attained it, I dwelled therein.

“Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ –

“Then, monks, I went to where Udaka Rāmaputta was. Having approached, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta:

‘Ettāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti?

‘Friend, was it to this extent that Rāma made known this Dhamma, having personally known it by direct knowledge, realized it, and attained it for himself?’

‘Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti.

‘Indeed, friend, it was to this extent that Rāma made known this Dhamma, having personally known it by direct knowledge, realized it, and attained it for himself.’

‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ [T 1.0322] dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti.

‘Indeed, friend, I too, to this extent, having personally known this Dhamma by direct knowledge, realized it, and attained it, dwell therein.’

‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi, taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi. Yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi, taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi, yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi, taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi. Iti yādiso rāmo ahosi tādiso tuvaṃ, yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso rāmo ahosi. Ehi dāni, āvuso, tuvaṃ imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharā’ti[M 1.0223]. Iti kho, bhikkhave[V 1.0226], udako rāmaputto sabrahmacārī me samāno ācariyaṭṭhāne maṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great blessing for us, that we see such a venerable companion in the holy life. So, the Dhamma that Rāma made known, having personally known it by direct knowledge, realized it, and attained it, is the very Dhamma that you, having personally known it by direct knowledge, realized it, and attained it, dwell in. And the Dhamma that you dwell in, having personally known it by direct knowledge, realized it, and attained it, is the very Dhamma that Rāma made known, having personally known it by direct knowledge, realized it, and attained it. Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma knew by direct knowledge, you know; the Dhamma that you know, Rāma knew by direct knowledge. Thus, as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma. Come now, friend, you lead this group.’ Thus, monks, Udaka Rāmaputta, while being my companion in the holy life, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with high honor. To me, monks, this thought occurred: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna; it leads only to rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ So, monks, not finding that Dhamma sufficient, I became disenchanted with it and departed.

279. “So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, kiṃ kusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno magadhesu anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena uruvelā senānigamo tadavasariṃ. Tatthaddasaṃ [P 1.0167] ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ, pāsādikañca vanasaṇḍaṃ, nadiñca sandantiṃ setakaṃ supatitthaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, samantā sāmantā (?) ca gocaragāmaṃ[T 1.0323]. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘ramaṇīyo vata, bho, bhūmibhāgo, pāsādiko ca vanasaṇḍo, nadī ca sandati setakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā, samantā ca gocaragāmo. Alaṃ vatidaṃ kulaputtassa padhānatthikassa padhānāyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, tattheva nisīdiṃ – alamidaṃ padhānāyāti.

279. “Indeed, monks, I, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace, while wandering by stages through the land of Magadha, arrived at the market town of Senā in Uruvelā. There I saw a delightful stretch of land, an inspiring grove, a flowing river with clear water and pleasant bathing places, and a village for alms nearby. It occurred to me, monks: ‘Indeed, this stretch of land is delightful, the grove is inspiring, the river flows with clear water and pleasant bathing places, and there is a village for alms nearby. This is suitable for a clansman intent on striving.’ So, monks, I sat down right there, thinking, ‘This is suitable for striving.’”

280. “So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, attanā jātidhammo samāno jātidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajātaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesamāno ajātaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃ, attanā jarādhammo samāno jarādhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajaraṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesamāno ajaraṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃ, attanā byādhidhammo samāno byādhidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā abyādhiṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesamāno abyādhiṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃ, attanā maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā amataṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃ, attanā sokadhammo samāno sokadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asokaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃ, attanā saṃkilesadhammo samāno saṃkilesadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesamāno asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃ. Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi – ‘akuppā me vimutti, ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo’ti.

280. Indeed, monks, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, I sought the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna—and I attained it. Being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, I sought the unaging, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna—and I attained it. Being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in what is subject to illness, I sought the illness-free, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna—and I attained it. Being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, I sought the deathless, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna—and I attained it. Being myself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in what is subject to sorrow, I sought the sorrowless, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna—and I attained it. Being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, I sought the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage—Nibbāna—and I attained it. And knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Unshakable is my liberation; this is the last birth; now there is no further becoming.’

281. “Tassa [M 1.0224] mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo gambhīro duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto atakkāvacaro nipuṇo paṇḍitavedanīyo. Ālayarāmā kho panāyaṃ pajā ālayaratā ālayasammuditā. Ālayarāmā kho panāyaṃ [V 1.0227] pajā ālayaratāya ālayasammuditāya duddasaṃ idaṃ ṭhānaṃ yadidaṃ – idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo. Idampi kho ṭhānaṃ duddasaṃ yadidaṃ – sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo [T 1.0324] virāgo nirodho nibbānaṃ. Ahañceva [P 1.0168] kho pana dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, pare ca me na ājāneyyuṃ, so mamassa kilamatho, sā mamassa vihesā’ti. Apissu maṃ, bhikkhave, imā anacchariyā gāthāyo paṭibhaṃsu pubbe assutapubbā –

281. Then, monks, it occurred to me: ‘This Dhamma that I have attained is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise. But this generation delights in attachment, takes pleasure in attachment, and rejoices in attachment. For a generation that delights in attachment, takes pleasure in attachment, and rejoices in attachment, this principle is hard to see, namely, specific conditionality, dependent origination. This state, too, is hard to see, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. If I were to teach the Dhamma and others were not to understand me, that would be wearisome for me, that would be vexing for me.’ Then, monks, these amazing verses, never heard before, occurred to me:

‘Kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ;

Rāgadosaparetehi, nāyaṃ dhammo susambudho.

‘It is not fitting now to proclaim what I have realized with difficulty. This Dhamma is not easily understood by those overcome by lust and hate.

‘Paṭisotagāmiṃ nipuṇaṃ, gambhīraṃ duddasaṃ aṇuṃ;

Rāgarattā na dakkhanti, tamokhandhena āvuṭā’”ti āvaṭāti (sī.), āvutā (syā.).

‘Going against the stream, subtle, profound, hard to see, and fine; those impassioned with lust will not see it, shrouded as they are in a mass of darkness.’

282. “Itiha me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato appossukkatāya cittaṃ namati, no dhammadesanāya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, brahmuno sahampatissa mama cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya etadahosi – ‘nassati vata bho loko, vinassati vata bho loko, yatra hi nāma tathāgatassa arahato sammāsambuddhassa appossukkatāya cittaṃ namati namissati (?), no dhammadesanāyā’ti. Atha kho, bhikkhave, brahmā sahampati – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – brahmaloke antarahito mama purato pāturahosi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, brahmā sahampati ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yenāhaṃ tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā maṃ etadavoca – ‘desetu, bhante, bhagavā dhammaṃ, desetu [T 1.0325] sugato dhammaṃ. Santi sattā apparajakkhajātikā, assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti. Bhavissanti dhammassa aññātāro’ti. Idamavoca, bhikkhave, brahmā sahampati. Idaṃ vatvā athāparaṃ etadavoca –

282. Thus, monks, as I reflected, my mind inclined toward inaction, not toward teaching the Dhamma. Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, knowing with his own mind the thought in my mind, thought: ‘Alas, the world is lost! Alas, the world is destroyed! For the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines toward inaction, not toward teaching the Dhamma.’ Then, monks, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his stretched-out arm, so too Brahmā Sahampati disappeared from the Brahmā world and reappeared before me. Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward me, and said: ‘Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Well-Gone One teach the Dhamma! There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are declining from not hearing the Dhamma. There will be those who will understand the Dhamma.’ This is what Brahmā Sahampati said, monks. Having said this, he said further:

‘Pāturahosi [M 1.0225] magadhesu pubbe,

Dhammo asuddho samalehi cintito;

Apāpuretaṃ avāpuretaṃ (sī.) amatassa dvāraṃ,

Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhaṃ.

‘In Magadha there appeared in the past an impure Dhamma devised by the defiled. Open this door to the Deathless! Let them hear the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One.

‘Sele [V 1.0228] yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito,

Yathāpi passe janataṃ samantato;

Tathūpamaṃ dhammamayaṃ sumedha,

Pāsādamāruyha samantacakkhu;

Sokāvatiṇṇaṃ sokāvakiṇṇaṃ (syā.) janatamapetasoko,

Avekkhassu jātijarābhibhūtaṃ.

‘Just as one standing on a rocky mountain peak might see the people all around, so too, O wise one, O all-seeing one, ascend the palace made of Dhamma. Free from sorrow yourself, behold the people sunk in sorrow, oppressed by birth and aging.

‘Uṭṭhehi [P 1.0169] vīra vijitasaṅgāma,

Satthavāha aṇaṇa vicara loke;

Desassu desetu (syā. ka.) bhagavā dhammaṃ,

Aññātāro bhavissantī’”ti.

‘Arise, O hero, victor in battle! O caravan leader, debt-free one, wander in the world. Teach the Dhamma, O Blessed One; there will be those who understand.’

283. “Atha kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmuno ca ajjhesanaṃ viditvā sattesu ca kāruññataṃ paṭicca buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesiṃ. Addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento satte apparajakkhe [T 1.0326] mahārajakkhe, tikkhindriye mudindriye, svākāre dvākāre, suviññāpaye duviññāpaye, appekacce paralokavajjabhayadassāvine dassāvino (syā. kaṃ. ka.) viharante, appekacce na paralokavajjabhayadassāvine dassāvino (syā. kaṃ. ka.) viharante. Seyyathāpi nāma uppaliniyaṃ vā paduminiyaṃ vā puṇḍarīkiniyaṃ vā appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakānuggatāni antonimuggaposīni, appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakānuggatāni samodakaṃ ṭhitāni, appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni tiṭṭhanti (sī. syā. pī.) anupalittāni udakena; evameva kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, buddhacakkhunā [M 1.0226] lokaṃ volokento addasaṃ satte apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe, tikkhindriye mudindriye, svākāre dvākāre, suviññāpaye duviññāpaye, appekacce paralokavajjabhayadassāvine viharante, appekacce na paralokavajjabhayadassāvine viharante. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmānaṃ sahampatiṃ gāthāya paccabhāsiṃ –

283. “Then, monks, having understood Brahmā’s request and on account of my compassion for beings, I looked upon the world with the eye of a Buddha. Monks, as I looked upon the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, easy to instruct and difficult to instruct; and some dwelling who see fear in the next world and in faults, and some dwelling who do not see fear in the next world and in faults. Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or a pond of red lotuses, or a pond of white lotuses, some blue, red, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and thrive submerged within the water without rising from it; some blue, red, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand level with the water; and some blue, red, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand having risen above the water, unstained by the water. In the very same way, monks, as I looked upon the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, easy to instruct and difficult to instruct; and some dwelling who see fear in the next world and in faults, and some dwelling who do not see fear in the next world and in faults. Then, monks, I replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse:”

‘Apārutā [V 1.0229] tesaṃ amatassa dvārā,

Ye sotavanto pamuñcantu saddhaṃ;

Vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ,

Dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme’”ti.

“‘Opened for them are the doors to the Deathless, for those who have ears. Let them release their faith. O Brahmā, perceiving it as wearisome, I did not speak the proficient, excellent Dhamma among humans.’”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, brahmā sahampati ‘katāvakāso khomhi bhagavatā dhammadesanāyā’ti maṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyi.

“Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, ‘An opportunity has been made by the Blessed One for the teaching of the Dhamma,’ paid homage to me, circumambulated me to the right, and vanished right there.”

284. “Tassa [T 1.0327] mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ; ko imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho āḷāro kālāmo paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī dīgharattaṃ apparajakkhajātiko. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ āḷārassa kālāmassa [P 1.0170] paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ. So imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti. Atha kho maṃ, bhikkhave, devatā upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – ‘sattāhakālaṅkato, bhante, āḷāro kālāmo’ti. Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi – ‘sattāhakālaṅkato āḷāro kālāmo’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘mahājāniyo kho āḷāro kālāmo. Sace hi so imaṃ dhammaṃ suṇeyya, khippameva ājāneyyā’ti.

284. “Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma? Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?’ Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Āḷāra Kālāma is wise, skilled, and intelligent; for a long time he has been of a nature to have little dust. What if I were to first teach the Dhamma to Āḷāra Kālāma? He will quickly understand this Dhamma.’ Then, monks, a deity approached me and said this: ‘Venerable sir, it has been seven days since Āḷāra Kālāma passed away.’ And the knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘It has been seven days since Āḷāra Kālāma passed away.’ Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma has met with a great loss. For if he had heard this Dhamma, he would have understood it quickly.’”

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ; ko imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho udako rāmaputto paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī dīgharattaṃ apparajakkhajātiko. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ udakassa rāmaputtassa paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ. So imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti. Atha kho maṃ, bhikkhave, devatā upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – ‘abhidosakālaṅkato, bhante, udako rāmaputto’ti. Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi – ‘abhidosakālaṅkato udako rāmaputto’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘mahājāniyo kho udako rāmaputto. Sace hi so imaṃ dhammaṃ suṇeyya[M 1.0227], khippameva ājāneyyā’ti.

“Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma? Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?’ Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Udaka Rāmaputta is wise, skilled, and intelligent; for a long time he has been of a nature to have little dust. What if I were to first teach the Dhamma to Udaka Rāmaputta? He will quickly understand this Dhamma.’ Then, monks, a deity approached me and said this: ‘Venerable sir, Udaka Rāmaputta passed away last night.’ And the knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Udaka Rāmaputta passed away last night.’ Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘Udaka Rāmaputta has met with a great loss. For if he had heard this Dhamma, he would have understood it quickly.’”

“Tassa mayhaṃ[T 1.0328], bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ; ko imaṃ dhammaṃ khippameva ājānissatī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘bahukārā [V 1.0230] kho me pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū, ye maṃ padhānapahitattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ pañcavaggiyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya’nti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘kahaṃ nu kho etarahi pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū viharantī’ti? Addasaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena pañcavaggiye bhikkhū bārāṇasiyaṃ viharante isipatane migadāye. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, uruvelāyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena bārāṇasī tena cārikaṃ pakkamiṃ pakkāmiṃ (syā. pī. ka.).

“Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma? Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?’ Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘The group of five monks were of great help to me; they attended upon me when I was intent on striving. What if I were to first teach the Dhamma to the group of five monks?’ Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘Where, indeed, are the group of five monks dwelling now?’ Monks, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw the group of five monks dwelling at Bārāṇasī in Isipatana, the Deer Park. Then, monks, having dwelt in Uruvelā for as long as I wished, I set out on a journey toward Bārāṇasī.”

285. “Addasā kho maṃ, bhikkhave, upako ājīvako antarā ājīviko (sī. pī. ka.) ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhiṃ addhānamaggappaṭipannaṃ. Disvāna maṃ etadavoca – ‘vippasannāni kho te, āvuso, indriyāni, parisuddho chavivaṇṇo pariyodāto! Kaṃsi tvaṃ, āvuso, uddissa pabbajito, ko vā te satthā, kassa vā tvaṃ dhammaṃ rocesī’ti[P 1.0171]? Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, upakaṃ ājīvakaṃ gāthāhi ajjhabhāsiṃ –

285. “Monks, the Ājīvaka Upaka saw me traveling on the long road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree. Having seen me, he said this: ‘Friend, your faculties are serene, the color of your skin is pure and radiant! On account of whom have you gone forth, friend? Who is your teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you approve of?’ When this was said, monks, I addressed the Ājīvaka Upaka in verses:”

‘Sabbābhibhū sabbavidūhamasmi, sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitto;

Sabbañjaho taṇhākkhaye vimutto, sayaṃ abhiññāya kamuddiseyyaṃ.

“‘I am the all-conqueror, the all-knower, unstained in all things. I am the abandoner of all, liberated through the destruction of craving. Having known for myself through direct knowledge, whom should I point to?’”

‘Na [T 1.0329] me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati;

Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi me paṭipuggalo.

“‘I have no teacher; one equal to me does not exist. In the world with its devas, there is no counterpart to me.’”

‘Ahañhi arahā loke, ahaṃ satthā anuttaro;

Ekomhi sammāsambuddho, sītibhūtosmi nibbuto.

“‘For I am the Arahant in the world; I am the unsurpassed Teacher. I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One; I have become cooled, I am extinguished.’”

‘Dhammacakkaṃ pavattetuṃ, gacchāmi kāsinaṃ puraṃ;

Andhībhūtasmiṃ andhabhūtasmiṃ (sī. syā. pī.) lokasmiṃ, āhañchaṃ amatadundubhi’nti.

To set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma, I go to the city of the Kāsīs. In a world that has become blind, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.

‘Yathā kho tvaṃ, āvuso, paṭijānāsi, arahasi anantajino’ti!

Friend, according to your claim, you are worthy to be the Victor without end.

‘Mādisā [V 1.0231] ve jinā honti, ye pattā āsavakkhayaṃ;

Jitā me pāpakā dhammā, tasmāhamupaka jino’ti.

Victors, indeed, are those like me who have reached the destruction of the taints. Evil states have been conquered by me; therefore, Upaka, I am a victor.

“Evaṃ [M 1.0228] vutte, bhikkhave, upako ājīvako ‘hupeyyapāvuso’ti huveyyapāvuso (sī. pī.), huveyyāvuso (syā.) vatvā sīsaṃ okampetvā ummaggaṃ gahetvā pakkāmi.

When this was said, monks, the Ājīvaka Upaka said, 'It may be so, friend,' shook his head, took a divergent path, and departed.

286. “Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena bārāṇasī isipatanaṃ migadāyo yena pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamiṃ. Addasaṃsu kho maṃ, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū dūrato āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna aññamaññaṃ saṇṭhapesuṃ aññamaññaṃ katikaṃ saṇṭhapesuṃ (vinayapiṭake mahāvagge) – ‘ayaṃ kho, āvuso, samaṇo gotamo āgacchati bāhulliko bāhuliko (sī. pī.) sāratthadīpanīṭīkāya sameti padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya. So neva abhivādetabbo, na paccuṭṭhātabbo; nāssa pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Api ca kho āsanaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ, sace ākaṅkhissati nisīdissatī’ti. Yathā yathā kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, upasaṅkamiṃ tathā [T 1.0330] tathā pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū nāsakkhiṃsu sakāya katikāya saṇṭhātuṃ. Appekacce maṃ paccuggantvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahesuṃ, appekacce āsanaṃ paññapesuṃ, appekacce pādodakaṃ upaṭṭhapesuṃ. Api ca kho maṃ nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācaranti.

286. Then, monks, wandering on tour by stages, I approached Isipatana, the Deer Park at Bārāṇasī, where the group of five monks were. The group of five monks saw me coming from afar. On seeing me, they made an agreement among themselves: ‘Friends, here comes the ascetic Gotama, who lives luxuriously, has abandoned his striving, and has reverted to a life of abundance. He is not to be paid homage to, nor are we to rise for him, nor is his bowl and robe to be received. However, a seat should be prepared; if he wishes, he may sit down.’ But as I gradually approached, monks, the group of five monks were unable to abide by their own agreement. Some came forward to meet me and received my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, and some set out water for my feet. Nevertheless, they addressed me by name and with the term ‘friend.’

“Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘mā, bhikkhave, tathāgataṃ nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācaratha samudācarittha (sī. syā. pī.). Arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho[P 1.0172]. Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ, amatamadhigataṃ, ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānā nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissathā’ti. Evaṃ vutte, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘tāyapi kho tvaṃ, āvuso gotama, iriyāya tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamā uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ, kiṃ pana tvaṃ etarahi bāhulliko padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya adhigamissasi uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa’nti? Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘na, bhikkhave, tathāgato bāhulliko, na padhānavibbhanto, na āvatto bāhullāya[M 1.0229][V 1.0232]. Arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho. Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ, amatamadhigataṃ, ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānā nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā [T 1.0331] sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissathā’ti. Dutiyampi kho, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘tāyapi kho tvaṃ, āvuso gotama, iriyāya tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamā uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ, kiṃ pana tvaṃ etarahi bāhulliko padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya adhigamissasi uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa’nti? Dutiyampi kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘na, bhikkhave, tathāgato bāhulliko…pe… upasampajja viharissathā’ti. Tatiyampi kho, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū maṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘tāyapi kho tvaṃ, āvuso gotama, iriyāya tāya paṭipadāya tāya dukkarakārikāya nājjhagamā uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ, kiṃ pana tvaṃ etarahi bāhulliko padhānavibbhanto āvatto bāhullāya adhigamissasi uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa’nti?

When this was said, monks, I addressed the group of five monks thus: ‘Do not, monks, address the Tathāgata by name or with the term “friend.” The Tathāgata, monks, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Lend ear, monks, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will, before long, in this very life, having realized it for yourselves with higher knowledge, enter upon and dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.’ When this was said, monks, the group of five monks replied to me: ‘Friend Gotama, even with that conduct, that practice, those severe austerities, you did not attain any state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How then, now that you live luxuriously, have abandoned striving, and reverted to a life of abundance, could you attain any state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?’ When this was said, monks, I addressed the group of five monks thus: ‘The Tathāgata, monks, does not live luxuriously, has not abandoned striving, nor has he reverted to a life of abundance. The Tathāgata, monks, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Lend ear, monks, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will, before long, enter upon and dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life.’ A second time, monks, the group of five monks said to me: ‘Friend Gotama, even with that conduct… could you attain any state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?’ A second time, monks, I addressed the group of five monks… A third time, monks, the group of five monks said to me: ‘Friend Gotama, even with that conduct, that practice, those severe austerities, you did not attain any state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How then, now that you live luxuriously, have abandoned striving, and reverted to a life of abundance, could you attain any state superior to the human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?’

“Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū etadavocaṃ – ‘abhijānātha me no tumhe, bhikkhave, ito pubbe evarūpaṃ pabhāvitameta’nti bhāsitametanti (sī. syā. vinayepi)? ‘No hetaṃ, bhante’. ‘Arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho. Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ, amatamadhigataṃ, ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ dhammaṃ desemi. Yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamānā nacirasseva [T 1.0332] – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā [P 1.0173] upasampajja viharissathā’ti.

When this was said, monks, I said this to the group of five monks: ‘Do you acknowledge, monks, that I have ever spoken to you in such a way before this?’ ‘Certainly not, venerable sir.’ ‘The Tathāgata, monks, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Lend ear, monks, the Deathless has been attained. I instruct, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will, before long, in this very life, having realized it for yourselves with higher knowledge, enter upon and dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.’

“Asakkhiṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiye bhikkhū saññāpetuṃ. Dvepi sudaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhū ovadāmi, tayo bhikkhū piṇḍāya caranti. Yaṃ tayo bhikkhū piṇḍāya caritvā āharanti tena chabbaggiyā chabbaggā (sī. syā.) yāpema. Tayopi sudaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhū ovadāmi, dve bhikkhū piṇḍāya caranti. Yaṃ dve bhikkhū piṇḍāya caritvā āharanti tena chabbaggiyā yāpema. Atha kho, bhikkhave, pañcavaggiyā [M 1.0230] bhikkhū mayā evaṃ ovadiyamānā evaṃ anusāsiyamānā attanā jātidhammā samānā jātidhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajātaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesamānā ajātaṃ anuttaraṃ [V 1.0233] yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃsu, attanā jarādhammā samānā jarādhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā ajaraṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesamānā ajaraṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃsu, attanā byādhidhammā samānā…pe… attanā maraṇadhammā samānā… attanā sokadhammā samānā… attanā saṃkilesadhammā samānā saṃkilesadhamme ādīnavaṃ viditvā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ pariyesamānā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ nibbānaṃ ajjhagamaṃsu. Ñāṇañca pana nesaṃ dassanaṃ udapādi – ‘akuppā no [T 1.0333] vimutti akuppā nesaṃ vimutti (ka.), ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo’ti.

“Monks, I was able to instruct the group of five monks. At times, monks, I would instruct two monks while three went for alms. We, a group of six, sustained ourselves on what the three monks brought back from their alms-round. At other times, monks, I would instruct three monks while two went for alms. We, a group of six, sustained ourselves on what the two monks brought back from their alms-round. Then, monks, while the group of five monks were being instructed and advised by me in this way—being themselves subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn, unsurpassed security from the yokes, Nibbāna—they attained the unborn, unsurpassed security from the yokes, Nibbāna.
