If, friends, the internal eye is intact and external forms come into range, but there is no corresponding advertence, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness does not occur. But when, friends, the internal eye is intact, external forms come into range, and there is corresponding advertence, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness occurs. Whatever form there is for one in such a state, that form is included in the form-aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever feeling there is for one in such a state, that feeling is included in the feeling-aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever perception there is for one in such a state, that perception is included in the perception-aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever formations there are for one in such a state, those formations are included in the formations-aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever consciousness there is for one in such a state, that consciousness is included in the consciousness-aggregate subject to clinging.”

“So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evañhi kira imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ saṅgaho sannipāto samavāyo hoti. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā – ‘yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati [P 1.0191] so dhammaṃ passati; yo dhammaṃ passati so paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passatīti. Paṭiccasamuppannā kho panime yadidaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhā. Yo imesu pañcasu [M 1.0249] upādānakkhandhesu chando ālayo anunayo ajjhosānaṃ so dukkhasamudayo. Yo imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, so dukkhanirodho’ti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hoti.

He understands thus: ‘Indeed, this is how the collection, coming together, and combination of these five aggregates subject to clinging occur. For the Blessed One has said: “One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.” These five aggregates subject to clinging are, indeed, dependently arisen. Whatever desire, attachment, inclination, and holding-on there is for these five aggregates subject to clinging: this is the origin of suffering. Whatever is the removal of desire and passion, the abandoning of desire and passion for these five aggregates subject to clinging: this is the cessation of suffering.’ Even to this extent, friends, much has been done by a monk.

“Ajjhattikañceva, āvuso, sotaṃ aparibhinnaṃ hoti…pe… ghānaṃ aparibhinnaṃ hoti… jivhā aparibhinnā hoti… kāyo aparibhinno hoti… mano aparibhinno hoti, bāhirā ca dhammā na āpāthaṃ āgacchanti [T 1.0360] no ca tajjo samannāhāro hoti, neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Ajjhattiko ceva, āvuso, mano aparibhinno hoti, bāhirā ca dhammā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, no ca tajjo samannāhāro hoti, neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yato ca kho, āvuso, ajjhattiko ceva mano aparibhinno hoti, bāhirā ca dhammā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, tajjo ca samannāhāro hoti, evaṃ tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yaṃ tathābhūtassa rūpaṃ taṃ rūpupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, yā tathābhūtassa vedanā sā vedanupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, yā tathābhūtassa saññā [V 1.0252] sā saññupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati, ye tathābhūtassa saṅkhārā te saṅkhārupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, yaṃ tathābhūtassa viññāṇaṃ taṃ viññāṇupādānakkhandhe saṅgahaṃ gacchati. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evañhi kira imesaṃ pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ saṅgaho sannipāto samavāyo hoti. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā – “yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati so dhammaṃ passati; yo dhammaṃ passati so paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passatī”ti. Paṭiccasamuppannā kho panime yadidaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhā. Yo imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chando ālayo anunayo ajjhosānaṃ so dukkhasamudayo. Yo imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ so dukkhanirodho’ti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno bahukataṃ hotī”ti.

“Friends, when the internal ear is intact… and so on… the nose is intact… the tongue is intact… the body is intact… the mind is intact, but external mental phenomena do not come into range and there is no corresponding advertence, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness does not occur. Friends, when the internal mind is intact and external mental phenomena come into range, but there is no corresponding advertence, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness does not occur. But, friends, when the internal mind is intact, external mental phenomena come into range, and there is a corresponding advertence, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness occurs. Whatever form pertains to one in such a state, that is included in the aggregate of form subject to clinging. Whatever feeling pertains to one in such a state, that is included in the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging. Whatever perception pertains to one in such a state, that is included in the aggregate of perception subject to clinging. Whatever formations pertain to one in such a state, they are included in the aggregate of formations subject to clinging. Whatever consciousness pertains to one in such a state, that is included in the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. He understands thus: ‘Indeed, this is how the collection, coming together, and combination of these five aggregates subject to clinging occur. For the Blessed One has said: “One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.” These five aggregates subject to clinging are, indeed, dependently arisen. Whatever desire, attachment, inclination, and holding-on there is for these five aggregates subject to clinging: this is the origin of suffering. Whatever is the removal of desire and passion, the abandoning of desire and passion for these five aggregates subject to clinging: this is the cessation of suffering.’ Even to this extent, friends, much has been done by a monk.”

Idamavoca [T 1.0361] āyasmā sāriputto. Attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

This was said by the Venerable Sāriputta. Those monks, being delighted, rejoiced at the words of the Venerable Sāriputta.

Mahāhatthipadopamasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Great Simile of the Elephant's Footprint, the eighth discourse, is concluded.

9. Mahāsāropamasuttaṃ

9. The Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Heartwood

307. Evaṃ [T 1.0362][M 1.0250][V 1.0253][P 1.0192] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate acirapakkante devadatte. Tatra kho bhagavā devadattaṃ ārabbha bhikkhū āmantesi –

307. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, on the Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks concerning Devadatta:

“Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attānukkaṃseti paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi lābhasakkārasilokavā lābhī silokavā (sī. pī.), lābhī sakkāra silokavā (syā.), ime panaññe bhikkhū appaññātā appesakkhā’ti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati.

“Here, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and fame. He is pleased with that gain, honor, and fame, and his intention is fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he exalts himself and disparages others: ‘I am one who has gain, honor, and fame, but these other monks are unknown and of little influence.’ Due to that gain, honor, and fame, he becomes intoxicated, becomes heedless, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi [T 1.0363] sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ tathāpāyaṃ (ka.) bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto[M 1.0251], appeva nāma imassa kevalassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito [V 1.0254] samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti [P 1.0193] ‘ahamasmi lābhasakkārasilokavā, ime panaññe bhikkhū appaññātā appesakkhā’ti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sākhāpalāsaṃ aggahesi brahmacariyassa; tena ca vosānaṃ āpādi.

“Suppose, monks, a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to come upon a great, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the bark, and passing over the outer bark, he might cut off the branches and leaves and depart with them, thinking them to be heartwood. A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say: ‘This good man did not know the heartwood, did not know the sapwood, did not know the bark, did not know the outer bark, and did not know the branches and leaves. So it is that this good man, in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came upon a great, standing tree possessing heartwood, yet, passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the bark, and passing over the outer bark, he has cut off the branches and leaves and departed with them, thinking them to be heartwood. And whatever purpose was to be served by the heartwood, that purpose of his he will not accomplish.’ So too, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and fame. He is pleased with that gain, honor, and fame, and his intention is fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he exalts himself and disparages others: ‘I am one who has gain, honor, and fame, but these other monks are unknown and of little influence.’ Due to that gain, honor, and fame, he becomes intoxicated, becomes heedless, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering. This, monks, is called a monk who has grasped the branches and leaves of the holy life; and with that, he has come to an end.”

308. “Idha pana, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi [T 1.0364] paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati. Appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo, ime panaññe bhikkhū dussīlā pāpadhammā’ti. So tāya sīlasampadāya majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati.

308. “Here, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I am beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, he brings about gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased by that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his intention fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become intoxicated, does not become negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of virtue. He is pleased by that accomplishment of virtue, and his intention is fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: ‘I am virtuous, of good character, whereas these other monks are immoral, of evil character.’ On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ, papaṭikaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ [M 1.0252] atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma [T 1.0365] tacaṃ, papaṭikaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno; yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.

“Suppose, monks, a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to come upon a great, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, and passing over the bark, he might cut off the outer bark and depart with it, thinking it to be heartwood. A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say: ‘Indeed, this good man did not know the heartwood, did not know the sapwood, did not know the bark, did not know the outer bark, and did not know the branches and leaves. So it is that this good man, in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came upon a great, standing tree possessing heartwood, and passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, and passing over the bark, he has cut off the outer bark and departed with it, thinking it to be heartwood. And whatever purpose was to be served by the heartwood, that purpose of his he will not accomplish.’”

“Evameva [V 1.0255] kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā”ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati. Appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo, ime panaññe bhikkhū dussīlā pāpadhammā’ti. So tāya sīlasampadāya majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati. Ayaṃ [P 1.0194] vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu papaṭikaṃ aggahesi brahmacariyassa; tena ca vosānaṃ āpādi.

“So too, monks, here a certain clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and fame. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and fame, nor is his intention fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not become intoxicated, does not become negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of virtue. He is pleased with that accomplishment of virtue, and his intention is fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: ‘I am virtuous, of good character, whereas these other monks are immoral, of evil character.’ On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering. This, monks, is called a monk who has grasped the outer bark of the holy life; and with that, he has come to an end.”

309. “Idha pana, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi [T 1.0366] paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati. Appamatto samāno samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti[M 1.0253]. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi samāhito ekaggacitto, ime panaññe bhikkhū asamāhitā vibbhantacittā’ti. So tāya samādhisampadāya majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati.

309. Here in this Dispensation, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I am beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, he brings about gain, honor, and renown. He is not gladdened by that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become intoxicated, he does not become negligent, he does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of virtue. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of virtue, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, he does not become negligent, he does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of concentration. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of concentration, and his aspiration is fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of concentration, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: ‘I am concentrated, with a mind of single-pointed focus, whereas these other monks are unconcentrated, with agitated minds.’ On account of that accomplishment of concentration, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering.

“Seyyathāpi[V 1.0256], bhikkhave, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ tacaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ[T 1.0367], na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ tacaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.

Monks, it is like a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, who would come upon a great, standing tree possessed of heartwood. He would pass right over the heartwood, pass over the sapwood, cut the bark, and take it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say thus: ‘Indeed, this good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know bark, did not know the outer crust, did not know branches and leaves. So it is that this good man, in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came upon a great, standing tree possessed of heartwood, yet passed right over the heartwood, passed over the sapwood, cut the bark, and departed with it, thinking, “This is heartwood.” And whatever purpose was to be served by the heartwood, that purpose of his he will not accomplish.’

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā”ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi [T 1.0368] samāhito ekaggacitto, ime panaññe bhikkhū asamāhitā vibbhantacittā’ti. So tāya [M 1.0254] samādhisampadāya majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati[P 1.0195], bhikkhave, bhikkhu tacaṃ aggahesi brahmacariyassa; tena ca vosānaṃ āpādi.

So it is, monks, that in this Dispensation a certain clansman goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I am beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is not gladdened by that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of virtue. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of virtue, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of concentration. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of concentration, and his aspiration is fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of concentration, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: ‘I am concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, but these other monks are unconcentrated, with distracted minds.’ On account of that accomplishment of concentration, he becomes intoxicated, is negligent, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering. This, monks, is called a monk who has grasped the bark of the holy life; and with that, he has settled for that attainment.

310. “Idha pana, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa [V 1.0257] antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati. Appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya na majjati nappamajjati [T 1.0369] na pamādaṃ āpajjati appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena ñāṇadassanena attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi jānaṃ passaṃ viharāmi. Ime panaññe bhikkhū ajānaṃ apassaṃ viharantī’ti. So tena ñāṇadassanena majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati.

310. “Here, bhikkhus, a certain clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am overwhelmed by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I am overwhelmed by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he accomplishes the perfection of virtue. He is pleased with that perfection of virtue, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. Because of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that perfection of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he accomplishes the perfection of concentration. He is pleased with that perfection of concentration, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. Because of that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that perfection of concentration, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he accomplishes knowledge and vision. He is pleased with that knowledge and vision, and his aspiration is fulfilled. Because of that knowledge and vision, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: ‘I dwell knowing and seeing, but these other bhikkhus dwell not knowing and not seeing.’ Because of that knowledge and vision, he becomes intoxicated, is negligent, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ phegguṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ na aññāsi phegguṃ na aññāsi tacaṃ na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa [M 1.0255] tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ phegguṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti. Evameva [P 1.0196] kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena [T 1.0370] na attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So [V 1.0258] tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena ñāṇadassanena attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi jānaṃ passaṃ viharāmi, ime panaññe bhikkhū ajānaṃ apassaṃ viharantī’ti. So tena ñāṇadassanena majjati pamajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati, pamatto samāno dukkhaṃ viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu phegguṃ aggahesi brahmacariyassa; tena ca vosānaṃ āpādi.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to come to a great standing tree possessed of heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, he might cut away the sapwood and take it away, thinking it to be heartwood. A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘Indeed, this good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know bark, did not know outer bark, did not know branches and leaves. Thus this good man, in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, yet passed over the heartwood, cut away the sapwood, and departed with it, thinking it to be heartwood. Whatever was to be done with heartwood, he will not accomplish that purpose.’ So too, bhikkhus, a certain clansman goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am overwhelmed by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I am overwhelmed by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he accomplishes the perfection of virtue. He is pleased with that perfection of virtue, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. Because of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that perfection of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he accomplishes the perfection of concentration. He is pleased with that perfection of concentration, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. Because of that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that perfection of concentration, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he accomplishes knowledge and vision. He is pleased with that knowledge and vision, and his aspiration is fulfilled. Because of that knowledge and vision, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: ‘I dwell knowing and seeing, but these other bhikkhus dwell not knowing and not seeing.’ Because of that knowledge and vision, he becomes intoxicated, is negligent, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has grasped the sapwood of the holy life; and with that, he has reached a conclusion.

311. “Idha pana, bhikkhave, ekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi [T 1.0371] paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti[M 1.0256], na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena ñāṇadassanena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno asamayavimokkhaṃ [V 1.0259] ārādheti. Aṭṭhānametaṃ aṭṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ (ka.), bhikkhave, anavakāso yaṃ so bhikkhu tāya asamayavimuttiyā parihāyetha.

311. Here, bhikkhus, some clansman goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, he brings about gain, honor, and renown. He is not gladdened by that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of virtue. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of virtue, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of concentration. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of concentration, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that accomplishment of concentration, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that accomplishment of concentration, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains knowledge and vision. He is gladdened by that knowledge and vision, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that knowledge and vision, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that knowledge and vision, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains timeless liberation. It is impossible, bhikkhus, it is not possible that that bhikkhu would fall away from that timeless liberation.

“Seyyathāpi[T 1.0372], bhikkhave, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraññeva chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘aññāsi vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāraṃ, aññāsi phegguṃ, aññāsi tacaṃ, aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato [P 1.0197] rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraññeva chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ anubhavissatī’ti.

Suppose, bhikkhus, a man in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to come upon a great, standing tree possessed of heartwood, and he were to cut just the heartwood and depart with it, knowing it to be heartwood. A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘Indeed, this good man knew heartwood, knew sapwood, knew bark, knew outer bark, and knew branches and leaves. Thus this good man, in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came upon a great, standing tree possessed of heartwood, cut just the heartwood, and departed with it, knowing it to be heartwood. And whatever was to be done with heartwood, he will accomplish that purpose.’

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco kulaputto saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So [M 1.0257] evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti, na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya na majjati nappamajjati [T 1.0373] na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena ñāṇadassanena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena na majjati nappamajjati na pamādaṃ āpajjati, appamatto samāno asamayavimokkhaṃ [V 1.0260] ārādheti. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso yaṃ so bhikkhu tāya asamayavimuttiyā parihāyetha.

So it is, bhikkhus. Here a certain clansman goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, he brings about gain, honor, and renown. He is not gladdened by that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of virtue. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of virtue, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains the accomplishment of concentration. He is gladdened by that accomplishment of concentration, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that accomplishment of concentration, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that accomplishment of concentration, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains knowledge and vision. He is gladdened by that knowledge and vision, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that knowledge and vision, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that knowledge and vision, he does not become intoxicated, is not negligent, and does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains timeless liberation. It is impossible, bhikkhus, it is not possible that that bhikkhu would fall away from that timeless liberation.

“Iti kho, bhikkhave, nayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsaṃ, na sīlasampadānisaṃsaṃ, na samādhisampadānisaṃsaṃ, na ñāṇadassanānisaṃsaṃ. Yā ca kho ayaṃ, bhikkhave, akuppā cetovimutti – etadatthamidaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ, etaṃ sāraṃ etaṃ pariyosāna”nti.

Thus, bhikkhus, this holy life is not for the sake of the benefit of gain, honor, and renown; it is not for the sake of the benefit of the accomplishment of virtue; it is not for the sake of the benefit of the accomplishment of concentration; it is not for the sake of the benefit of knowledge and vision. But, bhikkhus, that which is the unshakeable liberation of mind—for this purpose, bhikkhus, is this holy life. This is its essence, this is its culmination.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Pleased, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

Mahāsāropamasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The ninth, the Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Heartwood, is concluded.

10. Cūḷasāropamasuttaṃ

10. The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Heartwood

312. Evaṃ [T 1.0374][V 1.0261][P 1.0198] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo yena [M 1.0258] bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “yeme, bho gotama, samaṇabrāhmaṇā saṅghino gaṇino gaṇācariyā ñātā yasassino titthakarā sādhusammatā, bahujanassa, seyyathidaṃ – pūraṇo kassapo, makkhali gosālo, ajito kesakambalo, pakudho kaccāyano, sañcayo sañjayo (sī. syā. pī. ka.) belaṭṭhaputto, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto, sabbete sakāya paṭiññāya abbhaññaṃsu sabbeva nābbhaññaṃsu, udāhu ekacce abbhaññaṃsu ekacce nābbhaññaṃsū”ti? “Alaṃ, brāhmaṇa, tiṭṭhatetaṃ – sabbete sakāya paṭiññāya abbhaññaṃsu sabbeva nābbhaññaṃsu, udāhu ekacce abbhaññaṃsu ekacce nābbhaññaṃsūti. Dhammaṃ te, brāhmaṇa, desessāmi, taṃ suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

312. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging pleasant and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Gotama, those ascetics and brahmins who are leaders of orders, heads of groups, and teachers of groups, well-known and famous, founders of sects, regarded as worthy by many people—such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, and Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta—did all of them, by their own declaration, attain full knowledge, or did none of them attain it? Or did some attain it and some not?” “Enough, brahmin, let this be: ‘Did all of them, by their own declaration, attain full knowledge, or did none of them attain it? Or did some attain it and some not?’ I shall teach you the Dhamma, brahmin. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

313. “Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ [T 1.0375] atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.

313. “Suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, should come to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, passing over the outer bark, he would cut off the branches and leaves and take them away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘Surely, this good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know inner bark, did not know outer bark, and did not know branches and leaves. So it is that this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, passing over the outer bark, he cut off the branches and leaves and has taken them away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ And whatever purpose was to be served by the heartwood, that purpose he will not accomplish.’”

314. “Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno [V 1.0262] mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ[P 1.0199], papaṭikaṃ chetvā ādāya [M 1.0259] pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ papaṭikaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.

314. “Or suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, should come to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, he would cut off the outer bark and take it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘Surely, this good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know inner bark, did not know outer bark, and did not know branches and leaves. So it is that this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, he cut off the outer bark and has taken it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ And whatever purpose was to be served by the heartwood, that purpose he will not accomplish.’”

315. “Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato [T 1.0376] sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ, tacaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ, tacaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.

315. “Or suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, should come to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, he would cut off the inner bark and take it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘Surely, this good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know inner bark, did not know outer bark, and did not know branches and leaves. So it is that this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, he cut off the inner bark and has taken it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ And whatever purpose was to be served by the heartwood, that purpose he will not accomplish.’”

316. “Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ, phegguṃ chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘na vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso aññāsi sāraṃ, na aññāsi phegguṃ, na aññāsi tacaṃ, na aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, na aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ, phegguṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissatī’ti.

316. “Or suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, should come to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, he would cut off the sapwood and take it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ A man with vision, seeing him, would say: ‘Surely, this good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know inner bark, did not know outer bark, and did not know branches and leaves. So it is that this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a large, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, he cut off the sapwood and has taken it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’ And whatever purpose was to be served by the heartwood, that purpose he will not accomplish.’”

317. “Seyyathāpi vā pana, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno [V 1.0263] mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraññeva [M 1.0260] chetvā ādāya pakkameyya ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā[T 1.0377] puriso disvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘aññāsi vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāraṃ, aññāsi phegguṃ, aññāsi tacaṃ, aññāsi papaṭikaṃ, aññāsi sākhāpalāsaṃ. Tathā hayaṃ bhavaṃ puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraññeva chetvā ādāya [P 1.0200] pakkanto ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ anubhavissatī’ti.

317. Or again, brahmin, suppose a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, should come to a great, standing tree endowed with heartwood. He would cut off just the heartwood and take it away, knowing, ‘This is heartwood.’ A discerning man, seeing him, would say: ‘Surely, this good man knows heartwood, knows sapwood, knows inner bark, knows outer bark, and knows branches and leaves. Thus, this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great, standing tree endowed with heartwood. He cut off just the heartwood and has taken it away, knowing, ‘This is heartwood.’ And whatever is to be done with the heartwood, he will accomplish that purpose.’”

318. “Evameva kho, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco puggalo saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi lābhasakkārasilokavā, ime panaññe bhikkhū appaññātā appesakkhā’ti. Lābhasakkārasilokena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya na chandaṃ janeti, na vāyamati, olīnavuttiko ca hoti sāthaliko. Seyyathāpi so, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ atikkamma papaṭikaṃ, sākhāpalāsaṃ chetvā [T 1.0378] ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi.

318. “Just so, brahmin, some person here goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. I am beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. If only an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned!’ Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, and his aspiration is fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he exalts himself and disparages others: ‘I possess gain, honor, and renown, but these other monks are unknown and of little influence.’ Because of gain, honor, and renown, he does not generate desire nor make an effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime; he becomes sluggish and lax in his conduct. It is as if that man, brahmin, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passed over the heartwood of a great, standing tree possessing heartwood, and also passed over the sapwood, the inner bark, and the outer bark, and cutting off the branches and leaves, took them away, thinking them to be heartwood. And whatever is to be done with the heartwood, he will not accomplish that purpose. I say, brahmin, that this person is comparable to that man.”

319. “Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na [M 1.0261] attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Lābhasakkārasilokena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati[V 1.0264], anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo, ime panaññe bhikkhū dussīlā pāpadhammā’ti. Sīlasampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ [P 1.0201] sacchikiriyāya na chandaṃ janeti, na vāyamati, olīnavuttiko ca hoti sāthaliko. Seyyathāpi so, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī [T 1.0379] sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ atikkamma tacaṃ, papaṭikaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ, tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi.

319. “Here, brahmin, some person goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. I am beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. If only an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. He generates desire and makes an effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime than gain, honor, and renown; and he is ardent and not lax in his conduct. He achieves accomplishment in virtue. He is pleased with that accomplishment in virtue, and his aspiration is fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment in virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others: ‘I am virtuous, of good character, but these other monks are immoral, of bad character.’ Because of his accomplishment in virtue, he does not generate desire or make an effort for the realization of those other states that are higher and more sublime; and he becomes sluggish and lax in his conduct. Suppose, brahmin, a man in need of heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, comes across a great, standing tree with heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, and passing over the inner bark, he cuts off the outer bark and takes it away, thinking, ‘This is heartwood!’ Whatever is to be done with the heartwood, he will not accomplish that purpose. I say, brahmin, that this person is comparable to that man.”

320. “Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto, appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti, na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Lābhasakkārasilokena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Sīlasampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko[M 1.0262]. So samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti, paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi samāhito ekaggacitto, ime panaññe bhikkhū [T 1.0380] asamāhitā vibbhantacittā’ti. Samādhisampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca, tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya na chandaṃ janeti, na vāyamati, olīnavuttiko ca hoti sāthaliko. Seyyathāpi so, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ atikkamma phegguṃ, tacaṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa [V 1.0265] sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi.

320. Here, brahmin, a certain person goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: 'I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. I am beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. If only an end to this entire mass of suffering could be discerned!' Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and fame. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and fame, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. For the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than gain, honor, and fame, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unshrinking disposition, and is not lax. He achieves the accomplishment of virtue. He is pleased with that accomplishment of virtue, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. For the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than the accomplishment of virtue, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unshrinking disposition, and is not lax. He achieves the accomplishment of concentration. He is pleased with that accomplishment of concentration, and his aspiration is fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of concentration, he exalts himself and disparages others, saying: 'I am concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, but these other monks are unconcentrated, with scattered minds.' For the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than the accomplishment of concentration, he does not generate desire, does not make an effort, is of a shrinking disposition, and is lax. Suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to come upon a great, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood and passing over the sapwood, he would cut off the bark, take it away, and depart, thinking it to be heartwood. And whatever purpose could be served by heartwood, that purpose of his he would not accomplish. Brahmin, I say this person is of such a likeness.

321. “Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena…pe… [P 1.0202] antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Lābhasakkārasilokena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Sīlasampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Samādhisampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ [T 1.0381] sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena attamano hoti, paripuṇṇasaṅkappo[M 1.0263]. So tena ñāṇadassanena attānukkaṃseti, paraṃ vambheti – ‘ahamasmi jānaṃ passaṃ viharāmi, ime panaññe bhikkhū ajānaṃ apassaṃ viharantī’ti. Ñāṇadassanena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya na chandaṃ janeti, na vāyamati, olīnavuttiko ca hoti sāthaliko. Seyyathāpi so, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato atikkammeva sāraṃ, phegguṃ chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti maññamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ nānubhavissati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi.

321. Here, brahmin, a certain person goes forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: 'I am beset by birth, aging, and death… If only an end to this entire mass of suffering could be discerned!' Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and fame. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and fame, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. For the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than gain, honor, and fame, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unshrinking disposition, and is not lax. He achieves the accomplishment of virtue. He is pleased with that accomplishment of virtue, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. For the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than the accomplishment of virtue, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unshrinking disposition, and is not lax. He achieves the accomplishment of concentration. He is pleased with that accomplishment of concentration, but his aspiration is not yet fulfilled. On account of that accomplishment of concentration, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. For the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than the accomplishment of concentration, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unshrinking disposition, and is not lax. He achieves knowledge and vision. He is pleased with that knowledge and vision, and his aspiration is fulfilled. On account of that knowledge and vision, he exalts himself and disparages others, saying: 'I dwell knowing and seeing, but these other monks dwell unknowing and unseeing.' For the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision, he does not generate desire, does not make an effort, is of a shrinking disposition, and is lax. Suppose, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to come upon a great, standing tree possessing heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, he would cut off the sapwood, take it away, and depart, thinking it to be heartwood. And whatever purpose could be served by heartwood, that purpose of his he would not accomplish. Brahmin, I say this person is of such a likeness.

322. “Idha pana, brāhmaṇa, ekacco puggalo saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti – ‘otiṇṇomhi jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi[V 1.0266], dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto[T 1.0382], appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno [P 1.0203] lābhasakkārasilokaṃ abhinibbatteti. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attamano hoti, na paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena lābhasakkārasilokena na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Lābhasakkārasilokena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So sīlasampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya sīlasampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya sīlasampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Sīlasampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So samādhisampadaṃ ārādheti. So tāya samādhisampadāya attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tāya samādhisampadāya na attānukkaṃseti, na paraṃ vambheti. Samādhisampadāya ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko. So ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādheti. So tena ñāṇadassanena attamano hoti, no ca kho paripuṇṇasaṅkappo. So tena ñāṇadassanena na attānukkaṃseti, na [M 1.0264] paraṃ vambheti. Ñāṇadassanena ca ye aññe dhammā uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā [T 1.0383] ca tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sacchikiriyāya chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, anolīnavuttiko ca hoti asāthaliko.

322. Here, Brahmin, a certain person goes forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I am beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’ Having thus gone forth, he brings about gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. And for the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than gain, honor, and renown, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unflagging disposition, and is not lax. He attains the accomplishment of virtue. He is pleased with that accomplishment of virtue, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that accomplishment of virtue, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. And for the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than the accomplishment of virtue, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unflagging disposition, and is not lax. He attains the accomplishment of concentration. He is pleased with that accomplishment of concentration, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that accomplishment of concentration, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. And for the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than the accomplishment of concentration, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unflagging disposition, and is not lax. He attains knowledge and vision. He is pleased with that knowledge and vision, but his aspiration is not fulfilled. Because of that knowledge and vision, he does not exalt himself or disparage others. And for the realization of other states that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision, he generates desire, makes an effort, is of unflagging disposition, and is not lax.

323. “Katame ca, brāhmaṇa, dhammā ñāṇadassanena uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca? Idha, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

323. And what, Brahmin, are the states that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision? Here, Brahmin, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, with the subsiding of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno [V 1.0267] sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho[P 1.0204], brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body. He enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells happily.’ This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is without pain and pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, a bhikkhu, thinking, ‘Space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, a bhikkhu, thinking, ‘Consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Furthermore, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking, ‘There is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. Furthermore, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, a bhikkhu, perceiving ‘There is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna [M 1.0265] caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca [T 1.0384] paṇītataro ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Ayampi kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammo ñāṇadassanena uttaritaro ca paṇītataro ca. Ime kho, brāhmaṇa, dhammā ñāṇadassanena uttaritarā ca paṇītatarā ca.

Furthermore, Brahmin, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. And having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This, too, Brahmin, is a state that is higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision. These, Brahmin, are the states that are higher and more sublime than knowledge and vision.

324. “Seyyathāpi [V 1.0268] so, brāhmaṇa, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāraṃyeva chetvā ādāya pakkanto ‘sāra’nti jānamāno. Yañcassa sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ tañcassa atthaṃ anubhavissati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi.

324. “Brahmin, it is like a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, who would come to a great, standing tree possessing heartwood. Knowing it to be heartwood, he would cut away only the heartwood, take it, and depart. And whatever was to be accomplished with heartwood, he would achieve that purpose. Brahmin, I say this person is comparable to that.

“Iti kho, brāhmaṇa, nayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsaṃ, na sīlasampadānisaṃsaṃ, na samādhisampadānisaṃsaṃ, na ñāṇadassanānisaṃsaṃ. Yā ca kho ayaṃ[P 1.0205], brāhmaṇa, akuppā cetovimutti – etadatthamidaṃ, brāhmaṇa, brahmacariyaṃ, etaṃ sāraṃ etaṃ pariyosāna”nti.

“So, Brahmin, this holy life is not for the benefit of gains, honor, and renown; it is not for the benefit of the accomplishment of virtue; it is not for the benefit of the accomplishment of concentration; it is not for the benefit of knowledge and vision. But, Brahmin, this unshakeable liberation of mind—this is the purpose of this holy life, this is its essence, this is its final goal.”

Evaṃ vutte, piṅgalakoccho brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama…pe… upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

When this was said, the brahmin Piṅgalakoccha said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! … May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life, from this day forward.”

Cūḷasāropamasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Heartwood, the tenth, is concluded.

Opammavaggo niṭṭhito tatiyo.

The Chapter of Similes, the third, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for this is:

Moḷiyaphaggunariṭṭhañca [T 1.0385] nāmo, andhavane kathipuṇṇaṃ nivāpo;

Rāsikaṇerumahāgajanāmo, sārūpamo sāravaro (syā.), sāravano (ka.) puna piṅgalakoccho.

The Kakacūpama, the Alagaddūpama, the Vammika, the Rathavinīta, the Nivāpa, the Pāsarāsi, the Cūḷahatthipadopama, the Mahāhatthipadopama, the Mahāsāropama, and the Cūḷasāropama.

4. Mahāyamakavaggo

4. The Great Chapter of Pairs

1. Cūḷagosiṅgasuttaṃ

1. The Shorter Gosiṅga Discourse

325. Evaṃ [M 1.0266][V 1.0269][T 1.0386] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā nātike nādike (sī. syā. pī.), ñātike (ka.) viharati giñjakāvasathe. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā ca anuruddho āyasmā ca nandiyo āyasmā ca kimilo kimbilo (sī. pī. ka.) gosiṅgasālavanadāye viharanti. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena gosiṅgasālavanadāyo tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho dāyapālo bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “mā, samaṇa, etaṃ dāyaṃ pāvisi. Santettha tayo kulaputtā attakāmarūpā viharanti. Mā tesaṃ aphāsumakāsī”ti.

325. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nātika in the Brick Hall. At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sāla-wood Grove. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One arose from seclusion and approached the Gosiṅga Sāla-wood Grove. The grove keeper saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One: “Do not enter this grove, recluse. There are three clansmen dwelling here, intent on their own welfare. Do not cause them discomfort.”

Assosi kho āyasmā anuruddho dāyapālassa bhagavatā saddhiṃ mantayamānassa. Sutvāna dāyapālaṃ etadavoca – “mā, āvuso dāyapāla, bhagavantaṃ vāresi. Satthā no bhagavā anuppatto”ti. Atha kho āyasmā anuruddho yenāyasmā ca nandiyo āyasmā ca kimilo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantañca nandiyaṃ āyasmantañca kimilaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkamathāyasmanto, abhikkamathāyasmanto, satthā no bhagavā [P 1.0206] anuppatto”ti. Atha [T 1.0387] kho āyasmā ca anuruddho āyasmā ca nandiyo āyasmā ca kimilo bhagavantaṃ paccuggantvā – eko bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahesi, eko āsanaṃ paññapesi, eko pādodakaṃ upaṭṭhāpesi. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nisajja kho bhagavā pāde pakkhālesi. Tepi kho āyasmanto bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ bhagavā etadavoca –

The Venerable Anuruddha heard the grove keeper conversing with the Blessed One. Having heard, he said this to the grove keeper: “Friend grove keeper, do not hinder the Blessed One. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.” Then the Venerable Anuruddha went to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimbila. Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimbila: “Come forth, venerable sirs, come forth! Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.” Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila went to meet the Blessed One.
