When he hears a sound with the ear... smells an odor with the nose... tastes a flavor with the tongue... feels a tactile object with the body... cognizes a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary features. Inasmuch as, if he were to dwell with the mind faculty unguarded, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail him, he practices for its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. In this way, monks, a bhikkhu is one who covers a wound.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhūmaṃ kattā hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ desetā hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhūmaṃ kattā hoti.

“And how, monks, is a bhikkhu one who makes smoke? Here, monks, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to others in detail, just as he has heard it and learned it. In this way, monks, a bhikkhu is one who makes smoke.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu titthaṃ jānāti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ye te bhikkhū bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammadharā vinayadharā mātikādharā te kālena kālaṃ [T 1.0416] upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati, paripañhati – ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ? Imassa ko attho’ti? Tassa te āyasmanto avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttānī karonti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhāṭhānīyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu titthaṃ jānāti.

And how, monks, does a monk know the ford? Here, monks, a monk approaches from time to time those monks who are learned, who have mastered the traditions, who are upholders of the Dhamma, upholders of the Vinaya, and upholders of the matrices, and he questions and inquires of them: ‘Venerable sirs, how is this? What is its meaning?’ Then those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been made clear, and dispel his doubt concerning the various points that occasion doubt. It is in this way, monks, that a monk knows the ford.

“Kathañca bhikkhave, bhikkhu [P 1.0224] pītaṃ jānāti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye desiyamāne labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pītaṃ jānāti.

And how, monks, does a monk know that he has drunk? Here, monks, when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a monk gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. It is in this way, monks, that a monk knows that he has drunk.

“Kathañca[M 1.0286], bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīthiṃ jānāti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīthiṃ jānāti.

And how, monks, does a monk know the path? Here, monks, a monk understands the Noble Eightfold Path as it really is. In this way, monks, a monk knows the path.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gocarakusalo hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāro satipaṭṭhāne yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gocarakusalo hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk skilled in his range? Here, monks, a monk understands the four foundations of mindfulness as they really are. In this way, monks, a monk is skilled in his range.

“Kathañca [V 1.0289] bhikkhave, bhikkhu sāvasesadohī hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṃ saddhā gahapatikā abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavārenti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi. Tatra bhikkhu mattaṃ jānāti paṭiggahaṇāya. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sāvasesadohī hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk one who milks leaving a remainder? Here, monks, faithful householders invite him to accept robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. Therein, the monk knows the proper measure in accepting. Thus, monks, is a monk one who milks leaving a remainder.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ye te bhikkhū therā rattaññū cirapabbajitā saṅghapitaro saṅghapariṇāyakā, te atirekapūjāya pūjetā hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ye te bhikkhū therā rattaññū cirapabbajitā saṅghapitaro saṅghapariṇāyakā tesu mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti āvi ceva raho [T 1.0417] ca; mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti āvi ceva raho ca; mettaṃ manokammaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti āvi ceva raho ca. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ye te bhikkhū therā rattaññū cirapabbajitā saṅghapitaro saṅghapariṇāyakā te atirekapūjāya pūjetā hoti.

And how, monks, does a monk honor with exceeding honor those monks who are elders, of long standing, long-ordained, fathers of the Saṅgha, leaders of the Saṅgha? Here, monks, a monk directs bodily acts of loving-kindness toward those monks who are elders, of long standing, long-ordained, fathers of the Saṅgha, leaders of the Saṅgha, both openly and in private. He directs verbal acts of loving-kindness toward them, both openly and in private. He directs mental acts of loving-kindness toward them, both openly and in private. In this way, monks, a monk honors with exceeding honor those monks who are elders, of long standing, long-ordained, fathers of the Saṅgha, leaders of the Saṅgha.

“Imehi kho, bhikkhave, ekādasahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu bhabbo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjitu”nti.

Monks, a monk endowed with these eleven qualities is capable of attaining growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Those monks, being delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

Mahāgopālakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Great Cowherd Sutta, the third, is finished.

4. Cūḷagopālakasuttaṃ

4. The Shorter Discourse on the Cowherd

350. Evaṃ [T 1.0418][V 1.0290][P 1.0225] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vajjīsu viharati ukkacelāyaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

4. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjis at Ukkacelā, on the bank of the river Ganges. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Bhūtapubbaṃ[M 1.0287], bhikkhave, māgadhako gopālako duppaññajātiko, vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye, asamavekkhitvā gaṅgāya nadiyā orimaṃ tīraṃ, asamavekkhitvā pārimaṃ tīraṃ, atittheneva gāvo patāresi uttaraṃ tīraṃ suvidehānaṃ. Atha kho, bhikkhave, gāvo majjhegaṅgāya nadiyā sote āmaṇḍaliyaṃ karitvā tattheva anayabyasanaṃ āpajjiṃsu. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, māgadhako gopālako duppaññajātiko, vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye, asamavekkhitvā gaṅgāya nadiyā orimaṃ tīraṃ, asamavekkhitvā pārimaṃ tīraṃ, atittheneva gāvo patāresi uttaraṃ tīraṃ suvidehānaṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye hi keci ye keci (syā. kaṃ.) samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā akusalā imassa lokassa akusalā parassa lokassa, akusalā māradheyyassa akusalā amāradheyyassa, akusalā maccudheyyassa akusalā amaccudheyyassa, tesaṃ ye sotabbaṃ saddahātabbaṃ maññissanti, tesaṃ taṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya.

350. “Once upon a time, monks, there was a Magadhan cowherd who was foolish by nature. In the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, without inspecting this shore of the river Ganges, and without inspecting the far shore, he drove his cattle across by an unsuitable ford to the northern shore, to the land of the Videhans. Then, monks, the cattle, in the middle of the current of the river Ganges, were caught in a whirlpool and there met with ruin and disaster. For what reason? Because, monks, that Magadhan cowherd, being foolish by nature, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, without inspecting this shore of the river Ganges, and without inspecting the far shore, drove his cattle across by an unsuitable ford to the northern shore, to the land of the Videhans. In the same way, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be who are unskilled regarding this world and unskilled regarding the next world; unskilled regarding Māra’s domain and unskilled regarding what is not Māra’s domain; unskilled regarding Death’s domain and unskilled regarding what is not Death’s domain—for those who think their words should be listened to and believed, that will be for their long-term harm and suffering.”

351. “Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, māgadhako gopālako sappaññajātiko, vassānaṃ [T 1.0419] pacchime māse saradasamaye, samavekkhitvā gaṅgāya nadiyā orimaṃ tīraṃ, samavekkhitvā pārimaṃ tīraṃ, tittheneva gāvo patāresi uttaraṃ tīraṃ suvidehānaṃ. So paṭhamaṃ patāresi ye te usabhā gopitaro gopariṇāyakā. Te tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu. Athāpare patāresi balavagāvo dammagāvo. Tepi tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu. Athāpare patāresi vacchatare vacchatariyo. Tepi tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu. Athāpare patāresi vacchake kisābalake kisabalake (sī. syā. pī.). Tepi tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, vacchako taruṇako tāvadeva jātako mātugoravakena vuyhamāno, sopi tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamāsi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā [V 1.0291] hi so, bhikkhave, māgadhako gopālako sappaññajātiko[P 1.0226], vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye, samavekkhitvā gaṅgāya nadiyā orimaṃ [M 1.0288] tīraṃ, samavekkhitvā pārimaṃ tīraṃ, tittheneva gāvo patāresi uttaraṃ tīraṃ suvidehānaṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kusalā imassa lokassa kusalā parassa lokassa, kusalā māradheyyassa kusalā amāradheyyassa, kusalā maccudheyyassa kusalā amaccudheyyassa, tesaṃ ye sotabbaṃ saddahātabbaṃ maññissanti, tesaṃ taṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya.

351. “Once upon a time, monks, there was a Magadhan cowherd who was wise by nature. In the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, having inspected this shore of the river Ganges, and having inspected the far shore, he drove his cattle across by a suitable ford to the northern shore, to the land of the Videhans. First, he drove across those bulls who were the fathers and leaders of the herd. They cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore. Then he drove across the strong, tamed cattle. They too cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore. Then he drove across the young bullocks and heifers. They too cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore. Then he drove across the lean and weak calves. They too cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore. Once, monks, a tender, newborn calf, being carried along by its mother’s lowing, also cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore. For what reason? Because, monks, that Magadhan cowherd, being wise by nature, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, having inspected this shore of the river Ganges, and having inspected the far shore, drove his cattle across by a suitable ford to the northern shore, to the land of the Videhans. In the same way, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins there may be who are skilled regarding this world and skilled regarding the next world; skilled regarding Māra’s domain and skilled regarding what is not Māra’s domain; skilled regarding Death’s domain and skilled regarding what is not Death’s domain—for those who think their words should be listened to and believed, that will be for their long-term welfare and happiness.”

352. “Seyyathāpi[T 1.0420], bhikkhave, ye te usabhā gopitaro gopariṇāyakā te tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu, evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye te bhikkhū arahanto khīṇāsavā vusitavanto katakaraṇīyā ohitabhārā anuppattasadatthā parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanā sammadaññā vimuttā, te tiriyaṃ mārassa sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gatā.

352. “Monks, just as those bulls, the fathers and leaders of the herd, cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore, so too, monks, those monks who are arahants—whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through right knowledge—they have cut across Māra’s current and gone safely to the far shore.”

“Seyyathāpi te, bhikkhave, balavagāvo dammagāvo tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu, evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye te bhikkhū pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā opapātikā tattha parinibbāyino anāvattidhammā tasmā lokā, tepi tiriyaṃ mārassa sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gamissanti.

“Just as, monks, the strong, tamed cattle cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore, so too, monks, those monks who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, are spontaneously reborn, attain final Nibbāna there, and are of a nature not to return from that world—they too will cut across Māra’s current and safely reach the far shore.”

“Seyyathāpi te, bhikkhave, vacchatarā vacchatariyo tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu, evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye te bhikkhū tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmino sakiṃdeva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karissanti, tepi tiriyaṃ mārassa sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gamissanti.

“Just as, monks, those young bullocks and heifers cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore, so too, monks, those monks who, with the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners—who, having come to this world just once more, will make an end of suffering—they too will cut across Māra’s current and safely reach the far shore.”

“Seyyathāpi te, bhikkhave, vacchakā kisābalakā tiriyaṃ gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ agamaṃsu, evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye te bhikkhū tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpannā avinipātadhammā niyatā sambodhiparāyanā, tepi tiriyaṃ mārassa sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gamissanti.

“Just as, monks, those lean and weak calves cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore, so too, monks, those monks who, with the destruction of the three fetters, are stream-enterers, no longer subject to downfall, assured, and destined for enlightenment—they too will cut across Māra’s current and safely reach the far shore.”

“Seyyathāpi so, bhikkhave, vacchako taruṇako tāvadeva jātako mātugoravakena [T 1.0421] vuyhamāno tiriyaṃ [V 1.0292] gaṅgāya sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā [M 1.0289] pāraṃ agamāsi, evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye te bhikkhū dhammānusārino saddhānusārino, tepi tiriyaṃ mārassa sotaṃ chetvā sotthinā pāraṃ gamissanti.

“Just as, monks, that tender, newborn calf, being carried along by its mother’s lowing, cut across the current of the Ganges and safely reached the far shore, so too, monks, those monks who are Dhamma-followers and faith-followers—they too will cut across Māra’s current and safely reach the far shore.”

“Ahaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, kusalo [P 1.0227] imassa lokassa kusalo parassa lokassa, kusalo māradheyyassa kusalo amāradheyyassa, kusalo maccudheyyassa kusalo amaccudheyyassa. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, ye sotabbaṃ saddahātabbaṃ maññissanti, tesaṃ taṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.

“Indeed, monks, I am skilled in this world and skilled in the next world; skilled in what is under Māra's domain and skilled in what is not under Māra's domain; skilled in what is under Death's domain and skilled in what is not under Death's domain. Monks, for those who will think that my words should be heard and should be believed, that will be for their welfare and happiness for a long time.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Idaṃ vatvā sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then said further:

“Ayaṃ loko paro loko, jānatā suppakāsito;

Yañca mārena sampattaṃ, appattaṃ yañca maccunā.

“This world and the next world have been well proclaimed by the Knower; and also that which is reached by Māra, and that which is not reached by Death.

“Sabbaṃ lokaṃ abhiññāya, sambuddhena pajānatā;

Vivaṭaṃ amatadvāraṃ, khemaṃ nibbānapattiyā.

“By the Sambuddha who comprehends, having directly known the entire world, the door to the Deathless has been opened for the attainment of secure Nibbāna.

“Chinnaṃ pāpimato sotaṃ, viddhastaṃ vinaḷīkataṃ;

Pāmojjabahulā hotha, khemaṃ pattattha patthetha (syā. kaṃ. ka. aṭṭhakathāyaṃ saṃvaṇṇetabbapāṭho) bhikkhavo”ti.

“The stream of the Evil One has been cut, shattered, and uprooted. Monks, be full of joy and aspire to the secure state!”

Cūḷagopālakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Lesser Discourse on the Cowherd, the fourth, is finished.

5. Cūḷasaccakasuttaṃ

5. The Lesser Discourse to Saccaka

353. Evaṃ [T 1.0422][V 1.0293] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena saccako nigaṇṭhaputto vesāliyaṃ paṭivasati bhassappavādako paṇḍitavādo sādhusammato bahujanassa. So vesāliyaṃ parisati evaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – “nāhaṃ taṃ passāmi samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā, saṅghiṃ gaṇiṃ gaṇācariyaṃ, api arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ paṭijānamānaṃ, yo mayā vādena vādaṃ samāraddho na saṅkampeyya na sampakampeyya na sampavedheyya, yassa na kacchehi sedā mucceyyuṃ. Thūṇaṃ cepāhaṃ acetanaṃ vādena vādaṃ samārabheyyaṃ, sāpi mayā vādena vādaṃ samāraddhā [M 1.0290] saṅkampeyya sampakampeyya sampavedheyya. Ko pana vādo manussabhūtassā”ti?

353. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Now at that time Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, was residing at Vesālī—a debater, a clever speaker, esteemed as a good person by many people. He would speak these words in the assembly at Vesālī: "I do not see any ascetic or brahmin, any head of an order, leader of a group, or teacher of a group, not even one who claims to be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, who, when engaged in debate with me, would not tremble, quake, and shake, and from whose armpits sweat would not pour. Even if I were to engage a mindless post in debate, it too, when engaged in debate with me, would tremble, quake, and shake. What then to say of a human being?"

Atha kho āyasmā assaji pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya vesāliṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Addasā kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto vesāliyaṃ jaṅghāvihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno [P 1.0228] āyasmantaṃ assajiṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna yenāyasmā assaji tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā assajinā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto āyasmantaṃ assajiṃ etadavoca – “kathaṃ pana, bho assaji, samaṇo gotamo sāvake vineti, kathaṃbhāgā [T 1.0423] ca pana samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakesu anusāsanī bahulā pavattatī”ti? “Evaṃ kho, aggivessana, bhagavā sāvake vineti, evaṃbhāgā ca pana bhagavato sāvakesu anusāsanī bahulā pavattati – ‘rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā, saññā aniccā, saṅkhārā aniccā, viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā, vedanā anattā, saññā anattā, saṅkhārā anattā, viññāṇaṃ anattā. Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’ti. Evaṃ kho, aggivessana, bhagavā sāvake vineti, evaṃbhāgā ca pana bhagavato sāvakesu anusāsanī bahulā pavattatī”ti. “Dussutaṃ vata, bho assaji, assumha ye mayaṃ evaṃvādiṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ assumha. Appeva nāma mayaṃ kadāci karahaci tena bhotā gotamena saddhiṃ samāgaccheyyāma[V 1.0294], appeva nāma siyā kocideva kathāsallāpo, appeva nāma tasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā viveceyyāmā”ti.

Then, in the morning, the venerable Assaji dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms. Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, while walking and wandering for exercise in Vesālī, saw the venerable Assaji coming from afar. Seeing him, he approached the venerable Assaji; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Assaji. When this courteous and memorable conversation was concluded, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, said this to the venerable Assaji: “Venerable Assaji, how does the ascetic Gotama train his disciples, and what is the nature of the instruction that is frequently given to the ascetic Gotama’s disciples?” “Aggivessana, this is how the Blessed One trains his disciples, and this is the nature of the instruction that is frequently given to the Blessed One’s disciples: ‘Bhikkhus, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent. Bhikkhus, form is not-self, feeling is not-self, perception is not-self, formations are not-self, consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent; all things are not-self.’ This, Aggivessana, is how the Blessed One trains his disciples, and this is the nature of the instruction that is frequently given to the Blessed One’s disciples.” “Venerable Assaji, we have indeed heard what is ill-heard, we who have heard that the ascetic Gotama is one who speaks thus. Perhaps at some time we might meet with that venerable Gotama. Perhaps there might be some conversation. Perhaps we might wean him away from that evil view.”

354. Tena kho pana samayena pañcamattāni licchavisatāni santhāgāre sandhāgāre (ka.) sannipatitāni honti kenacideva karaṇīyena. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto yena te licchavī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā te licchavī etadavoca – “abhikkamantu bhonto licchavī, abhikkamantu bhonto licchavī, ajja me samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo bhavissati. Sace me samaṇo gotamo tathā patiṭṭhissati yathā ca me yathāssa me (sī. pī.) ñātaññatarena sāvakena assajinā nāma bhikkhunā patiṭṭhitaṃ, seyyathāpi [T 1.0424] nāma balavā puriso dīghalomikaṃ eḷakaṃ lomesu gahetvā ākaḍḍheyya parikaḍḍheyya samparikaḍḍheyya[M 1.0291], evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ ākaḍḍhissāmi parikaḍḍhissāmi samparikaḍḍhissāmi. Seyyathāpi nāma balavā soṇḍikākammakāro mahantaṃ soṇḍikākiḷañjaṃ gambhīre udakarahade pakkhipitvā kaṇṇe gahetvā ākaḍḍheyya parikaḍḍheyya samparikaḍḍheyya, evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ ākaḍḍhissāmi parikaḍḍhissāmi samparikaḍḍhissāmi. Seyyathāpi nāma balavā soṇḍikādhutto vālaṃ [P 1.0229] thālaṃ (ka.) kaṇṇe gahetvā odhuneyya niddhuneyya nipphoṭeyya nicchādeyya (sī. pī. ka.), nicchoṭeyya (ka.), nippoṭheyya (syā. kaṃ.) evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ odhunissāmi niddhunissāmi nipphoṭessāmi. Seyyathāpi nāma kuñjaro saṭṭhihāyano gambhīraṃ pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā sāṇadhovikaṃ nāma kīḷitajātaṃ kīḷati, evamevāhaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ sāṇadhovikaṃ maññe kīḷitajātaṃ kīḷissāmi. Abhikkamantu bhonto licchavī, abhikkamantu bhonto licchavī, ajja me samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo bhavissatī”ti. Tatrekacce licchavī evamāhaṃsu – “kiṃ samaṇo gotamo saccakassa nigaṇṭhaputtassa vādaṃ āropessati, atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto samaṇassa gotamassa vādaṃ āropessatī”ti? Ekacce licchavī evamāhaṃsu – “kiṃ so bhavamāno saccako nigaṇṭhaputto yo bhagavato vādaṃ āropessati, atha kho bhagavā saccakassa nigaṇṭhaputtassa vādaṃ āropessatī”ti? Atha kho saccako [T 1.0425] nigaṇṭhaputto pañcamattehi licchavisatehi parivuto yena mahāvanaṃ kūṭāgārasālā tenupasaṅkami.

354. Now at that time, about five hundred Licchavis were assembled in the council hall for some business. Then Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, approached those Licchavis and said to them: “Come forth, venerable Licchavis, come forth! Today I will have a conversation with the ascetic Gotama. If the ascetic Gotama stands his ground with me as his disciple, the bhikkhu named Assaji, one of the well-known ones, stood his ground with me, then just as a strong man, having seized a long-fleeced ram by its fleece, might drag it to and fro, drag it about, and thoroughly drag it around, even so will I, in debate, drag the ascetic Gotama to and fro with my words, drag him about, and thoroughly drag him around. Just as a strong distillery worker, having thrown a large distillery strainer into a deep pool of water and grabbed it by the corners, might drag it to and fro, drag it about, and thoroughly drag it around, even so will I, in debate, drag the ascetic Gotama to and fro with my words, drag him about, and thoroughly drag him around. Just as a strong drunkard, having grabbed a pot by the rim, might shake it down, shake it up, and thrash it about, even so will I, in debate, shake the ascetic Gotama down with my words, shake him up, and thrash him about. Just as an elephant sixty years old, having plunged into a deep lotus pond, plays the game called ‘hemp-washing,’ even so, I imagine, I will play the ‘hemp-washing’ game with the ascetic Gotama. Come forth, venerable Licchavis, come forth! Today I will have a conversation with the ascetic Gotama.” Thereupon, some of the Licchavis said: “How can the ascetic Gotama refute the statement of Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha? Surely it is Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, who will refute the statement of the ascetic Gotama.” But other Licchavis said: “Who is this Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, that he could refute the statement of the Blessed One? Surely it is the Blessed One who will refute the statement of Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha.” Then Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, surrounded by about five hundred Licchavis, approached the Great Wood, to the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

355. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū abbhokāse caṅkamanti. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā te bhikkhū etadavoca – “kahaṃ nu kho, bho, etarahi so bhavaṃ gotamo viharati? Dassanakāmā hi mayaṃ taṃ bhavantaṃ gotama”nti[V 1.0295]. “Esa, aggivessana, bhagavā mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisinno”ti. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto mahatiyā licchaviparisāya saddhiṃ mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tepi kho licchavī appekacce bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, appekacce bhagavatā [M 1.0292] saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, appekacce bhagavato santike nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, appekacce tuṇhībhūtā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

355. At that time, many monks were walking to and fro in the open. Then Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, approached those monks and said this: 'Venerables, where is the venerable Gotama dwelling now? We desire to see the venerable Gotama.' 'Aggivessana, the Blessed One has entered the Great Wood and is seated at the foot of a certain tree for his day's abiding.' Then Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, together with a great retinue of Licchavis, entered the Great Wood and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After concluding the courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. And some of those Licchavis, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after concluding the courteous and memorable talk, sat down to one side. Some, having raised their joined palms towards the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Some announced their name and clan in the Blessed One's presence and sat down to one side. And some, having become silent, sat down to one side.

356. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “puccheyyāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ kiñcideva desaṃ, sace me bhavaṃ gotamo okāsaṃ karoti pañhassa veyyākaraṇāyā”ti. “Puccha, aggivessana[T 1.0426], yadākaṅkhasī”ti[P 1.0230]. “Kathaṃ pana bhavaṃ gotamo sāvake vineti, kathaṃbhāgā ca pana bhoto gotamassa sāvakesu anusāsanī bahulā pavattatī”ti? “Evaṃ kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, sāvake vinemi, evaṃbhāgā ca pana me sāvakesu anusāsanī bahulā pavattati – ‘rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā, saññā aniccā, saṅkhārā aniccā, viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā, vedanā anattā, saññā anattā, saṅkhārā anattā, viññāṇaṃ anattā. Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’ti. Evaṃ kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, sāvake vinemi, evaṃbhāgā ca pana me sāvakesu anusāsanī bahulā pavattatī”ti.

356. When Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, was seated to one side, he said this to the Blessed One: 'I would ask the venerable Gotama about a certain matter, if the venerable Gotama would grant me the opportunity for an explanation to my question.' 'Ask, Aggivessana, whatever you wish.' 'How, venerable Gotama, do you discipline your disciples, and of what sort is the instruction that for the most part prevails among your disciples?' 'In this way, Aggivessana, I discipline my disciples, and of this sort is the instruction that for the most part prevails among my disciples: "Monks, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, volitional formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent. Monks, form is not-self, feeling is not-self, perception is not-self, volitional formations are not-self, consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self." In this way, Aggivessana, I discipline my disciples, and of this sort is the instruction that for the most part prevails among my disciples.'

“Upamā maṃ, bho gotama, paṭibhātī”ti. “Paṭibhātu taṃ, aggivessanā”ti bhagavā avoca.

“Venerable Gotama, an analogy occurs to me.” “Let it occur to you, Aggivessana,” the Blessed One said.

“Seyyathāpi, bho gotama, ye kecime bījagāmabhūtagāmā vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjanti, sabbe te pathaviṃ nissāya pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya. Evamete bījagāmabhūtagāmā vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjanti. Seyyathāpi vā pana, bho gotama, ye kecime balakaraṇīyā kammantā karīyanti, sabbe te pathaviṃ nissāya pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya. Evamete balakaraṇīyā kammantā karīyanti. Evameva kho, bho gotama, rūpattāyaṃ purisapuggalo rūpe patiṭṭhāya puññaṃ vā apuññaṃ vā pasavati, vedanattāyaṃ purisapuggalo vedanāyaṃ patiṭṭhāya puññaṃ vā [V 1.0296] apuññaṃ vā pasavati, saññattāyaṃ purisapuggalo saññāyaṃ patiṭṭhāya puññaṃ vā apuññaṃ vā pasavati, saṅkhārattāyaṃ purisapuggalo saṅkhāresu [T 1.0427] patiṭṭhāya puññaṃ vā apuññaṃ vā pasavati, viññāṇattāyaṃ purisapuggalo viññāṇe patiṭṭhāya puññaṃ vā apuññaṃ vā pasavatī”ti.

“Just as, Venerable Gotama, whatever kinds of seeds and plants there are attain growth, development, and abundance, all of them do so depending on the earth, established on the earth. In this way, these kinds of seeds and plants attain growth, development, and abundance. Or just as, Venerable Gotama, whatever actions requiring strength are performed, all of them are performed depending on the earth, established on the earth. In this way, these actions requiring strength are performed. In the very same way, Venerable Gotama, this person-being who has form as self, being established in form, produces merit or demerit; this person-being who has feeling as self, being established in feeling, produces merit or demerit; this person-being who has perception as self, being established in perception, produces merit or demerit; this person-being who has volitional formations as self, being established in volitional formations, produces merit or demerit; this person-being who has consciousness as self, being established in consciousness, produces merit or demerit.”

“Nanu tvaṃ, aggivessana, evaṃ vadesi – ‘rūpaṃ me attā, vedanā me attā, saññā me attā, saṅkhārā me attā, viññāṇaṃ me attā’”ti? “Ahañhi, bho gotama[M 1.0293], evaṃ vadāmi – ‘rūpaṃ me attā, vedanā me attā, saññā me attā, saṅkhārā me attā, viññāṇaṃ me attā’ti, ayañca mahatī janatā”ti.

“Do you not, Aggivessana, say thus: ‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, volitional formations are my self, consciousness is my self’?” “Indeed, Venerable Gotama, I say thus: ‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, volitional formations are my self, consciousness is my self,’ and so does this great populace.”

“Kiñhi te, aggivessana, mahatī janatā karissati? Iṅgha tvaṃ, aggivessana, sakaññeva vādaṃ nibbeṭhehī”ti. “Ahañhi, bho gotama, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘rūpaṃ me attā, vedanā me attā, saññā me attā, saṅkhārā me attā, viññāṇaṃ me attā’”ti.

“What will a great multitude do for you, Aggivessana? Come now, Aggivessana, clarify your own statement.” “For I, Venerable Gotama, say thus: ‘Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, volitional formations are my self, consciousness is my self.’”

357. “Tena hi, aggivessana, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi, yathā te khameyya tathā naṃ tathā taṃ (ka.) byākareyyāsi. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi[P 1.0231], aggivessana, vatteyya rañño khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa sakasmiṃ vijite vaso – ghātetāyaṃ vā ghātetuṃ, jāpetāyaṃ vā jāpetuṃ, pabbājetāyaṃ vā pabbājetuṃ, seyyathāpi rañño pasenadissa kosalassa, seyyathāpi vā pana rañño māgadhassa ajātasattussa vedehiputtassā”ti? “Vatteyya, bho gotama, rañño khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa sakasmiṃ vijite vaso – ghātetāyaṃ vā ghātetuṃ, jāpetāyaṃ vā jāpetuṃ, pabbājetāyaṃ vā pabbājetuṃ, seyyathāpi rañño pasenadissa kosalassa, seyyathāpi vā pana rañño māgadhassa ajātasattussa vedehiputtassa. Imesampi hi, bho gotama, saṅghānaṃ gaṇānaṃ – seyyathidaṃ, vajjīnaṃ mallānaṃ – vattati sakasmiṃ vijite vaso – ghātetāyaṃ vā ghātetuṃ, jāpetāyaṃ vā jāpetuṃ, pabbājetāyaṃ vā pabbājetuṃ. Kiṃ pana rañño khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa, seyyathāpi rañño pasenadissa kosalassa[T 1.0428], seyyathāpi vā pana rañño māgadhassa ajātasattussa vedehiputtassa? Vatteyya, bho gotama, vattituñca marahatī”ti.

357. “In that case, Aggivessana, I will question you in return on this very matter. You should answer as you see fit. What do you think, Aggivessana? Would the power of a consecrated khattiya king prevail in his own domain—to execute one who should be executed, to fine one who should be fined, or to banish one who should be banished—just as it would for King Pasenadi of Kosala, or for King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha?” “It would, Venerable Gotama. The power of a consecrated khattiya king would prevail in his own domain—to execute one who should be executed, to fine one who should be fined, or to banish one who should be banished—just as it would for King Pasenadi of Kosala, or for King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha. For even these federations and confederacies, Venerable Gotama—that is, the Vajjis and the Mallas—their power prevails in their own domain to execute one who should be executed, to fine one who should be fined, or to banish one who should be banished. How much more so for a consecrated khattiya king, like King Pasenadi of Kosala, or like King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha? It would prevail, Venerable Gotama, and it is fitting that it should prevail.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi – ‘rūpaṃ me attā’ti, vattati te [V 1.0297] tasmiṃ rūpe vaso – evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī”ti? Evaṃ vutte, saccako nigaṇṭhaputto tuṇhī ahosi. Dutiyampi kho bhagavā saccakaṃ nigaṇṭhaputtaṃ etadavoca – “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi – ‘rūpaṃ me attā’ti, vattati te tasmiṃ rūpe vaso – evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī”ti? Dutiyampi [M 1.0294] kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto tuṇhī ahosi. Atha kho bhagavā saccakaṃ nigaṇṭhaputtaṃ etadavoca – “byākarohi dāni, aggivessana, na dāni te tuṇhībhāvassa kālo. Yo koci, aggivessana tathāgatena yāvatatiyaṃ sahadhammikaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho na byākaroti, etthevassa sattadhā muddhā phalatī”ti.

“What do you think, Aggivessana? Since you say, ‘Form is my self,’ does your power prevail over that form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus’?” When this was said, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son remained silent. A second time, the Blessed One said this to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son: “What do you think, Aggivessana? Since you say, ‘Form is my self,’ does your power prevail over that form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus’?” A second time, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son remained silent. Then the Blessed One said this to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son: “Answer now, Aggivessana. This is not the time for you to be silent. Whoever, Aggivessana, when asked a question in accordance with the Dhamma by the Tathāgata up to a third time, does not answer, his head will split into seven pieces right on the spot.”

Tena kho pana samayena vajirapāṇi yakkho āyasaṃ vajiraṃ ādāya ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ saccakassa nigaṇṭhaputtassa uparivehāsaṃ ṭhito hoti – ‘sacāyaṃ [T 1.0429] saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavatā yāvatatiyaṃ sahadhammikaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho na byākarissati etthevassa sattadhā muddhaṃ phālessāmī’ti. Taṃ kho pana vajirapāṇiṃ yakkhaṃ bhagavā ceva passati saccako ca nigaṇṭhaputto. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhīto saṃviggo lomahaṭṭhajāto bhagavantaṃyeva [P 1.0232] tāṇaṃ gavesī bhagavantaṃyeva leṇaṃ gavesī bhagavantaṃyeva saraṇaṃ gavesī bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “pucchatu maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo, byākarissāmī”ti.

Now at that time, the yakkha Vajirapāṇi, holding an iron thunderbolt that was flaming, blazing, and glowing, stood in the air above Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son, thinking: “If this Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son, when asked a question in accordance with the Dhamma by the Blessed One up to a third time, does not answer, I will split his head into seven pieces right on the spot.” The Blessed One saw the yakkha Vajirapāṇi, and Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son saw him too. Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son—frightened, agitated, and with his hair standing on end—sought protection in the Blessed One alone, sought shelter in the Blessed One alone, and sought refuge in the Blessed One alone. He said to the Blessed One: “Let the Venerable Gotama question me; I will answer.”

358. “Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi – ‘rūpaṃ me attā’ti, vattati te tasmiṃ rūpe vaso – evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

358. “What do you think, Aggivessana? Since you say, ‘Form is my self,’ does your power prevail over that form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus’?” “This is not so, Venerable Gotama.”

“Manasi karohi, aggivessana; manasi karitvā kho, aggivessana, byākarohi. Na kho te sandhiyati purimena vā pacchimaṃ pacchimena vā purimaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi – ‘vedanā me attā’ti, vattati te tissaṃ vedanāyaṃ tāyaṃ vedanāyaṃ (sī. syā.) vaso – evaṃ me vedanā hotu, evaṃ me vedanā mā ahosī”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

“Pay attention, Aggivessana; having paid attention, Aggivessana, answer. Your earlier statement does not accord with your later, nor your later with your earlier. What do you think, Aggivessana? Since you say, ‘Feeling is my self,’ does your power prevail over that feeling: ‘Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling not be thus’?” “This is not so, Venerable Gotama.”

“Manasi karohi, aggivessana; manasi karitvā kho, aggivessana, byākarohi. Na kho te sandhiyati purimena vā pacchimaṃ, pacchimena vā purimaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana[V 1.0298], yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi – ‘saññā me attā’ti, vattati te tissaṃ saññāyaṃ vaso – evaṃ me saññā hotu, evaṃ me saññā mā ahosī”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

“Pay attention, Aggivessana; having paid attention, Aggivessana, answer. Your earlier statement does not accord with your later, nor your later with your earlier. What do you think, Aggivessana? Since you say, ‘Perception is my self,’ does your power prevail over that perception: ‘Let my perception be thus; let my perception not be thus’?” “This is not so, Venerable Gotama.”

“Manasi [M 1.0295] karohi, aggivessana[T 1.0430]; manasi karitvā kho, aggivessana, byākarohi. Na kho te sandhiyati purimena vā pacchimaṃ, pacchimena vā purimaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi – ‘saṅkhārā me attā’ti, vattati te tesu saṅkhāresu vaso – evaṃ me saṅkhārā hontu, evaṃ me saṅkhārā mā ahesu”nti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

“Pay attention, Aggivessana; having paid attention, Aggivessana, answer. Your earlier statement does not accord with your later, nor your later with your earlier. What do you think, Aggivessana? Since you say, ‘Formations are my self,’ does your power prevail over those formations: ‘Let my formations be thus; let my formations not be thus’?” “This is not so, Venerable Gotama.”

“Manasi karohi, aggivessana; manasi karitvā kho, aggivessana, byākarohi. Na kho te sandhiyati purimena vā pacchimaṃ, pacchimena vā purimaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadesi – ‘viññāṇaṃ me attā’ti, vattati te tasmiṃ viññāṇe vaso – evaṃ me viññāṇaṃ hotu, evaṃ me viññāṇaṃ mā ahosī”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

“Pay attention, Aggivessana; having paid attention, Aggivessana, answer. Your earlier statement does not accord with your later, nor your later with your earlier. What do you think, Aggivessana? Since you say, ‘Consciousness is my self,’ does your power prevail over that consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus’?” “This is not so, Venerable Gotama.”

“Manasi karohi, aggivessana; manasi karitvā kho, aggivessana, byākarohi. Na kho te sandhiyati purimena vā pacchimaṃ, pacchimena vā purimaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bho gotama”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bho gotama”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso [P 1.0233] me attā’”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

“Pay attention, Aggivessana; having paid attention, Aggivessana, answer. Your earlier statement does not accord with your later, nor your later with your earlier. What do you think of this, Aggivessana, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, Venerable Gotama.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, Venerable Gotama.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, Venerable Gotama.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, vedanā…pe… saññā…pe… saṅkhārā…pe… taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bho gotama”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bho gotama”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ [T 1.0431] – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”.

“What do you think of this, Aggivessana? Is feeling… perception… formations… What do you think of this, Aggivessana, is consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, Venerable Gotama.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, Venerable Gotama.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, Venerable Gotama.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, yo nu kho dukkhaṃ allīno dukkhaṃ upagato dukkhaṃ ajjhosito[V 1.0299], dukkhaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassati, api nu kho so sāmaṃ vā dukkhaṃ parijāneyya, dukkhaṃ vā parikkhepetvā vihareyyā”ti? “Kiñhi siyā, bho gotama? No hidaṃ, bho gotamā”ti.

“What do you think of this, Aggivessana? One who clings to suffering, has arrived at suffering, is attached to suffering, and regards suffering thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’—could such a one, on their own, fully understand suffering, or live having brought suffering to an end?” “How could that be, Venerable Gotama? Certainly not, Venerable Gotama.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, nanu tvaṃ evaṃ sante dukkhaṃ allīno dukkhaṃ upagato dukkhaṃ ajjhosito, dukkhaṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassasī”ti? “Kiñhi no siyā, bho gotama? Evametaṃ bho gotamā”ti.

“What do you think of this, Aggivessana? This being so, are you not one who clings to suffering, has arrived at suffering, is attached to suffering, and regards suffering thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “How could it not be so, Venerable Gotama? It is indeed so, Venerable Gotama.”

359. “Seyyathāpi[M 1.0296], aggivessana, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ kudhāriṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ādāya vanaṃ paviseyya. So tattha passeyya mahantaṃ kadalikkhandhaṃ ujuṃ navaṃ akukkukajātaṃ akukkuṭajātaṃ (syā. kaṃ.). Tamenaṃ mūle chindeyya, mūle chetvā agge chindeyya, agge chetvā pattavaṭṭiṃ vinibbhujeyya vinibbhujjeyya (ka.). So tattha pattavaṭṭiṃ vinibbhujanto pheggumpi nādhigaccheyya, kuto sāraṃ? Evameva kho tvaṃ, aggivessana, mayā sakasmiṃ vāde samanuyuñjiyamāno samanugāhiyamāno samanubhāsiyamāno ritto tuccho aparaddho. Bhāsitā kho pana te esā, aggivessana, vesāliyaṃ parisati vācā – ‘nāhaṃ taṃ passāmi samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā, saṅghiṃ gaṇiṃ gaṇācariyaṃ, api arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ paṭijānamānaṃ, yo mayā vādena vādaṃ samāraddho na saṅkampeyya na sampakampeyya na [T 1.0432] sampavedheyya, yassa na kacchehi sedā mucceyyuṃ. Thūṇaṃ cepāhaṃ acetanaṃ vādena vādaṃ samārabheyyaṃ sāpi mayā vādena vādaṃ samāraddhā saṅkampeyya sampakampeyya sampavedheyya. Ko pana vādo manussabhūtassā’ti? Tuyhaṃ kho pana, aggivessana, appekaccāni sedaphusitāni nalāṭā muttāni, uttarāsaṅgaṃ vinibhinditvā bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitāni. Mayhaṃ kho pana, aggivessana, natthi etarahi kāyasmiṃ sedo”ti. Iti bhagavā tasmiṃ tassaṃ (?) parisati suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ kāyaṃ vivari. Evaṃ [P 1.0234] vutte, saccako nigaṇṭhaputto tuṇhībhūto maṅkubhūto pattakkhandho adhomukho pajjhāyanto appaṭibhāno nisīdi.

359. “Suppose, Aggivessana, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There he would see a large banana trunk, straight, young, and unblemished. He would cut it at the root, and having cut it at the root, cut it at the top, and peel off the leaf-sheaths. As he peels off the leaf-sheaths, he would not even find pith, let alone heartwood. In the same way, Aggivessana, when questioned, pressed, and cross-examined by me regarding your own doctrine, you are found to be empty, hollow, and mistaken. And yet, Aggivessana, this was the statement you made in the assembly at Vesālī: ‘I do not see any ascetic or brahmin—be they the head of a community, the leader of a group, or the teacher of a group, even one claiming to be a perfected one, a fully enlightened Buddha—who, when engaged in debate with me, would not shake, quake, and tremble, from whose armpits sweat would not pour. Even if I were to engage in debate with a lifeless post, it too, when engaged in debate with me, would shake, quake, and tremble. What to say of a human being!’ But now, Aggivessana, some beads of sweat from your forehead have broken through your upper robe and settled on the ground. As for me, Aggivessana, at this time there is no sweat on my body.” So saying, the Blessed One revealed his golden-hued body to that assembly. When this was said, Saccaka, the Nigaṇṭha’s son, sat silent, dismayed, with drooping shoulders, face downcast, brooding, and with nothing to say.

360. Atha kho dummukho licchaviputto saccakaṃ nigaṇṭhaputtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ maṅkubhūtaṃ pattakkhandhaṃ adhomukhaṃ pajjhāyantaṃ appaṭibhānaṃ viditvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “upamā maṃ, bhagavā, paṭibhātī”ti. “Paṭibhātu taṃ, dummukhā”ti bhagavā avoca. “Seyyathāpi, bhante, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre pokkharaṇī. Tatrāssa kakkaṭako. Atha kho, bhante, sambahulā [V 1.0300] kumārakā vā kumārikā vā tamhā gāmā vā nigamā vā nikkhamitvā yena sā pokkharaṇī tenupasaṅkameyyuṃ; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā taṃ kakkaṭakaṃ udakā uddharitvā thale patiṭṭhāpeyyuṃ. Yaññadeva hi so, bhante, kakkaṭako aḷaṃ abhininnāmeyya taṃ tadeva te kumārakā vā kumārikā vā kaṭṭhena vā kathalena vā sañchindeyyuṃ sambhañjeyyuṃ [M 1.0297] sampalibhañjeyyuṃ. Evañhi [T 1.0433] so, bhante, kakkaṭako sabbehi aḷehi sañchinnehi sambhaggehi sampalibhaggehi abhabbo taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ puna otarituṃ, seyyathāpi pubbe. Evameva kho, bhante, yāni saccakassa nigaṇṭhaputtassa visūkāyitāni visevitāni vipphanditāni tānipi sabbāni vipphanditāni kānici kānici tāni (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bhagavatā sañchinnāni sambhaggāni sampalibhaggāni; abhabbo ca dāni, bhante, saccako nigaṇṭhaputto puna bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ yadidaṃ vādādhippāyo”ti. Evaṃ vutte, saccako nigaṇṭhaputto dummukhaṃ licchaviputtaṃ etadavoca – “āgamehi tvaṃ, dummukha, āgamehi tvaṃ, dummukha ( ) (mukharosi tvaṃ dummukha) (syā. kaṃ.) na mayaṃ tayā saddhiṃ mantema, idha mayaṃ bhotā gotamena saddhiṃ mantema.

360. Then the Licchavi prince Dummukha, seeing that Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son was silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping, downcast, brooding, and with nothing to say, said to the Blessed One: “An analogy occurs to me, Blessed One.” “Let it occur to you, Dummukha,” the Blessed One said. “Venerable sir, it is as if near a village or a town there were a pond with a crab in it. Then many boys or girls might leave that village or town, go to that pond, enter it, pull that crab out of the water, and place it on dry land. And whenever that crab would extend a claw, those boys or girls would cut it off, break it, and smash it with sticks or potsherds. Thus, venerable sir, with all its claws cut off, broken, and smashed, that crab would be unable to return to that pond as before. In the same way, venerable sir, all of Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son’s twists, turns, and contortions have been cut off, broken, and smashed by the Blessed One. And now, venerable sir, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son is unable to approach the Blessed One again for the purpose of debate.” When this was said, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son said to the Licchavi prince Dummukha: “Wait, Dummukha! Wait, Dummukha! We are not conversing with you; here we are conversing with Master Gotama.”

361. “Tiṭṭhatesā, bho gotama, amhākañceva aññesañca puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ vācā. Vilāpaṃ vilapitaṃ maññe. Kittāvatā ca nu kho bhoto gotamassa sāvako sāsanakaro hoti ovādapatikaro tiṇṇavicikiccho vigatakathaṃkatho vesārajjappatto aparappaccayo satthusāsane viharatī”ti? “Idha, aggivessana, mama sāvako yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ [P 1.0235] yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati; yā kāci vedanā…pe… yā kāci saññā…pe… ye keci saṅkhārā…pe… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Ettāvatā kho, aggivessana, mama sāvako sāsanakaro hoti ovādapatikaro tiṇṇavicikiccho vigatakathaṃkatho vesārajjappatto aparappaccayo satthusāsane viharatī”ti.

361. “Venerable Gotama, let that talk of ours and of other various ascetics and brahmins be set aside. I consider it to be mere rambling. But to what extent is a disciple of the Venerable Gotama one who follows the teaching, responds to advice, has crossed over doubt, is free from perplexity, has attained confidence, and dwells not dependent on another in the Teacher’s Dispensation?” “Here, Aggivessana, my disciple sees any form whatsoever—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ They see any feeling… they see any perception… they see any volitional formations… they see any consciousness whatsoever—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ It is to this extent, Aggivessana, that my disciple is one who follows the teaching, responds to advice, has crossed over doubt, is free from perplexity, has attained confidence, and dwells not dependent on another in the Teacher’s Dispensation.”

“Kittāvatā [V 1.0301] pana, bho gotama, bhikkhu arahaṃ hoti khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto”ti? “Idha, aggivessana, bhikkhu yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na [M 1.0298] meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā anupādā vimutto hoti; yā kāci vedanā…pe… yā kāci saññā…pe… ye keci saṅkhārā…pe… yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā [T 1.0434] paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya disvā anupādā vimutto hoti. Ettāvatā kho, aggivessana, bhikkhu arahaṃ hoti khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto. Evaṃ vimuttacitto kho, aggivessana, bhikkhu tīhi anuttariyehi samannāgato [T 1.0435] hoti – dassanānuttariyena, paṭipadānuttariyena, vimuttānuttariyena. Evaṃ vimuttacitto kho, aggivessana, bhikkhu tathāgataññeva sakkaroti garuṃ karoti māneti pūjeti – buddho so bhagavā bodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, danto so bhagavā damathāya dhammaṃ deseti, santo so bhagavā samathāya dhammaṃ deseti, tiṇṇo so bhagavā taraṇāya dhammaṃ deseti, parinibbuto so bhagavā parinibbānāya dhammaṃ desetī”ti.

“To what extent, Venerable Gotama, is a bhikkhu an arahant—one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated by right knowledge?” “Aggivessana, here a bhikkhu sees with right wisdom, as it really is, any kind of form—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, he is liberated without clinging. He sees with right wisdom, as it really is, any kind of feeling… any kind of perception… any kind of volitional formations… any kind of consciousness—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, he is liberated without clinging. To this extent, Aggivessana, a bhikkhu is an arahant—one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated by right knowledge. A bhikkhu whose mind is thus liberated, Aggivessana, is endowed with three unsurpassed qualities—unsurpassed vision, unsurpassed practice, and unsurpassed liberation. A bhikkhu whose mind is thus liberated, Aggivessana, only honors, respects, reveres, and venerates the Tathāgata, reflecting: ‘The Blessed One is awakened and teaches the Dhamma for awakening. The Blessed One is tamed and teaches the Dhamma for taming. The Blessed One is at peace and teaches the Dhamma for peace. The Blessed One has crossed over and teaches the Dhamma for crossing over. The Blessed One has attained Nibbāna and teaches the Dhamma for attaining Nibbāna.’”

362. Evaṃ vutte, saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [P 1.0236] – “mayameva, bho gotama, dhaṃsī, mayaṃ pagabbā, ye mayaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ āsādetabbaṃ amaññimha. Siyā hi, bho gotama, hatthiṃ pabhinnaṃ āsajja purisassa sotthibhāvo, na tveva bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ āsajja siyā purisassa sotthibhāvo. Siyā hi, bho gotama, pajjalitaṃ jalantaṃ (sī. pī.) aggikkhandhaṃ āsajja purisassa sotthibhāvo[V 1.0302], na tveva bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ āsajja siyā purisassa sotthibhāvo. Siyā hi, bho gotama, āsīvisaṃ ghoravisaṃ āsajja purisassa sotthibhāvo, na tveva bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ āsajja siyā purisassa sotthibhāvo. Mayameva, bho gotama, dhaṃsī, mayaṃ pagabbā, ye mayaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ vādena vādaṃ āsādetabbaṃ amaññimha. Adhivāsetu adhivāsetu ca (pī. ka.) me bhavaṃ gotamo svātanāya bhattaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghenā”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

362. When this was said, Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, said this to the Blessed One: “It is we, Master Gotama, who are assailants; it is we who are reckless, who thought to attack Master Gotama with argument. Indeed, Master Gotama, there might be safety for a person who encounters a maddened elephant, but there would surely be no safety for a person who encounters Master Gotama. Indeed, Master Gotama, there might be safety for a person who encounters a blazing mass of fire, but there would surely be no safety for a person who encounters Master Gotama. Indeed, Master Gotama, there might be safety for a person who encounters a snake of swift and terrible venom, but there would surely be no safety for a person who encounters Master Gotama. It is we, Master Gotama, who are assailants; it is we who are reckless, who thought to attack Master Gotama with argument. May Master Gotama accept my meal for tomorrow, together with the community of bhikkhus.” The Blessed One consented by silence.

363. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā te licchavī āmantesi – “suṇantu me bhonto licchavī, samaṇo [M 1.0299] me gotamo nimantito svātanāya saddhiṃ [T 1.0436] bhikkhusaṅghena. Tena me abhihareyyātha yamassa patirūpaṃ maññeyyāthā”ti. Atha kho te licchavī tassā rattiyā accayena saccakassa nigaṇṭhaputtassa pañcamattāni thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāraṃ abhihariṃsu. Atha kho nigaṇṭhaputto sake ārāme paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā bhagavato kālaṃ ārocāpesi – “kālo, bho gotama, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta”nti. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena saccakassa nigaṇṭhaputtassa ārāmo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresi. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavantaṃ bhuttāviṃ onītapattapāṇiṃ aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “yamidaṃ, bho gotama, dāne puññañca puññamahī ca taṃ dāyakānaṃ sukhāya hotū”ti. “Yaṃ kho, aggivessana, tādisaṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ āgamma avītarāgaṃ avītadosaṃ avītamohaṃ, taṃ [P 1.0237] dāyakānaṃ bhavissati. Yaṃ kho, aggivessana, mādisaṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ āgamma vītarāgaṃ vītadosaṃ vītamohaṃ, taṃ tuyhaṃ bhavissatī”ti.

363. Then Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, knowing the Blessed One's consent, addressed those Licchavis: “Good Licchavis, listen to my words. The ascetic Gotama has been invited by me for tomorrow, together with the community of monks. Therefore, you should bring to me what you think is suitable for him.” Then, when that night had passed, those Licchavis brought an offering of food of five hundred cooking pots to Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha. Then Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, having had excellent hard and soft food prepared in his own park, had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, Master Gotama, the meal is ready.” Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, approached the park of Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks. Then Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, with his own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks with the Buddha at its head with excellent hard and soft food. Then, when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, took a certain low seat and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, whatever merit and abundance of merit there is in this gift, may that be for the happiness of the donors.” “Aggivessana, whatever arises on account of a recipient for offerings such as that, who is not free from greed, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion, that will be for the donors. But whatever arises on account of a recipient for offerings like me, who is free from greed, free from hatred, and free from delusion, that will be for you.”

Cūḷasaccakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Cūḷasaccaka Sutta, the fifth, is finished.

6. Mahāsaccakasuttaṃ

6. The Greater Discourse to Saccaka

364. Evaṃ [T 1.0437][V 1.0303] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ sunivattho hoti pattacīvaramādāya vesāliṃ piṇḍāya pavisitukāmo pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya… pavisitukāmo hoti (sī.). Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto jaṅghāvihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno yena mahāvanaṃ kūṭāgārasālā tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho āyasmā ānando saccakaṃ nigaṇṭhaputtaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ, bhante, saccako [M 1.0300] nigaṇṭhaputto āgacchati bhassappavādako paṇḍitavādo sādhusammato bahujanassa. Eso kho, bhante, avaṇṇakāmo buddhassa, avaṇṇakāmo dhammassa, avaṇṇakāmo saṅghassa. Sādhu, bhante, bhagavā muhuttaṃ nisīdatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

364. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Vesālī, in the Great Wood, at the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Now at that time, the Blessed One, in the morning, was properly dressed and, taking his bowl and robe, intended to enter Vesālī for alms. Then Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, while walking back and forth and wandering about for exercise, approached the Great Wood, the Hall with the Peaked Roof. The Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, coming from afar. Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, this Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, is coming—a debater, one who proclaims himself wise, esteemed as good by the populace. He, venerable sir, desires to speak in dispraise of the Buddha, in dispraise of the Dhamma, and in dispraise of the Saṅgha. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would sit for a moment out of compassion.” The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Then Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and when the courteous and memorable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, said this to the Blessed One:

365. “Santi, bho gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāyabhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā viharanti, no cittabhāvanaṃ. Phusanti hi te, bho gotama, sārīrikaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bho gotama, sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭhassa sato ūrukkhambhopi nāma bhavissati, hadayampi nāma [T 1.0438] phalissati, uṇhampi lohitaṃ mukhato uggamissati, ummādampi pāpuṇissati pāpuṇissanti (syā. kaṃ.) cittakkhepaṃ. Tassa kho etaṃ, bho gotama, kāyanvayaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kāyassa vasena vattati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Abhāvitattā [P 1.0238] cittassa. Santi pana, bho gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā cittabhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā viharanti, no kāyabhāvanaṃ. Phusanti hi te, bho gotama, cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bho gotama, cetasikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭhassa sato ūrukkhambhopi nāma bhavissati, hadayampi nāma phalissati, uṇhampi lohitaṃ mukhato uggamissati, ummādampi pāpuṇissati cittakkhepaṃ. Tassa kho eso, bho gotama, cittanvayo kāyo hoti, cittassa vasena vattati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Abhāvitattā kāyassa[V 1.0304]. Tassa mayhaṃ, bho gotama, evaṃ hoti – ‘addhā bhoto gotamassa sāvakā cittabhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā viharanti, no kāyabhāvana’”nti.

365. “There are, venerable Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who dwell devoted to the practice of bodily development, but not to mental development. For they, venerable Gotama, experience bodily painful feeling. I say what has happened in the past, venerable Gotama: for one who is touched by bodily painful feeling, their thighs might indeed become stiff, their heart might indeed burst, hot blood might indeed gush from their mouth, and they might indeed go mad and become mentally deranged. For that person, venerable Gotama, this mind follows the body; it proceeds according to the body's will. For what reason? Because of the undeveloped state of the mind. Then there are, venerable Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who dwell devoted to the practice of mental development, but not to bodily development. For they, venerable Gotama, experience mental painful feeling. I say what has happened in the past, venerable Gotama: for one who is touched by mental painful feeling, their thighs might indeed become stiff, their heart might indeed burst, hot blood might indeed gush from their mouth, and they might indeed go mad and become mentally deranged. For that person, venerable Gotama, this body follows the mind; it proceeds according to the mind's will. For what reason? Because of the undeveloped state of the body. To me, venerable Gotama, this occurs: ‘Surely, the venerable Gotama's disciples dwell devoted to the practice of mental development, but not to bodily development.’”

366. “Kinti pana te, aggivessana, kāyabhāvanā sutā”ti? “Seyyathidaṃ – nando vaccho, kiso saṃkicco, makkhali gosālo – etehi, bho gotama, acelakā muttācārā hatthāpalekhanā naehibhaddantikā natiṭṭhabhaddantikā naehibhadantikā, natiṭṭhabhadantikā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) na abhihaṭaṃ na uddissakataṃ na nimantanaṃ sādiyanti, te na kumbhimukhā [M 1.0301] paṭiggaṇhanti na kaḷopimukhā paṭiggaṇhanti na eḷakamantaraṃ na daṇḍamantaraṃ na musalamantaraṃ na dvinnaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ na gabbhiniyā na pāyamānāya na purisantaragatāya na saṅkittīsu na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti na yattha makkhikā saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī[T 1.0439], na macchaṃ na maṃsaṃ na suraṃ na merayaṃ na thusodakaṃ pivanti. Te ekāgārikā vā honti ekālopikā, dvāgārikā vā honti dvālopikā…pe… sattāgārikā vā honti sattālopikā. Ekissāpi dattiyā yāpenti, dvīhipi dattīhi yāpenti…pe… sattahipi dattīhi yāpenti. Ekāhikampi āhāraṃ āhārenti, dvīhikampi āhāraṃ āhārenti…pe… sattāhikampi āhāraṃ āhārenti. Iti evarūpaṃ addhamāsikampi pariyāyabhattabhojanānuyogamanuyuttā viharantī”ti.

366. “But of what sort, Aggivessana, is the bodily development you have heard of?” “It is like this: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla—these, venerable Gotama, are naked ascetics, of unrestrained habits, who lick their hands. They do not come when invited with ‘Come, venerable sir,’ nor do they stop when told ‘Stop, venerable sir.’ They do not consent to food brought to them, to food prepared specifically for them, or to an invitation. They do not accept food from the mouth of a pot or from the mouth of a basket. They do not accept it across a threshold, across a stick, or across a pestle; nor from one of two people eating; nor from a pregnant woman, a nursing woman, or a woman consorting with a man; nor from food collected by subscription; nor where a dog is waiting; nor where flies are swarming. They do not eat fish or meat; they do not drink liquor, spirits, or fermented gruel. They are one-house-dwellers, one-morsel-eaters; or two-house-dwellers, two-morsel-eaters… or seven-house-dwellers, seven-morsel-eaters. They subsist on one small bowl, or on two small bowls… or on seven small bowls. They take food once a day, or once every two days… or once every seven days. Thus they dwell devoted to the practice of eating meals by turns, even up to half a month.”

“Kiṃ pana te, aggivessana, tāvatakeneva yāpentī”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama. Appekadā, bho gotama, uḷārāni uḷārāni khādanīyāni khādanti, uḷārāni uḷārāni bhojanāni bhuñjanti, uḷārāni uḷārāni sāyanīyāni sāyanti, uḷārāni uḷārāni pānāni pivanti. Te imaṃ kāyaṃ balaṃ gāhenti nāma, brūhenti nāma, medenti nāmā”ti.

“But, Aggivessana, do they subsist on just that much?” “Not so, venerable Gotama. Sometimes, venerable Gotama, they eat excellent hard foods, they consume excellent staple foods, they taste excellent soft foods, and they drink excellent beverages. By these, they are said to build up this body's strength, to make it flourish, and to fatten it.”

“Yaṃ kho te, aggivessana, purimaṃ pahāya pacchā upacinanti, evaṃ imassa kāyassa ācayāpacayo hoti. Kinti pana te, aggivessana, cittabhāvanā sutā”ti? Cittabhāvanāya kho [P 1.0239] saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavatā puṭṭho samāno na sampāyāsi.

“Aggivessana, what they, having abandoned their former practice, later build up—thus there is accumulation and dispersal for this body. But of what sort, Aggivessana, is the mental development you have heard of?” When questioned by the Blessed One about mental development, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son was unable to give a satisfactory answer.

367. Atha kho bhagavā saccakaṃ nigaṇṭhaputtaṃ etadavoca – “yāpi kho te esā, aggivessana, purimā kāyabhāvanā bhāsitā sāpi ariyassa vinaye no dhammikā kāyabhāvanā. Kāyabhāvanampi kāyabhāvanaṃ hi (sī. pī. ka.) kho tvaṃ, aggivessana, na aññāsi, kuto pana tvaṃ cittabhāvanaṃ [V 1.0305] jānissasi[T 1.0440]? Api ca, aggivessana, yathā abhāvitakāyo ca hoti abhāvitacitto ca, bhāvitakāyo ca hoti bhāvitacitto ca. Taṃ suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

367. Then the Blessed One said this to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son: “Aggivessana, that former bodily development which was spoken of by you is not, in the discipline of the Noble One, a legitimate bodily development. You do not even know bodily development, Aggivessana, so how could you know mental development? Furthermore, Aggivessana, listen to how one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind, and developed in body and developed in mind. Listen to it, attend to it carefully, and I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

368. “Kathañca[M 1.0302], aggivessana, abhāvitakāyo ca hoti abhāvitacitto ca? Idha, aggivessana, assutavato puthujjanassa uppajjati sukhā vedanā. So sukhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno sukhasārāgī ca hoti sukhasārāgitañca āpajjati. Tassa sā sukhā vedanā nirujjhati. Sukhāya vedanāya nirodhā uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. So dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati. Tassa kho esā, aggivessana, uppannāpi sukhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati abhāvitattā kāyassa, uppannāpi dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati abhāvitattā cittassa. Yassa kassaci, aggivessana, evaṃ ubhatopakkhaṃ uppannāpi sukhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati abhāvitattā kāyassa, uppannāpi dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati abhāvitattā cittassa, evaṃ kho, aggivessana, abhāvitakāyo ca hoti abhāvitacitto ca.

368. “And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind? Here, Aggivessana, for an uninstructed worldling, a pleasant feeling arises. Being touched by that pleasant feeling, he is full of lust for pleasure and falls into a state of being full of lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of his ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by that painful feeling, he sorrows, is weary, laments, beats his breast and wails, and falls into delusion. For him, Aggivessana, that pleasant feeling, having arisen, persists overwhelming his mind because of the undeveloped state of the body. And that painful feeling, having arisen, persists overwhelming his mind because of the undeveloped state of the mind. For whomever, Aggivessana, in this way on both sides, an arisen pleasant feeling persists overwhelming his mind because of the undeveloped state of the body, and an arisen painful feeling persists overwhelming his mind because of the undeveloped state of the mind—thus, Aggivessana, one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.”

369. “Kathañca, aggivessana, bhāvitakāyo ca hoti bhāvitacitto ca? Idha, aggivessana, sutavato ariyasāvakassa uppajjati sukhā vedanā. So sukhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno na sukhasārāgī [T 1.0441] ca hoti, na sukhasārāgitañca āpajjati. Tassa sā sukhā vedanā nirujjhati. Sukhāya vedanāya nirodhā uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. So dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno na socati na kilamati na paridevati na urattāḷiṃ kandati na sammohaṃ āpajjati. Tassa kho esā, aggivessana, uppannāpi sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati bhāvitattā kāyassa, uppannāpi dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati bhāvitattā cittassa. Yassa kassaci, aggivessana, evaṃ ubhatopakkhaṃ uppannāpi sukhā vedanā cittaṃ [P 1.0240] na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati bhāvitattā kāyassa, uppannāpi dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati bhāvitattā cittassa. Evaṃ kho, aggivessana, bhāvitakāyo ca hoti bhāvitacitto cā”ti.

369. “And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind? Here, Aggivessana, for a learned noble disciple, a pleasant feeling arises. Being touched by that pleasant feeling, they are not full of lust for pleasure, nor do they fall into a state of being full of lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of theirs ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by that painful feeling, they do not grieve, nor are they weary, nor do they lament, nor do they beat their breast and wail, nor do they fall into delusion. For them, Aggivessana, that pleasant feeling, having arisen, does not persist overwhelming their mind because of the developed state of the body. And that painful feeling, having arisen, does not persist overwhelming their mind because of the developed state of the mind. For whomever, Aggivessana, in this way on both sides, an arisen pleasant feeling does not persist overwhelming their mind because of the developed state of the body, and an arisen painful feeling does not persist overwhelming their mind because of the developed state of the mind—thus, Aggivessana, one is developed in body and developed in mind.”

370. “Evaṃ pasanno ahaṃ bhoto gotamassa! Bhavañhi gotamo bhāvitakāyo ca hoti bhāvitacitto cā”ti[V 1.0306]. “Addhā kho te ayaṃ, aggivessana, āsajja upanīya vācā bhāsitā, api ca te ahaṃ byākarissāmi[M 1.0303]. Yato kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, taṃ vata me uppannā vā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati, uppannā vā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ netaṃ khoṭhānaṃ (sī. pī.) vijjatī”ti.

370. “Thus I am confident in Master Gotama! For the venerable Gotama is one who has developed the body and developed the mind.” “Certainly, Aggivessana, this statement of yours is spoken contentiously and comparatively, but still I will explain to you. Since I, Aggivessana, shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness, there is no possibility that a pleasant feeling that has arisen could persist, overwhelming my mind, or that a painful feeling that has arisen could persist, overwhelming my mind.”

“Na hi nūna na hanūna (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) bhoto gotamassa uppajjati tathārūpā sukhā vedanā yathārūpā uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyya; na hi nūna bhoto gotamassa uppajjati [T 1.0442] tathārūpā dukkhā vedanā yathārūpā uppannā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyyā”ti.

“Surely, for the Venerable Gotama there does not arise such a pleasant feeling that, once arisen, would persist overwhelming his mind; surely, for the Venerable Gotama there does not arise such a painful feeling that, once arisen, would persist overwhelming his mind.”

371. “Kiñhi no siyā, aggivessana? Idha me, aggivessana, pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘sambādho gharāvāso rajāpatho, abbhokāso pabbajjā. Nayidaṃ sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ ekantaparisuddhaṃ saṅkhalikhitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, aparena samayena daharova samāno, susukāḷakeso bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato paṭhamena vayasā, akāmakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ assumukhānaṃ rudantānaṃ, kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajiṃ. So evaṃ pabbajito samāno kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso kālāma, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, aggivessana, āḷāro kālāmo maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā, tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca [T 1.0443] vadāmi theravādañca, ‘jānāmi passāmī’ti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā [M 1.0304] sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti, addhā āḷāro kālāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ viharatī’”ti.

371. “Why should they not arise, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: ‘The household life is confining, a path for dust; going forth is the open air. It is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life that is utterly complete, utterly pure, polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?’ So, Aggivessana, at a later time, while still a young man with jet-black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life—though my parents, unwilling, were weeping with tearful faces—I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness. Having gone forth thus, seeking what is skillful, searching for the supreme, unsurpassed state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him: ‘Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.’ When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma replied: ‘Let the venerable one stay. This Dhamma is such that a wise person can, in no long time, realize for themselves with direct knowledge their own teacher’s doctrine, and having attained it, abide therein.’ Before long, Aggivessana, I quickly mastered that Dhamma. As far as mere lip-reciting and rote repetition went, I spoke the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders, and I claimed, as did others, ‘I know, I see.’ Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me: ‘It is not out of mere faith that Āḷāra Kālāma declares of this Dhamma: “Having realized it for myself with direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in it.” Surely, Āḷāra Kālāma abides knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’”

“Atha khvāhaṃ, aggivessana, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ [V 1.0307] kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso kālāma, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, aggivessana, āḷāro kālāmo ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi vīriyaṃ, mayhaṃpatthi vīriyaṃ; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi sati, mayhaṃpatthi sati; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi samādhi, mayhaṃpatthi samādhi; na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā; yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ āḷāro kālāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedeti tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

“Then, Aggivessana, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him: ‘Friend Kālāma, to what extent do you declare that you have entered upon and abide in this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge?’ When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the base of nothingness. Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘It is not that Āḷāra Kālāma alone has faith, for I too have faith. It is not that Āḷāra Kālāma alone has energy, for I too have energy. It is not that Āḷāra Kālāma alone has mindfulness, for I too have mindfulness. It is not that Āḷāra Kālāma alone has concentration, for I too have concentration.
