It is not that Āḷāra Kālāma alone has wisdom, for I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declares he abides in, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge?’ Then, Aggivessana, in no long time, I quickly entered upon and abided in that Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge.”

“Atha khvāhaṃ, aggivessana, yena āḷāro kālāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā āḷāraṃ kālāmaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso kālāma[T 1.0444], imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho ahaṃ, āvuso, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedemi. Iti yāhaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi tamahaṃ dhammaṃ jānāmi. Iti yādiso ahaṃ tādiso tuvaṃ, yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso ahaṃ. Ehi dāni, āvuso, ubhova santā imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharāmā’ti. Iti [M 1.0305] kho, aggivessana, āḷāro kālāmo ācariyo me samāno (attano) ( ) natthi (sī. pī.) antevāsiṃ maṃ samānaṃ attanā samasamaṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva ākiñcaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

“Then, Aggivessana, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it to this extent that you declare this Dhamma, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge and entered upon it?’ ‘Friend, it is to this extent that I declare this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and entered upon it.’ I said: ‘I too, friend, to this extent, having realized this Dhamma for myself with direct knowledge and entered upon it, now abide.’ He said: ‘It is a gain for us, friend, a great gain for us, that we see such a venerable fellow practitioner of the holy life. The Dhamma that I declare, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and entered upon it, is the Dhamma in which you now abide, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge and entered upon it. The Dhamma in which you abide, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge and entered upon it, is the Dhamma that I declare, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge and entered upon it. Thus, the Dhamma I know, you know; the Dhamma you know, I know. As I am, so are you; as you are, so am I. Come now, friend, let us both, being good men, lead this community.’ Thus, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma, being my teacher, placed me, his student, on an equal footing with himself and honored me with the highest honor. Then, Aggivessana, it occurred to me: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna, but only as far as rebirth in the sphere of nothingness.’ So I, Aggivessana, not finding that Dhamma sufficient, became disenchanted with it and departed.”

372. “So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ [T 1.0445] pariyesamāno [V 1.0308] yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso passa ma. ni. 1.278 pāsarāsisutte imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu’nti. Evaṃ vutte, aggivessana, udako rāmaputto maṃ etadavoca – ‘viharatāyasmā, tādiso ayaṃ dhammo yattha viññū puriso nacirasseva sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihareyyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇiṃ. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tāvatakeneva oṭṭhapahatamattena lapitalāpanamattena ñāṇavādañca vadāmi theravādañca, ‘jānāmi passāmī’ti ca paṭijānāmi, ahañceva aññe ca. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ kevalaṃ saddhāmattakena sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesi. Addhā rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ vihāsī’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, aggivessana, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā no, āvuso rāmo, imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, aggivessana, udako rāmaputto nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘na kho rāmasseva ahosi saddhā, mayhaṃpatthi saddhā; na kho rāmasseva ahosi vīriyaṃ, mayhaṃpatthi vīriyaṃ; na kho rāmasseva ahosi sati, mayhaṃpatthi sati; na kho rāmasseva ahosi samādhi, mayhaṃpatthi [T 1.0446] samādhi; na kho rāmasseva ahosi paññā, mayhaṃpatthi paññā; yaṃnūnāhaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmīti pavedesi tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya [M 1.0306] padaheyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, nacirasseva khippameva taṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsiṃ.

372. “So I, Aggivessana, seeking what is skillful, searching for the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace, approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached, I said to Udaka Rāmaputta: ‘Friend, I wish to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.’ When this was said, Aggivessana, Udaka Rāmaputta said to me: ‘Let the venerable one stay. This Dhamma is such that a wise person can, in no long time, realize for himself with direct knowledge his own teacher's doctrine, and having entered upon it, abide.’ So I, Aggivessana, in no long time, very quickly, learned that Dhamma. And I, Aggivessana, to that extent, by mere lip-recital and repetition of speech, spoke the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders; I myself professed, ‘I know, I see,’ and others did as well. Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Rāma did not declare that he abided having realized this Dhamma for himself with direct knowledge and entered upon it based on mere faith alone. Surely, Rāma abided knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’ Then, Aggivessana, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta and asked: ‘To what extent, friend, did Rāma declare this Dhamma, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge and entered upon it?’ When this was said, Aggivessana, Udaka Rāmaputta declared the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘It was not only Rāma who had faith; I too have faith. It was not only Rāma who had energy; I too have energy. It was not only Rāma who had mindfulness; I too have mindfulness. It was not only Rāma who had concentration; I too have concentration. It was not only Rāma who had wisdom; I too have wisdom. What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma declared he had realized for himself with direct knowledge and entered upon?’ So I, Aggivessana, in no long time, very quickly, having realized that Dhamma for myself with direct knowledge and having entered upon it, abided.”

“Atha khvāhaṃ, aggivessana, yena udako rāmaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā udakaṃ rāmaputtaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘ettāvatā no, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti? ‘Ettāvatā kho, āvuso, rāmo imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesī’ti. ‘Ahampi kho, āvuso, ettāvatā imaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharāmī’ti. ‘Lābhā no, āvuso, suladdhaṃ no, āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi, taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharasi, taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja pavedesi. Iti yaṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi taṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi; yaṃ tvaṃ dhammaṃ jānāsi taṃ dhammaṃ rāmo abhiññāsi. Iti [V 1.0309] yādiso rāmo ahosi tādiso tuvaṃ; yādiso tuvaṃ tādiso rāmo ahosi. Ehi dāni, āvuso, tuvaṃ imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharā’ti. Iti kho, aggivessana, udako [T 1.0447] rāmaputto sabrahmacārī me samāno ācariyaṭṭhāne ca maṃ ṭhapesi, uḷārāya ca maṃ pūjāya pūjesi. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘nāyaṃ dhammo nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, yāvadeva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpapattiyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, taṃ dhammaṃ analaṅkaritvā tasmā dhammā nibbijja apakkamiṃ.

“Then, Aggivessana, I went to Udaka Rāmaputta and, on arrival, said to him: ‘Friend, was it to this extent that Rāma declared this Dhamma, having realized it himself with direct knowledge and attained it?’ ‘Friend, it was to this extent that Rāma declared this Dhamma, having realized it himself with direct knowledge and attained it.’ I then said, ‘Friend, I too dwell having realized this Dhamma myself with direct knowledge and attained it to this extent.’ ‘It is a gain for us, friend, a great gain for us, that we see such a venerable fellow practitioner. Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma declared, having realized it himself with direct knowledge and attained it, is the Dhamma that you dwell in, having realized it yourself with direct knowledge and attained it. And the Dhamma that you dwell in, having realized it yourself with direct knowledge and attained it, is the Dhamma that Rāma declared, having realized it himself with direct knowledge and attained it. Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma knew with direct knowledge, you know; and the Dhamma that you know, Rāma knew with direct knowledge. As Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma. Come now, friend, you lead this group.’ In this way, Aggivessana, Udaka Rāmaputta, though my fellow practitioner, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with a great honor. Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna; it leads only as far as rebirth in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ And so, Aggivessana, not valuing that Dhamma, I became disenchanted with it and departed.”

373. “So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, kiṃkusalagavesī anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ pariyesamāno magadhesu anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena uruvelā senānigamo tadavasariṃ. Tatthaddasaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ, pāsādikañca vanasaṇḍaṃ, nadiñca sandantiṃ setakaṃ supatitthaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, samantā ca gocaragāmaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘ramaṇīyo vata, bho, bhūmibhāgo, pāsādiko ca vanasaṇḍo, nadī ca sandati setakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā, samantā ca gocaragāmo. Alaṃ vatidaṃ kulaputtassa padhānatthikassa [M 1.0307] padhānāyā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tattheva nisīdiṃ ‘alamidaṃ padhānāyā’ti.

373. “Then, Aggivessana, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed, excellent state of peace, I wandered by stages through the Magadhan country and in due course arrived at the market town of Senā in Uruvelā. There I saw a delightful portion of land, an inspiring grove, a flowing river with clear water and good, delightful fords, and a village for alms-food all around. Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘Indeed, this portion of land is delightful, the grove is inspiring, the river flows with clear water and good, delightful fords, and there is a village for alms-food all around. This is indeed suitable for a clansman intent on striving to exert himself.’ And so, Aggivessana, thinking, ‘This is a suitable place for striving,’ I sat down right there.”

374. “Apissumaṃ, aggivessana, tisso upamā paṭibhaṃsu anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ udake nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, api nu so puriso amuṃ allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ, udake nikkhittaṃ[T 1.0448], uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya, tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Aduñhi, bho gotama, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ, tañca pana udake [P 1.0241] nikkhittaṃ. Yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, aggivessana, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi avūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho, so ca ajjhattaṃ na suppahīno hoti, na suppaṭippassaddho, opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te bhonto [V 1.0310] samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, aggivessana, paṭhamā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.

374. “Then, Aggivessana, three similes occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before. Suppose, Aggivessana, there was a wet, sappy piece of wood that had been placed in water. Then a man would come with an upper fire-stick, thinking, ‘I will produce fire, I will generate heat.’ What do you think, Aggivessana? Could that man, by rubbing the upper fire-stick against that wet, sappy piece of wood which had been placed in water, produce fire and generate heat?” “No, venerable Gotama.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable Gotama, that wood is wet and sappy, and it has been placed in water. That man would only be a partaker of fatigue and vexation.” “Even so, Aggivessana, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell with body and mind not withdrawn from sensual pleasures, and whose sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, and sensual fever for sensual pleasures has not been well abandoned and well stilled internally—even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings born of striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter feelings born of striving, they are still incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed enlightenment. This, Aggivessana, was the first simile that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before.”

375. “Aparāpi kho maṃ, aggivessana, dutiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ, ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, api nu so puriso amuṃ allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ, ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ, uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya [T 1.0449] abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “No hidaṃ, bho gotama”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Aduñhi, bho gotama, allaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sasnehaṃ, kiñcāpi ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ. Yāvadeva ca pana so puriso kilamathassa vighātassa [M 1.0308] bhāgī assāti. Evameva kho, aggivessana, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi vūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho so ca ajjhattaṃ na suppahīno hoti, na suppaṭippassaddho, opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, abhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, aggivessana, dutiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā”.

375. “Furthermore, Aggivessana, a second simile occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before. Suppose, Aggivessana, there was a wet, sappy piece of wood, placed on dry land away from water. Then a man came along with an upper fire-stick, thinking, ‘I will produce fire, I will make heat appear.’ What do you think, Aggivessana? Could that man, by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing that wet, sappy piece of wood which was placed on dry land away from water, produce fire and make heat appear?” “No, venerable Gotama.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable Gotama, that wood is wet and sappy, even though it is placed on dry land away from water. That man would only become a partaker of weariness and vexation.” “Even so, Aggivessana, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures with body and mind, and that desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and fever for sensual pleasures which is in them has not been well abandoned internally, has not been well calmed—even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins feel painful, sharp, harsh, bitter feelings due to their striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed supreme enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, sharp, harsh, bitter feelings due to their striving, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed supreme enlightenment. This, Aggivessana, is the second simile that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before.”

376. “Aparāpi kho maṃ, aggivessana, tatiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā [P 1.0242] pubbe assutapubbā. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ, ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya – ‘aggiṃ abhinibbattessāmi, tejo pātukarissāmī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, aggivessana, api nu so puriso amuṃ sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ, ārakā udakā thale nikkhittaṃ, uttarāraṇiṃ ādāya [T 1.0450] abhimanthento aggiṃ abhinibbatteyya, tejo pātukareyyā”ti? “Evaṃ, bho gotama”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Aduñhi, bho gotama, sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ koḷāpaṃ, tañca pana ārakā udakā thale nikkhitta”nti[V 1.0311]. “Evameva kho, aggivessana, ye hi keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā kāyena ceva cittena ca kāmehi vūpakaṭṭhā viharanti, yo ca nesaṃ kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapipāsā kāmapariḷāho, so ca ajjhattaṃ suppahīno hoti suppaṭippassaddho, opakkamikā cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, bhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. No cepi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, bhabbāva te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya. Ayaṃ kho maṃ, aggivessana, tatiyā upamā paṭibhāsi anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā. Imā kho maṃ, aggivessana, tisso upamā paṭibhaṃsu anacchariyā pubbe assutapubbā.”

376. “Furthermore, Aggivessana, a third simile occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before. Suppose, Aggivessana, there was a dry, sapless piece of wood, placed on dry land far from water. Then a man came along with an upper fire-stick, thinking, ‘I will produce fire, I will make heat appear.’ What do you think, Aggivessana? Could that man, by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing that dry, sapless piece of wood which was placed on dry land far from water, produce fire and make heat appear?” “Yes, venerable Gotama.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable Gotama, that wood is dry and sapless, and it is placed on dry land, far from water.” “Even so, Aggivessana, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures with body and mind, and that desire, affection, infatuation, thirst, and fever for sensual pleasures which is in them has been well abandoned internally, has been well calmed—even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins feel painful, sharp, harsh, bitter feelings due to their striving, they are capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed supreme enlightenment. And even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not feel painful, sharp, harsh, bitter feelings due to their striving, they are capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed supreme enlightenment. This, Aggivessana, is the third simile that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before. These, Aggivessana, are the three similes that occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before.”

377. “Tassa [M 1.0309] mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ dantebhi dantamādhāya passa ma. ni. 1.221 vitakkasaṇṭhānasutte, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇheyyaṃ abhinippīḷeyyaṃ abhisantāpeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, dantebhi dantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhāmi abhinippīḷemi abhisantāpemi. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, dantebhi dantamādhāya jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato [T 1.0451] abhisantāpayato kacchehi sedā muccanti. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, balavā puriso dubbalataraṃ purisaṃ sīse vā gahetvā khandhe vā gahetvā abhiniggaṇheyya abhinippīḷeyya abhisantāpeyya, evameva kho me, aggivessana, dantebhi dantamādhāya, jivhāya tāluṃ āhacca, cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhato abhinippīḷayato abhisantāpayato kacchehi sedā muccanti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, aggivessana, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, sāraddho ca pana me kāyo [P 1.0243] hoti appaṭippassaddho teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

377. “Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against my palate, were to subdue, crush, and torment my mind with my mind?’ So, Aggivessana, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against my palate, I subdued, crushed, and tormented my mind with my mind. As I was doing so, Aggivessana, sweat poured from my armpits. Just as a strong man, having seized a weaker man by the head or shoulders, might subdue, crush, and torment him, even so, Aggivessana, as I, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against my palate, subdued, crushed, and tormented my mind with my mind, sweat poured from my armpits. My energy was aroused and unshrinking, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, yet my body was agitated and uncalmed on account of that painful striving, as I was overcome by the exertion. Aggivessana, even such a painful feeling that arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.”

378. “Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu kaṇṇasotehi vātānaṃ nikkhamantānaṃ adhimatto saddo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma kammāragaggariyā dhamamānāya adhimatto saddo hoti, evameva kho me, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca assāsapassāsesu [V 1.0312] uparuddhesu kaṇṇasotehi vātānaṃ nikkhamantānaṃ adhimatto saddo hoti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, aggivessana, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā. Sāraddho ca pana me [T 1.0452] kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

378. To me, Aggivessana, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the meditation that is simply without breath?' So I, Aggivessana, restrained the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose. For me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose were restrained, there was an exceedingly loud sound of winds exiting from my ear passages. Just as there is an exceedingly loud sound from a blacksmith's bellows when it is being blown, even so, for me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth and nose were restrained, there was an exceedingly loud sound of winds exiting from my ear passages. Indeed, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused. But my body was agitated and uncalmed on account of that very painful striving by which I was afflicted. Even such a painful feeling that had arisen in me, Aggivessana, did not overcome my mind and remain.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato [M 1.0310] ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā muddhani ūhananti ūhanti (sī.), ohananti (syā. kaṃ.), uhananti (ka.). Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, balavā puriso tiṇhena sikharena muddhani abhimattheyya muddhānaṃ abhimantheyya (sī. pī.), muddhānaṃ abhimattheyya (syā. kaṃ.), evameva kho me, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā muddhani ūhananti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, aggivessana, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā. Sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

To me, Aggivessana, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the meditation that is simply without breath?' So I, Aggivessana, restrained the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. For me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears were restrained, exceedingly strong winds struck my head. Just as, Aggivessana, a strong man might bore into one's head with a sharp point, even so, for me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears were restrained, exceedingly strong winds struck my head. Indeed, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused. But my body was agitated and uncalmed on account of that very painful striving by which I was afflicted. Even such a painful feeling that had arisen in me, Aggivessana, did not overcome my mind and remain.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu [T 1.0453] uparuddhesu adhimattā sīse sīsavedanā honti. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, balavā puriso daḷhena [P 1.0244] varattakkhaṇḍena varattakabandhanena (sī.) sīse sīsaveṭhaṃ dadeyya, evameva kho me, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā sīse sīsavedanā honti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, aggivessana, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā. Sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

To me, Aggivessana, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the meditation that is simply without breath?' So I, Aggivessana, restrained the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. For me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears were restrained, there were exceedingly strong pains in my head. Just as, Aggivessana, a strong man might tighten a tough leather strap around one's head as a headband, even so, for me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears were restrained, there were exceedingly strong pains in my head. Indeed, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused. But my body was agitated and uncalmed on account of that very painful striving by which I was afflicted. Even such a painful feeling that had arisen in me, Aggivessana, did not overcome my mind and remain.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā [V 1.0313] vātā kucchiṃ parikantanti. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā tiṇhena [M 1.0311] govikantanena kucchiṃ parikanteyya, evameva kho me, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimattā vātā kucchiṃ parikantanti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, aggivessana, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā. Sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho teneva dukkhappadhānena [T 1.0454] padhānābhitunnassa sato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

To me, Aggivessana, this thought occurred: 'What if I were to practice the meditation that is simply without breath?' So I, Aggivessana, restrained the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. For me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears were restrained, exceedingly strong winds cut through my belly. Just as, Aggivessana, a skilled butcher or his apprentice might carve up a cow's belly with a sharp butcher's knife, even so, for me, Aggivessana, when the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears were restrained, exceedingly strong winds cut through my belly. Indeed, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused. But my body was agitated and uncalmed on account of that very painful striving by which I was afflicted. Even such a painful feeling that had arisen in me, Aggivessana, did not overcome my mind and remain.

“Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ appāṇakaṃyeva jhānaṃ jhāyeyya’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāse uparundhiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimatto kāyasmiṃ ḍāho hoti. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, dve balavanto purisā dubbalataraṃ purisaṃ nānābāhāsu gahetvā aṅgārakāsuyā santāpeyyuṃ samparitāpeyyuṃ, evameva kho me, aggivessana, mukhato ca nāsato ca kaṇṇato ca assāsapassāsesu uparuddhesu adhimatto kāyasmiṃ ḍāho hoti. Āraddhaṃ kho pana me, aggivessana, vīriyaṃ hoti asallīnaṃ upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā. Sāraddho ca pana me kāyo hoti appaṭippassaddho teneva dukkhappadhānena padhānābhitunnassa sato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā dukkhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Apissu maṃ, aggivessana, devatā [P 1.0245] disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekaccā devatā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo, api ca kālaṅkarotī’ti. Ekaccā devatā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kālaṅkato samaṇo gotamo, napi kālaṅkaroti, arahaṃ samaṇo gotamo, vihārotveva so vihārotveveso (sī.) arahato evarūpo hotī’ti vihārotveveso arahato”ti (?).

Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to practice the meditation without breath?’ So, Aggivessana, I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears. As I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths through my mouth, nose, and ears, an extreme burning arose in my body. Just as, Aggivessana, two strong men might seize a weaker man by the arms and roast and scorch him over a pit of hot coals, so too, Aggivessana, an extreme burning arose in my body as my in-breaths and out-breaths were stopped through the mouth, nose, and ears. My energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, but my body was agitated and uncalmed, afflicted as I was by that painful striving. Even such painful feelings that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not invade my mind and remain. Then, Aggivessana, some deities, seeing me, said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is dead.’ Other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’ Still other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither dead nor dying; he is an Arahant, for such is the abiding of an Arahant.’

379. “Tassa [T 1.0455] mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajjeyya’nti. Atha kho maṃ, aggivessana, devatā upasaṅkamitvā [M 1.0312] etadavocuṃ – ‘mā kho tvaṃ, mārisa, sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajji. Sace kho tvaṃ, mārisa, sabbaso āhārupacchedāya paṭipajjissasi, tassa te mayaṃ dibbaṃ ojaṃ lomakūpehi ajjhohāressāma ajjhoharissāma (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.), tāya tvaṃ yāpessasī’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘ahañceva kho pana sabbaso ajajjitaṃ ajaddhukaṃ (sī. pī.), jaddhukaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) paṭijāneyyaṃ, imā ca me devatā dibbaṃ ojaṃ lomakūpehi ajjhohāreyyuṃ ajjhohareyyuṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.), tāya [V 1.0314] cāhaṃ yāpeyyaṃ, taṃ mamassa musā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tā devatā paccācikkhāmi, ‘hala’nti vadāmi.

379. Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to practice complete abstinence from food?’ Then, Aggivessana, deities approached me and said: ‘Good sir, do not practice complete abstinence from food. If you, good sir, practice complete abstinence from food, we will infuse divine nutriment into the pores of your skin, and by that you will be sustained.’ Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘If I were to profess complete abstinence from food, while these deities infuse divine nutriment into the pores of my skin by which I would be sustained, that would be a falsehood on my part.’ So, Aggivessana, I refused those deities, saying, ‘That will not do.’

380. “Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyyaṃ, pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ, yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ, yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ, yadi vā hareṇukayūsa’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ, pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ, yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ, yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ, yadi vā hareṇukayūsaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, thokaṃ thokaṃ āhāraṃ āhārayato, pasataṃ pasataṃ, yadi vā muggayūsaṃ, yadi vā kulatthayūsaṃ, yadi vā kaḷāyayūsaṃ, yadi vā hareṇukayūsaṃ, adhimattakasimānaṃ patto kāyo hoti. Seyyathāpi nāma āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vā, evamevassu [T 1.0456] me aṅgapaccaṅgāni bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma oṭṭhapadaṃ, evamevassu me ānisadaṃ hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma vaṭṭanāvaḷī, evamevassu me piṭṭhikaṇṭako uṇṇatāvanato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma jarasālāya gopāṇasiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti, evamevassu me phāsuḷiyo oluggaviluggā bhavanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti, evamevassu me akkhikūpesu akkhitārakā gambhīragatā okkhāyikā dissanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Seyyathāpi nāma tittakālābu [P 1.0246] āmakacchinno vātātapena saṃphuṭito hoti sammilāto, evamevassu me sīsacchavi saṃphuṭitā hoti sammilātā [M 1.0313] tāyevappāhāratāya.

380. Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘What if I were to take very little food, a hollowed handful at a time, whether of green gram soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup?’ So, Aggivessana, I took very little food, a hollowed handful at a time, whether of green gram soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup. As I did so, Aggivessana, my body reached an extreme state of emaciation. Because of that meager diet, my major and minor limbs became like the joints of an āsītika creeper or a kāḷa creeper. Because of that meager diet, my buttocks became like a camel’s footprint. Because of that meager diet, my spine became uneven, like a string of beads. Because of that meager diet, my ribs jutted out, like the rafters of a dilapidated old hall. Because of that meager diet, my eyeballs, sunk deep in their sockets, appeared like the reflection of stars in a deep well. Because of that meager diet, the skin of my head became shriveled and withered, like a bitter gourd cut fresh and withered by wind and sun.

“So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, udaracchaviṃ parimasissāmīti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ parimasissāmīti udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmi, yāvassu me, aggivessana, udaracchavi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karissāmīti tattheva avakujjo papatāmi tāyevappāhāratāya. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, imameva kāyaṃ assāsento pāṇinā gattāni anumajjāmi. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, pāṇinā gattāni anumajjato pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā papatanti tāyevappāhāratāya. Apissu maṃ, aggivessana, manussā [T 1.0457] disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kāḷo samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekacce manussā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kāḷo samaṇo gotamo, sāmo samaṇo gotamo’ti. Ekacce manussā evamāhaṃsu – ‘na kāḷo samaṇo gotamo[V 1.0315], napi sāmo, maṅguracchavi samaṇo gotamo’ti. Yāvassu me, aggivessana, tāva parisuddho chavivaṇṇo pariyodāto upahato hoti tāyevappāhāratāya.

Then, Aggivessana, when I thought, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I would grasp my spine. When I thought, ‘I will touch my spine,’ I would grasp the skin of my belly. So much had the skin of my belly clung to my spine because of that meager diet. Then, Aggivessana, when I thought, ‘I will relieve myself of feces or urine,’ I would fall down right there on my face because of that meager diet. Then, Aggivessana, to comfort this very body, I would rub my limbs with my hand. As I rubbed my limbs, the hairs, their roots rotted, fell from my body because of that meager diet. Then, Aggivessana, people who saw me said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black; he is golden-brown.’ Other people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor golden-brown; he has a dusky complexion.’ So much had my clear, bright complexion been ruined because of that meager diet.

381. “Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘ye kho keci atītamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayiṃsu, etāvaparamaṃ, nayito bhiyyo. Yepi hi keci anāgatamaddhānaṃ samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayissanti, etāvaparamaṃ, nayito bhiyyo. Yepi hi keci etarahi samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā opakkamikā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti, etāvaparamaṃ, nayito bhiyyo. Na kho panāhaṃ imāya kaṭukāya dukkarakārikāya adhigacchāmi uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ. Siyā nu kho añño maggo bodhāyā’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ pitu sakkassa kammante sītāya jambucchāyāya nisinno vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharitā. Siyā nu kho eso maggo bodhāyā’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, satānusāri [T 1.0458] viññāṇaṃ ahosi – ‘eseva maggo bodhāyā’ti. Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ [P 1.0247] tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi, yaṃ taṃ sukhaṃ aññatreva kāmehi aññatra [M 1.0314] akusalehi dhammehī’ti? Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘na kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi, yaṃ taṃ sukhaṃ aññatreva kāmehi aññatra akusalehi dhammehī’ti.

381. Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have experienced painful feelings due to exertion that were sharp, harsh, and severe, this was the utmost; there is nothing beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful feelings due to exertion that are sharp, harsh, and severe, this will be the utmost; there will be nothing beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience painful feelings due to exertion that are sharp, harsh, and severe, this is the utmost; there is nothing beyond this. Yet by this severe and difficult practice, I do not attain any state superior to human states, any special knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to awakening?’ Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘I recall that while my father, the Sakyan, was at work, I was sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree; quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Could this be the path to awakening?’ Then, Aggivessana, a consciousness in accordance with that memory arose in me: ‘This is indeed the path to awakening.’ Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘Why should I fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?’ Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: ‘I do not fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.’

382. “Tassa mayhaṃ, aggivessana, etadahosi – ‘na kho taṃ sukaraṃ sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ evaṃ adhimattakasimānaṃ pattakāyena, yaṃnūnāhaṃ oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyyaṃ odanakummāsa’nti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ odanakummāsaṃ. Tena kho pana maṃ, aggivessana, samayena pañca pañcavaggiyā (aññasuttesu) bhikkhū paccupaṭṭhitā honti – ‘yaṃ kho samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ adhigamissati, taṃ no ārocessatī’ti. Yato kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāresiṃ odanakummāsaṃ, atha me te pañca bhikkhū nibbijja pakkamiṃsu – ‘bāhulliko bāhuliko (sī. pī.) saṃghabhedasikkhāpadaṭīkāya sameti samaṇo gotamo, padhānavibbhanto, āvatto bāhullāyā’ti.

382. Then, Aggivessana, this thought occurred to me: 'It is not easy to attain that happiness with a body that has become so extremely emaciated. What if I were to take coarse food, namely rice and barley-meal?' So, Aggivessana, I took coarse food: rice and barley-meal. Now at that time, Aggivessana, five monks were attending on me, thinking: 'Whatever Dhamma the ascetic Gotama realizes, he will declare it to us.' But when, Aggivessana, I took coarse food—rice and barley-meal—those five monks, becoming disgusted, departed from me, saying: 'The ascetic Gotama has become one who lives in abundance; he has abandoned his striving and reverted to a life of abundance.'

383. “So [V 1.0316] kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāretvā, balaṃ gahetvā, vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca vihāsiṃ, sato ca sampajāno. Sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedesiṃ yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ [T 1.0459] upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihāsiṃ. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

383. So, Aggivessana, having taken coarse food and regained my strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Even when such a pleasant feeling arose in me, Aggivessana, it did not consume my mind and remain. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and abided in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is filled with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. Even when such a pleasant feeling arose in me, Aggivessana, it did not consume my mind and remain. With the fading away of rapture, I abided equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and I experienced pleasure with the body. I entered and abided in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'One abides equanimous, mindful, and happy.' Even when such a pleasant feeling arose in me, Aggivessana, it did not consume my mind and remain. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and abided in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Even when such a pleasant feeling arose in me, Aggivessana, it did not consume my mind and remain.

384. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya [P 1.0248] cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi[M 1.0315], seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Ayaṃ kho me, aggivessana, rattiyā paṭhame yāme paṭhamā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

384. When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and had attained imperturbability, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives. I recollected many kinds of past lives, that is: one birth… and so on… Thus with their aspects and details I recollected many kinds of past lives. This, Aggivessana, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute. But even when such a pleasant feeling arose in me, Aggivessana, it did not consume my mind and remain.

385. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passāmi cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāmi…pe… ayaṃ kho me, aggivessana, rattiyā majjhime yāme dutiyā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo [P 1.0249] vihato, āloko uppanno; yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato[V 1.0317]. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana[T 1.0460], uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

385. When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and had attained imperturbability, I inclined my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and in bad destinations—and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions… This, Aggivessana, was the second true knowledge I attained in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute. But even when such a pleasant feeling arose in me, Aggivessana, it did not consume my mind and remain.

386. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesiṃ. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. ‘Ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccittha. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ ahosi. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsiṃ. Ayaṃ kho me, aggivessana, rattiyā pacchime yāme tatiyā vijjā adhigatā; avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā; tamo vihato, āloko uppanno; yathā [M 1.0316] taṃ appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato. Evarūpāpi kho me, aggivessana, uppannā sukhā vedanā cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati.

386. With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliable, workable, firm, and having attained imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; ‘This is the origin of suffering’; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew, as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; ‘This is the origin of the taints’; ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ Knowing and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there was the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’ This, Aggivessana, was the third knowledge I attained in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was dispelled, knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute. But even such a pleasant feeling that arose in me did not take possession of my mind and remain.

387. “Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, aggivessana, anekasatāya parisāya dhammaṃ desetā. Apissu maṃ ekameko evaṃ maññati – ‘mamevārabbha samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ desetī’ti. ‘Na kho panetaṃ, aggivessana, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ; yāvadeva viññāpanatthāya tathāgato paresaṃ dhammaṃ [T 1.0461] deseti. So kho ahaṃ, aggivessana, tassāyeva kathāya pariyosāne, tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi samādahāmi, yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī’”ti.

387. I recall, Aggivessana, teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. And yet each and every one thinks: ‘The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma just for me.’ But it should not be seen in this way, Aggivessana. The Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others for the purpose of imparting knowledge. At the end of that talk, Aggivessana, at that very same, former sign of concentration, I inwardly establish my mind, settle it, make it one-pointed, and concentrate it, by which I abide constantly.

“Okappaniyametaṃ bhoto gotamassa yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Abhijānāti kho pana bhavaṃ gotamo divā supitā”ti? “Abhijānāmahaṃ, aggivessana, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno niddaṃ okkamitā”ti. “Etaṃ kho, bho gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammohavihārasmiṃ [V 1.0318] vadantī”ti[P 1.0250]? “Na kho, aggivessana, ettāvatā sammūḷho vā hoti asammūḷho vā. Api ca, aggivessana, yathā sammūḷho ca hoti asammūḷho ca, taṃ suṇāhi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“This is credible for the Venerable Gotama, as it is for an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. But does the Venerable Gotama recall sleeping during the day?” “I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of summer, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, spreading my outer robe folded in four, and lying down on my right side, mindful and fully aware, falling asleep.” “Some ascetics and brahmins, Venerable Gotama, call this dwelling in delusion.” “Not merely by that, Aggivessana, is one deluded or undeluded. But, Aggivessana, as to how one is deluded and how one is not, listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

388. “Yassa kassaci, aggivessana, ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā appahīnā, tamahaṃ ‘sammūḷho’ti vadāmi. Āsavānañhi, aggivessana, appahānā sammūḷho hoti. Yassa kassaci, aggivessana, ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā pahīnā, tamahaṃ ‘asammūḷho’ti vadāmi. Āsavānañhi, aggivessana, pahānā asammūḷho hoti.

388. “Aggivessana, for whomever those taints that are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by vexation, result in suffering, and in the future lead to birth, aging, and death, are unabandoned, that one I call ‘deluded.’ For, Aggivessana, through the non-abandonment of the taints, one is deluded. For whomever, Aggivessana, those taints that are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by vexation, result in suffering, and in the future lead to birth, aging, and death, are abandoned, that one I call ‘undeluded.’ For, Aggivessana, through the abandonment of the taints, one is undeluded.

“Tathāgatassa [T 1.0462] kho, aggivessana, ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā[M 1.0317]. Seyyathāpi, aggivessana, tālo matthakacchinno abhabbo puna virūḷhiyā, evameva kho, aggivessana, tathāgatassa ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā”ti.

“For the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, those taints that are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by vexation, result in suffering, and in the future lead to birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. Just as, Aggivessana, a palm tree with its top cut off is incapable of further growth, even so, Aggivessana, for the Tathāgata, those taints that are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are accompanied by vexation, result in suffering, and in the future lead to birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise in the future.”

389. Evaṃ vutte, saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bho gotama, abbhutaṃ, bho gotama! Yāvañcidaṃ bhoto gotamassa evaṃ āsajja āsajja vuccamānassa, upanītehi vacanappathehi samudācariyamānassa, chavivaṇṇo ceva pariyodāyati, mukhavaṇṇo ca vippasīdati, yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Abhijānāmahaṃ, bho gotama, pūraṇaṃ kassapaṃ vādena vādaṃ samārabhitā. Sopi mayā vādena vādaṃ samāraddho aññenaññaṃ paṭicari, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmesi, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātvākāsi. Bhoto pana bhoto kho pana (sī.) gotamassa evaṃ āsajja āsajja vuccamānassa, upanītehi vacanappathehi samudācariyamānassa, chavivaṇṇo ceva pariyodāyati, mukhavaṇṇo ca vippasīdati, yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Abhijānāmahaṃ, bho gotama, makkhaliṃ gosālaṃ…pe… ajitaṃ kesakambalaṃ… pakudhaṃ kaccāyanaṃ… sañjayaṃ belaṭṭhaputtaṃ… nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ vādena vādaṃ samārabhitā[V 1.0319]. Sopi mayā [T 1.0463] vādena vādaṃ samāraddho aññenaññaṃ [P 1.0251] paṭicari, bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmesi, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātvākāsi. Bhoto pana gotamassa evaṃ āsajja āsajja vuccamānassa, upanītehi vacanappathehi samudācariyamānassa, chavivaṇṇo ceva pariyodāyati, mukhavaṇṇo ca vippasīdati, yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Handa ca dāni mayaṃ, bho gotama, gacchāma. Bahukiccā mayaṃ, bahukaraṇīyā”ti. “Yassadāni tvaṃ, aggivessana, kālaṃ maññasī”ti.

389. When this was said, Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭha, said this to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is amazing, Master Gotama! How, when the honorable Gotama is spoken to so pressingly, and challenged with these brought-forward lines of speech, his skin-complexion becomes exceedingly clear, and his facial complexion is especially serene, just as that of an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. I know, Master Gotama, of having engaged Pūraṇa Kassapa in debate. He, having been engaged by me in debate, responded with one thing and another, led the talk to external matters, and manifested anger, ill will, and displeasure. But when the honorable Gotama is spoken to so pressingly, and challenged with these brought-forward lines of speech, his skin-complexion becomes exceedingly clear, and his facial complexion is especially serene, just as that of an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. I know, Master Gotama, of having engaged Makkhali Gosāla… Ajita Kesakambala… Pakudha Kaccāyana… Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta… the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta in debate. He too, having been engaged by me in debate, responded with one thing and another, led the talk to external matters, and manifested anger, ill will, and displeasure. But when the honorable Gotama is spoken to so pressingly, and challenged with these brought-forward lines of speech, his skin-complexion becomes exceedingly clear, and his facial complexion is especially serene, just as that of an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Well then, Master Gotama, we shall now go. We have many duties, much to be done.” “Now, Aggivessana, is the time for whatever you think fit.”

Atha kho saccako nigaṇṭhaputto bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmīti.

Then Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭha, having delighted in and rejoiced at the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and departed.

Mahāsaccakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Great Discourse to Saccaka, the sixth, is concluded.

7. Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayasuttaṃ

7. The Shorter Discourse on the Destruction of Craving

390. Evaṃ [M 1.0318][V 1.0320][T 1.0464] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde. Atha kho sakko devānamindo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho sakko devānamindo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bhikkhu saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussāna”nti?

390. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra's Mother. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One: "To what extent, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu, in brief, liberated through the destruction of craving, one who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate consummation, the best among devas and humans?"

“Idha, devānaminda, bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti – ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti. Evañcetaṃ, devānaminda, bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti – ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti. So sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānāti; sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya sabbaṃ dhammaṃ parijānāti; sabbaṃ dhammaṃ pariññāya yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ vedeti – sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, so tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati. So tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharanto, virāgānupassī viharanto, nirodhānupassī viharanto, paṭinissaggānupassī viharanto na kiñci loke upādiyati. Anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ paccattaññeva parinibbāyati [P 1.0252] – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti [T 1.0465] pajānāti. Ettāvatā kho, devānaminda, bhikkhu saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussāna”nti.

“Here, Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu has heard: ‘All phenomena are not fit for adherence.’ And so, Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu has heard: ‘All phenomena are not fit for adherence.’ He directly knows every phenomenon; having directly known every phenomenon, he fully understands every phenomenon; having fully understood every phenomenon, whatever feeling he experiences—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, he dwells contemplating dispassion, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment. As he dwells contemplating impermanence, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment in those feelings, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Unagitated, he personally attains Parinibbāna. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ To this extent, Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu is, in brief, liberated through the destruction of craving, one who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate consummation, the best among devas and humans.”

Atha kho sakko devānamindo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyi.

Then Sakka, the lord of the devas, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and vanished right there.

391. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato avidūre nisinno hoti. Atha kho āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa etadahosi – “kiṃ nu kho so yakkho bhagavato [V 1.0321] bhāsitaṃ abhisamecca anumodi udāhu no; yaṃnūnāhaṃ taṃ yakkhaṃ jāneyyaṃ – yadi vā so yakkho bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhisamecca [M 1.0319] anumodi yadi vā no”ti? Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde antarahito devesu tāvatiṃsesu pāturahosi. Tena kho pana samayena sakko devānamindo ekapuṇḍarīke uyyāne dibbehi pañcahi tūriyasatehi turiyasatehi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti. Addasā kho sakko devānamindo āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna tāni dibbāni pañca tūriyasatāni paṭippaṇāmetvā yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ [T 1.0466] etadavoca – “ehi kho, mārisa moggallāna, svāgataṃ, mārisa moggallāna! Cirassaṃ kho, mārisa moggallāna, imaṃ pariyāyaṃ akāsi yadidaṃ idhāgamanāya. Nisīda, mārisa moggallāna, idamāsanaṃ paññatta”nti. Nisīdi kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno paññatte āsane. Sakkopi kho devānamindo aññataraṃ nīcaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca – “yathā kathaṃ pana kho, kosiya, bhagavā saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ abhāsi? Sādhu mayampi etissā kathāya bhāgino assāma savanāyā”ti.

391. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was seated not far from the Blessed One. Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'Did that yakkha rejoice in the Blessed One’s discourse having understood it with wisdom, or did he rejoice without having understood it? It would be good if I were to ascertain about that yakkha whether he rejoiced in the Blessed One’s discourse having understood it with wisdom, or whether he did not.' Then, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his stretched-out arm, even so, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having vanished from the Eastern Park, the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother, reappeared among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. At that time, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, was enjoying himself in the Ekapuṇḍarīka Park, being provided with and attended by five hundred celestial musical instruments. Sakka, the Lord of Devas, saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar. Having seen him, he dismissed those five hundred celestial musical instruments and approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'Come, venerable Moggallāna, welcome, venerable Moggallāna! It has been a long time, venerable Moggallāna, since you have made this occasion, that is, of coming here. Sit, venerable Moggallāna, this seat has been prepared.' The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sat down on the prepared seat. Sakka, the Lord of Devas, also took a certain low seat and sat to one side. To Sakka, the Lord of Devas, who was seated to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: 'How then, Kosiya, did the Blessed One speak in brief on the liberation through the destruction of craving? It would be good if we too might have a share of this discourse for the hearing.'

392. “Mayaṃ kho, mārisa moggallāna, bahukiccā bahukaraṇīyā – appeva sakena karaṇīyena, api ca devānaṃyeva tāvatiṃsānaṃ karaṇīyena. Api ca, mārisa moggallāna, sussutaṃyeva hoti suggahitaṃ sumanasikataṃ [P 1.0253] sūpadhāritaṃ, yaṃ no khippameva antaradhāyati. Bhūtapubbaṃ, mārisa moggallāna, devāsurasaṅgāmo samupabyūḷho samūpabyuḷho (syā. kaṃ.), samūpabbūḷho (sī.) ahosi. Tasmiṃ kho pana, mārisa moggallāna, saṅgāme devā jiniṃsu, asurā parājiniṃsu. So kho ahaṃ, mārisa moggallāna, taṃ saṅgāmaṃ abhivijinitvā vijitasaṅgāmo tato paṭinivattitvā vejayantaṃ nāma pāsādaṃ māpesiṃ. Vejayantassa kho, mārisa moggallāna, pāsādassa ekasataṃ niyyūhaṃ. Ekekasmiṃ niyyūhe satta satta kūṭāgārasatāni. Ekamekasmiṃ kūṭāgāre satta satta accharāyo[T 1.0467]. Ekamekissā accharāya satta satta paricārikāyo. Iccheyyāsi no tvaṃ[M 1.0320], mārisa moggallāna, vejayantassa pāsādassa rāmaṇeyyakaṃ daṭṭhu”nti? Adhivāsesi kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno tuṇhībhāvena.

392. ‘Venerable Moggallāna, we have many duties and many things to do—not so much with our own duties as with the duties of the Tāvatiṃsa devas themselves. Moreover, venerable Moggallāna, that which is well-heard, well-grasped, well-considered in the mind, and well-retained, even that quickly vanishes for us. Once in the past, venerable Moggallāna, a battle between the devas and asuras was arrayed. In that battle, venerable Moggallāna, the devas were victorious; the asuras were defeated. I, venerable Moggallāna, having conquered in that battle and being victorious, returned from there and had the palace named Vejayanta created. The Vejayanta palace, venerable Moggallāna, has one hundred and one turrets. In each turret, there are seven hundred pinnacled mansions. In each pinnacled mansion, there are seven nymphs. For each nymph, there are seven attendants. Would you wish, venerable Moggallāna, to see the delightfulness of the Vejayanta palace?’ The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna consented by means of silence.

393. Atha [V 1.0322] kho sakko ca devānamindo vessavaṇo ca mahārājā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ purakkhatvā yena vejayanto pāsādo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Addasaṃsu kho sakkassa devānamindassa paricārikāyo āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ; disvā ottappamānā hirīyamānā sakaṃ sakaṃ ovarakaṃ pavisiṃsu. Seyyathāpi nāma suṇisā sasuraṃ disvā ottappati hirīyati, evameva sakkassa devānamindassa paricārikāyo āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ disvā ottappamānā hirīyamānā sakaṃ sakaṃ ovarakaṃ pavisiṃsu. Atha kho sakko ca devānamindo vessavaṇo ca mahārājā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ vejayante pāsāde anucaṅkamāpenti anuvicarāpenti – “idampi, mārisa moggallāna, passa vejayantassa pāsādassa rāmaṇeyyakaṃ; idampi, mārisa moggallāna, passa vejayantassa pāsādassa rāmaṇeyyaka”nti. “Sobhati idaṃ āyasmato kosiyassa, yathā taṃ pubbe katapuññassa. Manussāpi kiñcideva rāmaṇeyyakaṃ disvā diṭṭhā (sī. pī. ka.) evamāhaṃsu – ‘sobhati vata bho yathā devānaṃ tāvatiṃsāna’nti. Tayidaṃ āyasmato kosiyassa sobhati, yathā taṃ pubbe katapuññassā”ti. Atha kho āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa [T 1.0468] etadahosi – “atibāḷhaṃ kho ayaṃ yakkho pamatto viharati. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ yakkhaṃ saṃvejeyya”nti. Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi abhisaṅkhāresi (ka.), abhisaṅkhāreti (syā. kaṃ.) yathā vejayantaṃ pāsādaṃ pādaṅguṭṭhakena saṅkampesi sampakampesi sampavedhesi[P 1.0254]. Atha kho sakko ca devānamindo, vessavaṇo ca mahārājā, devā ca tāvatiṃsā acchariyabbhutacittajātā ahesuṃ – “acchariyaṃ vata, bho, abbhutaṃ vata, bho, samaṇassa mahiddhikatā mahānubhāvatā, yatra hi nāma dibbabhavanaṃ pādaṅguṭṭhakena saṅkampessati sampakampessati sampavedhessatī”ti! Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ saṃviggaṃ lomahaṭṭhajātaṃ viditvā sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ etadavoca – “yathā kathaṃ pana kho, kosiya, bhagavā saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ abhāsi? Sādhu mayampi etissā kathāya bhāgino assāma savanāyā”ti.

393. Then Sakka, the Lord of Devas, and Vessavaṇa the great king, having placed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna at the forefront, approached the Vejayanta Palace. The female attendants of Sakka, the Lord of Devas, saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar; seeing him, they, out of moral dread and shame, each retreated into their own chambers. Just as a daughter-in-law, upon seeing her father-in-law, feels moral dread and shame, even so, the female attendants of Sakka, the Lord of Devas, seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, out of moral dread and shame, each retreated into their own chambers. Then Sakka, the Lord of Devas, and Vessavaṇa the great king, led the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to walk up and down, and wander around the Vejayanta Palace, saying, "Behold, venerable Moggallāna, this delightfulness of the Vejayanta Palace! Behold, venerable Moggallāna, this delightfulness of the Vejayanta Palace!" "This is resplendent for the venerable Kosiya, as befits one who has made merit in the past. Even humans, upon seeing something delightful, say, 'How splendid, sirs, just like that of the Tāvatiṃsa devas!' So this of the venerable Kosiya is resplendent, as befits one who has made merit in the past." Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: "This yakkha is living with excessive heedlessness. What if I were to stir a sense of urgency in this yakkha?" Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna performed such a feat of psychic power that he made the Vejayanta Palace shake, quake, and tremble with his big toe. Then Sakka, the Lord of Devas, Vessavaṇa the great king, and the Tāvatiṃsa devas were filled with astonishment and amazement, thinking, "How amazing, sirs, how wonderful, sirs, is the great psychic power and might of the ascetic, that he can make the divine mansion shake, quake, and tremble with his big toe!" Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing that Sakka, the Lord of Devas, was agitated and his hair was standing on end, said to him, "In what way, Kosiya, did the Blessed One teach in brief the liberation through the destruction of craving? It would be good if we too could have a share in hearing this discourse."

394. “Idhāhaṃ[M 1.0321], mārisa moggallāna, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsiṃ. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho ahaṃ, mārisa moggallāna, bhagavantaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bhikkhu saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussāna’”nti?

394. "Here, venerable Moggallāna, I approached the Blessed One. Having approached, I paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, venerable Moggallāna, I said to the Blessed One: 'To what extent, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu, in brief, liberated through the destruction of craving, one who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate consummation, the best among devas and humans?'"

“Evaṃ [V 1.0323] vutte, mārisa moggallāna, bhagavā maṃ etadavoca – ‘idha, devānaminda, bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti – sabbe dhammā nālaṃ [T 1.0469] abhinivesāyā’ti. Evaṃ cetaṃ devānaminda bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti. So sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānāti, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya sabbaṃ dhammaṃ parijānāti, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ pariññāya yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ vedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā. So tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati. So tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharanto, virāgānupassī viharanto, nirodhānupassī viharanto, paṭinissaggānupassī viharanto na kiñci loke upādiyati, anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ paccattaññeva parinibbāyati – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Ettāvatā kho, devānaminda, bhikkhu saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussānanti. Evaṃ kho me, mārisa moggallāna, bhagavā saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ abhāsī”ti.

When this was said, venerable Moggallāna, the Blessed One said to me: ‘Here, Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu has heard: “All things are not fit for adherence.” If a bhikkhu has heard this, “All things are not fit for adherence,” he directly knows all things; having directly known all things, he fully understands all things; having fully understood all things, whatever feeling he experiences—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. Dwelling thus, contemplating impermanence, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment in those feelings, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Parinibbāna. He understands: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.” To this extent, Lord of Devas, a bhikkhu is, in brief, liberated through the destruction of craving—one who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate consummation, the best among devas and humans.’ Thus, venerable Moggallāna, the Blessed One briefly explained to me the liberation through the destruction of craving.

Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno sakkassa devānamindassa bhāsitaṃ [P 1.0255] abhinanditvā anumoditvā – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya evameva – devesu tāvatiṃsesu antarahito pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde pāturahosi. Atha kho sakkassa devānamindassa paricārikāyo acirapakkante āyasmante mahāmoggallāne sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ [T 1.0470] etadavocuṃ – “eso nu te, mārisa, so bhagavā satthā”ti? “Na kho me, mārisa, so bhagavā satthā. Sabrahmacārī me eso āyasmā mahāmoggallāno”ti. “Lābhā te, mārisa, (suladdhaṃ te, mārisa) ( ) natthi (sī. pī.) yassa te sabrahmacārī evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo! Aho nūna te so bhagavā satthā”ti.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having delighted in and rejoiced at the words of Sakka, the Lord of Devas, vanished from among the Tāvatiṃsa devas and reappeared in the Eastern Park, in the Palace of Migāra's Mother, just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm. Soon after the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had departed, the female attendants of Sakka, the Lord of Devas, said to him: “Venerable sir, is that the Blessed One, your Teacher?” “No, ladies, that is not the Blessed One, my Teacher. That is my companion in the holy life, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.” “It is a great gain for you, venerable sir, it is well-gained by you, that your companion in the holy life is of such great psychic power and might! How wonderful, then, must the Blessed One, your Teacher, be!”

395. Atha [M 1.0322] kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhijānāti no, bhante, bhagavā ahu ahunaññeva (sī. syā. kaṃ.) ñātaññatarassa mahesakkhassa yakkhassa saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ bhāsitā”ti abhāsitthāti (ka.)? “Abhijānāmahaṃ, moggallāna, idha sakko devānamindo yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho, moggallāna, sakko devānamindo maṃ etadavoca – ‘kittāvatā nu kho, bhante[V 1.0324], bhikkhu saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussāna”nti.

395. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Blessed One: “Does the Blessed One recall, venerable sir, having spoken in brief on the liberation by the destruction of craving to a certain well-known, powerful yakkha?” “I recall, Moggallāna. Here, Sakka, the lord of the devas, approached me; having approached, he paid homage to me and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Moggallāna, Sakka, the lord of the devas, said this to me: ‘To what extent, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu one who is liberated by the destruction of craving in brief, one who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate security from the yokes, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate conclusion, the best among devas and humans?’”

Evaṃ vutte ahaṃ, moggallāna, sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ etadavocaṃ “idha devānaminda bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti. Evaṃ cetaṃ devānaminda bhikkhuno sutaṃ hoti ‘sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyā’ti. So sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānāti, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya sabbaṃ dhammaṃ parijānāti[T 1.0471], sabbaṃ dhammaṃ pariññāya yaṃ kiñci vedanaṃ vedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā. So tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati. So tāsu vedanāsu aniccānupassī viharanto, virāgānupassī viharanto, nirodhānupassī viharanto, paṭinissaggānupassī viharanto na kiñci loke upādiyati, anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ paccattaññeva parinibbāyati – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ[P 1.0256], kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Ettāvatā kho, devānaminda, bhikkhu saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti accantaniṭṭho accantayogakkhemī accantabrahmacārī accantapariyosāno seṭṭho devamanussānanti. Evaṃ kho ahaṃ, moggallāna, abhijānāmi sakkassa devānamindassa saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ bhāsitā”ti.

When this was said, Moggallāna, I said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas: ‘Here, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu has heard: “All phenomena are unfit for adherence.” And if, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu has heard that “All phenomena are unfit for adherence,” he directly knows every phenomenon; having directly known every phenomenon, he fully understands every phenomenon; having fully understood every phenomenon, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, he dwells contemplating dispassion, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment. Dwelling thus contemplating impermanence, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment in those feelings, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains final Nibbāna. He understands: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.” To this extent, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu is, in brief, one who is liberated by the destruction of craving—one who has reached the ultimate end, the ultimate security from the yokes, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate conclusion, the best among devas and humans.’ Thus, Moggallāna, I recall having spoken to Sakka, the lord of the devas, on the liberation by the destruction of craving in brief.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, pleased, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ sattamaṃ.

The seventh, the Shorter Discourse on the Destruction of Craving, is concluded.

8. Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasuttaṃ

8. The Greater Discourse on the Destruction of Craving

396. Evaṃ [T 1.0472][M 1.0323][V 1.0325] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena sātissa nāma bhikkhuno kevaṭṭaputtassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati anañña”nti. Assosuṃ kho sambahulā bhikkhū – “sātissa kira nāma bhikkhuno kevaṭṭaputtassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati, anañña’”nti. Atha kho te bhikkhū yena sāti bhikkhu kevaṭṭaputto tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā sātiṃ bhikkhuṃ kevaṭṭaputtaṃ etadavocuṃ – “saccaṃ kira te, āvuso sāti, evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ – ‘tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati, anañña’”nti? “Evaṃ byā kho ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi yathā tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati, anañña”nti.
