Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo; alamettāvatā [P 1.0273] katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho[T 1.0499], natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti [V 1.0345] tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.

420. “And what more, monks, is to be done? ‘Our livelihood will be pure, open, unconcealed, without flaw, and restrained. And by means of this pure livelihood, we will neither exalt ourselves nor disparage others.’ Thus, monks, should you train. It might occur to you, monks: ‘We are endowed with moral shame and moral dread, our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, our mental conduct is pure, our livelihood is pure; this much is enough, this much has been accomplished, the goal of recluseship has been reached by us, there is nothing further for us to do,’ and you might become content with just that. I declare to you, monks, I announce to you, monks: ‘Let not the goal of recluseship decline for you who are seekers of the goal of recluseship, while there is still something further to be done.’”

421. “Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Indriyesu guttadvārā bhavissāma; cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī nānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjissāma, rakkhissāma cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjissāma. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya na nimittaggāhī nānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjissāma, rakkhissāma manindriyaṃ, manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjissāmā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha [M 1.0341] samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ [T 1.0500] āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi, sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.

421. “And what more, monks, is to be done? ‘We will be those with guarded sense faculties. Having seen a form with the eye, we will not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics. For, should one dwell with the eye faculty unguarded, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail one on that account; we will practice for its restraint, we will guard the eye faculty, and we will undertake restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear… Having smelled an odor with the nose… Having tasted a flavor with the tongue… Having felt a tangible object with the body… Having cognized a mental object with the mind, we will not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics. For, should one dwell with the mind faculty unguarded, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail one on that account; we will practice for its restraint, we will guard the mind faculty, and we will undertake restraint of the mind faculty.’ Thus, monks, should you train. It might occur to you, monks: ‘We are endowed with moral shame and moral dread, our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, our mental conduct is pure, our livelihood is pure, we are those with guarded sense faculties; this much is enough, this much has been accomplished, the goal of recluseship has been reached by us, there is nothing further for us to do,’ and you might become content with just that. I declare to you, monks, I announce to you, monks: ‘Let not the goal of recluseship decline for you who are seekers of the goal of recluseship, while there is still something further to be done.’”

422. “Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Bhojane mattaññuno bhavissāma, paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āharissāma, neva davāya na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya, vihiṃsūparatiyā, brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāma navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāma, yātrā ca no bhavissati, anavajjatā ca, phāsu vihāro cā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo, sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.

422. “And what more, monks, is to be done? ‘We will be moderate in eating. Reflecting wisely, we will take food not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and continuance of this body, for the cessation of affliction, and for the support of the holy life, thinking: “Thus, we will eliminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling. And there will be sustenance for us, and blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.”’ Thus, monks, should you train. It might occur to you, monks: ‘We are endowed with moral shame and moral dread, our bodily conduct is pure, our verbal conduct is pure, our mental conduct is pure, our livelihood is pure, we are those with guarded sense faculties, and we are moderate in eating; this much is enough, this much has been accomplished, the goal of recluseship has been reached by us, there is nothing further for us to do,’ and you might become content with just that. I declare to you, monks, I announce to you, monks: ‘Let not the goal of recluseship decline for you who are seekers of the goal of recluseship, while there is still something further to be done.’”

423. “Kiñca[V 1.0346], bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā bhavissāma, divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhessāma. Rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ caṅkamena [P 1.0274] nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi [T 1.0501] cittaṃ parisodhessāma. Rattiyā majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappessāma pāde pādaṃ accādhāya, sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā. Rattiyā pacchimaṃ yāmaṃ paccuṭṭhāya caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhessāmā’ti, evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho [M 1.0342] manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti, tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo, sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.

423. “And what, bhikkhus, is the further task to be done? ‘We shall be devoted to wakefulness. During the day, by walking and by sitting, we shall cleanse our minds of obstructive states. In the first watch of the night, by walking and by sitting, we shall cleanse our minds of obstructive states. In the middle watch of the night, we shall lie down on the right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having established in our minds the perception of rising. In the last watch of the night, having risen, by walking and by sitting, we shall cleanse our minds of obstructive states.’ Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves. It may be, bhikkhus, that this thought occurs to you: ‘We are endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct is purified, our verbal conduct is purified, our mental conduct is purified, our livelihood is purified, our sense doors are guarded, we are moderate in eating, we are devoted to wakefulness; this is enough, the task is done by this much, the goal of the ascetic life has been attained by us, there is nothing further for us to do,’ and you might be content with just that. I declare to you, bhikkhus, I announce to you, bhikkhus: ‘Let not the goal of asceticism decline for you who are seekers of it, while there is still a further task to be done.’”

424. “Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? ‘Satisampajaññena samannāgatā bhavissāma, abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī’ti, evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Siyā kho pana, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ evamassa [T 1.0502] – ‘hirottappenamha samannāgatā, parisuddho no kāyasamācāro, parisuddho vacīsamācāro, parisuddho manosamācāro, parisuddho ājīvo, indriyesumha guttadvārā, bhojane mattaññuno, jāgariyaṃ anuyuttā, satisampajaññena samannāgatā; alamettāvatā katamettāvatā, anuppatto no sāmaññattho, natthi no kiñci uttariṃ karaṇīya’nti tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyātha. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave – ‘mā vo, sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyi sati uttariṃ karaṇīye’.

424. “And what, bhikkhus, is the further task to be done? ‘We shall be endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, acting with clear comprehension when going forward and returning, when looking ahead and looking aside, when bending and stretching, when wearing the robes and carrying the bowl, when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, when defecating and urinating, when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.’ Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves. It may be, bhikkhus, that this thought occurs to you: ‘We are endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, our bodily conduct is purified, our verbal conduct is purified, our mental conduct is purified, our livelihood is purified, we are guarded in the sense faculties, we are moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension; this much is enough, the task is done by this much, the goal of the ascetic life has been attained by us, there is nothing further to be done,’ and you might be content with just this much. I declare to you, bhikkhus, I announce to you, bhikkhus: ‘Let not the goal of asceticism decline for you who are seekers of it, while there is still a further task to be done.’”

425. “Kiñca, bhikkhave, uttariṃ karaṇīyaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati – araññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ pabbataṃ kandaraṃ giriguhaṃ susānaṃ vanappatthaṃ abbhokāsaṃ palālapuñjaṃ. So pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā, ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya [V 1.0347] parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So abhijjhaṃ loke pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā viharati, abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti; byāpādapadosaṃ pahāya abyāpannacitto viharati, sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī[P 1.0275], byāpādapadosā cittaṃ parisodheti; thīnamiddhaṃ pahāya vigatathīnamiddho viharati, ālokasaññī sato sampajāno, thīnamiddhā cittaṃ parisodheti; uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahāya anuddhato viharati[M 1.0343], ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto, uddhaccakukkuccā cittaṃ parisodheti; vicikicchaṃ pahāya tiṇṇavicikiccho viharati, akathaṃkathī kusalesu dhammesu, vicikicchāya cittaṃ parisodheti.

425. “And what further, bhikkhus, is to be done? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu resorts to a secluded dwelling—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw. Having returned from his alms-round after the meal, he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind devoid of covetousness; he cleanses his mind of covetousness. Abandoning ill will and aversion, he dwells with a mind devoid of ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he cleanses his mind of ill will and aversion. Abandoning sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he cleanses his mind of sloth and torpor. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly stilled; he cleanses his mind of restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, with no perplexity about wholesome states; he cleanses his mind of doubt.”

426. “Seyyathāpi[T 1.0503], bhikkhave, puriso iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojeyya. Tassa te kammantā samijjheyyuṃ sampajjeyyuṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.). So yāni ca porāṇāni iṇamūlāni tāni ca byantī byantiṃ (ka.), byanti (pī.) kareyya, siyā cassa uttariṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ dārabharaṇāya. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojesiṃ, tassa me te kammantā samijjhiṃsu. Sohaṃ yāni ca porāṇāni iṇamūlāni tāni ca byantī akāsiṃ, atthi ca me uttariṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ dārabharaṇāyā’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

426. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man, having taken a loan, were to engage in business. His business ventures would succeed. He would pay off the old, original debts, and there would be a surplus remaining for the support of his wife. The thought would occur to him: ‘Formerly, having taken a loan, I engaged in business, and my business ventures succeeded. I have paid off the old, original debts, and there is a surplus remaining for the support of my wife.’ On that account, he would obtain joy and attain gladness.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso ābādhiko assa dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, bhattañcassa nacchādeyya, na cassa kāye balamattā. So aparena samayena tamhā ābādhā mucceyya, bhattañcassa chādeyya, siyā cassa kāye balamattā. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe ābādhiko ahosiṃ dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, bhattañca me nacchādesi, na ca me āsi kāye balamattā, somhi etarahi tamhā ābādhā mutto, bhattañca me chādeti, atthi ca me kāye balamattā’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to be sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. Food would not be agreeable to him, and there would be no measure of strength in his body. Then, after some time, he would be freed from that sickness. Food would be agreeable to him, and there would be a measure of strength in his body. The thought would occur to him: ‘Formerly, I was sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. Food was not agreeable to me, and there was no measure of strength in my body. But now I am freed from that sickness. Food is agreeable to me, and there is a measure of strength in my body.’ On that account, he would obtain joy and attain gladness.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso bandhanāgāre baddho assa. So aparena samayena tamhā bandhanā mucceyya sotthinā abbhayena abyayena (sī. pī.), na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe bandhanāgāre baddho ahosiṃ, somhi etarahi [T 1.0504] tamhā bandhanā mutto, sotthinā abbhayena, natthi ca me kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were imprisoned in a jail. After some time he would be released from that imprisonment, safe and sound, with no loss of his possessions. It would occur to him: ‘Formerly, I was imprisoned in a jail. Now I have been released from that imprisonment, safe and sound, with no loss of my possessions.’ On that account, he would obtain joy and attain gladness.”

“Seyyathāpi[V 1.0348], bhikkhave, puriso dāso assa anattādhīno parādhīno na yenakāmaṃgamo. So aparena samayena tamhā dāsabyā mucceyya attādhīno aparādhīno bhujisso yenakāmaṃgamo. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe dāso ahosiṃ [M 1.0344] anattādhīno parādhīno na yenakāmaṃgamo, somhi etarahi tamhā dāsabyā mutto attādhīno aparādhīno [P 1.0276] bhujisso yenakāmaṃgamo’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were a slave, not his own master, dependent on others, unable to go where he wished. Then after some time, he might be freed from that slavery, become his own master, independent, a freed man, able to go where he wished. It would occur to him: ‘Formerly, I was a slave, not my own master, dependent on others, unable to go where I wished. Now I am freed from that slavery, my own master, independent, a freed man, able to go where I wish.’ On that account, he would obtain joy and attain gladness.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sadhano sabhogo kantāraddhānamaggaṃ paṭipajjeyya sīlakkhandhavaggapāḷiyā kiñci visadisaṃ. So aparena samayena tamhā kantārā nitthareyya sotthinā abbhayena, na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho pubbe sadhano sabhogo kantāraddhānamaggaṃ paṭipajjiṃ. Somhi etarahi tamhā kantārā nitthiṇṇo sotthinā abbhayena, natthi ca me kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo’ti. So tatonidānaṃ labhetha pāmojjaṃ, adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man with wealth and possessions were to travel a long road through a perilous wilderness. After some time, he might cross beyond that wilderness safely and without fear, with no loss of his possessions. It would occur to him: ‘Formerly, with wealth and possessions, I traveled a long road through a perilous wilderness. Now I have crossed beyond that wilderness safely and without fear, and there has been no loss of my possessions.’ On that account, he would obtain joy and attain gladness.”

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathā iṇaṃ yathā rogaṃ yathā bandhanāgāraṃ yathā dāsabyaṃ yathā kantāraddhānamaggaṃ, ime pañca nīvaraṇe appahīne attani samanupassati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āṇaṇyaṃ yathā ārogyaṃ yathā bandhanāmokkhaṃ yathā bhujissaṃ yathā khemantabhūmiṃ; evameva bhikkhu ime pañca nīvaraṇe [T 1.0505] pahīne attani samanupassati.

“In this very way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees these five hindrances, when unabandoned in himself, as a debt, as a sickness, as a prison, as slavery, and as a long, perilous road through a wilderness. Just as freedom from debt, as health, as release from prison, as the state of a freed man, and as a place of safety; in the same way, a bhikkhu sees these five hindrances, when abandoned in himself.”

427. “So ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe, vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi, savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ vivekajena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho nhāpako nahāpako (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vā nhāpakantevāsī vā kaṃsathāle nhānīyacuṇṇāni nahānīyacuṇṇāni (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ākiritvā udakena paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ sanneyya. Sāyaṃ nhānīyapiṇḍi snehānugatā snehaparetā santarabāhirā, phuṭā snehena na ca pagghariṇī. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ vivekajena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.

427. “Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled bath attendant or his apprentice would pour bath powder into a bronze basin and, sprinkling it again and again with water, would knead it together, so that the ball of bath powder—permeated by moisture, saturated with moisture, pervaded by moisture inside and out—would not drip. In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”

428. “Puna [M 1.0345] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ [V 1.0349] cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ samādhijena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, udakarahado ubbhidodako [P 1.0277] ubbhitodako (ka.). Tassa [T 1.0506] nevassa puratthimāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na pacchimāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na uttarāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, na dakkhiṇāya disāya udakassa āyamukhaṃ, devo ca na kālena kālaṃ sammādhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya. Atha kho tamhāva udakarahadā sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvā tameva udakarahadaṃ sītena vārinā abhisandeyya parisandeyya paripūreyya paripphareyya, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato udakarahadassa sītena vārinā apphuṭaṃ assa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ samādhijena pītisukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa samādhijena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.

428. “Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the stilling of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of concentration. Just as, bhikkhus, there might be a great lake with an upwelling of water. It would have no inlet for water on the eastern side, the western side, the northern side, or the southern side, and the sky-god would not from time to time supply it with proper showers. Then, from that very lake, a cool stream of water, having welled up, would drench, steep, fill, and pervade that very lake with cool water, so that there would be no part of that entire lake unpervaded by the cool water. In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.”

429. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ nippītikena sukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa nippītikena sukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, uppaliniyaṃ vā paduminiyaṃ vā puṇḍarīkiniyaṃ vā appekaccāni uppalāni vā padumāni vā puṇḍarīkāni vā udake jātāni udake saṃvaḍḍhāni udakānuggatāni antonimuggaposīni, tāni yāva caggā yāva ca mūlā [T 1.0507] sītena vārinā abhisannāni parisannāni paripūrāni paripphuṭāni, nāssa na nesaṃ (sī.) kiñci sabbāvataṃ uppalānaṃ vā padumānaṃ vā puṇḍarīkānaṃ vā sītena vārinā apphuṭaṃ assa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ nippītikena sukhena abhisandeti parisandeti paripūreti parippharati, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa nippītikena sukhena apphuṭaṃ hoti.

429. Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimously, is mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body. He enters and remains in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells happily.’ He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with pleasure devoid of rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by pleasure devoid of rapture. Just as, monks, in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some lotuses—born and grown in the water, developing in the water, nourished while submerged—are drenched, steeped, filled, and suffused with cool water from their tips to their roots, so that there is no part of those lotuses unpervaded by cool water; in the same way, monks, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with pleasure devoid of rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by pleasure devoid of rapture.

430. “Puna [M 1.0346] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So imameva kāyaṃ parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena pharitvā nisinno hoti[V 1.0350], nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena apphuṭaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso odātena vatthena sasīsaṃ pārupetvā nisinno assa, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato [P 1.0278] kāyassa odātena vatthena apphuṭaṃ assa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena pharitvā nisinno hoti, nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena apphuṭaṃ hoti.

430. Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and remains in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has a purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits pervading this very body with a pure and bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the pure and bright mind. Just as, monks, a man might sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by the white cloth; in the same way, monks, a monk sits pervading this very body with a pure and bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the pure and bright mind.

431. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ [T 1.0508] anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ, dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sakamhā gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ gaccheyya, tamhāpi gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ gaccheyya, so tamhā gāmā sakaṃyeva gāmaṃ paccāgaccheyya. Tassa evamassa – ‘ahaṃ kho sakamhā gāmā amuṃ gāmaṃ agacchiṃ agacchiṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), tatrapi evaṃ aṭṭhāsiṃ evaṃ nisīdiṃ evaṃ abhāsiṃ evaṃ tuṇhī ahosiṃ; tamhāpi gāmā amuṃ gāmaṃ agacchiṃ, tatrapi evaṃ aṭṭhāsiṃ evaṃ nisīdiṃ evaṃ abhāsiṃ evaṃ tuṇhī ahosiṃ; somhi tamhā gāmā sakaṃyeva gāmaṃ paccāgato’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati.

431. When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, firm, and immovable, he directs it to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births… and so on, with their aspects and details. Just as, monks, a man might go from his own village to another village, from that village to yet another village, and then return from that village back to his own village. He would think: ‘I went from my own village to that village, where I stood in this way, sat in this way, spoke in this way, and remained silent in this way. From that village I went to another village, where I stood in this way, sat in this way, spoke in this way, and remained silent in this way. And then I returned from that village back to my own village.’ In the same way, monks, a monk recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births… and so on, with their aspects and details.

432. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte [M 1.0347] suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate, yathākammūpage satte pajānāti…pe… [P 1.0279] seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dve agārā sadvārā sannadvārā (ka.). Tattha cakkhumā puriso majjhe ṭhito passeyya manusse gehaṃ pavisantepi nikkhamantepi, anucaṅkamantepi anuvicarantepi[T 1.0509]. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti…pe….

432. When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, firm, and immovable, he directs it to the knowledge of the passing away and arising of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and arising—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their actions… Just as, monks, if there were two houses with doors, and a man with good eyesight standing in between them would see people entering and leaving the house, walking and wandering about; in the same way, monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and arising—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their actions…

433. “So evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye [V 1.0351] ṭhite āneñjappatte āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti. So ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. ‘Ime āsavā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ āsavanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, bhavāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati, avijjāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.

433. When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, firm, and immovable, he directs it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.’ As he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of being, and his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pabbatasaṅkhepe udakarahado accho vippasanno anāvilo. Tattha cakkhumā puriso tīre ṭhito passeyya sippisambukampi sippikasambukampi (syā. kaṃ. ka.) sakkharakathalampi macchagumbampi, carantampi tiṭṭhantampi. Tassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho udakarahado accho vippasanno anāvilo. Tatrime sippisambukāpi [P 1.0280] sakkharakathalāpi macchagumbāpi carantipi tiṭṭhantipīti[T 1.0510]. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti.

Just as, monks, if on a mountain slope there were a lake of water—clear, very clear, and undisturbed—a man with good eyesight standing on the bank would see oysters and shells, gravel and potsherds, and also shoals of fish moving about or staying still. It would occur to him: 'This lake of water is clear, very clear, and undisturbed. Herein are these oysters and shells, this gravel and these potsherds, and these shoals of fish moving about and staying still.' In the very same way, monks, a monk understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'... and so on... he understands: 'There is nothing further for this state of being.'

434. “Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘samaṇo’ itipi ‘brāhmaṇo’itipi ‘nhātako’itipi ‘vedagū’itipi ‘sottiyo’itipi ‘ariyo’itipi ‘arahaṃ’itipi. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samaṇo hoti? Samitāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā, saṃkilesikā, ponobbhavikā, sadarā, dukkhavipākā[M 1.0348], āyatiṃ, jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samaṇo hoti.

434. This monk, monks, is called a 'recluse,' a 'brahmin,' one who is cleansed, one who has attained the goal through knowledge, one who is pure, a noble one, and an 'arahant.' And how, monks, is a monk a 'recluse'? For him, evil, unwholesome states—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are fraught with distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—have been pacified. In this way, monks, a monk is a 'recluse.'

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu brāhmaṇo hoti? Bāhitāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā[V 1.0352], saṃkilesikā, ponobbhavikā, sadarā, dukkhavipākā, āyatiṃ, jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu brāhmaṇo hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk a 'brahmin'? For him, evil, unwholesome states—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are fraught with distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—have been excluded. In this way, monks, a monk is a 'brahmin.'

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nhātako nahātako (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) hoti? Nhātāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā, saṃkilesikā, ponobbhavikā, sadarā, dukkhavipākā, āyatiṃ, jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nhātako hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk one who is cleansed? For him, evil, unwholesome states—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are fraught with distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—have been washed away. In this way, monks, a monk is one who is cleansed.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedagū hoti? Viditāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā, saṃkilesikā, ponobbhavikā, sadarā, dukkhavipākā, āyatiṃ, jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedagū hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk one who has attained the goal through knowledge? For him, evil, unwholesome states—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are fraught with distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—have been fully known. In this way, monks, a monk is one who has attained the goal through knowledge.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sottiyo hoti? Nissutāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā, saṃkilesikā, ponobbhavikā, sadarā, dukkhavipākā, āyatiṃ, jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sottiyo hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk one who is pure? For him, evil, unwholesome states—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are fraught with distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—have been cast out. In this way, monks, a monk is one who is pure.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ariyo hoti[T 1.0511]? Ārakāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā, saṃkilesikā, ponobbhavikā, sadarā, dukkhavipākā, āyatiṃ, jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ariyo hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk a noble one? For him, evil, unwholesome states—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are fraught with distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—are far away. In this way, monks, a monk is a noble one.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṃ hoti? Ārakāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā, saṃkilesikā, ponobbhavikā, sadarā, dukkhavipākā, āyatiṃ, jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṃ hotī”ti.

And how, monks, is a monk an 'arahant'? For him, evil, unwholesome states—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are fraught with distress, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death—are far away. In this way, monks, a monk is an 'arahant.'

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Those monks, being pleased, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Mahāassapurasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The ninth, the Greater Discourse at Assapura, is finished.

10. Cūḷaassapurasuttaṃ

10. The Shorter Discourse at Assapura

435. Evaṃ [M 1.0349][V 1.0353][P 1.0281][T 1.0512] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā aṅgesu viharati assapuraṃ nāma aṅgānaṃ nigamo. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “samaṇā samaṇāti vo, bhikkhave, jano sañjānāti. Tumhe ca pana ‘ke tumhe’ti puṭṭhā samānā ‘samaṇāmhā’ti paṭijānātha. Tesaṃ vo, bhikkhave, evaṃsamaññānaṃ sataṃ evaṃpaṭiññānaṃ sataṃ – ‘yā samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadā taṃ paṭipajjissāma; evaṃ no ayaṃ amhākaṃ samaññā ca saccā bhavissati paṭiññā ca bhūtā; yesañca mayaṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paribhuñjāma, tesaṃ te kārā amhesu mahapphalā bhavissanti mahānisaṃsā, amhākañcevāyaṃ pabbajjā avañjhā bhavissati saphalā saudrayā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

435. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Aṅgas, at Assapura, a market town of the Aṅgas. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, people recognize you as ‘recluses.’ And when asked, ‘Who are you?’ you declare, ‘We are recluses.’ With such a designation and such a declaration, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will practice the conduct proper to recluses, so that this designation of ours will be true, and our declaration factual. And for those whose robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick we use, their actions toward us will be of great fruit and great benefit, and this our going forth will not be barren, but fruitful and with increase.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”

436. “Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu na samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti? Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno abhijjhālussa abhijjhā appahīnā hoti, byāpannacittassa byāpādo appahīno hoti, kodhanassa kodho appahīno hoti, upanāhissa upanāho appahīno hoti, makkhissa makkho appahīno hoti, paḷāsissa paḷāso appahīno hoti, issukissa issā appahīnā hoti, maccharissa macchariyaṃ appahīnaṃ hoti[T 1.0513], saṭhassa sāṭheyyaṃ appahīnaṃ hoti, māyāvissa māyā appahīnā hoti, pāpicchassa pāpikā icchā appahīnā hoti, micchādiṭṭhikassa micchādiṭṭhi appahīnā hoti – imesaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, samaṇamalānaṃ samaṇadosānaṃ samaṇakasaṭānaṃ āpāyikānaṃ ṭhānānaṃ duggativedaniyānaṃ appahānā ‘na samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno’ti vadāmi. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, matajaṃ nāma āvudhajātaṃ ubhatodhāraṃ pītanisitaṃ. Tadassa saṅghāṭiyā sampārutaṃ sampaliveṭhitaṃ. Tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imassa bhikkhuno pabbajjaṃ vadāmi.

436. And how, monks, is a monk not one who has entered upon the practice proper to recluses? For whatever monk who is covetous, monks, covetousness is not abandoned; for one with a mind of ill will, ill will is not abandoned; for one who is angry, anger is not abandoned; for one who is resentful, resentment is not abandoned; for one who is contemptuous, contempt is not abandoned; for one who is given to rivalry, rivalry is not abandoned; for one who is envious, envy is not abandoned; for one who is stingy, stinginess is not abandoned; for one who is deceitful, deceit is not abandoned; for one who is fraudulent, fraud is not abandoned; for one with evil desires, evil desire is not abandoned; for one with wrong view, wrong view is not abandoned. Because of the non-abandonment of these stains of a recluse, faults of a recluse, and dregs of a recluse, which lead to the plane of misery and are to be experienced in a woeful destination, I say that he has not entered upon the practice proper to recluses. Just as, monks, a type of weapon named ‘mataja,’ double-edged and well-honed, might be covered and wrapped up in an outer robe, so too, monks, do I declare the going forth of this monk to be.

437. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saṅghāṭikassa saṅghāṭidhāraṇamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, acelakassa acelakamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, rajojallikassa rajojallikamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave[M 1.0350][V 1.0354], udakorohakassa udakorohaṇamattena udakorohakamattena (sī. pī.) sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlikassa rukkhamūlikamattena [P 1.0282] sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, abbhokāsikassa abbhokāsikamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ubbhaṭṭhakassa ubbhaṭṭhakamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, pariyāyabhattikassa pariyāyabhattikamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, mantajjhāyakassa mantajjhāyakamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi. Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, jaṭilakassa jaṭādhāraṇamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi.

437. “Monks, I do not declare recluseship for a wearer of the patchwork robe merely by the wearing of a patchwork robe. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for a naked ascetic merely by being naked. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for one covered in dust and dirt merely by being covered in dust and dirt. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for one who descends into water merely by descending into water. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for one who dwells at the root of a tree merely by dwelling at the root of a tree. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for one who dwells in the open air merely by dwelling in the open air. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for one who stands upright merely by standing upright. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for one who eats food periodically merely by eating food periodically. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for a chanter of mantras merely by chanting mantras. Monks, I do not declare recluseship for one with matted hair merely by wearing matted hair.”

“Saṅghāṭikassa ce, bhikkhave, saṅghāṭidhāraṇamattena abhijjhālussa [T 1.0514] abhijjhā pahīyetha, byāpannacittassa byāpādo pahīyetha, kodhanassa kodho pahīyetha, upanāhissa upanāho pahīyetha, makkhissa makkho pahīyetha, paḷāsissa paḷāso pahīyetha, issukissa issā pahīyetha, maccharissa macchariyaṃ pahīyetha, saṭhassa sāṭheyyaṃ pahīyetha, māyāvissa māyā pahīyetha, pāpicchassa pāpikā icchā pahīyetha, micchādiṭṭhikassa micchādiṭṭhi pahīyetha, tamenaṃ mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā jātameva naṃ saṅghāṭikaṃ kareyyuṃ, saṅghāṭikattameva saṃghāṭīkatte ceva (ka.) samādapeyyuṃ – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhadramukha, saṅghāṭiko hohi, saṅghāṭikassa te sato saṅghāṭidhāraṇamattena abhijjhālussa abhijjhā pahīyissati, byāpannacittassa byāpādo pahīyissati, kodhanassa kodho pahīyissati, upanāhissa upanāho pahīyissati, makkhissa makkho pahīyissati, paḷāsissa paḷāso pahīyissati, issukissa issā pahīyissati, maccharissa macchariyaṃ pahīyissati, saṭhassa sāṭheyyaṃ pahīyissati, māyāvissa māyā pahīyissati, pāpicchassa pāpikā icchā pahīyissati, micchādiṭṭhikassa micchādiṭṭhi pahīyissatī’ti. Yasmā ca kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, saṅghāṭikampi idhekaccaṃ passāmi abhijjhāluṃ byāpannacittaṃ kodhanaṃ upanāhiṃ makkhiṃ paḷāsiṃ issukiṃ macchariṃ saṭhaṃ māyāviṃ pāpicchaṃ micchādiṭṭhikaṃ, tasmā na saṅghāṭikassa saṅghāṭidhāraṇamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi.

“Monks, if for a wearer of the patchwork robe, merely by wearing a patchwork robe, covetousness were to be abandoned in one who is covetous, ill will in one with a mind of ill will, anger in one who is angry, resentment in one who is resentful, disparagement in one who is disparaging, rivalry in one given to rivalry, envy in one who is envious, stinginess in one who is stingy, deceit in one who is deceitful, hypocrisy in one who is hypocritical, evil desire in one with evil desires, and wrong view in one with wrong view—then his friends, companions, and blood relatives would make him a wearer of the patchwork robe from the moment he is born and would have him undertake the state of being a wearer of the patchwork robe, saying: ‘Come, good sir, be a wearer of the patchwork robe. For you, being a wearer of the patchwork robe, merely by wearing a patchwork robe, covetousness will be abandoned in you who are covetous, ill will in you with a mind of ill will, anger in you who are angry, resentment in you who are resentful, disparagement in you who are disparaging, rivalry in you given to rivalry, envy in you who are envious, stinginess in you who are stingy, deceit in you who are deceitful, hypocrisy in you who are hypocritical, evil desire in you with evil desires, and wrong view in you with wrong view.’ But because, monks, I see here a certain wearer of the patchwork robe who is covetous, has a mind of ill will, is angry, resentful, disparaging, given to rivalry, envious, stingy, deceitful, hypocritical, has evil desires, and has wrong view, therefore I do not declare recluseship for a wearer of the patchwork robe merely by the wearing of a patchwork robe.”

“Acelakassa ce, bhikkhave…pe… rajojallikassa ce, bhikkhave…pe… udakorohakassa ce, bhikkhave…pe… rukkhamūlikassa [T 1.0515] ce, bhikkhave…pe… abbhokāsikassa ce, bhikkhave…pe… ubbhaṭṭhakassa ce, bhikkhave…pe… pariyāyabhattikassa ce, bhikkhave…pe… mantajjhāyakassa ce, bhikkhave…pe… jaṭilakassa [M 1.0351] ce, bhikkhave, jaṭādhāraṇamattena abhijjhālussa abhijjhā pahīyetha, byāpannacittassa byāpādo pahīyetha[V 1.0355], kodhanassa kodho pahīyetha, upanāhissa upanāho pahīyetha, makkhissa makkho pahīyetha, paḷāsissa paḷāso pahīyetha, issukissa issā pahīyetha, maccharissa macchariyaṃ pahīyetha, saṭhassa sāṭheyyaṃ pahīyetha, māyāvissa māyā pahīyetha, pāpicchassa pāpikā icchā pahīyetha, micchādiṭṭhikassa micchādiṭṭhi pahīyetha, tamenaṃ mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā jātameva naṃ jaṭilakaṃ kareyyuṃ, jaṭilakattameva jaṭilakatte ceva (ka.) samādapeyyuṃ – ‘ehi tvaṃ, bhadramukha, jaṭilako hohi, jaṭilakassa te sato jaṭādhāraṇamattena abhijjhālussa abhijjhā pahīyissati byāpannacittassa [P 1.0283] byāpādo pahīyissati, kodhanassa kodho pahīyissati…pe… pāpicchassa pāpikā icchā pahīyissati micchādiṭṭhikassa micchādiṭṭhi pahīyissatī’ti. Yasmā ca kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, jaṭilakampi idhekaccaṃ passāmi abhijjhāluṃ byāpannacittaṃ kodhanaṃ upanāhiṃ makkhiṃ palāsiṃ issukiṃ macchariṃ saṭhaṃ māyāviṃ pāpicchaṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ, tasmā [T 1.0516] na jaṭilakassa jaṭādhāraṇamattena sāmaññaṃ vadāmi.

“Monks, if for a naked ascetic... if for one covered in dust and dirt... if for one who descends into water... if for one dwelling at the root of a tree... if for one dwelling in the open air... if for one who stands upright... if for one who eats food periodically... if for one who recites mantras... if, monks, for a matted-hair ascetic, merely by wearing matted hair, covetousness would be abandoned in the covetous person, ill will in the person with a mind of ill will, anger in the angry person, resentment in the resentful person, dispraise in the disparaging person, rivalry in the competitive person, envy in the envious person, stinginess in the stingy person, deceit in the deceitful person, hypocrisy in the hypocritical person, evil desires in the person with evil desires, and wrong view in the person with wrong view—then his friends, companions, and blood relatives would make him a matted-hair ascetic from birth and would encourage him only to undertake the state of being a matted-hair ascetic, saying: ‘Come, good sir, be a matted-hair ascetic. For you, being a matted-hair ascetic, merely by wearing matted hair, covetousness will be abandoned in you who are covetous, ill will will be abandoned in you who have a mind of ill will, anger will be abandoned in you who are angry... evil desires will be abandoned in you who have evil desires, and wrong view will be abandoned in you who have wrong view.’ But because, monks, I see here a certain matted-hair ascetic who is covetous, has a mind of ill will, is angry, resentful, disparaging, competitive, envious, stingy, deceitful, hypocritical, has evil desires, and holds wrong view, therefore I do not declare recluseship for a matted-hair ascetic merely by the wearing of matted hair.”

438. “Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti? Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno abhijjhālussa abhijjhā pahīnā hoti, byāpannacittassa byāpādo pahīno hoti, kodhanassa kodho pahīno hoti, upanāhissa upanāho pahīno hoti, makkhissa makkho pahīno hoti, paḷāsissa paḷāso pahīno hoti, issukissa issā pahīnā hoti, maccharissa macchariyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, saṭhassa sāṭheyyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, māyāvissa māyā pahīnā hoti, pāpicchassa pāpikā icchā pahīnā hoti, micchādiṭṭhikassa micchādiṭṭhi pahīnā hoti – imesaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, samaṇamalānaṃ samaṇadosānaṃ samaṇakasaṭānaṃ āpāyikānaṃ ṭhānānaṃ duggativedaniyānaṃ pahānā ‘samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno’ti vadāmi. So sabbehi imehi pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehi visuddhamattānaṃ samanupassati ( ) (vimuttamattānaṃ samanupassati) (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Tassa sabbehi imehi pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehi visuddhamattānaṃ samanupassato [M 1.0352] ( ) (vimuttamattānaṃ samanupassato) (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati.

438. And how, Bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has undertaken the practice suitable for a recluse? When, for any bhikkhu, covetousness is abandoned in one who is covetous, ill will is abandoned in one with a mind of ill will, anger is abandoned in one who is angry, resentment is abandoned in one who is resentful, contempt is abandoned in one who is contemptuous, rivalry is abandoned in one who is competitive, envy is abandoned in one who is envious, stinginess is abandoned in one who is stingy, deceit is abandoned in one who is deceitful, fraud is abandoned in one who is fraudulent, evil desire is abandoned in one with evil desires, and wrong view is abandoned in one with wrong view—because of the abandoning of these stains of a recluse, faults of a recluse, and dregs of a recluse, which are states leading to the woeful planes and entailing miserable destinations, I declare him to be one who has undertaken the practice suitable for a recluse. He sees himself as purified from all these evil, unwholesome states. For him, seeing himself as purified from all these evil, unwholesome states, gladness is born. For one who is gladdened, rapture is born. For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.

“So mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena [T 1.0517] averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Karuṇāsahagatena [V 1.0356] cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pokkharaṇī acchodakā sātodakā sītodakā setakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā. Puratthimāya [P 1.0284] cepi disāya puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito. So taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ āgamma vineyya udakapipāsaṃ vineyya ghammapariḷāhaṃ…pe… pacchimāya cepi disāya puriso āgaccheyya…pe… uttarāya cepi disāya puriso āgaccheyya…pe… dakkhiṇāya cepi disāya puriso āgaccheyya. Yato kuto cepi naṃ puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto, kilanto tasito pipāsito. So taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ āgamma vineyya udakapipāsaṃ, vineyya ghammapariḷāhaṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, khattiyakulā cepi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti, so ca tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ āgamma, evaṃ mettaṃ karuṇaṃ muditaṃ upekkhaṃ bhāvetvā labhati ajjhattaṃ tamahaṃ (ka.) vūpasamaṃ tamahaṃ (ka.). Ajjhattaṃ vūpasamā ‘samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno’ti vadāmi. Brāhmaṇakulā cepi…pe… vessakulā cepi…pe… suddakulā cepi…pe… yasmā kasmā cepi kulā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti[T 1.0518], so ca tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ āgamma, evaṃ mettaṃ karuṇaṃ muditaṃ upekkhaṃ bhāvetvā labhati ajjhattaṃ vūpasamaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ vūpasamā ‘samaṇasāmīcippaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno’ti vadāmi.

He dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. He dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion… with a mind accompanied by appreciative joy… with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. Just as, Bhikkhus, there might be a pond with clear water, sweet water, cool water, pure water, with good banks, and delightful. If a man were to come from the eastern direction, afflicted by heat, overcome by heat, weary, thirsty, and parched, upon reaching that pond, he would dispel his thirst for water and dispel his great burning heat. Likewise, if a man were to come from the western direction… from the northern direction… from the southern direction… From whatever direction a man might come, afflicted by heat, overcome by heat, weary, thirsty, and parched, upon reaching that pond, he would dispel his thirst for water and dispel his great burning heat. In the same way, Bhikkhus, if one from a warrior family has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, and having come to the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, he develops loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity in this way, he attains internal pacification. Because of internal pacification, I declare him to be one who has undertaken the practice suitable for a recluse. If one from a brahmin family… if one from a merchant family… if one from a worker family… from whatever family one has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, and having come to the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, he develops loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity in this way, he attains internal pacification. Because of internal pacification, I declare him to be one who has undertaken the practice suitable for a recluse.

“Khattiyakulā [M 1.0353] cepi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti. So ca āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hoti. Brāhmaṇakulā cepi…pe… vessakulā cepi… suddakulā cepi… yasmā kasmā cepi kulā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti, so ca āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ [V 1.0357] diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī”ti.

Even if one from a warrior family has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, and he, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having made it manifest, enters and dwells therein; through the destruction of the taints, he is a recluse. Even if one is from a brahmin family... even if one is from a merchant family... even if one is from a worker family... from whatever family one has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, and he, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having made it manifest, enters and dwells therein; through the destruction of the taints, he is a recluse.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Those bhikkhus, being delighted, greatly rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Cūḷaassapurasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Cūḷaassapura Sutta, the tenth, is concluded.

Mahāyamakavaggo niṭṭhito catuttho.

The Mahāyamaka Vagga, the fourth, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Giñjakasālavanaṃ pariharituṃ, paññavato puna saccakanisedho;

Mukhavaṇṇapasīdanatāpindo, kevaṭṭaassapurajaṭilena.

The Brick Hall and the Sāla Grove; for the wise one, again the refutation of Saccaka; the radiant facial complexion; with the fisherman, Assapura, and the matted-hair ascetic.

5. Cūḷayamakavaggo

5. The Cūḷayamaka Vagga

1. Sāleyyakasuttaṃ

1. The Sāleyyaka Sutta

439. Evaṃ [T 1.0519][M 1.0354][V 1.0358][P 1.0285] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ yena sālā nāma kosalānaṃ brāhmaṇagāmo tadavasari. Assosuṃ kho sāleyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā – “samaṇo khalu, bho, gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ sālaṃ anuppatto. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā. So imaṃ lokaṃ sadevakaṃ samārakaṃ sabrahmakaṃ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ sadevamanussaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti. So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ; kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti’. Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ dassanaṃ hotī”ti.

439. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour in the Kosala country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, arrived at Sālā, a brahmin village of the Kosalans. The brahmin householders of Sālā heard: “Indeed, friends, the recluse Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan, while wandering on tour in the Kosala country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, has arrived at Sālā. Regarding that Master Gotama, a good report of his fame has spread thus: ‘That Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Farer, Knower of the world, an unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ He, having realized it for himself with higher knowledge, makes known this world with its devas, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, with its devas and humans. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, utterly complete and pure. It is indeed good to see such Arahants.”

Atha kho sāleyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā appekacce bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ [T 1.0520] sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce bhagavato santike nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu; appekacce tuṇhībhūtā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho sāleyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “ko nu kho, bho gotama, hetu, ko paccayo, yena midhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti[V 1.0359]? Ko pana, bho gotama, hetu, ko paccayo, yena midhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantī”ti?

Then the brahmin householders of Sālā approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after concluding the courteous and memorable talk, sat down to one side. Some, raising their joined palms toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Some announced their name and clan in the Blessed One's presence and sat down to one side. Some, remaining silent, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin householders of Sālā said this to the Blessed One: “What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, an unhappy destination, a place of ruin, in hell? And what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world?”

“Adhammacariyāvisamacariyāhetu kho, gahapatayo, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Dhammacariyāsamacariyāhetu [M 1.0355] kho, gahapatayo, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantī”ti[P 1.0286].

“Householders, it is because of unrighteous and uneven conduct that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, an unhappy destination, a place of ruin, in hell. It is because of righteous and even conduct that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.”

“Na kho mayaṃ imassa bhoto gotamassa saṃkhittena bhāsitassa, vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa, vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāma. Sādhu no bhavaṃ gotamo tathā dhammaṃ desetu, yathā mayaṃ imassa bhoto gotamassa saṃkhittena bhāsitassa, vitthārena atthaṃ avibhattassa, vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyyāmā”ti. “Tena hi, gahapatayo, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho sāleyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā [T 1.0521] etadavoca –

“We do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by Master Gotama, which has not been analyzed in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach us the Dhamma in such a way that we might understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief, which has not been analyzed in detail.” “In that case, householders, listen and apply your minds well; I will speak.” “So be it, Master,” the brahmin householders of Sālā replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

440. “Tividhaṃ kho, gahapatayo, kāyena adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti, catubbidhaṃ vācāya adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti, tividhaṃ manasā adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti.

440. “Householders, unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of the body is threefold; unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of speech is fourfold; and unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of the mind is threefold.”

“Kathañca, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ kāyena adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti? Idha, gahapatayo, ekacco pāṇātipātī hoti, luddo luddo dāruṇo (ka.) ṭīkā oloketabbā lohitapāṇi hatappahate niviṭṭho adayāpanno pāṇabhūtesu sabbapāṇabhūtesu (syā. kaṃ. ka.).

“And how, householders, is unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of the body threefold? Here, householders, someone is a destroyer of life, cruel, with bloody hands, devoted to striking and killing, without compassion for living beings.

“Adinnādāyī kho pana hoti. Yaṃ taṃ parassa paravittūpakaraṇaṃ, gāmagataṃ vā araññagataṃ vā, taṃ adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādātā hoti.

“Furthermore, one takes what is not given. Whatever property or belongings of another, whether in a village or in a forest, that is not given, one takes with thievish intent.

“Kāmesumicchācārī kho pana hoti. Yā tā māturakkhitā piturakkhitā mātāpiturakkhitā bhāturakkhitā bhaginirakkhitā ñātirakkhitā gottarakkhitā dhammarakkhitā sassāmikā saparidaṇḍā antamaso mālāguḷaparikkhittāpi, tathārūpāsu cārittaṃ āpajjitā hoti. Evaṃ kho, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ kāyena adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti.

“Furthermore, one engages in sexual misconduct. One transgresses with women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both mother and father, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, or protected by the Dhamma; with women who have a husband, who are subject to punishment, and even with those who are garlanded as a token of engagement. In this way, householders, unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of the body is threefold.”

“Kathañca[V 1.0360], gahapatayo, catubbidhaṃ vācāya adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti? Idha, gahapatayo, ekacco musāvādī hoti. Sabhāgato vā parisāgato vā, ñātimajjhagato vā pūgamajjhagato vā rājakulamajjhagato vā, abhinīto sakkhipuṭṭho – ‘ehambho purisa, yaṃ jānāsi taṃ vadehī’ti[M 1.0356], so ajānaṃ vā āha – ‘jānāmī’ti, jānaṃ vā āha – ‘na jānāmī’ti, apassaṃ vā āha – ‘passāmī’ti, passaṃ vā āha – ‘na passāmī’ti so āha ajānaṃ vā ahaṃ jānāmīti jānaṃ vā ahaṃ na jānāmīti apassaṃ vā ahaṃ passāmīti passaṃ vā ahaṃ na passāmīti (ka.). Iti attahetu vā parahetu vā āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā sampajānamusā bhāsitā hoti.

“And how, householders, is unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of speech fourfold? Here, householders, someone is a liar. When summoned to an assembly, a gathering, among relatives, in a guild, or in the royal court, and brought forward as a witness, being asked: ‘Good man, tell what you know,’ he, not knowing, says ‘I know’; or knowing, says ‘I do not know’; or not seeing, says ‘I see’; or seeing, says ‘I do not see.’ Thus, for his own sake, or for another’s sake, or for some trifling material gain, he is one who speaks a deliberate lie.

“Pisuṇavāco kho pana hoti. Ito sutvā amutra akkhātā [T 1.0522] imesaṃ bhedāya, amutra vā sutvā imesaṃ akkhātā amūsaṃ bhedāya. Iti samaggānaṃ vā bhettā bhedakā (ka.), bhedetā (syā. kaṃ.), tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana bhettāti dissati, bhinnānaṃ vā anuppadātā, vaggārāmo vaggarato vagganandī vaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

“He is one who speaks divisively. Having heard something here, he reports it there to create dissension among these people; or having heard something there, he reports it to these people to create dissension among those people. Thus, he is a divider of those who are united or an encourager of those who are divided; he delights in disunity, is fond of disunity, rejoices in disunity, and is one who speaks words that create disunity.”

“Pharusavāco kho pana hoti. Yā sā vācā aṇḍakā kaṇḍakā (ka.) kakkasā parakaṭukā parābhisajjanī kodhasāmantā asamādhisaṃvattanikā[P 1.0287], tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

“Furthermore, he is one of harsh speech. That speech of his is thorny, rough, bitter to others, offensive to others, close to anger, and not conducive to concentration. Such is the speech he is one to utter.”

“Samphappalāpī kho pana hoti. Akālavādī abhūtavādī anatthavādī adhammavādī avinayavādī. Anidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti akālena anapadesaṃ apariyantavatiṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ. Evaṃ kho, gahapatayo, catubbidhaṃ vācāya adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti.

He is given to frivolous chatter. He speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is not true, speaks what is unbeneficial, speaks what is not the Dhamma, and speaks what is not the discipline. He is one who speaks words not worth treasuring, at the wrong time, without reason, without limit, and unconnected with benefit. Thus, householders, unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of speech is fourfold.

“Kathañca, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ manasā adhammacariyāvisamacariyā hoti? Idha, gahapatayo, ekacco abhijjhālu hoti, yaṃ taṃ parassa paravittūpakaraṇaṃ taṃ abhijjhātā hoti – ‘aho vata yaṃ parassa taṃ mamassā’”ti!

And how, householders, is there a threefold unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of mind? Here, householders, someone is covetous. He covets the wealth and property of others, thinking, ‘Oh, that what belongs to others would be mine!’

“Byāpannacitto kho pana hoti paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo – ‘ime sattā haññantu vā vajjhantu vā ucchijjantu vā vinassantu vā mā vā ahesu’”nti mā vā ahesuṃ iti vāti (sī. pī. ka.).

He is of a mind affected by ill will, with thoughts corrupted by malice: ‘May these beings be struck down, or be slain, or be annihilated, or perish, or may they not exist at all!’

“Micchādiṭṭhiko kho pana hoti viparītadassano – ‘natthi dinnaṃ natthi yiṭṭhaṃ natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko natthi paro loko, natthi mātā natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā[M 1.0357], natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā [V 1.0361] ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti. Evaṃ kho, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ manasā adhammacariyāvisamacariyā [T 1.0523] hoti.

One is of wrong view, with a distorted perspective, holding: ‘There is nothing given, nothing sacrificed, nothing offered. There is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father. There are no spontaneously reborn beings. There are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are well-gone and well-practicing, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves with direct knowledge, make them known.’ Thus, householders, unrighteous and uneven conduct by way of mind is threefold.

“Evaṃ adhammacariyāvisamacariyāhetu kho, gahapatayo, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti.

Thus, householders, it is because of such unrighteous and uneven conduct that some beings here, on the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, an unhappy destination, the downfall, in hell.

441. “Tividhaṃ kho, gahapatayo, kāyena dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti, catubbidhaṃ vācāya dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti, tividhaṃ manasā dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti.

441. Householders, there is a threefold righteous and even conduct by way of the body, a fourfold righteous and even conduct by way of speech, and a threefold righteous and even conduct by way of mind.

“Kathañca, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ kāyena dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti? Idha, gahapatayo, ekacco pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho lajjī dayāpanno sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī viharati.

And how, householders, is there a threefold righteous and even conduct by way of the body? Here, householders, someone, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from the killing of living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, scrupulous, endowed with kindness, he dwells compassionate for the welfare of all living beings.

“Adinnādānaṃ pahāya adinnādānā paṭivirato hoti. Yaṃ taṃ parassa paravittūpakaraṇaṃ, gāmagataṃ vā araññagataṃ vā, taṃ nādinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādātā hoti.

Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. Whatever property or possession of another there is, whether in a village or in the wilderness, he is not one to take with thievish intent what has not been given.

“Kāmesumicchācāraṃ pahāya kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato hoti. Yā tā māturakkhitā piturakkhitā mātāpiturakkhitā bhāturakkhitā bhaginirakkhitā ñātirakkhitā gottarakkhitā dhammarakkhitā sassāmikā saparidaṇḍā antamaso mālāguḷaparikkhittāpi, tathārūpāsu na cārittaṃ āpajjitā hoti. Evaṃ kho, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ kāyena dhammacariyāsamacariyā [P 1.0288] hoti.

Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct. He is not one to transgress with such women as are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both mother and father, protected by a brother, protected by a sister, protected by relatives, those who have a husband, those protected by law, or even those betrothed with a garland of flowers. Thus, householders, righteous and even conduct by way of the body is threefold.

“Kathañca, gahapatayo, catubbidhaṃ vācāya dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti? Idha, gahapatayo, ekacco musāvādaṃ pahāya musāvādā paṭivirato hoti. Sabhāgato vā parisāgato vā, ñātimajjhagato vā pūgamajjhagato vā rājakulamajjhagato vā, abhinīto sakkhipuṭṭho – ‘ehambho purisa, yaṃ jānāsi taṃ vadehī’ti, so [T 1.0524] ajānaṃ vā āha – ‘na jānāmī’ti, jānaṃ vā āha – ‘jānāmī’ti, apassaṃ vā āha – ‘na passāmī’ti, passaṃ vā āha [M 1.0358] – ‘passāmī’ti. Iti attahetu vā parahetu vā āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā na sampajānamusā bhāsitā hoti.

And how, householders, is there a fourfold righteous and even conduct by way of speech? Here, householders, a certain person, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech. When summoned to an assembly, a gathering, among relatives, in a guild, or in the royal court, and brought forward as a witness, being asked: ‘Come, good man, speak what you know’—not knowing, he says, ‘I do not know’; knowing, he says, ‘I know’; not seeing, he says, ‘I do not see’; seeing, he says, ‘I see.’ Thus, he is not one who knowingly speaks a lie for his own sake, for another’s sake, or for some trifling material gain.

“Pisuṇaṃ [V 1.0362] vācaṃ pahāya pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti, ito sutvā na amutra akkhātā imesaṃ bhedāya, amutra vā sutvā na imesaṃ akkhātā amūsaṃ bhedāya. Iti bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātā, sahitānaṃ vā anuppadātā, samaggārāmo samaggarato samagganandī samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech. What he has heard here, he does not repeat there so as to cause division among those people; nor does he repeat what he has heard there so as to cause division among these people. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and an encourager of those who are united. He delights in concord, is fond of concord, rejoices in concord, and is one who speaks words that promote concord.

“Pharusaṃ vācaṃ pahāya pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti. Yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā pemanīyā hadayaṅgamā porī bahujanakantā bahujanamanāpā – tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He is one who speaks words that are faultless, pleasant to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, urbane, liked by many, and agreeable to many.

“Samphappalāpaṃ pahāya samphappalāpā paṭivirato hoti. Kālavādī bhūtavādī atthavādī dhammavādī vinayavādī nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti kālena sāpadesaṃ pariyantavatiṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ. Evaṃ kho, gahapatayo, catubbidhaṃ vācāya dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti.

Having abandoned frivolous talk, he abstains from frivolous talk. He speaks at the proper time, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Discipline. He speaks words worth treasuring, uttered at the proper time, with a basis, with a limit, and connected with benefit. Thus, householders, righteous and even conduct by way of speech is fourfold.

“Kathañca, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ manasā dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti? Idha, gahapatayo, ekacco anabhijjhālu hoti, yaṃ taṃ parassa paravittūpakaraṇaṃ taṃ nābhijjhātā hoti – ‘aho vata yaṃ parassa taṃ mamassā’ti!

And how, householders, is righteous and even conduct by way of mind threefold? Here, householders, a certain person is not covetous; he does not covet the wealth and property of another, thinking: ‘Oh, that what belongs to another were mine!’

“Abyāpannacitto kho pana hoti appaduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo – ‘ime sattā averā abyābajjhā anīghā sukhī attānaṃ pariharantū’ti.

Furthermore, he has a mind free from ill will and intentions not corrupted by hate. He thinks: ‘May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness.’

“Sammādiṭṭhiko kho pana hoti aviparītadassano – ‘atthi dinnaṃ atthi yiṭṭhaṃ [T 1.0525] atthi hutaṃ, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, atthi ayaṃ loko atthi paro loko, atthi mātā atthi pitā, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti. Evaṃ kho, gahapatayo, tividhaṃ manasā dhammacariyāsamacariyā hoti.

Furthermore, he is of right view, with an undistorted vision, holding that: ‘There is what is given, what is offered, and what is sacrificed. There is fruit and result of good and bad actions. There is this world and the other world. There is mother and father. There are beings who are spontaneously reborn. There are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are well-gone and well-practicing, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves with direct knowledge, make them known.’ Thus, householders, righteous and even conduct by way of mind is threefold.

“Evaṃ dhammacariyāsamacariyāhetu kho, gahapatayo, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti.

Householders, it is because of such righteous and harmonious conduct that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world.

442. “Ākaṅkheyya [M 1.0359][V 1.0363][P 1.0289] ce, gahapatayo, dhammacārī samacārī – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya’nti; ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so dhammacārī samacārī.

442. Householders, if one who practices the Dhamma and lives harmoniously should wish: ‘Oh, that with the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn into companionship with wealthy nobles!’—this possibility exists, that with the breakup of the body, after death, he might be reborn into companionship with wealthy nobles. For what reason? Because he is one who practices the Dhamma and lives harmoniously.

“Ākaṅkheyya ce, gahapatayo, dhammacārī samacārī – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṃ…pe… gahapatimahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya’nti; ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā gahapatimahāsālānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so dhammacārī samacārī.

Householders, if one who practices the Dhamma and lives harmoniously should wish: ‘Oh, that with the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn into companionship with wealthy brahmins… or with wealthy householders!’—this possibility exists, that with the breakup of the body, after death, he might be reborn into companionship with wealthy householders. For what reason? Because he is one who practices the Dhamma and lives harmoniously.

“Ākaṅkheyya ce, gahapatayo, dhammacārī samacārī – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeya’nti; ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ [T 1.0526] vijjati, yaṃ so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so dhammacārī samacārī.

Householders, if one who practices the Dhamma and lives harmoniously should wish: ‘Oh, that with the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn into companionship with the devas of the Four Great Kings!’—this possibility exists, that with the breakup of the body, after death, he might be reborn into companionship with the devas of the Four Great Kings. For what reason? Because he is one who practices the Dhamma and lives harmoniously.

“Ākaṅkheyya ce, gahapatayo, dhammacārī samacārī – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā tāvatiṃsānaṃ devānaṃ…pe… yāmānaṃ devānaṃ… tusitānaṃ devānaṃ… nimmānaratīnaṃ devānaṃ… paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ devānaṃ… brahmakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya’nti; ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brahmakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so dhammacārī samacārī.
