“Sukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo”ti.

Friend Visākha, in pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to lust is to be abandoned; in painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion is to be abandoned; in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to ignorance is to be abandoned.

“Sabbāya [V 1.0385] nu kho, ayye, sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, sabbāya dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo, sabbāya adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo”ti?

Venerable lady, is the underlying tendency to lust to be abandoned in all pleasant feeling, is the underlying tendency to aversion to be abandoned in all painful feeling, and is the underlying tendency to ignorance to be abandoned in all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?

“Na kho, āvuso visākha, sabbāya sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, na sabbāya dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo[T 1.0554], na sabbāya adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo. Idhāvuso visākha, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Rāgaṃ tena pajahati, na tattha rāgānusayo anuseti. Idhāvuso visākha, bhikkhu iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘kudāssu nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharissāmi yadariyā etarahi āyatanaṃ upasampajja viharantī’ti? Iti anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato [P 1.0304] uppajjati pihāppaccayā domanassaṃ. Paṭighaṃ tena pajahati, na tattha paṭighānusayo anuseti. Idhāvuso visākha, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā, dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Avijjaṃ tena pajahati, na tattha avijjānusayo anusetī”ti.

It is not, friend Visākha, that the underlying tendency to lust is to be abandoned in all pleasant feeling, nor that the underlying tendency to aversion is to be abandoned in all painful feeling, nor that the underlying tendency to ignorance is to be abandoned in all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Here, friend Visākha, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by directed thought and evaluation, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. By that, he abandons lust, and the underlying tendency to lust does not lie dormant therein. Here, friend Visākha, a bhikkhu reflects thus: ‘When shall I enter and dwell in that sphere that the noble ones now enter and dwell in?’ As he generates longing for the unsurpassed liberations, grief arises in him on account of that longing. By that, he abandons aversion, and the underlying tendency to aversion does not lie dormant therein. Here, friend Visākha, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. By that, he abandons ignorance, and the underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie dormant therein.

466. “Sukhāya panāyye, vedanāya kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti?

466. And, venerable lady, what is the counterpart to pleasant feeling?

“Sukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya dukkhā vedanā paṭibhāgo”ti.

Friend Visākha, painful feeling is the counterpart to pleasant feeling.

“Dukkhāya pannāyye, vedanāya kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti?

Venerable lady, what is the counterpart to painful feeling?

“Dukkhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya sukhā vedanā paṭibhāgo”ti.

Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is the counterpart to painful feeling.

“Adukkhamasukhāya panāyye, vedanāya kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti?

But, venerable lady, what is the counterpart to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?

“Adukkhamasukhāya kho, āvuso visākha, vedanāya avijjā paṭibhāgo”ti.

Friend Visākha, ignorance is the counterpart to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

“Avijjāya panāyye, kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti?

But, venerable lady, what is the counterpart to ignorance?

“Avijjāya kho, āvuso visākha, vijjā paṭibhāgo”ti.

Friend Visākha, knowledge is the counterpart to ignorance.

“Vijjāya panāyye, kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti?

Venerable lady, what is the counterpart to knowledge?

“Vijjāya kho, āvuso visākha, vimutti paṭibhāgo”ti.

Friend Visākha, liberation is the counterpart to knowledge.

“Vimuttiyā panāyye[T 1.0555], kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti?

But, venerable lady, what is the counterpart to liberation?

“Vimuttiyā kho, āvuso visākha, nibbānaṃ paṭibhāgo”ti.

Friend Visākha, Nibbāna is the counterpart to liberation.

“Nibbānassa panāyye, kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti? “Accayāsi, āvuso accasarāvuso (sī. pī.), accassarāvuso (syā. kaṃ.) visākha, pañhaṃ, nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetuṃ. Nibbānogadhañhi, āvuso visākha, brahmacariyaṃ, nibbānaparāyanaṃ nibbānapariyosānaṃ. Ākaṅkhamāno ca tvaṃ, āvuso visākha, bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ puccheyyāsi, yathā ca te bhagavā byākaroti tathā naṃ dhāreyyāsī”ti.

“Venerable lady, what is the counterpart to Nibbāna?” “You have gone beyond the question, friend Visākha; you were not able to grasp the limit of questions. For the holy life, friend Visākha, plunges into Nibbāna, has Nibbāna as its destination, and Nibbāna as its final end. If you wish, friend Visākha, you may approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter. And as the Blessed One explains it to you, so you should bear it in mind.”

467. Atha kho visākho upāsako dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā dhammadinnaṃ bhikkhuniṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho visākho upāsako yāvatako ahosi dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Evaṃ vutte, bhagavā visākhaṃ upāsakaṃ etadavoca – “paṇḍitā, visākha, dhammadinnā bhikkhunī, mahāpaññā, visākha, dhammadinnā bhikkhunī. Maṃ cepi tvaṃ, visākha, etamatthaṃ puccheyyāsi, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyaṃ, yathā [P 1.0305] taṃ dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā byākataṃ. Eso cevetassa esovetassa (syā. kaṃ.) attho. Evañca naṃ evametaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.) dhārehī”ti.

467. Then the lay follower Visākha, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the nun Dhammadinnā, rose from his seat, paid homage to the nun Dhammadinnā, circumambulated her respectfully, and went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the lay follower Visākha reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the nun Dhammadinnā. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the lay follower Visākha: “The nun Dhammadinnā is wise, Visākha; the nun Dhammadinnā has great wisdom. If you were to ask me about this matter, Visākha, I would explain it in exactly the same way as the nun Dhammadinnā explained it. This is indeed its meaning. And you should bear it in mind thus.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano visākho upāsako bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

The Blessed One said this. Pleased, the lay follower Visākha greatly rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

Cūḷavedallasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the fourth, is finished.

5. Cūḷadhammasamādānasuttaṃ

5. The Shorter Discourse on the Undertaking of Practices

468. Evaṃ [T 1.0556][V 1.0387] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānāni. Katamāni cattāri? Atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave[M 1.0380], dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ”.

468. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four undertakings of practices. What four? There is, bhikkhus, an undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future; there is, bhikkhus, an undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future; there is, bhikkhus, an undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future; there is, bhikkhus, an undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.”

469. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ? Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘natthi kāmesu doso’ti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te kho moḷibaddhāhi moḷibandhāhi (syā. kaṃ. ka.) paribbājikāhi paricārenti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃsu nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti? Sukho imissā paribbājikāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya bāhāya samphasso’ti te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ [T 1.0557] duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Te tattha dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘idaṃ kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti, ime hi mayaṃ kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ [P 1.0306] dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayāmā’ti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse māluvāsipāṭikā phaleyya. Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, māluvābījaṃ aññatarasmiṃ sālamūle nipateyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, yā tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthā devatā sā bhītā saṃviggā santāsaṃ āpajjeyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthāya devatāya mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā ārāmadevatā vanadevatā rukkhadevatā osadhitiṇavanappatīsu adhivatthā devatā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samassāseyyuṃ – ‘mā bhavaṃ bhāyi, mā bhavaṃ bhāyi; appeva nāmetaṃ māluvābījaṃ [V 1.0388] moro vā gileyya moro vā gileyya, godhā vā khādeyya (ka.), mago vā khādeyya, davaḍāho vanadāho (ka.) vā ḍaheyya, vanakammikā vā uddhareyyuṃ, upacikā vā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ udrabheyyuṃ (sī. pī. ka.), abījaṃ vā panassā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, māluvābījaṃ neva moro gileyya, na mago khādeyya, na davaḍāho ḍaheyya, na vanakammikā uddhareyyuṃ, na upacikā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ, bījañca panassa taṃ pāvussakena meghena abhippavuṭṭhaṃ [M 1.0381] sammadeva viruheyya. Sāssa māluvālatā taruṇā mudukā lomasā vilambinī, sā taṃ sālaṃ upaniseveyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthāya devatāya evamassa – ‘kiṃsu nāma te [T 1.0558] bhonto mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā ārāmadevatā vanadevatā rukkhadevatā osadhitiṇavanappatīsu adhivatthā devatā māluvābīje anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samassāsesuṃ samassāseyyuṃ (ka.) – “mā bhavaṃ bhāyi mā bhavaṃ bhāyi, appeva nāmetaṃ māluvābījaṃ moro vā gileyya, mago vā khādeyya, davaḍāho vā ḍaheyya, vanakammikā vā uddhareyyuṃ, upacikā vā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ, abījaṃ vā panassā”ti; sukho imissā māluvālatāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya vilambiniyā samphasso’ti. Sā taṃ sālaṃ anuparihareyya. Sā taṃ sālaṃ anupariharitvā upari viṭabhiṃ viṭapaṃ (syā. ṭṭha.) kareyya. Upari viṭabhiṃ karitvā oghanaṃ janeyya. Oghanaṃ janetvā ye tassa sālassa mahantā mahantā khandhā te padāleyya. Atha kho, bhikkhave, tasmiṃ sāle adhivatthāya devatāya evamassa – ‘idaṃ kho te bhonto mittāmaccā ñātisālohitā ārāmadevatā vanadevatā rukkhadevatā osadhitiṇavanappatīsu adhivatthā devatā māluvābīje anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā saṅgamma samāgamma evaṃ samassāsesuṃ samassāseyyuṃ (ka.) – “mā bhavaṃ bhāyi mā bhavaṃ bhāyi, appeva nāmetaṃ māluvābījaṃ moro vā gileyya, mago [P 1.0307] vā khādeyya, davaḍāho vā ḍaheyya, vanakammikā vā uddhareyyuṃ, upacikā vā uṭṭhaheyyuṃ abījaṃ vā panassā”ti. Yañcāhaṃ yaṃ vāhaṃ (ka.), svāhaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) māluvābījahetu dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayāmī’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, santi eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino ‘natthi kāmesu doso’ti[T 1.0559]. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te moḷibaddhāhi paribbājikāhi paricārenti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘kiṃsu nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti? Sukho imissā paribbājikāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya bāhāya samphasso’ti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjanti. Te kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjitvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Te tattha dukkhā tibbā kharā [M 1.0382] kaṭukā vedanā vedayanti. Te evamāhaṃsu – ‘idaṃ kho te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā kāmesu anāgatabhayaṃ sampassamānā kāmānaṃ pahānamāhaṃsu, kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapenti. Ime hi [V 1.0389] mayaṃ kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vedayāmā’ti. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ.

469. “And what, bhikkhus, is the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present but ripens as painful in the future? Here, bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine, such a view: ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. They take their pleasure with female wanderers with braided hair. They say thus: ‘For what reason do those venerable ascetics and brahmins, seeing future danger in sensual pleasures, speak of abandoning sensual pleasures and propound the full understanding of sensual pleasures? Pleasant is the touch of this young, tender, soft-haired female wanderer’s arm!’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. Having indulged in sensual pleasures, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. There they experience feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and severe. They say thus: ‘It was this future danger in sensual pleasures that those venerable ascetics and brahmins saw when they spoke of abandoning sensual pleasures and propounded the full understanding of sensual pleasures. For it is on account of sensual pleasures, because of sensual pleasures, that we now experience these painful, sharp, harsh, and severe feelings.’

“Suppose, bhikkhus, in the last month of the hot season, a māluvā creeper pod were to split open. Then, bhikkhus, that māluvā seed might fall at the root of a certain sāl tree. Then, bhikkhus, the deity dwelling in that sāl tree would be frightened, agitated, and fall into a panic. Then, bhikkhus, the friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen of the deity dwelling in that sāl tree—the park deities, forest deities, tree deities, and the deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and trees of the forest—gathering and assembling together, would console her thus: ‘Do not fear, venerable one, do not fear! Perhaps a peacock might swallow this māluvā seed, or a wild animal might eat it, or a forest fire might burn it, or foresters might pull it up, or termites might consume it, or perhaps it is not a viable seed.’

“But, bhikkhus, that māluvā seed is neither swallowed by a peacock, nor eaten by a wild animal, nor burned by a forest fire, nor pulled up by foresters, nor consumed by termites, and it is indeed a viable seed. Drenched by a monsoon cloud, it would sprout properly. That māluvā creeper, being young, tender, soft-haired, and trailing, would settle upon that sāl tree. Then, bhikkhus, the deity dwelling in that sāl tree would think thus: ‘For what reason did those venerable friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen—the park deities, forest deities, tree deities, and the deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and trees of the forest—seeing a future danger in the māluvā seed, gather and assemble together to console me thus: “Do not fear, venerable one, do not fear! Perhaps a peacock might swallow this māluvā seed… or perhaps it is not a viable seed”? Pleasant is the touch of this young, tender, soft-haired, trailing māluvā creeper!’ That creeper would wind itself around the sāl tree. Having wound itself around the sāl tree, it would form a canopy above. Having formed a canopy above, it would create a dense thicket. Having created a dense thicket, it would break apart the great trunks of that sāl tree. Then, bhikkhus, the deity dwelling in that sāl tree would think thus: ‘It was this future danger in the māluvā seed that my venerable friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen… saw when they gathered and assembled together to console me thus: “Do not fear, venerable one, do not fear!… or perhaps it is not a viable seed.” And now, on account of that māluvā seed, I experience feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and severe.’

“So too, bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine, such a view: ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. They take their pleasure with female wanderers with braided hair. They say thus: ‘For what reason do those venerable ascetics and brahmins, seeing future danger in sensual pleasures, speak of abandoning sensual pleasures and propound the full understanding of sensual pleasures? Pleasant is the touch of this young, tender, soft-haired female wanderer’s arm!’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. Having indulged in sensual pleasures, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. There they experience feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and severe. They say thus: ‘It was this future danger in sensual pleasures that those venerable ascetics and brahmins saw when they spoke of abandoning sensual pleasures and propounded the full understanding of sensual pleasures. For it is on account of sensual pleasures, because of sensual pleasures, that we now experience these painful, sharp, harsh, and severe feelings.’ This, bhikkhus, is called the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present but ripens as painful in the future.”

470. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco acelako hoti muttācāro hatthāpalekhano, naehibhaddantiko, natiṭṭhabhaddantiko, nābhihaṭaṃ, na uddissakataṃ, na nimantanaṃ sādiyati, so na kumbhimukhā paṭiggaṇhāti, na kaḷopimukhā paṭiggaṇhāti, na eḷakamantaraṃ, na daṇḍamantaraṃ, na musalamantaraṃ, na dvinnaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ, na gabbhiniyā, na pāyamānāya, na purisantaragatāya, na saṅkittīsu, na yattha sā upaṭṭhito [T 1.0560] hoti, na yattha makkhikā saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī, na macchaṃ, na maṃsaṃ, na suraṃ, na merayaṃ, na thusodakaṃ pivati. So ekāgāriko vā hoti ekālopiko, dvāgāriko vā hoti dvālopiko…pe… sattāgāriko vā hoti sattālopiko. Ekissāpi dattiyā yāpeti, dvīhipi dattīhi yāpeti… sattahipi dattīhi yāpeti. Ekāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāreti, dvīhikampi āhāraṃ āhāreti… sattāhikampi āhāraṃ āhāreti. Iti evarūpaṃ addhamāsikampi pariyāyabhattabhojanānuyogamanuyutto viharati. So sākabhakkho vā hoti[P 1.0308], sāmākabhakkho vā hoti, nīvārabhakkho vā hoti, daddulabhakkho vā hoti, haṭabhakkho vā hoti, kaṇabhakkho vā hoti, ācāmabhakkho vā hoti, piññākabhakkho vā hoti, tiṇabhakkho vā hoti, gomayabhakkho vā hoti, vanamūlaphalāhāro yāpeti pavattaphalabhojī. So sāṇānipi dhāreti, masāṇānipi dhāreti, chavadussānipi dhāreti, paṃsukūlānipi dhāreti, tirīṭānipi dhāreti, ajinampi dhāreti, ajinakkhipampi dhāreti, kusacīrampi dhāreti, vākacīrampi dhāreti, phalakacīrampi dhāreti, kesakambalampi dhāreti, vāḷakambalampi dhāreti, ulūkapakkhampi dhāreti, kesamassulocakopi hoti, kesamassulocanānuyogamanuyutto, ubbhaṭṭhakopi hoti, āsanapaṭikkhitto, ukkuṭikopi hoti ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutto, kaṇṭakāpassayikopi hoti, kaṇṭakāpassaye seyyaṃ [M 1.0383] kappeti passa ma. ni. 1.155 mahāsīhanādasutte, sāyatatiyakampi udakorohanānuyogamanuyutto viharati. Iti evarūpaṃ anekavihitaṃ kāyassa ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto viharati[T 1.0561]. So kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ.

470. And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present and ripens in suffering in the future? Here, monks, someone goes naked, free from conventions, licking his hands; he does not come when asked, ‘Venerable sir, please come,’ nor does he stop when asked, ‘Venerable sir, please stop’; he does not accept food brought to him, food prepared specifically for him, or an invitation. He does not receive food from the mouth of a pot or from the mouth of a bowl. He does not accept it across a threshold, across a stick, or across a pestle; nor from two people eating together, from a pregnant woman, from a nursing woman, from a woman in the midst of men, from a place of food distribution, from where a dog is waiting, or from where flies are swarming. He does not eat fish or meat; he does not drink liquor, wine, or fermented gruel. He is one who takes alms from only one house, a one-morsel man; from two houses, a two-morsel man… from seven houses, a seven-morsel man. He sustains himself on one serving, on two servings… on seven servings. He takes food once a day, or once every two days… up to once every seven days. Thus he lives devoted to the practice of taking food at regular intervals, even up to half a month. He is an eater of greens, or millet, or wild rice, or leather parings, or scum, or rice bran, or rice scum, or sesame flour, or grass, or cow dung. He subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating fallen fruits. He wears coarse hemp, or coarse mixed fabrics, or shrouds from charnel grounds, or rags from dust heaps, or bark garments, or antelope hides, or strips of antelope hide, or kusa-grass garments, or bark-fiber garments, or wood-shaving garments, or human hair blankets, or horse-hair blankets, or owl’s feathers. He is a hair-and-beard plucker, devoted to the practice of plucking out hair and beard. He stands continuously, rejecting seats. He squats continuously, devoted to the practice of squatting. He is a thorn-bed user, making his bed on thorns. He lives devoted to the practice of descending into water three times a day, including the evening. Thus he lives devoted to various kinds of practices of heating and tormenting the body. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present and ripens in suffering in the future.

471. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ? Idha[V 1.0390], bhikkhave, ekacco pakatiyā tibbarāgajātiko hoti, so abhikkhaṇaṃ rāgajaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; pakatiyā tibbadosajātiko hoti, so abhikkhaṇaṃ dosajaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; pakatiyā tibbamohajātiko hoti, so abhikkhaṇaṃ mohajaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. So sahāpi dukkhena, sahāpi domanassena, assumukhopi rudamāno paripuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carati. So kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ.

471. And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present but ripens in happiness in the future? Here, monks, a certain person is by nature of intense lust, and he frequently experiences suffering and displeasure born of lust; by nature of intense hatred, and he frequently experiences suffering and displeasure born of hatred; by nature of intense delusion, and he frequently experiences suffering and displeasure born of delusion. With suffering and with displeasure, with a tearful face, weeping, he lives the complete and pure holy life. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present but ripens in happiness in the future.

472. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco pakatiyā na tibbarāgajātiko hoti, so na abhikkhaṇaṃ rāgajaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; pakatiyā na tibbadosajātiko hoti, so na abhikkhaṇaṃ dosajaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; pakatiyā na tibbamohajātiko hoti[P 1.0309], so na abhikkhaṇaṃ mohajaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. So vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ [T 1.0562] pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri dhammasamādānānī”ti.

472. And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and ripens in happiness in the future? Here, monks, someone is by nature not of intense lust, and he does not frequently experience suffering and displeasure born of lust; by nature not of intense hatred, and he does not frequently experience suffering and displeasure born of hatred; by nature not of intense delusion, and he does not frequently experience suffering and displeasure born of delusion. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied thought and sustained thought, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and ripens in happiness in the future. These, monks, are the four undertakings of practices.

Idamavoca [M 1.0384] bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

This is what the Blessed One said. The monks, gratified, rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

Cūḷadhammasamādānasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Shorter Discourse on the Undertaking of Practices, the fifth, is finished.

6. Mahādhammasamādānasuttaṃ

6. The Greater Discourse on the Undertaking of Practices

473. Evaṃ [V 1.0391][T 1.0563] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, sattā evaṃkāmā evaṃchandā evaṃadhippāyā – ‘aho vata aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā parihāyeyyuṃ, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍheyyu’nti. Tesaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃkāmānaṃ evaṃchandānaṃ evaṃadhippāyānaṃ aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā parihāyanti. Tatra tumhe, bhikkhave, kaṃ hetuṃ paccethā”ti? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā [P 1.0310] no, bhante, dhammā, bhagavaṃnettikā, bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaññeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho; bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

473. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “For the most part, monks, beings have such desires, such wishes, such intentions: ‘Oh, that undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable things would diminish, and desirable, pleasing, and agreeable things would increase!’ But for those beings, monks, having such desires, such wishes, such intentions, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable things increase, and desirable, pleasing, and agreeable things diminish. What reason do you perceive for this, monks?” “Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would reveal the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.” “Then listen, monks, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

474. “Idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano, ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto, sevitabbe dhamme na jānāti asevitabbe dhamme na jānāti, bhajitabbe [T 1.0564] dhamme na jānāti abhajitabbe dhamme na jānāti. So sevitabbe dhamme ajānanto asevitabbe dhamme ajānanto, bhajitabbe dhamme ajānanto abhajitabbe dhamme ajānanto, asevitabbe dhamme sevati sevitabbe dhamme na sevati, abhajitabbe dhamme bhajati bhajitabbe dhamme na bhajati. Tassa asevitabbe dhamme sevato sevitabbe dhamme asevato, abhajitabbe dhamme bhajato bhajitabbe dhamme abhajato aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā [M 1.0385] abhivaḍḍhanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā parihāyanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ aviddasuno.

474. “Here, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the noble Dhamma, and untrained in the noble Dhamma; who has not seen true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and untrained in the Dhamma of true persons, does not know which things should be resorted to and which things should not be resorted to; does not know which things should be associated with and which things should not be associated with. Not knowing which things should be resorted to and which things should not be resorted to, not knowing which things should be associated with and which things should not be associated with, they resort to things that should not be resorted to and do not resort to things that should be resorted to; they associate with things that should not be associated with and do not associate with things that should be associated with. For one who resorts to things that should not be resorted to and does not resort to things that should be resorted to, who associates with things that should not be associated with and does not associate with things that should be associated with, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable things increase, and desirable, pleasing, and agreeable things diminish. For what reason? Because, monks, that is how it is for one without wisdom.”

“Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako, ariyānaṃ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme [V 1.0392] suvinīto, sappurisānaṃ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto, sevitabbe dhamme jānāti asevitabbe dhamme jānāti, bhajitabbe dhamme jānāti abhajitabbe dhamme jānāti. So sevitabbe dhamme jānanto asevitabbe dhamme jānanto, bhajitabbe dhamme jānanto abhajitabbe dhamme jānanto, asevitabbe dhamme na sevati sevitabbe dhamme sevati, abhajitabbe dhamme na bhajati bhajitabbe dhamme bhajati. Tassa asevitabbe dhamme asevato sevitabbe dhamme sevato, abhajitabbe dhamme abhajato bhajitabbe dhamme bhajato, aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā parihāyanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti. Taṃ [T 1.0565] kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ viddasuno.

“But, monks, a learned noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the noble Dhamma, and well-trained in the noble Dhamma; who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons, knows which things should be resorted to and which things should not be resorted to; knows which things should be associated with and which things should not be associated with. Knowing which things should be resorted to and which things should not be resorted to, knowing which things should be associated with and which things should not be associated with, they do not resort to things that should not be resorted to and resort to things that should be resorted to; they do not associate with things that should not be associated with and associate with things that should be associated with. For one who does not resort to things that should not be resorted to and resorts to things that should be resorted to, who does not associate with things that should not be associated with and associates with things that should be associated with, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable things diminish, and desirable, pleasing, and agreeable things increase. For what reason? Because, monks, that is how it is for one with wisdom.”

475. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānāni. Katamāni cattāri? Atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ [P 1.0311] paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ; atthi, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ.

475. “Monks, there are these four undertakings of practices. What four? There is, monks, an undertaking of practices that is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future. There is, monks, an undertaking of practices that is pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future. There is, monks, an undertaking of practices that is painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future. There is, monks, an undertaking of practices that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.”

476. “Tatra, bhikkhave, yamidaṃ yadidaṃ (sī.) dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ, taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti – ‘idaṃ kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipāka’nti. Taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto taṃ sevati, taṃ na parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ sevato, taṃ aparivajjayato, aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā parihāyanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ aviddasuno.

476. “Among these, monks, is the undertaking of practices that is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future. One without wisdom, overcome by ignorance, does not know it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future.’ Not knowing it as it really is, being without wisdom and overcome by ignorance, they resort to it and do not avoid it. For one who resorts to it and does not avoid it, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable things increase, and desirable, pleasing, and agreeable things diminish. For what reason? Because, monks, that is how it is for one without wisdom.”

“Tatra, bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti – ‘idaṃ kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ [M 1.0386] āyatiṃ dukkhavipāka’nti. Taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto taṃ sevati, taṃ na parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ sevato, taṃ [T 1.0566] aparivajjayato, aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā parihāyanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ aviddasuno.

“Among these, monks, is the undertaking of practices that is pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future. One without wisdom, overcome by ignorance, does not know it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future.’ Not knowing it as it really is, being without wisdom and overcome by ignorance, they resort to it and do not avoid it. For one who resorts to it and does not avoid it, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable things increase, and desirable, pleasing, and agreeable things diminish. For what reason? Because, monks, that is how it is for one without wisdom.”

“Tatra[V 1.0393], bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ, taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti – ‘idaṃ kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipāka’nti. Taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto taṃ na sevati, taṃ parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ asevato, taṃ parivajjayato, aniṭṭhā [P 1.0312] akantā amanāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā parihāyanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ aviddasuno.

Monks, among these, regarding that undertaking of practices which is painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future, an unwise person, one endowed with ignorance, does not know it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is indeed painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.’ Not knowing it as it really is, that unwise person, endowed with ignorance, does not resort to it; they avoid it. For them, by not resorting to it and by avoiding it, unwished-for, disliked, and disagreeable states increase, while wished-for, liked, and agreeable states decline. For what reason? Monks, it is so for them, just as it is for an unwise person.

“Tatra, bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ, taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti – ‘idaṃ kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipāka’nti. Taṃ avidvā avijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ appajānanto taṃ na sevati, taṃ parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ asevato, taṃ parivajjayato, aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā parihāyanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ aviddasuno.

Monks, among these, regarding that undertaking of practices which is pleasant in the present and also has a pleasant result in the future, an unwise person, one endowed with ignorance, does not know it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is indeed pleasant in the present and also has a pleasant result in the future.’ Not knowing it as it really is, that unwise person, endowed with ignorance, does not resort to it; they avoid it. For them, by not resorting to it and by avoiding it, unwished-for, disliked, and disagreeable states increase, while wished-for, liked, and agreeable states decline. For what reason? Monks, it is so for them, just as it is for an unwise person.

477. “Tatra, bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti – ‘idaṃ [T 1.0567] kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipāka’nti. Taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanto taṃ na sevati, taṃ parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ asevato, taṃ parivajjayato, aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā parihāyanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ viddasuno.

477. Monks, among these, regarding that undertaking of practices which is painful in the present and also has a painful result in the future, a wise person, one endowed with true knowledge, knows it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is indeed painful in the present and also has a painful result in the future.’ Knowing it as it really is, that wise person, endowed with true knowledge, does not resort to it; they avoid it. For them, by not resorting to it and by avoiding it, unwished-for, disliked, and disagreeable states decline, while wished-for, liked, and agreeable states increase. For what reason? Monks, it is so for them, just as it is for a wise person.

“Tatra, bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti – ‘idaṃ kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipāka’nti. Taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanto taṃ na sevati, taṃ parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ asevato, taṃ parivajjayato[M 1.0387], aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā parihāyanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ viddasuno.

Monks, among these, regarding that undertaking of practices which is pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future, a wise person, one endowed with true knowledge, knows it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is indeed pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future.’ Knowing it as it really is, that wise person, endowed with true knowledge, does not resort to it; they avoid it. For them, by not resorting to it and by avoiding it, unwished-for, disliked, and disagreeable states decline, while wished-for, liked, and agreeable states increase. For what reason? Monks, it is so for them, just as it is for a wise person.

“Tatra[V 1.0394], bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti – ‘idaṃ kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipāka’nti. Taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanto taṃ sevati, taṃ na parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ sevato, taṃ aparivajjayato, aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā parihāyanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ viddasuno.

Monks, among these, regarding that undertaking of practices which is painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future, a wise person, one endowed with true knowledge, knows it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is indeed painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.’ Knowing it as it really is, that wise person, endowed with true knowledge, resorts to it; they do not avoid it. For them, by resorting to it and by not avoiding it, unwished-for, disliked, and disagreeable states decline, while wished-for, liked, and agreeable states increase. For what reason? Monks, it is so for them, just as it is for a wise person.

“Tatra, bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ [T 1.0568] taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti – ‘idaṃ kho dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipāka’nti. Taṃ vidvā vijjāgato yathābhūtaṃ pajānanto taṃ sevati, taṃ na parivajjeti. Tassa taṃ sevato, taṃ aparivajjayato, aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā dhammā parihāyanti, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti yathā taṃ viddasuno.

Monks, among these, regarding that undertaking of practices which is pleasant in the present and also has a pleasant result in the future, a wise person, one endowed with true knowledge, knows it as it really is: ‘This undertaking of practices is indeed pleasant in the present and also has a pleasant result in the future.’ Knowing it as it really is, that wise person, endowed with true knowledge, resorts to it; they do not avoid it. For them, by resorting to it and by not avoiding it, unwished-for, disliked, and disagreeable states decline, while wished-for, liked, and agreeable states increase. For what reason? Monks, it is so for them, just as it is for a wise person.

478. “Katamañca[P 1.0313], bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena pāṇātipātī hoti, pāṇātipātapaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena adinnādāyī hoti, adinnādānapaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena kāmesu micchācārī hoti, kāmesu micchācārapaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena musāvādī hoti, musāvādapaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena pisuṇavāco hoti, pisuṇavācāpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena pharusavāco hoti, pharusavācāpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena samphappalāpī hoti, samphappalāpapaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi [M 1.0388] dukkhena sahāpi domanassena abhijjhālu [T 1.0569] hoti, abhijjhāpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena byāpannacitto hoti, byāpādapaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena micchādiṭṭhi hoti, micchādiṭṭhipaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. So [V 1.0395] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ.

478. And what, bhikkhus, is the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, with pain and with distress, destroys life; and on account of destroying life, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they take what is not given; and on account of taking what is not given, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they engage in sexual misconduct; and on account of sexual misconduct, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they speak falsely; and on account of false speech, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they speak divisively; and on account of divisive speech, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they speak harshly; and on account of harsh speech, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they engage in idle chatter; and on account of idle chatter, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they are covetous; and on account of covetousness, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they have a mind of ill will; and on account of ill will, they experience pain and distress. With pain and with distress, they have wrong view; and on account of wrong view, they experience pain and distress. After the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the downfall, in hell. This, bhikkhus, is called the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future.

479. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena pāṇātipātī hoti, pāṇātipātapaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena adinnādāyī hoti, adinnādānapaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena kāmesumicchācārī hoti, kāmesumicchācārapaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena musāvādī hoti, musāvādapaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena pisuṇavāco hoti, pisuṇavācāpaccayā ca sukhaṃ [P 1.0314] somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena pharusavāco hoti, pharusavācāpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena samphappalāpī hoti, samphappalāpapaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi [T 1.0570] sukhena sahāpi somanassena abhijjhālu hoti, abhijjhāpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena byāpannacitto hoti, byāpādapaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena micchādiṭṭhi hoti, micchādiṭṭhipaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. So kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ.

479. And what, bhikkhus, is the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, with pleasure and with joy, destroys life; and on account of destroying life, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they take what is not given; and on account of taking what is not given, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they engage in sexual misconduct; and on account of sexual misconduct, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they speak falsely; and on account of false speech, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they speak divisively; and on account of divisive speech, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they speak harshly; and on account of harsh speech, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they engage in idle chatter; and on account of idle chatter, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they are covetous; and on account of covetousness, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they have a mind of ill will; and on account of ill will, they experience pleasure and joy. With pleasure and with joy, they have wrong view; and on account of wrong view, they experience pleasure and joy. After the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the downfall, in hell. This, bhikkhus, is called the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and has a painful result in the future.

480. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, pāṇātipātā veramaṇīpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti[M 1.0389]; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena adinnādānā paṭivirato hoti, adinnādānā veramaṇīpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato hoti, kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇīpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena musāvādā paṭivirato hoti, musāvādā veramaṇīpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti[V 1.0396], pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇīpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti[T 1.0571]; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti, pharusāya vācāya veramaṇīpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena samphappalāpā paṭivirato hoti, samphappalāpā veramaṇīpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena anabhijjhālu hoti, anabhijjhāpaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassena abyāpannacitto hoti, abyāpādapaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi dukkhena [P 1.0315] sahāpi domanassena sammādiṭṭhi hoti, sammādiṭṭhipaccayā ca dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. So kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ.

480. And what, Bhikkhus, is the undertaking of practices that is painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future? Here, Bhikkhus, a certain person, accompanied by pain and distress, refrains from the destruction of life; and because of refraining from the destruction of life, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they refrain from taking what is not given; and because of refraining from taking what is not given, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they refrain from sexual misconduct; and because of refraining from sexual misconduct, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they refrain from false speech; and because of refraining from false speech, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they refrain from divisive speech; and because of refraining from divisive speech, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they refrain from harsh speech; and because of refraining from harsh speech, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they refrain from frivolous talk; and because of refraining from frivolous talk, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they are not covetous; and because of not being covetous, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they have a mind without ill will; and because of the absence of ill will, they experience pain and distress. Accompanied by pain and distress, they have right view; and because of having right view, they experience pain and distress. With the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This, Bhikkhus, is called the undertaking of practices that is painful in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.

481. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti, pāṇātipātā veramaṇīpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena adinnādānā paṭivirato hoti, adinnādānā veramaṇīpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato hoti, kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇīpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena [T 1.0572] sahāpi somanassena musāvādā paṭivirato hoti, musāvādā veramaṇīpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti, pisuṇāya vācāya [M 1.0390] veramaṇīpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti, pharusāya vācāya veramaṇīpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena samphappalāpā paṭivirato hoti, samphappalāpā veramaṇīpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena anabhijjhālu hoti, anabhijjhāpaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena abyāpannacitto hoti, abyāpādapaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti; sahāpi sukhena sahāpi somanassena sammādiṭṭhi hoti, sammādiṭṭhipaccayā ca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. So kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Idaṃ, vuccati, bhikkhave, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva [V 1.0397] āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri dhammasamādānāni.

481. And what, Bhikkhus, is the undertaking of practices that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future? Here, Bhikkhus, a certain person, accompanied by pleasure and joy, refrains from the destruction of life; and because of refraining from the destruction of life, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they refrain from taking what is not given; and because of refraining from taking what is not given, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they refrain from sexual misconduct; and because of refraining from sexual misconduct, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they refrain from false speech; and because of refraining from false speech, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they refrain from divisive speech; and because of refraining from divisive speech, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they refrain from harsh speech; and because of refraining from harsh speech, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they refrain from frivolous talk; and because of refraining from frivolous talk, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they are not covetous; and because of not being covetous, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they have a mind without ill will; and because of the absence of ill will, they experience pleasure and joy. Accompanied by pleasure and joy, they have right view; and because of having right view, they experience pleasure and joy. With the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This, Bhikkhus, is called the undertaking of practices that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future. These, Bhikkhus, are the four undertakings of practices.

482. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, tittakālābu visena saṃsaṭṭho. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikūlo. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ambho purisa, ayaṃ tittakālābu visena saṃsaṭṭho, sace ākaṅkhasi piva pipa (sī. pī.). Tassa [P 1.0316] te pivato pipato (sī. pī.) ceva nacchādessati [T 1.0573] vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā pītvā (sī.) ca pana maraṇaṃ vā nigacchasi maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha’nti. So taṃ appaṭisaṅkhāya piveyya, nappaṭinissajjeyya. Tassa taṃ pivato ceva nacchādeyya vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā ca pana maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ vadāmi, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ.

482. Bhikkhus, suppose there was a bitter gourd mixed with poison. Then a person would come along, desiring to live, not wishing to die, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering. They might say to him: 'Good man, this bitter gourd is mixed with poison. If you wish, drink it. While you are drinking it, it will not be pleasing in color, smell, or taste. And having drunk it, you will come to death or to suffering equal to death.' Then that person, without reflecting, might drink it and not reject it. For him, while drinking it, it would not be pleasing in color, smell, or taste. And having drunk it, he would come to death or to suffering equal to death. Bhikkhus, I declare this undertaking of practices to be comparable to that, namely, the undertaking of practices that is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future.

483. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āpānīyakaṃso vaṇṇasampanno gandhasampanno rasasampanno. So ca kho visena saṃsaṭṭho. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikūlo. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ambho purisa, ayaṃ āpānīyakaṃso vaṇṇasampanno gandhasampanno rasasampanno. So ca kho visena saṃsaṭṭho, sace ākaṅkhasi piva. Tassa te pivatohi pivatopi (ka.) kho chādessati vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā ca pana maraṇaṃ vā nigacchasi maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkha’nti. So taṃ appaṭisaṅkhāya [M 1.0391] piveyya, nappaṭinissajjeyya. Tassa taṃ pivatohi kho chādeyya vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā ca pana maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ vadāmi, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ.

483. Bhikkhus, suppose there were a bronze cup full of a sweet drink, endowed with color, endowed with scent, and endowed with taste, but it was mixed with poison. Then a man would come along, desiring to live, not wishing to die, longing for happiness, and averse to suffering. They would say to him: ‘Good man, this bronze cup full of a sweet drink is endowed with color, scent, and taste, but it is mixed with poison. If you wish, drink it. As you drink it, it will gratify you with its color, scent, and taste, but having drunk it, you will come to death or suffering equivalent to death.’ Without reflecting, he would drink it and not reject it. As he drinks it, it would gratify him with its color, scent, and taste, but having drunk it, he would come to death or suffering equivalent to death. Bhikkhus, I declare this undertaking of a practice to be comparable to that, namely, the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present but has a painful result in the future.

484. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pūtimuttaṃ nānābhesajjehi saṃsaṭṭhaṃ. Atha [T 1.0574] puriso āgaccheyya paṇḍukarogī. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ambho purisa, idaṃ pūtimuttaṃ nānābhesajjehi saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, sace ākaṅkhasi piva. Tassa te pivatohi kho nacchādessati vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā ca pana sukhī bhavissasī’ti. So taṃ paṭisaṅkhāya piveyya, nappaṭinissajjeyya. Tassa taṃ pivatohi kho nacchādeyya vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā [V 1.0398] ca pana sukhī assa. Tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ vadāmi, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ.

484. Bhikkhus, suppose there was fermented urine mixed with various medicines. Then a man suffering from a wasting disease would come along. They would say to him: ‘Good man, this fermented urine is mixed with various medicines. If you wish, drink it. As you drink it, it will not please you with its color, scent, or taste, but having drunk it, you will be well.’ Reflecting, he would drink it and not reject it. As he drinks it, it would not please him with its color, scent, or taste, but having drunk it, he would be well. Bhikkhus, I declare this undertaking of a practice to be comparable to that, namely, the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present but has a pleasant result in the future.

485. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dadhi ca madhu ca sappi ca phāṇitañca ekajjhaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya lohitapakkhandiko. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ambho purisa, idaṃ [P 1.0317] dadhiṃ ca madhuṃ ca sappiṃ ca phāṇitañca ekajjhaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, sace ākaṅkhasi piva. Tassa te pivato ceva chādessati vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā ca pana sukhī bhavissasī’ti. So taṃ paṭisaṅkhāya piveyya, nappaṭinissajjeyya. Tassa taṃ pivato ceva chādeyya vaṇṇenapi gandhenapi rasenapi, pivitvā ca pana sukhī assa. Tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ vadāmi, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ.

485. Bhikkhus, suppose curd, honey, ghee, and molasses were mixed together. Then a man suffering from dysentery would come along. They would say to him: ‘Good man, this curd, honey, ghee, and molasses are mixed together. If you wish, drink it. As you drink it, it will please you with its color, scent, and taste, and after drinking it, you will be well.’ Reflecting, he would drink it and not reject it. As he drinks it, it would please him with its color, scent, and taste, and after drinking it, he would be well. Bhikkhus, I declare this undertaking of a practice to be comparable to that, namely, the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.

486. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye viddhe vigatavalāhake deve ādicco nabhaṃ abbhussakkamāno sabbaṃ ākāsagataṃ tamagataṃ abhivihacca bhāsate ca tapate ca virocate ca; evameva [T 1.0575] kho, bhikkhave, yamidaṃ dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ tadaññe puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇaparappavāde abhivihacca bhāsate ca tapate ca virocate cā”ti.

486. Bhikkhus, just as in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the sun, rising into the sky, having dispelled all darkness in the sky, shines, blazes, and glows; even so, bhikkhus, this undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future, having dispelled the many other views of ascetics and brahmins, shines, blazes, and glows.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Those bhikkhus, delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.

Mahādhammasamādānasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Great Discourse on the Undertaking of a Practice, the sixth, is concluded.

7. Vīmaṃsakasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Investigator

487. Evaṃ [T 1.0576][M 1.0392][V 1.0399] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “vīmaṃsakena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā parassa cetopariyāyaṃ ajānantena ājānantena (pī. ka.), ajānantena kinti (?) tathāgate samannesanā kātabbā ‘sammāsambuddho vā no vā’ iti viññāṇāyā”ti. “Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā, bhagavaṃnettikā bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā; sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho; bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti[P 1.0318]. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

487. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, an investigating bhikkhu, not knowing the range of another's mind, should undertake an inquiry of the Tathāgata in order to know: ‘Is he a Perfectly Enlightened One or not?’ ” “For us, venerable sir, the teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will bear it in mind.” “In that case, bhikkhus, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

488. “Vīmaṃsakena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā parassa cetopariyāyaṃ ajānantena dvīsu dhammesu tathāgato samannesitabbo cakkhusotaviññeyyesu dhammesu – ‘ye saṃkiliṭṭhā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti vā te tathāgatassa no vā’ti? Tamenaṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘ye saṃkiliṭṭhā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, na te tathāgatassa saṃvijjantī’ti.

488. “Bhikkhus, an investigating bhikkhu, not knowing the range of another's mind, should investigate the Tathāgata in regard to two kinds of phenomena, those cognizable by the eye and ear: ‘Do defiled phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear exist for the Tathāgata, or not?’ Investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘Defiled phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do not exist for the Tathāgata.’”

“Yato naṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘ye saṃkiliṭṭhā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, na te tathāgatassa saṃvijjantī’ti, tato naṃ uttariṃ samannesati – ‘ye vītimissā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti vā te tathāgatassa no [T 1.0577] vā’ti? Tamenaṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘ye vītimissā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, na te tathāgatassa saṃvijjantī’ti.

“Since, investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘Defiled phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do not exist for the Tathāgata,’ he therefore investigates him further: ‘Do mixed phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear exist for the Tathāgata, or not?’ Investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘Mixed phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do not exist for the Tathāgata.’”

“Yato naṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘ye vītimissā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, na te tathāgatassa saṃvijjantī’ti, tato naṃ uttariṃ samannesati – ‘ye vodātā cakkhusotaviññeyyā [V 1.0400] dhammā, saṃvijjanti vā te tathāgatassa no vā’ti? Tamenaṃ samannesamāno evaṃ [M 1.0393] jānāti – ‘ye vodātā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti te tathāgatassā’ti.

“Since, investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘Mixed phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do not exist for the Tathāgata,’ he therefore investigates him further: ‘Do pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear exist for the Tathāgata, or not?’ Investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘Pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do exist for the Tathāgata.’”

“Yato naṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘ye vodātā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti te tathāgatassā’ti, tato naṃ uttariṃ samannesati – ‘dīgharattaṃ samāpanno ayamāyasmā imaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, udāhu ittarasamāpanno’ti? Tamenaṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘dīgharattaṃ samāpanno ayamāyasmā imaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, nāyamāyasmā ittarasamāpanno’ti.

“Since, investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘Pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do exist for the Tathāgata,’ he therefore investigates him further: ‘Has this venerable one been endowed with this wholesome state for a long time, or only for a short while?’ Investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘This venerable one has been endowed with this wholesome state for a long time; this venerable one has not been endowed with it for only a short while.’”

“Yato naṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘dīgharattaṃ samāpanno ayamāyasmā imaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, nāyamāyasmā ittarasamāpanno’ti, tato naṃ uttariṃ samannesati – ‘ñattajjhāpanno ayamāyasmā bhikkhu yasappatto, saṃvijjantassa idhekacce ādīnavā’ti? Na tāva, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno idhekacce ādīnavā saṃvijjanti yāva na ñattajjhāpanno hoti yasappatto. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ñattajjhāpanno hoti yasappatto[T 1.0578], athassa idhekacce ādīnavā saṃvijjanti. Tamenaṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘ñattajjhāpanno ayamāyasmā bhikkhu yasappatto, nāssa idhekacce ādīnavā saṃvijjantī’ti.

“Since, investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘This venerable one has been endowed with this wholesome state for a long time; this venerable one has not been endowed with it for only a short while,’ he therefore investigates him further: ‘Is this venerable bhikkhu well-known and renowned, and do certain dangers exist for him on that account?’ Bhikkhus, certain dangers do not yet exist for a bhikkhu so long as he is not well-known and renowned. But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is well-known and renowned, then certain dangers exist for him. Investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘This venerable bhikkhu is well-known and renowned, but certain dangers do not exist for him.’”

“Yato naṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘ñattajjhāpanno ayamāyasmā [P 1.0319] bhikkhu yasappatto, nāssa idhekacce ādīnavā saṃvijjantī’ti, tato naṃ uttariṃ samannesati – ‘abhayūparato ayamāyasmā, nāyamāyasmā bhayūparato; vītarāgattā kāme na sevati khayā rāgassā’ti? Tamenaṃ samannesamāno evaṃ jānāti – ‘abhayūparato ayamāyasmā, nāyamāyasmā bhayūparato; vītarāgattā kāme na sevati khayā rāgassā’ti. Tañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṃ pare evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘ke panāyasmato ākārā, ke anvayā, yenāyasmā evaṃ vadesi – abhayūparato ayamāyasmā, nāyamāyasmā bhayūparato; vītarāgattā kāme na sevati khayā rāgassā’ti. Sammā byākaramāno, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ byākareyya – ‘tathā hi pana ayamāyasmā saṅghe vā viharanto eko vā viharanto, ye ca tattha sugatā ye ca tattha duggatā, ye ca tattha gaṇamanusāsanti, ye ca idhekacce āmisesu saṃdissanti, ye ca idhekacce āmisena anupalittā, nāyamāyasmā taṃ tena avajānāti[M 1.0394]. Sammukhā kho pana metaṃ bhagavato [V 1.0401] sutaṃ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ – abhayūparatohamasmi, nāhamasmi bhayūparato, vītarāgattā kāme na sevāmi khayā rāgassā’ti.

“Since, investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘This venerable bhikkhu is well-known and renowned, but certain dangers do not exist for him,’ he therefore investigates him further: ‘Has this venerable one abstained through fearlessness, not through fear? Being free from lust, does he not indulge in sensual pleasures due to the destruction of lust?’ Investigating him, he comes to know thus: ‘This venerable one has abstained through fearlessness, not through fear. Being free from lust, he does not indulge in sensual pleasures due to the destruction of lust.’ If, bhikkhus, others were to ask that bhikkhu: ‘But what are the venerable one’s grounds, what are the reasons, that the venerable one says: “This venerable one has abstained through fearlessness, not through fear. Being free from lust, he does not indulge in sensual pleasures due to the destruction of lust”?’ Answering correctly, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu should reply thus: ‘It is because this venerable one, whether dwelling in the Saṅgha or dwelling alone, does not on that account despise those who are faring well or those who are faring badly, those who are instructing a group, those here who are seen to be attached to material things, or those here who are untainted by material things. Furthermore, I have heard this in the Blessed One’s presence, I have received it in his presence: “I have abstained through fearlessness, I have not abstained through fear. Being free from lust, I do not indulge in sensual pleasures due to the destruction of lust.”’”

489. “Tatra[T 1.0579], bhikkhave, tathāgatova uttariṃ paṭipucchitabbo – ‘ye saṃkiliṭṭhā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti vā te tathāgatassa no vā’ti? Byākaramāno, bhikkhave, tathāgato evaṃ byākareyya – ‘ye saṃkiliṭṭhā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, na te tathāgatassa saṃvijjantī’”ti.

489. “Therein, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata himself should be questioned further: ‘Do defiled phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear exist for the Tathāgata, or not?’ Answering, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata would reply thus: ‘Defiled phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do not exist for the Tathāgata.’”

“Ye vītimissā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti vā te tathāgatassa no vāti? Byākaramāno, bhikkhave, tathāgato evaṃ byākareyya – ‘ye vītimissā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, na te tathāgatassa saṃvijjantī’ti.

“‘Do mixed phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear exist for the Tathāgata or not?’ Answering, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata would answer thus: ‘Mixed phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do not exist for the Tathāgata.’”

“Ye vodātā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti vā te tathāgatassa no vāti? Byākaramāno, bhikkhave, tathāgato evaṃ byākareyya – ‘ye vodātā cakkhusotaviññeyyā dhammā, saṃvijjanti te tathāgatassa; etaṃpathohamasmi, etaṃgocaro etapathohamasmi etagocaro (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), no ca tena tammayo’ti.

“‘Do pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear exist for the Tathāgata or not?’ Answering, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata would answer thus: ‘Pure phenomena cognizable by the eye and ear do exist for the Tathāgata. This is my path, this is my domain, but I do not identify with it.’”

“Evaṃvādiṃ kho, bhikkhave, satthāraṃ arahati sāvako upasaṅkamituṃ dhammassavanāya. Tassa satthā dhammaṃ deseti uttaruttariṃ paṇītapaṇītaṃ kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaṃ. Yathā yathā kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno satthā dhammaṃ deseti uttaruttariṃ paṇītapaṇītaṃ kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaṃ tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme abhiññāya idhekaccaṃ dhammaṃ dhammesu [P 1.0320] niṭṭhaṃ gacchati, satthari pasīdati – ‘sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho’ti. Tañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṃ pare evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘ke panāyasmato ākārā, ke anvayā, yenāyasmā evaṃ vadesi – sammāsambuddho bhagavā[T 1.0580], svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho’ti? Sammā byākaramāno, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ byākareyya – ‘idhāhaṃ, āvuso, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃ dhammassavanāya. Tassa me bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti uttaruttariṃ paṇītapaṇītaṃ kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaṃ. Yathā yathā me, āvuso[M 1.0395], bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti uttaruttariṃ paṇītapaṇītaṃ kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaṃ tathā tathāhaṃ tasmiṃ dhamme abhiññāya idhekaccaṃ dhammaṃ dhammesu niṭṭhamagamaṃ, satthari pasīdiṃ – sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto bhagavatā, dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho’ti.

“Bhikkhus, a disciple is worthy to approach a Teacher who speaks thus for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. That Teacher teaches him the Dhamma that is progressively higher, progressively more sublime, with its dark and bright counterparts. As the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhu in this way—progressively higher, progressively more sublime, with its dark and bright counterparts—so that bhikkhu, by directly knowing a certain teaching here among the teachings, arrives at a conclusion among the teachings and gains confidence in the Teacher: ‘The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha is of good conduct.’ If, bhikkhus, others were to ask that bhikkhu: ‘But by what aspects, by what reasons does the venerable one speak thus: “The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha is of good conduct”?’ Answering rightly, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu would answer thus: ‘Here, friends, I approached the Blessed One for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma that is progressively higher, progressively more sublime, with its dark and bright counterparts. As the Blessed One taught me the Dhamma in this way—progressively higher, progressively more sublime, with its dark and bright counterparts—so I, by directly knowing a certain teaching here among the teachings, arrived at a conclusion among the teachings and gained confidence in the Teacher, thinking: “The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha is of good conduct.”’”

490. “Yassa [V 1.0402] kassaci, bhikkhave, imehi ākārehi imehi padehi imehi byañjanehi tathāgate saddhā niviṭṭhā hoti mūlajātā patiṭṭhitā, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ākāravatī saddhā dassanamūlikā, daḷhā; asaṃhāriyā samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tathāgate dhammasamannesanā hoti. Evañca pana tathāgato dhammatāsusamanniṭṭho hotī”ti.

490. “Bhikkhus, for anyone in whom faith in the Tathāgata is settled, rooted, and established by these aspects, these terms, and these expressions, this is called, bhikkhus, faith endowed with aspects, rooted in vision, firm, and unshakable by any ascetic or brahmin, by a deva, by Māra, by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. Thus, bhikkhus, there is an investigation of the Dhamma concerning the Tathāgata. And thus the Tathāgata is well-investigated in accordance with the nature of things.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Gladdened, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s speech.

Vīmaṃsakasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ sattamaṃ.

The seventh Discourse on Investigation is concluded.

8. Kosambiyasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse at Kosambī

491. Evaṃ [T 1.0581][V 1.0403] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme. Tena kho pana samayena kosambiyaṃ bhikkhū bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharanti. Te na ceva aññamaññaṃ saññāpenti na ca saññattiṃ upenti, na ca aññamaññaṃ nijjhāpenti, na ca nijjhattiṃ upenti. Atha kho aññataro [P 1.0321] bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idha, bhante, kosambiyaṃ bhikkhū bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharanti, te na ceva aññamaññaṃ saññāpenti, na ca saññattiṃ upenti, na ca aññamaññaṃ nijjhāpenti, na ca nijjhattiṃ upentī”ti.

491. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Now at that time, the bhikkhus at Kosambī had become quarrelsome, had become contentious, had fallen into disputes, and were living wounding one another with verbal spears. They could neither convince one another nor be convinced; they could neither persuade one another nor be persuaded. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, here in Kosambī, the bhikkhus have become quarrelsome, have become contentious, have fallen into disputes, and are living wounding one another with verbal spears. They can neither convince one another nor be convinced; they can neither persuade one another nor be persuaded.”

Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena te bhikkhū āmantehi – ‘satthā vo āyasmante āmantetī’”ti. “Evaṃ[M 1.0396], bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā te bhikkhū etadavoca – “satthā āyasmante āmantetī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.
