Ekamantaṃ [T 1.0582] nisinne kho te bhikkhū bhagavā etadavoca – “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharatha, te na ceva aññamaññaṃ saññāpetha, na ca saññattiṃ upetha, na ca aññamaññaṃ nijjhāpetha, na ca nijjhattiṃ upethā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ tumhe samaye bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ [P 1.0322] mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharatha, api nu tumhākaṃ tasmiṃ samaye mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca, mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ…pe… mettaṃ manokammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho cā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Iti kira, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ tumhe samaye bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharatha, neva tumhākaṃ [V 1.0404] tasmiṃ samaye mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca, na mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ…pe… na mettaṃ manokammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Atha kiñcarahi tumhe, moghapurisā, kiṃ jānantā kiṃ passantā bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharatha, te na ceva aññamaññaṃ saññāpetha, na ca saññattiṃ upetha, na ca aññamaññaṃ nijjhāpetha, na ca nijjhattiṃ upetha[T 1.0583]? Tañhi tumhākaṃ, moghapurisā, bhavissati dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti.

Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk: “Come, monk, go to those monks and, in my name, say to them: ‘The Teacher calls the venerable ones.’” “Yes, venerable sir,” that monk replied to the Blessed One. He then approached those monks and said to them: “The Teacher calls the venerable ones.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to that monk. Then they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One said to those monks: “Is it true, monks, as is said, that you are living having become quarrelsome, having become contentious, having fallen into disputes, wounding one another with verbal spears, unable to convince one another or to be convinced, unable to reconcile with one another or to be reconciled?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “What do you think, monks? At a time when you are living having become quarrelsome, contentious, and having fallen into disputes, wounding one another with verbal spears, is loving bodily action established toward your companions in the holy life, both openly and in private? Is loving verbal action… is loving mental action established toward your companions in the holy life, both openly and in private?” “No, venerable sir.” “Thus, monks, it is so that at a time when you are living having become quarrelsome, contentious, and having fallen into disputes, wounding one another with verbal spears, loving bodily action is not established toward your companions in the holy life, either openly or in private; loving verbal action is not… loving mental action is not established toward your companions in the holy life, either openly or in private. Why then, you foolish men, knowing what, seeing what, do you live having become quarrelsome, contentious, and having fallen into disputes, wounding one another with verbal spears, unable to convince one another or to be convinced, unable to reconcile with one another or to be reconciled? This, you foolish men, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.”

492. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “chayime, bhikkhave, dhammā sāraṇīyā piyakaraṇā garukaraṇā saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattanti. Katame cha? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

492. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, there are these six principles that are to be remembered, that create affection and respect, and that conduce to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity. What are the six? Here, monks, a monk’s loving bodily action is established toward his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private. This, too, is a principle that is to be remembered, that creates affection and respect, and that conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo [M 1.0397] garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekibhāvāya saṃvattati.

“Furthermore, monks, a monk’s loving verbal action is established toward his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private. This, too, is a principle that is to be remembered, that creates affection and respect, and that conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno mettaṃ manokammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

“Furthermore, monks, a monk’s loving mental action is established toward his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private. This, too, is a principle that is to be remembered, that creates affection and respect, and that conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ye te lābhā dhammikā dhammaladdhā antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampi, tathārūpehi lābhehi appaṭivibhattabhogī hoti sīlavantehi sabrahmacārīhi sādhāraṇabhogī. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

“Furthermore, monks, with regard to those gains that are righteous and righteously obtained, even down to the mere contents of his alms-bowl, a monk is one who enjoys them without apportionment, who enjoys them in common with his virtuous companions in the holy life. This, too, is a principle that is to be remembered, that creates affection and respect, and that conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni [T 1.0584] aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni tathārūpesu sīlesu sīlasāmaññagato viharati sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo [V 1.0405] sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

“Furthermore, monks, with regard to those virtues that are unbroken, unpierced, unspotted, and unblemished, which are liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, and conducive to concentration—with regard to such virtues, a monk dwells having attained to sameness in virtue with his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private. This, too, is a principle that is to be remembered, that creates affection and respect, and that conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharati sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

“Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells with his companions in the holy life, both openly and in private, having attained to sameness in that view which is noble, emancipating, and which, for one who practices it, leads rightly to the complete destruction of suffering. This, too, is a principle that is to be remembered, that creates affection and respect, and that conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

“Ime kho, bhikkhave, cha sāraṇīyā dhammā piyakaraṇā garukaraṇā saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattanti. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, channaṃ sāraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ etaṃ aggaṃ etaṃ saṅgāhikaṃ saṅgāhakaṃ (?) etaṃ saṅghāṭanikaṃ – yadidaṃ yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kūṭāgārassa etaṃ aggaṃ etaṃ saṅgāhikaṃ etaṃ saṅghāṭanikaṃ yadidaṃ kūṭaṃ; evameva kho, bhikkhave[P 1.0323], imesaṃ channaṃ sāraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ etaṃ aggaṃ etaṃ saṅgāhikaṃ etaṃ saṅghāṭanikaṃ [M 1.0398] yadidaṃ yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

“These, monks, are the six principles of cordiality that lead to affection and respect, and conduce to cohesion, non-dispute, concord, and unity. Among these six principles of cordiality, monks, this is the foremost, this is the most inclusive, this is the most cohesive: namely, that noble view which is emancipating and leads one who practices it rightly to the complete destruction of suffering. Just as, monks, the roof-peak is the foremost, the most inclusive, and the most cohesive part of a gabled house; so too, monks, among these six principles of cordiality, that noble view is the foremost, the most inclusive, and the most cohesive—the one that is emancipating and leads one who practices it rightly to the complete destruction of suffering.”

493. “Kathañca, bhikkhave, yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘atthi nu [T 1.0585] kho me taṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ ajjhattaṃ appahīnaṃ, yenāhaṃ pariyuṭṭhānena pariyuṭṭhitacitto yathābhūtaṃ nappajāneyyaṃ na passeyya’nti? Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhito hoti, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu byāpādapariyuṭṭhito hoti, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu thīnamiddhapariyuṭṭhito hoti, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu uddhaccakukkuccapariyuṭṭhito hoti, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vicikicchāpariyuṭṭhito hoti, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu idhalokacintāya pasuto hoti, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paralokacintāya pasuto hoti, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhaṇḍanajāto kalahajāto vivādāpanno aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudanto viharati, pariyuṭṭhitacittova hoti[V 1.0406]. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘natthi kho me taṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ ajjhattaṃ appahīnaṃ, yenāhaṃ pariyuṭṭhānena pariyuṭṭhitacitto yathābhūtaṃ nappajāneyyaṃ na passeyyaṃ. Suppaṇihitaṃ me mānasaṃ saccānaṃ bodhāyā’ti. Idamassa paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti ariyaṃ lokuttaraṃ asādhāraṇaṃ puthujjanehi.

493. “And how, monks, is that view noble, emancipating, and for one who practices it, leads rightly to the complete destruction of suffering? Here, monks, a monk, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, reflects thus: ‘Is there any obsession within me that is unabandoned, due to which, with my mind obsessed, I might not know and see things as they really are?’ If, monks, a monk is obsessed with sensual lust, his mind is indeed obsessed. If, monks, a monk is obsessed with ill will, his mind is indeed obsessed. If, monks, a monk is obsessed with sloth and torpor, his mind is indeed obsessed. If, monks, a monk is obsessed with restlessness and remorse, his mind is indeed obsessed. If, monks, a monk is obsessed with doubt, his mind is indeed obsessed. If, monks, a monk is devoted to thinking about this world, his mind is indeed obsessed. If, monks, a monk is devoted to thinking about the next world, his mind is indeed obsessed. If, monks, a monk dwells having created quarrels, created strife, entered into disputes, and is piercing others with verbal spears, his mind is indeed obsessed. He understands thus: ‘There is no obsession within me that is unabandoned, due to which, with my mind obsessed, I might not know and see things as they really are. My mind is well-directed for the awakening to the truths.’ This is the first knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, unshared by ordinary people.

494. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘imaṃ nu kho ahaṃ diṭṭhiṃ āsevanto bhāvento bahulīkaronto labhāmi paccattaṃ samathaṃ, labhāmi paccattaṃ nibbuti’nti? So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘imaṃ kho ahaṃ diṭṭhiṃ āsevanto bhāvento bahulīkaronto labhāmi paccattaṃ [T 1.0586] samathaṃ, labhāmi paccattaṃ nibbuti’nti. Idamassa dutiyaṃ ñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti ariyaṃ lokuttaraṃ asādhāraṇaṃ puthujjanehi.

494. “Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘By practicing this view, developing it, and making much of it, do I personally attain serenity, do I personally attain extinguishment?’ He understands thus: ‘By practicing this view, developing it, and making much of it, I personally attain serenity, I personally attain extinguishment.’ This is the second knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, unshared by ordinary people.”

495. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yathā rūpāyāhaṃ diṭṭhiyā samannāgato, atthi nu kho ito bahiddhā añño samaṇo [M 1.0399] vā brāhmaṇo vā [P 1.0324] tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā samannāgato’ti? So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘yathārūpāyāhaṃ diṭṭhiyā samannāgato, natthi ito bahiddhā añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā samannāgato’ti. Idamassa tatiyaṃ ñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti ariyaṃ lokuttaraṃ asādhāraṇaṃ puthujjanehi.

495. “Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘With the kind of view I am endowed with, is there any other ascetic or brahmin outside of this Dispensation who is endowed with such a view?’ He understands thus: ‘With the kind of view I am endowed with, there is no other ascetic or brahmin outside of this Dispensation who is endowed with such a view.’ This is the third knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, unshared by ordinary people.”

496. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yathārūpāya dhammatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya dhammatāya samannāgato’ti. Kathaṃrūpāya ca, bhikkhave, dhammatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato? Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa – ‘kiñcāpi tathārūpiṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati, yathārūpāya āpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati, atha kho naṃ khippameva satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu deseti vivarati uttānīkaroti; desetvā vivaritvā uttānīkatvā āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjati’. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, daharo kumāro mando uttānaseyyako hatthena vā pādena vā aṅgāraṃ akkamitvā khippameva paṭisaṃharati; evameva kho, bhikkhave, dhammatā esā diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa – ‘kiñcāpi tathārūpiṃ [T 1.0587] āpattiṃ āpajjati yathārūpāya āpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati, atha kho naṃ khippameva satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu deseti vivarati [V 1.0407] uttānīkaroti; desetvā vivaritvā uttānīkatvā āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjati’. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘yathārūpāya dhammatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya dhammatāya samannāgato’ti. Idamassa catutthaṃ ñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti ariyaṃ lokuttaraṃ asādhāraṇaṃ puthujjanehi.

496. “Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a quality, and I too am endowed with such a quality.’ And what, monks, is the quality with which a person accomplished in view is endowed? It is this quality, monks, of a person accomplished in view: ‘Even if one commits such an offense for which recovery is apparent, one quickly confesses, reveals, and discloses it to the Teacher or to wise spiritual companions; having confessed, revealed, and disclosed it, one undertakes restraint for the future.’ Just as, monks, a young, tender infant lying on its back, upon touching a hot ember with its hand or foot, quickly withdraws it; in the same way, monks, it is this quality of a person accomplished in view: ‘Even if one commits such an offense for which recovery is apparent, one quickly confesses, reveals, and discloses it to the Teacher or to wise spiritual companions; having confessed, revealed, and disclosed it, one undertakes restraint for the future.’ He understands thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a quality, and I too am endowed with such a quality.’ This is the fourth knowledge attained by him—noble, supramundane, unshared by ordinary people.”

497. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yathārūpāya dhammatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya dhammatāya samannāgato’ti. Kathaṃrūpāya ca, bhikkhave, dhammatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato? Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa – ‘kiñcāpi yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃkaraṇīyāni tattha ussukkaṃ āpanno hoti, atha khvāssa tibbāpekkhā hoti adhisīlasikkhāya adhicittasikkhāya adhipaññāsikkhāya’. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gāvī taruṇavacchā thambañca ālumpati vacchakañca apacinati; evameva kho, bhikkhave[M 1.0400], dhammatā esā diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa – ‘kiñcāpi yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃkaraṇīyāni tattha ussukkaṃ āpanno hoti, atha khvāssa tibbāpekkhā hoti adhisīlasikkhāya adhicittasikkhāya adhipaññāsikkhāya’. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘yathārūpāya dhammatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo [T 1.0588] samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya dhammatāya samannāgato’ti. Idamassa pañcamaṃ ñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti ariyaṃ lokuttaraṃ asādhāraṇaṃ puthujjanehi.

497. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a nature, and I too am endowed with such a nature.’ And with what kind of nature, monks, is a person accomplished in view endowed? This, monks, is the nature of a person accomplished in view: though one is diligent in the various higher and lower duties for one’s spiritual companions, one nevertheless has a strong aspiration for the higher training in moral conduct, the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom. Just as, monks, a cow with a young calf both munches on grass and watches over her calf; in the same way, monks, this is the nature of a person accomplished in view: though one is diligent in the various higher and lower duties for one’s spiritual companions, one nevertheless has a strong aspiration for the higher training in moral conduct, the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom. He understands thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a nature, and I too am endowed with such a nature.’ This is the fifth knowledge he has attained, which is noble, supramundane, and unshared by ordinary people.

498. “Puna [P 1.0325] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yathārūpāya balatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya balatāya samannāgato’ti. Kathaṃrūpāya ca, bhikkhave, balatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato? Balatā esā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa yaṃ tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye desiyamāne aṭṭhiṃkatvā manasikatvā sabbacetasā sabbacetaso (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), sabbaṃ cetasā (ka.) samannāharitvā ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇāti. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘yathārūpāya balatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya balatāya samannāgato’ti. Idamassa chaṭṭhaṃ ñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti ariyaṃ lokuttaraṃ asādhāraṇaṃ puthujjanehi.

498. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a strength, and I too am endowed with such a strength.’ And with what kind of strength, monks, is a person accomplished in view endowed? This, monks, is the strength of a person accomplished in view: when the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, one makes it a matter of importance, takes it to heart, attends to it with one’s whole mind, and listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear. He understands thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a strength, and I too am endowed with such a strength.’ This is the sixth knowledge he has attained, which is noble, supramundane, and unshared by ordinary people.

499. “Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yathārūpāya balatāya [V 1.0408] diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya balatāya samannāgato’ti. Kathaṃrūpāya ca, bhikkhave, balatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo samannāgato? Balatā esā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa yaṃ tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye desiyamāne labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘yathārūpāya balatāya diṭṭhisampanno puggalo [T 1.0589] samannāgato, ahampi tathārūpāya balatāya samannāgato’ti. Idamassa sattamaṃ ñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti ariyaṃ lokuttaraṃ asādhāraṇaṃ puthujjanehi.

499. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a strength, and I too am endowed with such a strength.’ And with what kind of strength, monks, is a person accomplished in view endowed? This, monks, is the strength of a person accomplished in view: when the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, one gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the teaching, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma. He understands thus: ‘A person accomplished in view is endowed with such a strength, and I too am endowed with such a strength.’ This is the seventh knowledge he has attained, which is noble, supramundane, and unshared by ordinary people.

500. “Evaṃ sattaṅgasamannāgatassa kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa dhammatā susamanniṭṭhā hoti sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya. Evaṃ sattaṅgasamannāgato [M 1.0401] kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sotāpattiphalasamannāgato hotī”ti.

500. Monks, for a noble disciple endowed with these seven factors, the principle for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is well ascertained. Monks, a noble disciple endowed with these seven factors is endowed with the fruit of stream-entry.

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. Those monks, being delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Kosambiyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Kosambiya Sutta, the eighth, is concluded.

9. Brahmanimantanikasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on the Invitation of a Brahmā

501. Evaṃ [T 1.0590][V 1.0409][P 1.0326] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

501. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, saying: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Ekamidāhaṃ, bhikkhave, samayaṃ ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharāmi subhagavane sālarājamūle. Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena bakassa brahmuno evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – ‘idaṃ niccaṃ, idaṃ dhuvaṃ, idaṃ sassataṃ, idaṃ kevalaṃ, idaṃ acavanadhammaṃ, idañhi na jāyati na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjati, ito ca panaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ natthī’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bakassa brahmuno cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya – seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva – ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ subhagavane sālarājamūle antarahito tasmiṃ brahmaloke pāturahosiṃ. Addasā kho maṃ, bhikkhave, bako brahmā dūratova āgacchantaṃ; disvāna maṃ etadavoca – ‘ehi kho, mārisa, svāgataṃ, mārisa! Cirassaṃ kho, mārisa, imaṃ pariyāyamakāsi yadidaṃ idhāgamanāya. Idañhi, mārisa, niccaṃ, idaṃ dhuvaṃ, idaṃ sassataṃ, idaṃ kevalaṃ, idaṃ acavanadhammaṃ, idañhi na jāyati na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjati. Ito ca panaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ natthī’”ti.

“Bhikkhus, at one time I was dwelling in Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Grove, at the foot of a kingly sāl tree. At that time, bhikkhus, this evil wrong view had arisen in Baka the Brahmā: ‘This is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal, this is complete, this is not subject to passing away; for this is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn. And there is no other, higher escape beyond this.’ Then, bhikkhus, having known with my mind the thought in the mind of Baka the Brahmā—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm, or bend his outstretched arm—even so, I vanished from the Subhaga Grove at the foot of the kingly sāl tree in Ukkaṭṭhā and appeared in that Brahmā world. Baka the Brahmā, bhikkhus, saw me coming from afar. Having seen me, he said this: ‘Come, good sir! Welcome, good sir! It has been a long time, good sir, since you have made this occasion to come here. For this, good sir, is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal, this is complete, this is not subject to passing away; for this is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn. And there is no other, higher escape beyond this.’”

Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, bakaṃ brahmānaṃ etadavocaṃ [T 1.0591] – “avijjāgato vata, bho, bako brahmā; avijjāgato vata, bho, bako brahmā; yatra hi nāma aniccaṃyeva samānaṃ niccanti vakkhati, addhuvaṃyeva samānaṃ dhuvanti vakkhati, asassataṃyeva samānaṃ sassatanti vakkhati, akevalaṃyeva samānaṃ [M 1.0402] kevalanti vakkhati, cavanadhammaṃyeva samānaṃ acavanadhammanti vakkhati; yattha ca pana jāyati jīyati mīyati cavati upapajjati tañca vakkhati – ‘idañhi na jāyati na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjatī’ti; santañca panaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ ‘natthaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇa’nti vakkhatī”ti.

When this was said, bhikkhus, I said this to Baka the Brahmā: ‘Alas, good sir, Baka the Brahmā has fallen into ignorance! Alas, good sir, Baka the Brahmā has fallen into ignorance! In that, being impermanent, he says it is permanent; being unstable, he says it is stable; being non-eternal, he says it is eternal; being incomplete, he says it is complete; being subject to passing away, he says it is not subject to passing away. And of that wherein one is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn, he says: “For this is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn.” And though there is another, higher escape, he says: “There is no other, higher escape.”’

502. “Atha [V 1.0410] kho, bhikkhave, māro pāpimā aññataraṃ brahmapārisajjaṃ anvāvisitvā maṃ etadavoca – ‘bhikkhu, bhikkhu, metamāsado metamāsado, eso hi, bhikkhu, brahmā mahābrahmā [P 1.0327] abhibhū anabhibhūto aññadatthudaso vasavattī issaro kattā nimmātā seṭṭho sajitā sajjitā (syā. kaṃ. ka.), sañjitā (sī. pī.) vasī pitā bhūtabhabyānaṃ. Ahesuṃ kho ye, bhikkhu, tayā pubbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā lokasmiṃ pathavīgarahakā pathavījigucchakā, āpagarahakā āpajigucchakā, tejagarahakā tejajigucchakā, vāyagarahakā vāyajigucchakā, bhūtagarahakā bhūtajigucchakā, devagarahakā devajigucchakā, pajāpatigarahakā pajāpatijigucchakā, brahmagarahakā brahmajigucchakā – te kāyassa bhedā pāṇupacchedā hīne kāye patiṭṭhitā ahesuṃ. Ye pana, bhikkhu, tayā pubbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā lokasmiṃ pathavīpasaṃsakā pathavābhinandino, āpapasaṃsakā āpābhinandino, tejapasaṃsakā tejābhinandino, vāyapasaṃsakā [T 1.0592] vāyābhinandino, bhūtapasaṃsakā bhūtābhinandino, devapasaṃsakā devābhinandino, pajāpatipasaṃsakā pajāpatābhinandino, brahmapasaṃsakā brahmābhinandino – te kāyassa bhedā pāṇupacchedā paṇīte kāye patiṭṭhitā. Taṃ tāhaṃ, bhikkhu, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘iṅgha tvaṃ, mārisa, yadeva te brahmā āha tadeva tvaṃ karohi, mā tvaṃ brahmuno vacanaṃ upātivattittho’. Sace kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, brahmuno vacanaṃ upātivattissasi, seyyathāpi nāma puriso siriṃ āgacchantiṃ daṇḍena paṭippaṇāmeyya, seyyathāpi vā pana, bhikkhu, puriso narakappapāte papatanto hatthehi ca pādehi ca pathaviṃ virādheyya, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ, bhikkhu, tuyhaṃ bhavissati. ‘Iṅghaṃ tvaṃ, mārisa, yadeva te brahmā āha tadeva tvaṃ karohi, mā tvaṃ brahmuno vacanaṃ upātivattittho. Nanu tvaṃ, bhikkhu, passasi brahmaparisaṃ sannipatita’nti? Iti kho maṃ, bhikkhave, māro pāpimā brahmaparisaṃ upanesi.

502. Then, bhikkhus, Māra the Evil One, having possessed a certain attendant of Brahmā’s assembly, said this to me: ‘Bhikkhu, bhikkhu, do not assail him, do not assail him! For this, bhikkhu, is Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the Wielder of Power, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Arranger, the Master, the Father of all that have been and will be. Bhikkhu, those ascetics and brahmins in the world before you who were revilers of earth, who were disgusted with earth; revilers of water, disgusted with water; revilers of fire, disgusted with fire; revilers of air, disgusted with air; revilers of beings, disgusted with beings; revilers of gods, disgusted with gods; revilers of Pajāpati, disgusted with Pajāpati; revilers of Brahmā, disgusted with Brahmā—they, with the breakup of the body, after the severing of the life faculty, were established in an inferior body. But, bhikkhu, those ascetics and brahmins in the world before you who were praisers of earth, who delighted in earth; praisers of water, who delighted in water; praisers of fire, who delighted in fire; praisers of air, who delighted in air; praisers of beings, who delighted in beings; praisers of gods, who delighted in gods; praisers of Pajāpati, who delighted in Pajāpati; praisers of Brahmā, who delighted in Brahmā—they, with the breakup of the body, after the severing of the life faculty, were established in a superior body. Therefore, bhikkhu, I say this to you: “Come now, good sir, do just what Brahmā tells you; do not transgress the word of Brahmā.” If you, bhikkhu, should transgress the word of Brahmā, it will be just as a man might beat back with a stick the fortune that is coming to him; or, bhikkhu, as a man falling into a hellish abyss might fail to get a hold on the earth with his hands and feet. Such, bhikkhu, will be your predicament. “Come now, good sir, do just what Brahmā tells you; do not transgress the word of Brahmā. Do you not see, bhikkhu, the assembly of Brahmā gathered here?”’ Thus, bhikkhus, Māra the Evil One tried to bring me into the fold of Brahmā's assembly.

“Evaṃ [M 1.0403] vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, māraṃ pāpimantaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘jānāmi kho tāhaṃ, pāpima; mā tvaṃ maññittho – na maṃ jānātī’ti. Māro tvamasi, pāpima. Yo ceva, pāpima, brahmā, yā ca brahmaparisā, ye ca brahmapārisajjā, sabbeva tava hatthagatā sabbeva tava vasaṃgatā. Tuyhañhi, pāpima, evaṃ hoti – ‘esopi me assa hatthagato, esopi me assa vasaṃgato’ti. Ahaṃ kho pana, pāpima, neva tava hatthagato neva tava vasaṃgato”ti.

When this was said, bhikkhus, I said this to Māra the Evil One: ‘I know you, Evil One. Do not think, “He does not know me.” You are Māra, Evil One. This Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the attendants of Brahmā's assembly—all have come into your hand, all have come under your power. For you, Evil One, think thus: “May this one too come into my hand! May this one too come under my power!” But I, Evil One, have not come into your hand, nor have I come under your power.’

503. “Evaṃ [T 1.0593] vutte, bhikkhave, bako brahmā maṃ etadavoca – ‘ahañhi, mārisa, niccaṃyeva [V 1.0411] samānaṃ niccanti vadāmi, dhuvaṃyeva [P 1.0328] samānaṃ dhuvanti vadāmi, sassataṃyeva samānaṃ sassatanti vadāmi, kevalaṃyeva samānaṃ kevalanti vadāmi, acavanadhammaṃyeva samānaṃ acavanadhamma’nti vadāmi, yattha ca pana na jāyati na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjati tadevāhaṃ vadāmi – ‘idañhi na jāyati na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjatī’ti. Asantañca panaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ ‘natthaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇa’nti vadāmi. Ahesuṃ kho, bhikkhu, tayā pubbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā lokasmiṃ yāvatakaṃ tuyhaṃ kasiṇaṃ āyu tāvatakaṃ tesaṃ tapokammameva ahosi. Te kho evaṃ jāneyyuṃ – ‘santañca panaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ atthaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇanti, asantaṃ vā aññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ natthaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇa’nti. Taṃ tāhaṃ, bhikkhu, evaṃ vadāmi – ‘na cevaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ dakkhissasi, yāvadeva ca pana kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī bhavissasi. Sace kho tvaṃ, bhikkhu, pathaviṃ ajjhosissasi, opasāyiko me bhavissasi vatthusāyiko, yathākāmakaraṇīyo bāhiteyyo. Sace āpaṃ… tejaṃ… vāyaṃ… bhūte… deve… pajāpatiṃ… brahmaṃ ajjhosissasi, opasāyiko me bhavissasi vatthusāyiko, yathākāmakaraṇīyo bāhiteyyo’ti.

503. When this was said, bhikkhus, Baka the Brahmā said this to me: ‘Good sir, being permanent, I declare it as “permanent”; being stable, I declare it as “stable”; being eternal, I declare it as “eternal”; being complete, I declare it as “complete”; being of a nature not to pass away, I declare it as “of a nature not to pass away.” And where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn, that very place I declare thus: “Here one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn.” And there being no other, further escape, I declare: “There is no other, further escape.” Bhikkhu, before you there were ascetics and brahmins in the world whose practice of austerity lasted for as long as your entire lifespan. They are the ones who would know whether there is another, further escape, or whether there is no other, further escape. Therefore, Bhikkhu, I say this to you: “You will not see another, further escape, and you will only become a partaker of weariness and vexation. If, Bhikkhu, you were to cling to earth, you will be my attendant, dwelling in my domain, to be dealt with as I please, and my subject. If you were to cling to water… fire… air… beings… gods… Pajāpati… Brahmā, you will be my attendant, dwelling in my domain, to be dealt with as I please, and my subject.’”

“Ahampi kho evaṃ, brahme, jānāmi – sace pathaviṃ ajjhosissāmi, opasāyiko te bhavissāmi vatthusāyiko, yathākāmakaraṇīyo [T 1.0594] bāhiteyyo. ‘Sace āpaṃ… tejaṃ… vāyaṃ… bhūte… deve… pajāpatiṃ… brahmaṃ ajjhosissāmi, opasāyiko te bhavissāmi vatthusāyiko, yathākāmakaraṇīyo bāhiteyyo’ti api ca te ahaṃ, brahme, gatiñca pajānāmi, jutiñca pajānāmi – evaṃ mahiddhiko bako brahmā, evaṃ mahānubhāvo bako brahmā, evaṃ mahesakkho bako brahmā”ti.

“I too, indeed, Brahmā, know this: ‘If I were to cling to earth, I would become your attendant, dwelling in your domain, to be dealt with as you please, and under your authority. If I were to cling to water… fire… air… beings… gods… Pajāpati… Brahmā, I would become your attendant, dwelling in your domain, to be dealt with as you please, and under your authority.’ Moreover, Brahmā, I know your state of existence and your radiance: ‘So powerful is Baka Brahmā, so great in majesty is Baka Brahmā, so great in sovereignty is Baka Brahmā.’”

“Yathākathaṃ [M 1.0404] pana me tvaṃ, mārisa, gatiñca pajānāsi, jutiñca pajānāsi – ‘evaṃ mahiddhiko bako brahmā, evaṃ mahānubhāvo bako brahmā, evaṃ mahesakkho bako brahmā’ti?

“But how, good sir, do you know my state of existence and my radiance, that: ‘So powerful is Baka Brahmā, so great in majesty is Baka Brahmā, so great in sovereignty is Baka Brahmā’?”

“Yāvatā candimasūriyā, pariharanti disā bhanti virocanā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko, ettha te vattate vattatī (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vaso.

“As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the directions, so far extends the thousandfold world-system. There your power prevails.”

“Paroparañca [V 1.0412] parovarañca (sī. pī.) jānāsi, atho rāgavirāginaṃ;

Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ, sattānaṃ āgatiṃ gati”nti.

“I know beings high and low, and also those with passion and those without passion; this state and other states, the coming and going of beings.”

“Evaṃ kho te ahaṃ, brahme, gatiñca pajānāmi jutiñca pajānāmi – ‘evaṃ mahiddhiko bako brahmā, evaṃ mahānubhāvo bako [P 1.0329] brahmā, evaṃ mahesakkho bako brahmā’ti.

“Thus indeed, Brahmā, I know your state of existence and your radiance: ‘So powerful is Baka Brahmā, so great in majesty is Baka Brahmā, so great in sovereignty is Baka Brahmā.’”

504. “Atthi kho, brahme, añño kāyo, taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi; tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. Atthi kho, brahme, ābhassarā nāma kāyo yato tvaṃ cuto idhūpapanno. Tassa te aticiranivāsena sā sati pamuṭṭhā, tena taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi; tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. Evampi kho ahaṃ, brahme, neva te samasamo abhiññāya, kuto nīceyyaṃ? Atha [T 1.0595] kho ahameva tayā bhiyyo. Atthi kho, brahme, subhakiṇho nāma kāyo, vehapphalo nāma kāyo, abhibhū nāma kāyo, taṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi na passasi; tamahaṃ jānāmi passāmi. Evampi kho ahaṃ, brahme, neva te samasamo abhiññāya, kuto nīceyyaṃ? Atha kho ahameva tayā bhiyyo. Pathaviṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme, pathavito abhiññāya yāvatā pathaviyā pathavattena ananubhūtaṃ tadabhiññāya pathaviṃ nāpahosiṃ, pathaviyā nāpahosiṃ, pathavito nāpahosiṃ, pathaviṃ meti nāpahosiṃ, pathaviṃ nābhivadiṃ. Evampi kho ahaṃ, brahme, neva te samasamo abhiññāya, kuto nīceyyaṃ? Atha kho ahameva tayā bhiyyo. Āpaṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… tejaṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… vāyaṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… bhūte kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… deve kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… pajāpatiṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… brahmaṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… ābhassare kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… subhakiṇhe kho ahaṃ, brahme… [M 1.0405] …pe… vehapphale kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… abhibhuṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme…pe… sabbaṃ kho ahaṃ, brahme, sabbato abhiññāya yāvatā sabbassa sabbattena ananubhūtaṃ tadabhiññāya sabbaṃ nāpahosiṃ sabbasmiṃ nāpahosiṃ sabbato nāpahosiṃ sabbaṃ meti nāpahosiṃ, sabbaṃ nābhivadiṃ. Evampi kho ahaṃ, brahme, neva te samasamo abhiññāya, kuto nīceyyaṃ? Atha kho ahameva tayā bhiyyo”ti.

504. “There is, Brahmā, another plane of existence, which you do not know or see; that I know and see. There is, Brahmā, the plane of existence called Ābhassara, from which you passed away and were reborn here. Due to your exceedingly long residence, that memory has been lost. Therefore, you do not know it or see it; that I know and see. In this way too, Brahmā, I am not your equal with regard to direct knowledge, so how could I be inferior? Rather, it is I who am superior to you. There is, Brahmā, the plane of existence called Subhakiṇha, the plane of existence called Vehapphala, and the plane of existence called Abhibhū, which you do not know or see; that I know and see. In this way too, Brahmā, I am not your equal with regard to direct knowledge, so how could I be inferior? Rather, it is I who am superior to you. Brahmā, having directly known earth as earth, and having directly known that which is not experienced through the nature of earth, I did not cling to earth, I did not cling in earth, I did not cling from earth, I did not cling to ‘earth is mine,’ and I did not assent to earth. In this way too, Brahmā, I am not your equal with regard to direct knowledge, so how could I be inferior? Rather, it is I who am superior to you. Brahmā, having directly known water… fire… air… beings… gods… Pajāpati… Brahmā… the Ābhassaras… the Subhakiṇhas… the Vehapphalas… Abhibhū… Brahmā, having directly known the all as the all, and having directly known that which is not experienced through the nature of the all, I did not cling to the all, I did not cling in the all, I did not cling from the all, I did not cling to ‘the all is mine,’ and I did not assent to the all. In this way too, Brahmā, I am not your equal with regard to direct knowledge, so how could I be inferior? Rather, it is I who am superior to you.”

“Sace [V 1.0413] kho, mārisa, sabbassa sabbattena ananubhūtaṃ, tadabhiññāya mā heva te rittakameva ahosi, tucchakameva ahosī”ti[T 1.0596].

“Good sir, if there is indeed something unexperienced by the nature of the all, then having directly known it, may your statement not prove to be merely empty, merely void.”

“‘Viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ anantaṃ sabbato pabhaṃ’, taṃ pathaviyā pathavattena ananubhūtaṃ, āpassa āpattena ananubhūtaṃ, tejassa tejattena ananubhūtaṃ, vāyassa vāyattena ananubhūtaṃ, bhūtānaṃ bhūtattena ananubhūtaṃ, devānaṃ devattena ananubhūtaṃ, pajāpatissa pajāpatittena ananubhūtaṃ, brahmānaṃ brahmattena ananubhūtaṃ, ābhassarānaṃ ābhassarattena ananubhūtaṃ, subhakiṇhānaṃ subhakiṇhattena ananubhūtaṃ, vehapphalānaṃ vehapphalatte [P 1.0330] ananubhūtaṃ, abhibhussa abhibhuttena ananubhūtaṃ, sabbassa sabbattena ananubhūtaṃ”.

“‘Consciousness that is non-manifest, infinite, radiant all around’—that is unexperienced by earth through the nature of earth, unexperienced by water through the nature of water, unexperienced by fire through the nature of fire, unexperienced by air through the nature of air, unexperienced by beings through the nature of beings, unexperienced by gods through the nature of a god, unexperienced by Pajāpati through the nature of Pajāpati, unexperienced by brahmās through the nature of a brahmā, unexperienced by the Ābhassaras through the nature of an Ābhassara, unexperienced by the Subhakiṇhas through the nature of a Subhakiṇha, unexperienced by the Vehapphalas through the nature of a Vehapphala, unexperienced by Abhibhū through the nature of Abhibhū, unexperienced by the all through the nature of the all.”

“Handa carahi handa ca hi (sī. pī.) te, mārisa, passa antaradhāyāmī”ti. ‘Handa carahi me tvaṃ, brahme, antaradhāyassu, sace visahasī’ti. Atha kho, bhikkhave, bako brahmā ‘antaradhāyissāmi samaṇassa gotamassa, antaradhāyissāmi samaṇassa gotamassā’ti nevassu me sakkoti antaradhāyituṃ.

“Come now, good sir, watch as I disappear.” “Come now, Brahmā, disappear from me, if you are able.” Then, monks, Baka the Brahmā, thinking, “I will disappear from the ascetic Gotama, I will disappear from the ascetic Gotama,” was not able to disappear from me.

“Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, bakaṃ brahmānaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘handa carahi te brahme antaradhāyāmī’ti. ‘Handa carahi me tvaṃ, mārisa, antaradhāyassu sace visahasī’ti. Atha kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsiṃ – ‘ettāvatā brahmā ca brahmaparisā ca brahmapārisajjā ca saddañca me sossanti saddameva suyyanti (ka.), na ca maṃ dakkhantī’ti. Antarahito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsiṃ –

When this was said, I, monks, said to Baka the Brahmā: ‘Well then, Brahmā, I will now disappear from you.’ ‘Well then, good sir, disappear from me if you can.’ Then, monks, I performed such a feat of psychic power that the Brahmā, the Brahmā assembly, and the Brahmā retinue would hear my voice but would not see me. Having disappeared, I uttered this verse:

“Bhavevāhaṃ bhayaṃ disvā, bhavañca vibhavesinaṃ;

Bhavaṃ nābhivadiṃ kiñci, nandiñca na upādiyi”nti.

‘Having seen the danger in existence, and in existence for one seeking the cessation of existence, I did not affirm any kind of existence, nor did I cling to delight.’”

“Atha [T 1.0597][M 1.0406] kho, bhikkhave, brahmā ca brahmaparisā ca brahmapārisajjā ca acchariyabbhutacittajātā ahesuṃ – ‘acchariyaṃ vata bho, abbhutaṃ vata bho! Samaṇassa gotamassa mahiddhikatā mahānubhāvatā, na ca vata no ito pubbe diṭṭho vā, suto vā, añño [V 1.0414] samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃ mahiddhiko evaṃ mahānubhāvo yathāyaṃ samaṇo gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito. Bhavarāmāya vata, bho, pajāya bhavaratāya bhavasammuditāya samūlaṃ bhavaṃ udabbahī’ti.

Then, monks, the Brahmā, the Brahmā assembly, and the Brahmā’s retinue were filled with wonder and amazement, saying: ‘It is wonderful, good sirs, it is marvelous! The ascetic Gotama has such great psychic power and might. Never before have we seen or heard of any other ascetic or brahmin with such great psychic power and might as this ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan, who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan. For this generation, good sirs, that delights in existence, takes pleasure in existence, and rejoices in existence, he has uprooted existence together with its root!’

505. “Atha kho, bhikkhave, māro pāpimā aññataraṃ brahmapārisajjaṃ anvāvisitvā maṃ etadavoca – ‘sace kho tvaṃ, mārisa, evaṃ pajānāsi, sace tvaṃ evaṃ anubuddho, mā sāvake upanesi, mā pabbajite; mā sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ desesi, mā pabbajitānaṃ; mā sāvakesu gedhimakāsi, mā pabbajitesu. Ahesuṃ kho, bhikkhu, tayā pubbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā lokasmiṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā paṭijānamānā[P 1.0331]. Te sāvake upanesuṃ pabbajite, sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ desesuṃ pabbajitānaṃ, sāvakesu gedhimakaṃsu pabbajitesu, te sāvake upanetvā pabbajite, sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā pabbajitānaṃ, sāvakesu gedhitacittā pabbajitesu, kāyassa bhedā pāṇupacchedā hīne kāye patiṭṭhitā. Ahesuṃ ye pana, bhikkhu, tayā pubbe samaṇabrāhmaṇā lokasmiṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā paṭijānamānā. Te na sāvake upanesuṃ na pabbajite, na sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ desesuṃ na pabbajitānaṃ, na sāvakesu [T 1.0598] gedhimakaṃsu na pabbajitesu, te na sāvake upanetvā na pabbajite, na sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā na pabbajitānaṃ, na sāvakesu gedhitacittā na pabbajitesu, kāyassa bhedā pāṇupacchedā paṇīte kāye patiṭṭhitā. Taṃ tāhaṃ, bhikkhu, evaṃ vadāmi – iṅgha tvaṃ, mārisa, appossukko diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāramanuyutto viharassu, anakkhātaṃ kusalañhi, mārisa, mā paraṃ ovadāhī’ti.

505. “Then, monks, Māra the Evil One, having possessed a certain member of the Brahmā’s retinue, said this to me: ‘If, good sir, you know thus, if you have awakened thus, do not lead lay disciples, do not lead the ordained; do not teach the Dhamma to lay disciples, do not teach it to the ordained; do not become attached to lay disciples, do not become attached to the ordained. There were, monk, before you in the world ascetics and brahmins who claimed to be arahants, fully enlightened ones. They led lay disciples and the ordained; they taught the Dhamma to lay disciples and the ordained; they became attached to lay disciples and the ordained. Because they led lay disciples and the ordained, taught the Dhamma to lay disciples and the ordained, and had minds attached to lay disciples and the ordained, with the breakup of the body, after the cutting off of life, they were established in an inferior realm. But there were also, monk, before you in the world ascetics and brahmins who claimed to be arahants, fully enlightened ones. They did not lead lay disciples or the ordained; they did not teach the Dhamma to lay disciples or the ordained; they did not become attached to lay disciples or the ordained. Because they did not lead lay disciples or the ordained, did not teach the Dhamma to lay disciples or the ordained, and did not have minds attached to lay disciples or the ordained, with the breakup of the body, after the cutting off of life, they were established in a sublime realm. Therefore, monk, I say this to you: Come now, good sir, dwell unconcerned, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life. For it is good not to declare it, good sir; do not advise others.’”

“Evaṃ vutte, ahaṃ, bhikkhave, māraṃ pāpimantaṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘jānāmi kho tāhaṃ, pāpima, mā tvaṃ maññittho – na maṃ jānātī’ti. Māro tvamasi, pāpima. Na maṃ tvaṃ, pāpima, hitānukampī evaṃ vadesi; ahitānukampī maṃ tvaṃ, pāpima, evaṃ vadesi. Tuyhañhi, pāpima, evaṃ hoti – ‘yesaṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ desessati, te me visayaṃ upātivattissantī’ti. Asammāsambuddhāva pana te[M 1.0407], pāpima, samānā sammāsambuddhāmhāti paṭijāniṃsu. Ahaṃ kho pana, pāpima, sammāsambuddhova samāno sammāsambuddhomhīti paṭijānāmi. Desentopi hi, pāpima, tathāgato sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ tādisova adesentopi hi, pāpima, tathāgato sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ tādisova. Upanentopi hi, pāpima, tathāgato sāvake [V 1.0415] tādisova, anupanentopi hi, pāpima, tathāgato sāvake tādisova. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathāgatassa, pāpima, ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā – te pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ [T 1.0599] anuppādadhammā. Seyyathāpi, pāpima, tālo matthakacchinno abhabbo puna virūḷhiyā; evameva kho, pāpima, tathāgatassa ye āsavā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā – te pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammāti.

When this was said, I spoke to Māra the Evil One, saying: ‘I know you, Evil One. Do not think, “He does not know me.” You are Māra, Evil One. You do not speak to me thus, Evil One, out of a desire for my welfare; you speak to me thus, Evil One, out of a desire for my non-welfare. For this thought occurs to you, Evil One: “Those to whom the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma will pass beyond my domain.” Evil One, those who were not Perfectly Enlightened, being not Perfectly Enlightened, claimed, “We are Perfectly Enlightened.” But I, Evil One, being Perfectly Enlightened, claim, “I am Perfectly Enlightened.” Indeed, Evil One, even when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to his disciples, he is just so; and even when the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma to his disciples, he is just so. Indeed, Evil One, even when the Tathāgata leads his disciples, he is just so; and even when the Tathāgata does not lead his disciples, he is just so. For what reason? Because, Evil One, the taints of the Tathāgata—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are distressing, have suffering as their result, and are subject to future birth, aging, and death—have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to a state of non-being, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. Just as, Evil One, a palm tree with its crown cut off is incapable of growing again; even so, Evil One, the taints of the Tathāgata—which are defiling, lead to renewed existence, are distressing, have suffering as their result, and are subject to future birth, aging, and death—have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to a state of non-being, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.’

“Iti hidaṃ mārassa ca anālapanatāya brahmuno ca abhinimantanatāya, tasmā imassa veyyākaraṇassa brahmanimantanikaṃteva adhivacana”nti.

Thus, because of disregarding Māra and inviting Brahmā, this exposition received the designation, 'The Invitation of a Brahmā'.

Brahmanimantanikasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The Brahmanimantanika Sutta, the ninth, is concluded.

10. Māratajjanīyasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Rebuking Māra

506. Evaṃ [T 1.0600][V 1.0416][P 1.0332] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhaggesu viharati susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahāmoggallāno abbhokāse caṅkamati. Tena kho pana samayena māro pāpimā āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa kucchigato hoti koṭṭhamanupaviṭṭho. Atha kho āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa etadahosi – “kiṃ nu kho me kucchi garugaro viya garu garu viya (sī. pī. ṭīkāyaṃ pāṭhantaraṃ)? Māsācitaṃ maññe”ti. Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno caṅkamā orohitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno paccattaṃ yoniso manasākāsi. Addasā kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno māraṃ pāpimantaṃ kucchigataṃ koṭṭhamanupaviṭṭhaṃ. Disvāna [M 1.0408] māraṃ pāpimantaṃ etadavoca – “nikkhama, pāpima; nikkhama, pāpima! Mā tathāgataṃ vihesesi, mā tathāgatasāvakaṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā”ti. Atha kho mārassa pāpimato etadahosi – “ajānameva kho maṃ ayaṃ samaṇo apassaṃ evamāha – ‘nikkhama, pāpima; nikkhama, pāpima! Mā tathāgataṃ vihesesi, mā tathāgatasāvakaṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā’ti. Yopissa so satthā sopi maṃ neva khippaṃ jāneyya, kuto pana kuto ca pana (syā.) maṃ ayaṃ sāvako jānissatī”ti? Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno [T 1.0601] māraṃ pāpimantaṃ etadavoca – “evampi kho tāhaṃ, pāpima, jānāmi, mā tvaṃ maññittho – ‘na maṃ jānātī’ti. Māro tvamasi, pāpima; tuyhañhi, pāpima, evaṃ hoti – ‘ajānameva kho maṃ ayaṃ samaṇo apassaṃ evamāha – nikkhama, pāpima; nikkhama, pāpima! Mā tathāgataṃ vihesesi, mā tathāgatasāvakaṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyāti. Yopissa so satthā sopi maṃ neva khippaṃ jāneyya, kuto pana maṃ ayaṃ sāvako jānissatī’”ti?

506. Thus have I heard. At one time the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Wood, in the deer sanctuary. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was practicing walking meditation in an open space. At that time, Māra the evil one had entered the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's belly and gone into his intestines. Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'Why is my belly so very heavy, as if filled with a meal of beans?' Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, descending from his walking path, entered his dwelling and sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna applied his mind properly to himself. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw Māra the evil one, who had entered his belly and gone into his intestines. Having seen him, he spoke to Māra the evil one, saying: 'Go forth, Evil One! Go forth, Evil One! Do not harass the Tathāgata; do not harass a disciple of the Tathāgata. Let it not be for your long-term detriment and suffering!' Then this thought occurred to Māra the evil one: 'This ascetic, without knowing me and without seeing me, says this: “Go forth, Evil One! Go forth, Evil One! Do not harass the Tathāgata; do not harass a disciple of the Tathāgata. Let it not be for your long-term detriment and suffering!” Even his teacher would not know me quickly; how then could this disciple know me?' Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spoke to Māra the evil one, saying: 'I know you even in this way, Evil One. Do not think, “He does not know me.” You are Māra, Evil One. For this thought occurs to you, Evil One: “This ascetic, without knowing me and without seeing me, says this: ‘Go forth, Evil One! Go forth, Evil One! Do not harass the Tathāgata; do not harass a disciple of the Tathāgata. Let it not be for your long-term detriment and suffering!’ Even his teacher would not know me quickly; how then could this disciple know me?”'

Atha kho mārassa pāpimato etadahosi – “jāname kho maṃ ayaṃ samaṇo passaṃ evamāha – ‘nikkhama, pāpima; nikkhama, pāpima! Mā tathāgataṃ vihesesi, mā tathāgatasāvakaṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā’”ti. Atha kho māro pāpimā āyasmato [P 1.0333] mahāmoggallānassa mukhato uggantvā paccaggaḷe aṭṭhāsi.

Then this thought occurred to Māra the evil one: ‘This ascetic, knowing me indeed and seeing me, says: “Go forth, Evil One! Go forth, Evil One! Do not harass the Tathāgata; do not harass a disciple of the Tathāgata. Let it not be for your long-term detriment and suffering!”’ Then Māra the evil one, having come up out of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s mouth, stood by the door-leaf.

507. Addasā [V 1.0417] kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno māraṃ pāpimantaṃ paccaggaḷe ṭhitaṃ; disvāna māraṃ pāpimantaṃ etadavoca – ‘etthāpi kho tāhaṃ, pāpima, passāmi; mā tvaṃ maññittho “na maṃ passatī”ti. Eso tvaṃ, pāpima, paccaggaḷe ṭhito. Bhūtapubbāhaṃ, pāpima, dūsī nāma māro ahosiṃ, tassa me kāḷī nāma bhaginī. Tassā tvaṃ putto. So me tvaṃ bhāgineyyo ahosi. Tena kho pana, pāpima, samayena kakusandho bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno hoti. Kakusandhassa kho pana, pāpima, bhagavato arahato [T 1.0602] sammāsambuddhassa vidhurasañjīvaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Yāvatā kho pana, pāpima, kakusandhassa bhagavato [M 1.0409] arahato sammāsambuddhassa sāvakā. Tesu na ca koci āyasmatā vidhurena samasamo hoti yadidaṃ dhammadesanāya. Iminā kho evaṃ etaṃ (sī. syā. pī.), pāpima, pariyāyena āyasmato vidhurassa vidhuroteva vidhurassa vidhuro vidhurotveva (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) samaññā udapādi.

507. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw Māra the evil one standing by the door-leaf. Having seen him, he spoke to Māra the evil one, saying: ‘Even here I see you, Evil One. Do not think, “He does not see me.” There you are, Evil One, standing by the door-leaf. In a former time, Evil One, I was a Māra named Dūsī, and I had a sister named Kāḷī. You were her son. Thus, you were my nephew. At that time, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had arisen in the world. And, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva, a foremost, excellent pair. Among all the disciples of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was none who was equal to the Venerable Vidhura in regard to the teaching of the Dhamma. It was for this reason, Evil One, that the designation ‘Vidhura’ arose for the Venerable Vidhura.’

“Āyasmā pana, pāpima, sañjīvo araññagatopi rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi appakasireneva saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjati. Bhūtapubbaṃ, pāpima, āyasmā sañjīvo aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno nisinno hoti. Addasaṃsu kho, pāpima, gopālakā pasupālakā kassakā pathāvino āyasmantaṃ sañjīvaṃ aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannaṃ nisinnaṃ; disvāna tesaṃ etadahosi – ‘acchariyaṃ vata, bho, abbhutaṃ vata, bho! Ayaṃ samaṇo nisinnakova kālaṅkato! Handa naṃ dahāmā’ti. Atha kho te, pāpima, gopālakā pasupālakā kassakā pathāvino tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca gomayañca saṃkaḍḍhitvā āyasmato sañjīvassa kāye upacinitvā aggiṃ datvā pakkamiṃsu. Atha kho, pāpima, āyasmā sañjīvo tassā rattiyā accayena tāya samāpattiyā vuṭṭhahitvā cīvarāni papphoṭetvā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Addasaṃsu kho te, pāpima, gopālakā pasupālakā kassakā pathāvino āyasmantaṃ sañjīvaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ; disvāna nesaṃ [T 1.0603] etadahosi – ‘acchariyaṃ vata, bho, abbhutaṃ vata, bho! Ayaṃ samaṇo nisinnakova kālaṅkato, svāyaṃ paṭisañjīvito’ti[P 1.0334]. Iminā kho evaṃ, pāpima, pariyāyena āyasmato sañjīvassa sañjīvoteva sañjīvo sañjīvotveva (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) samaññā udapādi.

Furthermore, Evil One, the Venerable Sañjīva, whether gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, attains the cessation of perception and feeling without any difficulty. Formerly, Evil One, the Venerable Sañjīva was seated at the root of a certain tree, having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. Cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva seated at the root of a certain tree, having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen him, this thought occurred to them: ‘Sirs, it is amazing! Sirs, it is wonderful! This ascetic has passed away while sitting! Come, let us cremate him!’ Then, Evil One, those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers, having gathered grass, wood, and cow dung, and having piled it upon the body of the Venerable Sañjīva, set fire to it and departed. Then, Evil One, the Venerable Sañjīva, at the passing of that night, having emerged from that attainment, shook out his robes, dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered the village for alms-food. Those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva wandering for alms-food. Having seen him, this thought occurred to them: ‘Sirs, it is amazing! Sirs, it is wonderful! This ascetic passed away while sitting, and now he has revived!’ It was in this way, Evil One, that the designation ‘Sañjīva’ arose for the Venerable Sañjīva.

508. “Atha kho, pāpima, dūsissa mārassa etadahosi – ‘imesaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ kalyāṇadhammānaṃ neva jānāmi āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatike anvāviseyyaṃ [V 1.0418] – etha, tumhe bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme akkosatha paribhāsatha rosetha vihesetha. Appeva nāma tumhehi akkosiyamānānaṃ paribhāsiyamānānaṃ rosiyamānānaṃ vihesiyamānānaṃ siyā cittassa aññathattaṃ, yathā taṃ dūsī [M 1.0410] māro labhetha otāra’nti. Atha kho te, pāpima, dūsī māro brāhmaṇagahapatike anvāvisi – ‘etha, tumhe bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme akkosatha paribhāsatha rosetha vihesetha. Appeva nāma tumhehi akkosiyamānānaṃ paribhāsiyamānānaṃ rosiyamānānaṃ vihesiyamānānaṃ siyā cittassa aññathattaṃ, yathā taṃ dūsī māro labhetha otāra’nti.

508. Then, Evil One, this thought occurred to Māra Dūsī: ‘I do not know the coming or the going of these monks who are virtuous and of good character. What if I were to possess the brahmins and householders, saying: “Come, revile, abuse, vex, and harass the monks who are virtuous and of good character. Perhaps, while being reviled, abused, vexed, and harassed by you, there might be an alteration of their minds, so that Māra Dūsī might find an opportunity.”’ Then, Evil One, Māra Dūsī possessed those brahmins and householders, saying: ‘Come, revile, abuse, vex, and harass the monks who are virtuous and of good character. Perhaps, while being reviled, abused, vexed, and harassed by you, there might be an alteration of their minds, so that Māra Dūsī might find an opportunity.’”

“Atha kho te, pāpima, brāhmaṇagahapatikā anvāvisiṭṭhā dūsinā mārena bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme akkosanti paribhāsanti rosenti vihesenti – ‘ime pana muṇḍakā samaṇakā ibbhā kiṇhā kaṇhā (syā. kaṃ. ka.) bandhupādāpaccā “jhāyinosmā jhāyinosmā”ti pattakkhandhā adhomukhā madhurakajātā jhāyanti pajjhāyanti nijjhāyanti apajjhāyanti. Seyyathāpi nāma ulūko [T 1.0604] rukkhasākhāyaṃ mūsikaṃ maggayamāno jhāyati pajjhāyati nijjhāyati apajjhāyati; evamevime muṇḍakā samaṇakā ibbhā kiṇhā bandhupādāpaccā “jhāyinosmā jhāyinosmā”ti pattakkhandhā adhomukhā madhurakajātā jhāyanti pajjhāyanti nijjhāyanti apajjhāyanti. Seyyathāpi nāma kotthu nadītīre macche maggayamāno jhāyati pajjhāyati nijjhāyati apajjhāyati; evamevime muṇḍakā samaṇakā ibbhā kiṇhā bandhupādāpaccā “jhāyinosmā jhāyinosmā”ti pattakkhandhā adhomukhā madhurakajātā jhāyanti pajjhāyanti nijjhāyanti apajjhāyanti. Seyyathāpi nāma biḷāro sandhisamalasaṅkaṭīre mūsikaṃ maggayamāno jhāyati pajjhāyati nijjhāyati apajjhāyati; evamevime muṇḍakā samaṇakā ibbhā kiṇhā bandhupādāpaccā “jhāyinosmā jhāyinosmā”ti pattakkhandhā adhomukhā madhurakajātā jhāyanti pajjhāyanti nijjhāyanti apajjhāyanti. Seyyathāpi nāma gadrabho vahacchinno sandhisamalasaṅkaṭīre jhāyati pajjhāyati nijjhāyati apajjhāyati, evamevime muṇḍakā samaṇakā ibbhā kiṇhā bandhupādāpaccā “jhāyinosmā jhāyinosmā”ti pattakkhandhā adhomukhā madhurakajātā jhāyanti pajjhāyanti nijjhāyanti apajjhāyantī”ti.

Then, Evil One, those brahmins and householders, possessed by Māra Dūsī, reviled, abused, vexed, and harassed the monks who are virtuous and of good character, saying: ‘These shaveling petty ascetics, these wealthy men, these black ones, offspring from the kinsman’s foot, saying, “We are meditators, we are meditators,” with drooping shoulders, with faces downcast, and listless, they meditate, contemplate, scrutinize, and reflect. Just as an owl on a tree branch, seeking a mouse, meditates, contemplates, scrutinizes, and reflects; even so, these shaveling petty ascetics, these wealthy men, these black ones, offspring from the kinsman’s foot, saying, “We are meditators, we are meditators,” with drooping shoulders, with faces downcast, and listless, they meditate, contemplate, scrutinize, and reflect. Just as a jackal on a riverbank, seeking fish, meditates, contemplates, scrutinizes, and reflects; even so, these shaveling petty ascetics, these wealthy men, these black ones, offspring from the kinsman’s foot, saying, “We are meditators, we are meditators,” with drooping shoulders, with faces downcast, and listless, they meditate, contemplate, scrutinize, and reflect. Just as a cat in a gap, a sewer, or on a rubbish heap, seeking a mouse, meditates, contemplates, scrutinizes, and reflects; even so, these shaveling petty ascetics, these wealthy men, these black ones, offspring from the kinsman’s foot, saying, “We are meditators, we are meditators,” with drooping shoulders, with faces downcast, and listless, they meditate, contemplate, scrutinize, and reflect. Just as a donkey with a sore back in a gap, a sewer, or on a rubbish heap, meditates, contemplates, scrutinizes, and reflects; even so, these shaveling petty ascetics, these wealthy men, these black ones, offspring from the kinsman’s foot, saying, “We are meditators, we are meditators,” with drooping shoulders, with faces downcast, and listless, they meditate, contemplate, scrutinize, and reflect.’”

“Ye kho pana, pāpima, tena samayena manussā kālaṅkaronti yebhuyyena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti.

Now, Evil One, those humans who passed away at that time, for the most part, with the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.

509. “Atha [M 1.0411][V 1.0419][P 1.0335] kho, pāpima, kakusandho bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho bhikkhū [T 1.0605] āmantesi – ‘anvāviṭṭhā kho, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇagahapatikā dūsinā mārena – etha, tumhe bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme akkosatha paribhāsatha rosetha vihesetha, appeva nāma tumhehi akkosiyamānānaṃ paribhāsiyamānānaṃ rosiyamānānaṃ vihesiyamānānaṃ siyā cittassa aññathattaṃ, yathā taṃ dūsī māro labhetha otāra’nti. Etha, tumhe, bhikkhave, mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatha, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharatha. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatha, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā viharathā’ti.

509. Then, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monks: ‘Monks, the brahmin householders have been possessed by Māra Dūsī, who said to them: “Come, revile, abuse, vex, and harass the monks who are virtuous and of good character. Perhaps, while being reviled, abused, vexed, and harassed by you, there might be an alteration of their minds, so that Māra Dūsī might find an opportunity.” Come, monks, dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. Dwell with a mind accompanied by compassion… with a mind accompanied by altruistic joy… dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.’”

“Atha kho te, pāpima, bhikkhū kakusandhena bhagavatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena evaṃ ovadiyamānā evaṃ anusāsiyamānā araññagatāpi rukkhamūlagatāpi suññāgāragatāpi mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihariṃsu, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihariṃsu. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā vihariṃsu, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyābajjhena pharitvā vihariṃsu[T 1.0606].

Then, Evil One, those monks, being thus advised and instructed by the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, whether they had gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, dwelt pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, they dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. They dwelt with a mind accompanied by compassion… with a mind accompanied by altruistic joy… they dwelt pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, they dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.

510. “Atha kho, pāpima, dūsissa mārassa etadahosi – ‘evampi kho ahaṃ karonto imesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ kalyāṇadhammānaṃ neva jānāmi āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā, yaṃnūnāhaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatike anvāviseyyaṃ – etha, tumhe bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme sakkarotha garuṃ karotha mānetha [M 1.0412] pūjetha[P 1.0336], appeva nāma tumhehi sakkariyamānānaṃ garukariyamānānaṃ māniyamānānaṃ pūjiyamānānaṃ siyā cittassa aññathattaṃ, yathā taṃ dūsī māro labhetha otāra’nti[V 1.0420]. Atha kho te, pāpima, dūsī māro brāhmaṇagahapatike anvāvisi – ‘etha, tumhe bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme sakkarotha garuṃ karotha mānetha pūjetha, appeva nāma tumhehi sakkariyamānānaṃ garukariyamānānaṃ māniyamānānaṃ pūjiyamānānaṃ siyā cittassa aññathattaṃ, yathā taṃ dūsī māro labhetha otāra’nti. Atha kho te, pāpima, brāhmaṇagahapatikā anvāviṭṭhā dūsinā mārena bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme sakkaronti garuṃ karonti mānenti pūjenti.

510. Then, Evil One, this thought occurred to Dūsī Māra: ‘Even while acting in this way, I do not know the destination or future course of these virtuous monks of good character. What if I were to possess the brahmin householders, with the thought: “Come, you, honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the virtuous monks of good character. Perhaps, while they are being honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated by you, there might be a change in their minds, whereby Dūsī Māra might gain an opportunity.”’ Then, Evil One, Dūsī Māra possessed those brahmin householders, with the thought: ‘Come, you, honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the virtuous monks of good character. Perhaps, while they are being honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated by you, there might be a change in their minds, whereby Dūsī Māra might gain an opportunity.’ Then, Evil One, those brahmin householders, possessed by Dūsī Māra, honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated the virtuous monks of good character.

“Ye kho pana, pāpima, tena samayena manussā kālaṅkaronti yebhuyyena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti.

Indeed, Evil One, at that time, most of the humans who passed away, after the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.

511. “Atha [T 1.0607] kho, pāpima, kakusandho bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘anvāviṭṭhā kho, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇagahapatikā dūsinā mārena – etha, tumhe bhikkhū sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme sakkarotha garuṃ karotha mānetha pūjetha, appeva nāma tumhehi sakkariyamānānaṃ garukariyamānānaṃ māniyamānānaṃ pūjiyamānānaṃ siyā cittassa aññathattaṃ, yathā taṃ dūsī māro labhetha otāranti. Etha, tumhe, bhikkhave, asubhānupassino kāye viharatha, āhāre paṭikūlasaññino, sabbaloke anabhiratisaññino anabhiratasaññīno (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), sabbasaṅkhāresu aniccānupassino’ti.

511. Then, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monks: ‘Monks, the brahmin householders have been possessed by Dūsī Māra. Come, you, honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the virtuous monks of good character. Perhaps, while they are being honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated by you, there might be a change in their minds, whereby Dūsī Māra might gain an opportunity. Come, monks, dwell contemplating the foulness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world, and contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena.’

“Atha kho te, pāpima, bhikkhū kakusandhena bhagavatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena evaṃ ovadiyamānā evaṃ anusāsiyamānā araññagatāpi rukkhamūlagatāpi suññāgāragatāpi asubhānupassino kāye vihariṃsu, āhāre paṭikūlasaññino, sabbaloke anabhiratisaññino, sabbasaṅkhāresu aniccānupassino.

Then, Evil One, those monks, being thus advised and instructed by the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, whether they had gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, dwelt contemplating the foulness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world, and contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena.

512. “Atha kho, pāpima, kakusandho bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya āyasmatā vidhurena pacchāsamaṇena gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha kho, pāpima, dūsī māro aññataraṃ kumārakaṃ [M 1.0413] kumāraṃ (sī. pī.) anvāvisitvā sakkharaṃ gahetvā āyasmato vidhurassa sīse pahāramadāsi; sīsaṃ vobhindi sīsaṃ te bhindissāmīti (ka.). Atha kho, pāpima, āyasmā vidhuro bhinnena sīsena lohitena gaḷantena kakusandhaṃyeva bhagavantaṃ [P 1.0337] arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi. Atha kho[T 1.0608], pāpima, kakusandho bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho nāgāpalokitaṃ apalokesi [V 1.0421] – ‘na vāyaṃ dūsī māro mattamaññāsī’ti. Sahāpalokanāya ca pana, pāpima, dūsī māro tamhā ca ṭhānā cavi mahānirayañca upapajji.

512. Then, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered a village for alms with the Venerable Vidhura as his attendant monk. Then, Evil One, Dūsī Māra, having possessed a certain boy, took a piece of gravel and struck a blow on the head of the Venerable Vidhura, splitting his head. Then, Evil One, the Venerable Vidhura, with his head split and blood flowing, followed right behind the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then, Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, cast an elephant-look, thinking: ‘This Dūsī Māra does not know his measure.’ And just with that look, Evil One, Dūsī Māra fell from that place and was reborn in the great hell.

“Tassa kho pana, pāpima, mahānirayassa tayo nāmadheyyā honti – chaphassāyataniko itipi, saṅkusamāhato itipi, paccattavedaniyo itipi. Atha kho maṃ, pāpima, nirayapālā upasaṅkamitvā etadavocuṃ – yadā kho te yato te (ka.), mārisa, saṅkunā saṅku hadaye samāgaccheyya. Atha naṃ tvaṃ jāneyyāsi – ‘vassasahassaṃ me niraye paccamānassā’ti. So kho ahaṃ, pāpima, bahūni vassāni bahūni vassasatāni bahūni vassasahassāni tasmiṃ mahāniraye apacciṃ. Dasavassasahassāni tasseva mahānirayassa ussade apacciṃ vuṭṭhānimaṃ nāma vedanaṃ vediyamāno. Tassa mayhaṃ, pāpima, evarūpo kāyo hoti, seyyathāpi manussassa. Evarūpaṃ sīsaṃ hoti, seyyathāpi macchassa.

Indeed, Evil One, that great hell has three names: ‘the Sixfold Sense-Base,’ ‘Struck with Stakes,’ and ‘Individually Experienced.’ Then, Evil One, the hell-wardens approached me and said this: ‘When, good sir, a stake meets a stake in your heart, then you should know: “For a thousand years I have been tormented in hell.”’ So I, Evil One, was tormented in that great hell for many years, for many hundreds of years, for many thousands of years. For ten thousand years I was tormented in the Ussada hell of that very great hell, experiencing the feeling called ‘the emergence.’ My body, Evil One, was of such a nature as a human’s, and my head was of such a nature as a fish’s.

513.

513.

“Kīdiso nirayo āsi, yattha dūsī apaccatha;

Vidhuraṃ sāvakamāsajja, kakusandhañca brāhmaṇaṃ.

What kind of hell was it, where Dūsī was tormented, for having assaulted the disciple Vidhura and the brahmin Kakusandha?

“Sataṃ āsi ayosaṅkū, sabbe paccattavedanā;

Īdiso nirayo āsi, yattha dūsī apaccatha;

Vidhuraṃ sāvakamāsajja, kakusandhañca brāhmaṇaṃ.

There were a hundred iron stakes, all individually experienced; such was the hell where Dūsī was tormented, for having assaulted the disciple Vidhura and the brahmin Kakusandha.

“Yo etamabhijānāti, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Tādisaṃ [T 1.0609] bhikkhumāsajja, kaṇha dukkhaṃ nigacchasi.

The monk, a disciple of the Buddha, who has direct knowledge of this—by assaulting such a monk, you will come to dark suffering.

“Majjhe sarassa tiṭṭhanti, vimānā kappaṭṭhāyino;

Veḷuriyavaṇṇā rucirā, accimanto pabhassarā;

Accharā tattha naccanti, puthu nānattavaṇṇiyo.

In the middle of the ocean stand mansions that endure for an eon; the color of beryl, lovely, radiant, and resplendent. There nymphs dance, many and of various colors.

“Yo [M 1.0414][V 1.0422][P 1.0338] etamabhijānāti, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Tādisaṃ bhikkhumāsajja, kaṇha dukkhaṃ nigacchasi.

The monk, a disciple of the Buddha, who has direct knowledge of this—by assaulting such a monk, you will come to dark suffering.

“Yo ve buddhena codito, bhikkhu saṅghassa pekkhato;

Migāramātupāsādaṃ, pādaṅguṭṭhena kampayi.

The disciple who, urged on by the Buddha, shook the palace of Migāra’s mother with his big toe while the community of monks looked on.

“Yo etamabhijānāti, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Tādisaṃ bhikkhumāsajja, kaṇha dukkhaṃ nigacchasi.

The monk, a disciple of the Buddha, who has direct knowledge of this—by assaulting such a monk, you will come to dark suffering.

“Yo vejayantaṃ pāsādaṃ, pādaṅguṭṭhena kampayi;

Iddhibalenupatthaddho, saṃvejesi ca devatā.

He who shook the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe, supported by his psychic power, and thereby stirred the devas.

“Yo etamabhijānāti, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Tādisaṃ bhikkhumāsajja, kaṇha dukkhaṃ nigacchasi.

The monk, a disciple of the Buddha, who has direct knowledge of this—by assaulting such a monk, you will come to dark suffering.

“Yo vejayantapāsāde, sakkaṃ so paripucchati;

Api vāsava jānāsi, taṇhākkhayavimuttiyo;

Tassa sakko viyākāsi, pañhaṃ puṭṭho yathātathaṃ.

He who in the Vejayanta Palace questioned Sakka: ‘Do you know, Vāsava, the liberations through the destruction of craving?’ Sakka, having been asked the question, answered him according to reality.

“Yo etamabhijānāti, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Tādisaṃ bhikkhumāsajja, kaṇha dukkhaṃ nigacchasi.

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha and who knows this as it truly is—by assaulting such a monk, you will come to dark suffering.

“Yo brahmaṃ paripucchati, sudhammāyābhito sabhaṃ;

Ajjāpi [T 1.0610] tyāvuso diṭṭhi, yā te diṭṭhi pure ahu;

Passasi vītivattantaṃ, brahmaloke pabhassaraṃ.

He who fearlessly questioned Brahmā near the Sudhammā assembly: ‘Friend, do you still today have that view which you had before? Do you see the brilliant radiance in the Brahma world passing away?’

“Tassa [V 1.0423] brahmā viyākāsi, anupubbaṃ yathātathaṃ;

Na me mārisa sā diṭṭhi, yā me diṭṭhi pure ahu.

Brahmā answered him sequentially, according to reality: ‘Good sir, I do not have now that view which I had before.’

“Passāmi vītivattantaṃ, brahmaloke pabhassaraṃ;

Sohaṃ ajja kathaṃ vajjaṃ, ahaṃ niccomhi sassato.

‘I see the brilliant radiance in the Brahma world passing away. How, then, could I say today: “I am permanent, eternal”?’

“Yo etamabhijānāti, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Tādisaṃ bhikkhumāsajja, kaṇha dukkhaṃ nigacchasi.

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha and who knows this as it truly is—by assaulting such a monk, you will come to dark suffering.

“Yo mahāmeruno kūṭaṃ, vimokkhena aphassayi;

Vanaṃ pubbavidehānaṃ, ye ca bhūmisayā narā.

The disciple who with liberation pervaded the peak of Mahā Meru, the people of Jambudīpa and Pubbavideha, and those humans who sleep on the ground.

“Yo etamabhijānāti, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Tādisaṃ bhikkhumāsajja, kaṇha dukkhaṃ nigacchasi.

The monk who is a disciple of the Buddha and who knows this as it truly is—by assaulting such a monk, you will come to dark suffering.

“Na [M 1.0415] ve aggi cetayati veṭhayati (sī.), ‘ahaṃ bālaṃ ḍahāmī’ti;

Bālo ca jalitaṃ aggiṃ, āsajja naṃ sa ḍayhati.

Fire does not think, ‘I am burning a fool.’ But the fool, by approaching the blazing fire, is burned by it.

“Evameva tuvaṃ māra, āsajja naṃ tathāgataṃ;

Sayaṃ ḍahissasi attānaṃ, bālo aggiṃva saṃphusaṃ.

Just so, Māra, by assaulting the Tathāgata, you will burn yourself, like a fool touching fire.

“Apuññaṃ pasavī māro, āsajja naṃ tathāgataṃ;

Kinnu maññasi pāpima, na me pāpaṃ vipaccati.

By assaulting the Tathāgata, Māra, you have produced demerit. What do you think, Wicked One? Do you imagine, ‘My evil will not ripen’?

“Karoto cīyati pāpaṃ, cirarattāya antaka;

Māra nibbinda buddhamhā, āsaṃ mākāsi bhikkhusu.

For the doer, evil accumulates for a long time, O Ender. Māra, turn away from the Buddha; do not place hope in the monks.

“Iti [T 1.0611] māraṃ atajjesi, bhikkhu bhesakaḷāvane;

Tato so dummano yakkho, natatthevantaradhāyathā”ti.

Thus the monk threatened Māra in the Bhesakaḷā Forest. Then that disheartened yakkha vanished right there.

Māratajjanīyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Māratajjanīya Sutta, the tenth, is concluded.

Cūḷayamakavaggo niṭṭhito pañcamo.

The Cūḷayamaka Vagga, the fifth, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ [V 1.0424] –

The summary of it:

Sāleyya verañjaduve ca tuṭṭhi, cūḷamahādhammasamādānañca;

Vīmaṃsakā kosambi ca brāhmaṇo, dūsī ca māro dasamo ca vaggo.

Sāleyya, Verañja, the two Vedallas, the Cūḷa and Mahā Dhammasamādāna, Vīmaṃsaka, Kosambī, the Brāhmaṇanimantanika, and Dūsī Māra as the tenth; this completes the chapter.

Sāleyyavaggo niṭṭhito pañcamo.

The Sāleyya Vagga, the fifth, is concluded.

Idaṃ vaggānamuddānaṃ –

This is the summary of the chapters:

Mūlapariyāyo ceva, sīhanādo ca uttamo;

Kakaco ceva gosiṅgo, sāleyyo ca ime pañca.

The Mūlapariyāya, and the excellent Sīhanāda; the Kakaca, the Gosiṅga, and the Sāleyya—these are the five.

Mūlapaṇṇāsakaṃ samattaṃ.

The Mūlapaṇṇāsaka is concluded.
